title: Ireland faces pressure to stop sending Russia an ingredient vital to its war on Ukraine
summary: A cargo ship is set to leave Ireland for Russia with alumina, a white powder that experts say is likely used to make weapons
story: A cargo ship is set to leave Ireland for Russia with alumina, a white powder that experts say is likely used to make weapons

AUGHINISH, Ireland -- The Karin, a 400-foot-long (120-meter-long) cargo ship, sat moored this week on Ireland’s boggy River Shannon estuary. Soon it set sail for Russia laden with a white powder that can be forged into weapons vital to Moscow’s war on Ukraine.

Alumina, a key ingredient in aluminum, goes into everything from toothpaste and lipstick to missiles and drones. A Russian-owned plant in southern Ireland is Europe’s biggest alumina refinery and regularly sends shiploads of the substance directly to St. Petersburg and other Russian ports.

Almost five years into Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, alumina has escaped European sanctions intended to hobble Russia’s economy. That leaves the refinery in Aughinish free to send its product to Russia, where some ends up in weapons, experts say.

“The material is clearly ending up in military supplies,” said Irish lawmaker Ivana Bacik, who leads the opposition Labour Party. “It would be unthinkable for Ireland to be contributing, even in that indirect way, to Putin’s war machine.”

Ireland is facing calls to stop the shipments as dozens of European leaders gather in Dublin this week to discuss support for Ukraine. A summit of the 47-nation European Political Community on Thursday is being followed by a meeting of European Union leaders.

Irish government minister Niall Collins told The Associated Press that “there’s absolutely no evidence” the material is ending up in military supply chains, though the government has declined to make public the findings of its investigation into the alumina shipments.

Aughinish Alumina said in a statement its product “has no connection to the Russian military supply chain” and that it hired an independent company to provide monthly audits to Irish authorities for “enhanced traceability.”

Alumina is a chemical compound refined from bauxite, a red ore mined primarily in Guinea, Australia and China. The chalky white substance can be smelted into aluminum, which is then forged with other, rarer elements to make strong, heat-resistant and flexible alloys used in missiles and aircraft; aluminum is also used in the manufacture of rocket fuel and explosives.

The Aughinish plant in County Limerick was built in the 1970s and bought in 2007 by Rusal, a Russian aluminum producer. The company was founded, and is still part-owned, by Oleg Deripaska, a sanctioned oligarch with ties to Russian President Vladimir Putin. Rusal makes virtually all of Russia's aluminum, according to the U.S. and Australian governments.
While many cargo ships leave Aughinish bound for Europe and beyond, a steady stream of them heads straight to the port of St. Petersburg, according to data from MarineTraffic analyzed by AP.

The activist group Alumina 22, which is lobbying to sanction the trade in alumina to Russia, estimated that between March and October some 491,307 metric tons of alumina from Ireland was shipped to Russia.

These shipments have grown in importance. Since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, two alumina factories — one in Australia, the other in Ukraine — stopped exporting to Russia, crimping its supplies by about 40%, according to a 2026 report by the Economic Security Council of Ukraine, or ESCU.
Roughly 17% of Rusal's alumina supply now comes from Ireland, according to ESCU.

An investigation by the Organized Crime and Corruption Reporting Project and the Irish Times published earlier this year found that alumina from Aughinish is smelted in Russia into aluminum, with some of it sold to a metals trading company that supplies Russian defense contractors.

“Virtually everything that comes from Rusal is with a high probability ending up in the hands of Russian military enterprises,” said Olena Yurchenko, director of analytics, research and investigations at the ESCU.

Standing next to Irish Prime Minister Micheál Martin in Dublin in June, Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said “Unfortunately, there are companies in Europe that are owned or effectively controlled by Russia and its sanctioned oligarchs. They keep supplying the aggressor with essential materials, even now.”
Martin acknowledged that “we do not want to be in a position where material emanating from a plant in Ireland goes to support the Russian war machine.”

Ireland has not found evidence that is happening — but also no proof it isn’t, said Enterprise Minister Peter Burke, who is in charge of the country's sanctions enforcement. He said in July it had been impossible to prove Rusal’s assertion that alumina from Ireland is only used to make aluminum for export from Russia.
The Irish government hasn't published its findings, but it handed them to the European Commission, which drafts EU sanctions packages.

EU sanctions envoy David O’Sullivan said there is little doubt that “the alumina goes to smelters in Russia who produce stuff which undoubtedly goes at least in part to the military-industrial complex.”

“I’ve read the government report. Personally, I think there’s no doubt the investigative journalists got it right,” he said last month in Dublin at a meeting organized by the Institute of International and European Affairs.

The European Parliament in July passed a non-binding motion calling for a ban on alumina exports to Russia. But alumina was not included in the EU’s 21st sanctions package against Russia that month. The EU’s executive European Commission, which draws up sanctions packages, is now sounding out member nations about the Irish alumina exports. Sanctions must be agreed upon unanimously by the bloc's 27 countries.

A commission spokesperson said in July that the bloc’s sanctions policy was “a delicate balance” between thwarting Russia’s war effort and limiting “negative impacts” on EU member nations, “especially considering that alumina is a critical raw material.”

Supporters of the plant point to the hundreds of jobs it provides, and to its role as a key source of alumina for European countries. Keeping supply lines open is especially important because of the chokehold on cargo traffic through the Strait of Hormuz caused by the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran.

Collins, who represents County Limerick in Ireland's parliament, said Ireland has been "hugely resolute in our support for the Ukrainians, and Ukraine hasn’t provided any evidence that Aughinish is doing anything adverse."

Opposition politicians remain skeptical. Bacik's left-of-center Labour Party supports a temporary nationalization of the refinery, similar to when Ireland seized banks in the wake of the 2008 financial crisis. She says the refinery can ban exports to Russia and find other eager customers in Europe.
“We need to see much stronger action being taken on this from other EU countries if the Irish government isn’t willing to do the right thing here,” she said.
In Foynes, the wind-swept port town beside the plant, many work at Aughinish or know someone who does. But some locals have mixed feelings.
“It's too big a business for them to close it down,” said retired docker Joe Hanlon. “Too much employment for the government to get involved.”
But he said “of course they should,” if Ireland wants “to stop the war on Ukraine.”
Associated Press writers M. Reo in Washington and Larry Fenn in New York contributed to this report.

title: How Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's extramarital affair could cause collateral damage in Washington
summary: Jensen Huang, CEO of Nvidia, is under scrutiny after revelations of an affair with a Chinese businesswoman, Alice Huang, who is suspected of spying
story: Jensen Huang, CEO of Nvidia, is under scrutiny after revelations of an affair with a Chinese businesswoman, Alice Huang, who is suspected of spying
WASHINGTON -- Extramarital affairs are usually private matters. Jensen Huang’s has global implications.

The 63-year-old is the leading face of the artificial intelligence revolution with his black leather jackets and fluff of grey hair. He runs the company Nvidia, which produces highly coveted computer chips. That's landed him on a late-night-phone-call basis with President Donald Trump, a promoter of the industry.

But Huang was also liaising with a Chinese businesswoman who has allegedly fed intelligence — as well as advanced chips — to China. The woman, Alice Huang, is a former executive at the Singapore-based cloud computing company Megaspeed.

It's a saga of personal betrayal, corporate espionage and high-tech development, and the fallout is spreading across Washington. There are bipartisan calls for investigations on Capitol Hill. The U.S. Department of Justice has opened its own probe. Nvidia, one of the most valuable companies in the world, is conducting an internal review.

Some expect the technology to reshape human civilization by imbuing computers with the vast powers of creation and analysis, and Trump has repeated that “whoever wins AI, wins." Nvidia is the backbone of America's plans for dominating the field.
When asked about Huang's affair, Trump said this week that he had spoken to the tech executive as the scandal grew.
“I think he’ll be in good shape," Trump said, adding that "he said he had absolutely no idea that the person in question was a spy.”
As for when the president first learned about the concerns involving Alice Huang, Trump brushed off the question.
“They could have been mentioned," he said. "Certainly it didn’t make much of an impact on me.”
With the AI race between the U.S. and China often framed as a fierce and consequential rivalry, the Justice Department has persistently warned of the espionage threat posed by Beijing.
That includes efforts to cultivate well-placed relationships in government and private industry, as well as to acquire sensitive technology such as AI chips developed in the U.S.

Last year, Megaspeed faced scrutiny from the U.S. Commerce Department over its alleged skirting of U.S. export laws and routing of a large amount of advanced Nvidia chips to Chinese users. The company denied those allegations. U.S. intelligence officials eventually concluded that Alice Huang had spied for China, according to The New York Times.

The Commerce Department's probe was handed off to the Justice Department, and its National Security Division is investigating whether Megaspeed violated export control laws in an inquiry that will also include scrutiny of Alice Huang, according to a person familiar with the matter who insisted on anonymity to discuss an ongoing law enforcement probe.
Megaspeed did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Tuesday, and The Associated Press was unable to reach Alice Huang.

Jensen Huang has apologized to his company about the affair, saying he hurt his wife and their children, but he didn’t address reports that Alice Huang was a suspected spy. Nvidia’s board said that it had “no reason to believe” that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, and that Huang would remain in charge while cooperating with the investigation.
Beijing has said the “Chinese spy allegation is unsubstantiated" and called it “nothing but smears.”
After their first dinner together at Mar-a-Lago in early 2025, Trump latched onto Huang as a tech titan positioned to deliver on the president’s own promises of an economic renaissance.

The computer chips produced by Nvidia would essentially turn data centers into factories that made raw intelligence, which could then be applied across the economy to produce cars, new pharmaceutical drugs, advanced weapons and seemingly unparalleled wealth.
Trump would regularly phone Huang to discuss this future.

“From the moment that I met him, the only thing that he’s ever talked to me about is creating more jobs, re-industrializing the United States, of protection, of national security,” Huang told AP in an interview this summer. "He knows that if America is wealthy, we have a lot of tax revenues. We can fund the military, we can fund our economy, we fund our communities, create more jobs.”

Trump saw his political fortunes — and that of the country — in Huang's Nvidia. Huang joined Trump on Air Force One for a state visit to Beijing earlier this year. Just last month, Trump awarded Huang with a National Medal of Science.
The president called him “a man whose determination laid the foundations for the explosion of super intelligence and put America at the front of the race, an amazing man, gotten to know him so well.”
Nvidia also donated $25 million to help fund the construction of Trump’s White House ballroom.
Multiple estimates suggest that more than half of the stock market gains during Trump's second term came from the growth of the AI industry and the construction of data centers.

Without that growth, consumer spending could slump, delivering another economic setback to a president who has already failed to deliver on his campaign promise of stopping inflation. Rising prices were among the reasons that voters delivered a harsh rebuke to Republicans in last week's midterm elections, returning control of Congress to the Democrats.

While Huang said his interests were in helping America succeed, he also expressed a strong view that Nvidia should be able to sell some of its less advanced chips such as the H200 to China. Nvidia long argued that the sales would help ensure that the broader AI ecosystem was tied to America, boxing out Chinese chipmakers that are developing semiconductors and systems to compete with his company.

Those arguments previously came under scrutiny, including from Massachusetts Democratic Sen. Elizabeth Warren, who wanted him to appear before the Senate Banking Committee to answer questions about his desire to loosen export restrictions.

Huang has so far refused to appear, and Democrats responded angrily when his infidelity came to light, raising concerns that a bulwark of American technology may have been compromised by the Chinese government.
Warren said in a statement Monday that Nvidia had reportedly gotten approvals to export “hundreds of thousands of advanced AI chips to China, including to companies tied to China’s military.”
And Huang's relationship with Alice Huang, Warren continued, “raises important questions NVIDIA must answer about the extent to which these activities were related."

Chan reported from Hong Kong and Ng from Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia. Associated Press journalists Wu Jia in Beijing, Didi Tang in Washington and Russ Bynum in Savannah, Georgia, contributed to this report.

title: US futures climb and Nvidia shares stabilize in a brutal week for the chipmaker
summary: U.S. futures are rising as Nvidia’s shares look to rebound and Brent crude remains below $100 a barrel
story: U.S. futures are rising as Nvidia’s shares look to rebound and Brent crude remains below $100 a barrel
U.S. futures are rising with crude still below $100 a barrel as shares of Nvidia stabilize in a brutal week for the chipmaker.
Futures for the S&P 500 gained 0.9% on Wednesday, while those for the Dow Jones Industrial Average edged up 0.2%. Nasdaq futures climbed 1.9%.
Nvidia was the single heaviest weight on the S&P 500 on Tuesday, but shares are up 3.7% in early trading Wednesday. They are still down almost 10% this week.

The company that is central to the artificial intelligence boom has been under pressure since the company’s board announced an investigation into its CEO, Jensen Huang, following revelations of his affair with a purported Chinese spy. President Donald Trump said the FBI is investigating the affair, which Huang has acknowledged and apologized for.
Among other technology stocks, CoreWeave jumped more than 15% before the market opened after posting better-than-expected third-quarter revenue and a boost in its 2026 revenue outlook.
The U.S. bond market is closed Wednesday for Veterans Day, but the stock markets remain open.

The price of Brent crude, the international standard, rose 1.9% to $93.22 a barrel. U.S. benchmark crude oil gained 1.2% to $87.05 per barrel. Brent remains well below $100 a barrel, with Trump saying late Monday that the war in Iran, which sent oil prices much higher, “militarily is effectively over.”
Oil prices are still about $30 higher per barrel than at this time last year.

New data on consumer inflation Tuesday upended markets and sent the 10-year Treasury yield charging above 5% again. On Friday, the U.S. releases its producer price index for October, which captures inflation before it reaches consumers. The September report showed the biggest increase since December 2022 and that data showed that rising fuel prices, particularly for diesel fuel, continue to push shipping and warehousing prices higher.

In Europe, Germany’s DAX rose 0.7% to 26,531.66 after inflation fell to 2.8% in October from a year earlier, according to the federal statistics office on Wednesday. The CAC 40 in Paris climbed 0.3% to 8,302.23. Britain’s FTSE 100 added 0.4% to 10,797.68.
Asian markets were mostly higher. China’s biggest online shopping festival, Singles Day, began Wednesday. Its sales data will offer a gauge of consumer demand in the world’s second-largest economy.
The U.S. dollar rose to 159.15 Japanese yen from 158.70 yen. The euro fell to $1.1133 from $1.1171.

title: At COP31, Turkey pushes zero-waste plan to curb climate change
summary: As world leaders arrive at United Nations climate talks in the Turkish resort town of Antalya, calling for urgent climate action, co-host Turkey also wants to halve the amount of global waste in the next decade
story: As world leaders arrive at United Nations climate talks in the Turkish resort town of Antalya, calling for urgent climate action, co-host Turkey also wants to halve the amount of global waste in the next decade

ANTALYA, Turkey -- As world leaders gathered for United Nations climate talks in the Turkish resort town of Antalya on Wednesday, host Turkey urged countries to commit to a zero-waste initiative aimed at reducing emissions and helping get global efforts to curb climate change back on track.

Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan touted his country's progress on recycling, saying its rate had risen from about 13% in 2017, when the zero waste movement began, to about 40% by the end of 2025.

"Some 90 million tons of waste have been brought back into our economy,” Erdogan told the leaders' summit. “We’ll not stop here and we will continue working and making every effort until we achieve the goal of zero waste."

Turkey has outlined 10 priorities for this year’s climate talks, known as COP31, with a pledge to accelerate electrification and the zero-waste initiatives emerging as major talking points during the opening days of the conference.

Turkish first lady Emine Erdogan, who attended Wednesday's talks, has been a driving force behind the zero-waste initiative, which aims to reduce methane emissions, cut food waste and promote a circular economy in which materials are reused and recycled.

“Recovered materials can be cheaper when reliable supplies, efficient processing and nearby demand outweigh the costs of collection, sorting and transport,” said Samed Agirbas, president of the nonprofit Zero Waste Foundation and a COP31 high-level climate champion.

If implemented, energy experts say the initiatives could slow global warming and reduce the environmental footprint of renewable energy technologies, like solar panels and batteries. But there is still a risk these climate ambitions may fall flat.
Conference agreements are often nonbinding and past hosts have been criticized for failing to follow through on promises. Turkey also faces scrutiny over its own climate record.

“The Zero Waste target is a good target. It definitely needs to be supported with concrete measures and further action,” said Berk Butan, who heads the waste campaign for Greenpeace Turkey. “But fundamentally, we also need to recognize its shortcomings.”

As the second biggest cause of climate change after carbon dioxide, the reduction of methane emissions could significantly slow global warming, according to the U.N. During the first three days of the climate talks, leaders repeatedly called for urgent climate action.
The U.N. recently had to readjust a decades-old goal of limiting the rise of global temperatures because the world was blowing past previous thresholds.

While Turkey wants countries to commit to reducing methane emissions, it has not signed the Global Methane Pledge. Launched at the 2021 climate talks in Glasgow, the initiative aims to reduce methane emissions by at least 30% from 2020 levels by 2030.
Turkey is also the world’s fifth-biggest emitter of methane from solid waste, according to nonprofit emissions tracker Climate TRACE.
“Methane emissions from waste disposal are an important challenge,” said Agirbas, with the Zero Waste Foundation.

A circular economy — an economic model that generally prioritizes recycling and other regenerative approaches that create less waste— would help reduce emissions, but not every country has the resources to take such steps.
Ke Wang, an energy expert at the WRI's Polsky Center for the Global Energy Transition, said that this is “a vital strategy for cutting greenhouse gas emissions."

But recycling food waste is difficult because it decomposes quickly, making separation and processing expensive. Collecting and transporting wet, smelly food waste also requires specialized logistics and infrastructure that many countries lack.
“Waste and food loss account for almost 10% of total emissions, so we need to integrate these actions,” Adalberto Maluf, a top official in Brazil’s environment ministry, told The Associated Press.

The recycling of already-mined materials is key to reducing the reliance on mining, according to experts, which will only become more important as the world relies more on critical mineral-dependent renewable technologies.
The International Energy Agency estimates that scaling up recycling could lower the need for new mining by between 25% and 40% by 2050.

Most countries don’t recycle critical materials because it’s cheaper to mine them. The technology and infrastructure needed to recycle these materials are also concentrated in a handful of nations, like China. The European Union and the U.S. will likely only have the capacity to recycle 30% of their raw materials by 2040, according to the IEA.

“We must do a better job with our materials retrieval, reuse and recycling,” said Aimee Boulanger, executive director of the Initiative for Responsible Mining Assurance. She stressed the need to create incentives for “retrieving the materials, taking things apart, being able to reuse them again in a circular way.”
Arasu reported from Bengaluru, India, Milko from Islamabad, Pakistan and Delgado from Bangkok.

title: Grand Theft Auto VI is almost here. What to know about the characters, music and billions at stake
summary: Grand Theft Auto VI is set to release on Nov. 19, marking a return to the neon-lit streets of Vice City
story: Grand Theft Auto VI is set to release on Nov. 19, marking a return to the neon-lit streets of Vice City
LOS ANGELES -- LOS ANGELES (AP) — Grand Theft Auto has never been much for following the rules.

Nearly three decades after a video game built around stealing cars, outrunning police and embracing criminal mayhem first arrived, the franchise has survived controversy, transformed open-world gaming and become one of the biggest sellers in entertainment.

Now, after a 13-year wait since its last main installment, Grand Theft Auto VI is preparing for another big score. The latest chapter arrives Nov. 19 with a return to the neon-soaked streets of Vice City with two protagonists.
For longtime fans, GTA VI is a highly anticipated return. For everyone else, here’s what to know about the blockbuster video game, its characters and the enormous business riding on its release:
The franchise began in 1997 as a relatively simple, top-down game that allowed players to roam fictional cities, steal vehicles, evade police and commit crimes.

The release of Grand Theft Auto III in 2001 helped redefine open-world gaming. It gave players greater freedom to explore a sprawling three-dimensional city, pursue missions and interact with their surroundings.
Later installments expanded that freedom with larger environments, cinematic storytelling, social satire and detailed worlds. The influence reached far beyond games about stealing cars.

Ubisoft’s Assassin’s Creed series brought open-world exploration to historical settings, while Bethesda’s The Elder Scrolls games expanded their own longstanding tradition of open-ended fantasy role-playing. Nintendo’s The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild later emphasized experimentation and discovery, allowing players to use the environment itself to solve problems.

For Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas and Grand Theft Auto V, Rockstar Games recruited real-life gang members to help bring authenticity to background characters and dialogue. Former writer and audio director Lazlow Jones has said some performers challenged scripted lines, prompting developers to let them use language drawn from their own experiences.
That attention to detail helped create the sense of a living world that became a hallmark of the franchise, even as the series drew criticism for its depictions of violence, crime and women.
But controversy did not stop the franchise’s commercial rise.

According to publisher Take-Two Interactive, the franchise has sold more than 470 million units worldwide. Grand Theft Auto V, released in 2013, accounts for more than 230 million of those units and reached $1 billion in retail sales in just three days.
Its online multiplayer component, Grand Theft Auto Online, has helped keep players engaged through years of updates, new activities and in-game purchases.

This time, the action returns to Vice City, Rockstar’s fictional version of Miami, and expands across the surrounding state of Leonida, a Florida-inspired setting filled with beaches, highways, nightlife and criminal enterprises.

At the center are Lucia Caminos and Jason Duval, a couple trying to improve their circumstances through a life of crime. Lucia has recently been released from prison while Jason, a former soldier who became involved with drug runners in the Leonida Keys, is looking for a different path.
Their plans become more complicated when a seemingly straightforward criminal job goes wrong, drawing them into a conspiracy that stretches across Leonida.
The trailers suggest a story mixing romance, robberies, betrayals and the series’ familiar satirical take on American culture.
Rockstar has revealed several supporting characters, including bank robber Raul Bautista, aspiring music executive Dre’Quan Priest and nightclub owner Boobie Ike.
Rockstar has kept much of the voice cast under wraps, including the performers behind Lucia and Jason.

One familiar actor has confirmed his involvement: Stephen Root, known for his work in “Office Space,” “King of the Hill” and “Barry.” He told The Associated Press in September that he appears in the game, adding that fans had already recognized his distinctive voice in promotional footage.

Root has been identified in reports as the voice of Brian Heder, an aging drug runner operating out of the Leonida Keys. Rockstar has introduced the character but has not publicly confirmed Root’s casting in that specific role.
Beyond the return to Vice City, one of the biggest changes is the focus on two protagonists whose relationship drives the story.
Grand Theft Auto V featured three playable main characters. The new installment centers on Lucia and Jason as partners navigating the criminal underworld together.

Rockstar has promoted a larger, more detailed setting that stretches beyond the city into the wider state of Leonida. The game also arrives in a vastly different technological landscape from its predecessor, with newer consoles capable of supporting more elaborate environments and character interactions.

But not every detail is known. Rockstar has offered trailers and promotional previews, while questions remain about the full range of activities, how the game’s systems will work and the future of its online multiplayer experience.
Music has long been part of Grand Theft Auto’s identity. It has included everything from fictional radio stations to the songs accompanying players as they cruise through the game’s cities.
Grand Theft Auto VI is expanding that tradition with an original score by Justice, the Grammy-winning French electronic duo of Gaspard Augé and Xavier de Rosnay.
Rockstar says the score adapts to players’ actions and experiences throughout the game, shifting with the environments and situations they encounter.
A 30-track score album is scheduled for Dec. 11, featuring collaborations with artists including Tame Impala, SZA, King Gizzard & The Lizard Wizard and Gesaffelstein.
The game also features in-game radio stations and a separate collection of original songs, continuing the franchise’s connection to popular music.

title: Leaders gather in Turkey for UN climate summit
summary: World leaders, delegates and climate activists are in Antalya, Turkey, for a U.N. climate summit
story: World leaders, delegates and climate activists are in Antalya, Turkey, for a U.N. climate summit

ANTALYA, Turkey -- World leaders, delegates and climate activists on Monday kicked off talks in Turkey on curbing climate change, which in the last year has led to rising temperatures and deadly heat waves in Europe and beyond, and played a role in disasters such as the devastating floods in Nepal.

This U.N. climate summit — called the Conference of the Parties, or COP31 — comes as the war in Iran has effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz, hiking global prices of gasoline, oil and products made with them, such as fertilizers and pesticides. The disruption has pushed governments to rethink energy policies and increased investment in renewable energy sources like wind and solar.

“COP31 must supercharge solutions,” U.N. climate chief Simon Stiell said at the opening session. An estimated 68,500 people are to attend the two-week event and nearly 25,000 people will help ensure the conference goes smoothly.

Stiell said that agreeing on practical solutions, such as reducing methane emissions, can be “planetary icepacks” that can help reduce global heating. Methane stays in the atmosphere for a shorter time but warms the planet much faster than other planet-heating gases. Using renewable-powered electricity instead of oil, gas and coal can also help reduce global warming.

Delegates, meeting in the Mediterranean resort city of Antalya, will come under pressure to develop new pledges for climate action while implementing previous promises. The stakes are high: Climate scientists say global warming is likely to exceed 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) above the preindustrial levels of the early 1800s.
Limiting temperature rise to that threshold was a goal established during the 2015 Paris Agreement. Since then, it's been a focus of international climate negotiations.

The fact that the goal is no longer realistic underscores how difficult it's been for the world to cut greenhouse gas emissions, which are released into the atmosphere when fossil fuels like oil, gas and coal are burned, leading to climate change.

“This is the first COP where it is clear beyond a reasonable doubt that the world will overshoot the 1.5-degree target,” said Turkish Environment Minister Murat Kurum. “We will not look away, and we will not lower our ambition.”
Kurum, the COP31 president, has said that rather than establishing new targets, he wants the summit to focus on turning previous climate commitments into action.

He has announced an “Action Agenda” that includes reducing methane emissions and building climate-resilient cities. There is also the aim of increasing the use of electricity — preferably from renewable energy such as solar and wind — from 21% to 35% by 2035, to reduce greenhouse emissions.
“Success begins when our decisions reach that last mile,” said Kurum. “If we are to share a future, we must share the responsibility for it.”

Delegates are also expected to discuss at the Nov. 9-20 summit how to help poorer countries pay to adapt to rising temperatures and extreme weather events, both tied to climate change, and transition away from fossil fuels.

Even as leaders delivered speeches talking about ambition and implementation, negotiators from nearly 200 countries were already wrangling in the backrooms about disagreements over funds for climate adaptation and recovery from climate disasters and other long-pending bottlenecks.
“Countries that did the least to cause this crisis shouldn’t have to borrow their way through it,” said Meena Raman from the Malaysia-based climate advocacy group Third World Network.
At the center of the disagreements are developing countries, which seek more discussions on financing for the goals agreed on at the 2015 Paris climate talks.

“After years of disappointment, developing countries want to know clearly how rich countries plan to provide the funds needed to tackle climate change,” said Iskander Erzini Vernoit, a veteran of many climate talks and advisor to African negotiators at this year’s talks.
“Agenda proposals from the 54-country African Group were backed by many developing countries but contested by rich countries from the European Union and Canada,” he said.

The last two summits, COP30 in Brazil and COP29 in Azerbaijan, came under criticism for ending with little agreement on how to reduce greenhouse emissions. The final texts of those conferences didn't even mention fuels. At COP28 in Dubai, delegates had agreed to transition away from fossil fuels.
The United States — the world’s second-largest polluter after China — is again absent from the summit.
During his first term, and again when he took office for a second time in January 2025, President Donald Trump withdrew the U.S. from climate negotiations.
“No single COP is a silver bullet that can stop climate change overnight,” said Stiell, the climate chief. “But every recent COP has made essential progress. COP31 in Antalya will, too.”

In a change from previous summits, Turkey and Australia are jointly holding this summit after the two jostled over which would be the host. As a compromise, Turkey is the official host while Australia is leading the negotiations. Both countries have come under criticism for their strong reliance on coal.
Arasu reported from Bengaluru, India.

title: China's trade surplus surpasses $1 trillion for a 2nd straight year, as exports surge 35%
summary: China says its trade surplus exceeded $1 trillion for a 2nd straight year
story: China says its trade surplus exceeded $1 trillion for a 2nd straight year
HONG KONG -- China’s trade surplus exceeded $1 trillion for a second straight year, according to official data released Tuesday, as pressure mounts for greater balance in trade with Beijing.

Exports in October surged 35.2% from a year earlier, the customs agency said. Exports have grown rapidly this year supported by high-tech goods like semiconductors and autos. Imports rose 41.6% year-on-year.
Between January and October, China logged a $1.04 trillion trade surplus, even as the trade surplus narrowed last month to $105.3 billion from $133.5bn in September as imports picked up pace.
That puts China on track for surpassing last year’s record $1.2 trillion trade surplus.
“We expect Chinese exports to stay strong for the rest of this year, led by electronics and autos,” said Dave Chia, an economist at Moody’s Analytics.

Overcapacity in many industries, excess domestic savings and weakened domestic demand are still forcing China to ship its goods abroad as some countries move to protect their own industries, said Alicia García-Herrero, chief economist for Asia Pacific at French bank Natixis.
The situation is not sustainable, she said.

Businesses are feeling the pressure of ferocious competition as China’s economy has slowed, said Cinders Zhou, who sells eyewear for a manufacturer in Linhai city in eastern China’s Zhejiang province.

“It comes down to product quality, or rather the increasingly the lack of it across the industry, since there’s significant homogenization,” said Zhou, whose company makes frames and lenses sold both in and outside China. “That has forced everyone to compete on price,” she said.
Trade curbs by the European Union pose an important risk at a time of heightened U.S. trade barriers and tariffs, Chia said.
Top Chinese officials insist Beijing is not seeking to expand the trade surplus but wants more balanced global trade.

China’s exports could be vulnerable to setbacks for the artificial intelligence industry, a concern that deepened with the Democratic victories in the U.S. midterm elections given the public backlash against expansion of data centers.
“If the AI boom slows or turns into a correction, lower chip and electronics prices and smaller shipping volumes would hit China’s exports hard,” Chia said.

Trade is among the top issues likely to be on the agenda in planned meetings between U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation leaders summit later this month in China’s technology hub Shenzhen.
A two-month extension of a trade truce until January has provided some relief to exporters, though it’s unclear how long that may last.

U.S. and European trade policies have added “a lot of difficulties” for Chinese businesses to expand in the markets, said Wang Xin, head of the Shenzhen Cross-Border E-Commerce Association, an industry group.

Strong exports have helped offset sluggish domestic demand in China, where the economy is forecast to meet Beijing’s official target of a 4.5% to 5% annual growth this year, slightly slower than last year’s 5% expansion.

title: Honda reports robust results on the back of healthy motorcycle sales
summary: Honda has reported a 66% rise in net profit for the first half of its fiscal year, driven by strong motorcycle sales
story: Honda has reported a 66% rise in net profit for the first half of its fiscal year, driven by strong motorcycle sales
TOKYO -- Honda’s net profit rose 66% in the first half of its fiscal year, the Japanese automaker reported Tuesday, driven by strong motorcycle sales.

Tokyo-based Honda Motor Co. reported a profit of 516.76 billion yen ($3.3 billion) for the six months through September, up from 311.83 billion yen a year earlier. First half sales rose 13% to 12 trillion yen from 10.6 trillion yen.
The robust results came despite costs in its electric vehicle program, where it dropped some models. Honda said EV-related losses erased 484.8 billion yen from its operating profits.
But officials stressed that Honda expects battery EVs might eventually become more popular and it will remain flexible enough to switch to EV production in the future.
Honda raised its full-year operating profit forecast to 780 billion yen from 650 billion yen.
Honda attributed the more optimistic forecast to favorable exchange rates and efforts to reduce the impact of U.S. tariffs, including shifting production to the United States.
The maker of the Super Cub motorcycle and Accord sedan also announced major production investments in North America and Brazil.

Honda plans to build a new auto production plant in Ohio, increasing production capacity in North America to 1.91 million vehicles by 2029 from 1.67 million. The company expects U.S. demand to grow, especially for its hybrid models.
Honda also plans to expand production of its motorcycle business at its Manaus factory in Brazil, increasing capacity to 2.3 million motorcycles by 2029 from the current 1.6 million.

Honda marked a record for fiscal first half sales in its motorcycle division, as its models proved popular in Brazil and India. It sold 11.9 million motorcycles during the six months, up from nearly 10.8 million the previous year.
However, Honda sold 1.57 million automobiles globally in the first half of the year, down from 1.68 million.
Honda shares, which have risen over the past year, had slipped 1.6% in Tokyo trading on Tuesday before the financial results were released.

title: Wall Street mixed in early trading ahead of a new peek at inflation
summary: Premarket trading on Wall Street was mixed but relatively calm and oil prices fell again, one day after stocks rallied to recover most of their big losses from last week
story: Premarket trading on Wall Street was mixed but relatively calm and oil prices fell again, one day after stocks rallied to recover most of their big losses from last week
Early trading on Wall Street was mixed and oil prices fell again, one day after stocks rallied to recover most of the big losses from last week.
Futures for the S&P 500 rose 0.1% before the opening bell, while futures for the Dow Jones Industrial Average gained 0.3%. Nasdaq futures dipped 0.3%.

Oil prices continue to decline, with Brent crude falling below $91 per barrel, the lowest level in three months. The declines came after President Donald Trump said that the war in Iran “militarily is effectively over,” a week after American voters, angered by skyrocketing costs, handed both chambers of Congress to Democrats in midterm elections.
Brent crude, the international standard, fell 2.2%, or $2.02, to $90.55 a barrel. U.S. benchmark crude oil slid 1.8%, or $1.65, to $84.94 per barrel.

Nvidia shares were off less than 1% before the bell. Shares fell 4.3% on Monday after the AI chip company said it’s investigating after its CEO, Jensen Huang, acknowledged an intimate relationship with a business executive who, according to The New York Times, U.S. intelligence determined was gathering information for China.

Nvidia’s board said it has “no reason to believe” that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised but its inquiry would examine all available information. China has rejected the allegations.
Artificial intelligence giant Anthropic filed papers with regulators Tuesday seeking a $1.3 trillion valuation ahead of its IPO, expected later this month.
Anthropic’s quarterly revenue swelled to $17 billion but it still posted a net loss for the latest three months, the artificial intelligence giant said in an updated IPO filing.
Last week, the San Francisco company behind the Claude chatbot said its quarterly revenue swelled to $17 billion though it still posted a loss for the last three-month period.
Anthropic said it has committed to spend $895.4 billion on AI computing and infrastructure like data centers, including $70 billion that’s due to be spent in the next 12 months.

Global demand for AI chips remains robust with AI chipmaker Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. reporting after the market closed that its October revenue was nearly six-fold that of a year earlier.
In Asian trading, Taiwan’s Taiex jumped 2.5%.
Japan’s benchmark Nikkei 225 closed 2.9% higher at 60,459.58.
Shares in OpenAI investor SoftBank Group jumped 13.9% ahead of the company’s earnings release. Its share price had fallen to its lowest level in a year on Monday.
SoftBank Group reported a $7 billion loss for the three months through September as worries about investments in artificial intelligence hurt the Japanese technology company’s bottom line.
Computer chip equipment maker Tokyo Electron surged 6.1% and testing equipment maker Advantest gained 4.6%.
South Korea’s Kospi climbed 4.4% to 5,239.13. Samsung Electronics gained 4.7% and SK Hynix climbed 6.7%.
In Hong Kong, the Hang Seng rose 0.6% to 24,584.81, while the Shanghai Composite index edged 0.1% higher to 3,663.72.
China’s exports in October climbed 35.2% from a year earlier, while imports grew 41.6%, according to customs data released on Tuesday.
That has put the country on track for another record for the year since the trade surplus for 2026 has already surpassed $1 trillion.
At midday in Europe, Germany’s DAX rose 1.2%, as did the CAC 40 in Paris. Britain’s FTSE 100 was up 0.5%.

Investors are waiting for the U.S. consumer price index report for October, which comes out later Tuesday. Data is expected to show inflation rose 3.9%, up from 3.7% in September, which many analysts expect will force the Federal Reserve to raise its benchmark interest rate in the coming months.

title: Paid recruits tied to banned group behind 3-day crude bomb attacks in Bangladesh, police say
summary: Unidentified individuals have exploded crude bombs and torched vehicles in Bangladesh's capital and other areas over the past three days
story: Unidentified individuals have exploded crude bombs and torched vehicles in Bangladesh's capital and other areas over the past three days

DHAKA, Bangladesh -- Dozens of crude bombs have exploded and passenger vehicles have been set on fire in Bangladesh’s capital and elsewhere over the past three days, leaving one person dead and others injured, authorities and media reports said Tuesday.
The violence coincided with reports that the ousted former prime minister, Sheikh Hasina, plans to return from exile next month, though any connection remained unclear.

Mohammad Akhtar Hossain, a police spokesman, said at least 33 people were arrested Monday in Dhaka and more arrests were made elsewhere. He said a banned group was behind the attacks but did not identify it.

As many as 15 crude bombs exploded in the central district of Manikganj, near Dhaka, early Tuesday, and a driver was killed when a parked bus was set on fire, the country's leading newspapers reported.
In Dhaka, crude bombs exploded over the three days, including at the Dhaka University campus and at the premises of a court on Tuesday, with two people injured. Several vehicles were also torched.
Hossain said seven crude bombs were recovered during search operations, and two motorcycles used in the attacks were also seized in Dhaka. He said security has been increased across the city.
The ruling Bangladesh Nationalist Party accused Hasina’s followers of the violence, saying they want to destabilize the country.

Hossain, without naming any suspected perpetrators, said: “We have found that those involved in these activities are linked to an organization whose activities have been banned, or to its affiliated groups. In many cases, we have also found that some individuals were paid to carry out these acts."
Hasina has been in India since Aug. 5, 2024, when she fled the country as a student-led mass uprising ended her 15-year rule.
A special tribunal sentenced her to death in 2025 for ordering a deadly crackdown on protesters.
On Monday, Hasina requested a new passport to facilitate her return from exile.
The government has been seeking her extradition from India and has dismissed suggestions she needed new identification documents to return home.
Hasina says she wants to return to Bangladesh in December voluntarily, despite being sentenced to death.

In a letter seen by The Associated Press that was emailed to Bangladesh’s diplomatic mission in New Delhi, Hasina’s counsel urged the top diplomat to take necessary action to provide her a passport and national identity card.

The government of Prime Minister Tarique Rahman said Hasina’s email seeking the passport was a mockery. It said Hasina would be required to submit her application in person, and that an emailed request is not enough.

title: Investigators recover the voice recorder from a jet crash in Florida that killed 9
summary: Investigators say they have recovered the cockpit voice recorder of a business jet that plummeted from the sky amid severe weather in Florida last week
story: Investigators say they have recovered the cockpit voice recorder of a business jet that plummeted from the sky amid severe weather in Florida last week
Investigators said Monday they have recovered the cockpit voice recorder from a business jet that plummeted from the sky amid severe weather in Florida last week, killing all nine people on board.

The recorder was found at the site where the Bahamas-bound Learjet slammed into the ground and erupted in a fireball Nov. 1, the National Transportation Safety Board said in a statement posted to social media.

If data from the device can be recovered, it could provide crucial details about what the pilots said to each other as they encountered turbulence, ice formed on the wings and they lost control of the aircraft.
It was not immediately known if the recorder had been damaged or if it was working in the first place. The NTSB said the device was being evaluated at a lab in Washington.
From photos the agency posted online, showing the recorder's orange-painted metal shell, it appeared to be in decent shape, aviation safety expert Jeff Guzzetti told The Associated Press.
“It's very plausible that any info on the recorder survived,” Guzzetti said. “If they can recover it, and it's from the accident flight, that will be a huge help to investigators.”

He noted that when the NTSB recovered the cockpit voice recorder from a medical transport plane that crashed in Philadelphia in January 2025, killing seven people, it turned out the device likely had not been functioning for several years.

Witnesses captured dramatic video as the business jet plunged nose-first into the ground, and air traffic control transmissions recorded the disturbing moments as the pilots realized their fate. But the cockpit voice recorder could shed light on other aspects of the crash, including why the Learjet appeared to steer around a large storm cell only to head directly into a rapidly developing smaller one.

Investigators have said pieces of a key part of the tail called the elevator, which controls the plane’s pitch, were found more than a mile away from the main crater, confirming the plane started to break apart before impact.
The co-pilot told air traffic controllers that the plane was being thrown up and down more than 700 feet (213 meters), and she asked them for a better route through the area.

Generally, it takes 12 to 18 months for the NTSB to complete a crash investigation, but complicated cases can take longer. The NTSB’s roughly 400 workers are pursuing more than 1,200 active investigations.

Investigators will review maintenance records and any history of problems with the plane. They will also interview officials at Upper Jets, the company that operated the flight, as well as air traffic controllers and people who work at the airport in Austin, Texas, from where the plane departed.

title: Explosion at steel plant in western Turkey leaves 10 dead and 4 missing
summary: Turkish officials say that a huge explosion and fire at an iron and steel works in western Turkey have left at least 10 people dead
story: Turkish officials say that a huge explosion and fire at an iron and steel works in western Turkey have left at least 10 people dead
ISTANBUL -- A huge explosion and fire at an iron and steelworks in western Turkey left 10 people dead Monday as rescuers searched for four missing workers, officials said.

The fire at the HABAS plant in Aliaga, Izmir province, also injured 15 people, two of them critically, Provincial Gov. Suleyman Elban said in a televised update of the latest casualties. Search teams were looking for four people still believed to be under the wreckage, he added.
An earlier statement from his office had put the death toll at three, with 14 wounded and 10 missing.
Izmir Mayor Cemil Tugay said that the exact number of casualties would only be known once the debris is cleared.
Broadcaster NTV showed images of a large fire inside the facility and a tall column of smoke rising.
“The ground shook. It was very intense,” witness Nuri Ali Ulker was quoted as saying by the state-run Anadolu news agency.
Another witness, Deniz Ulker, said that the explosion “felt like the earth’s crust was shifting beneath us. I thought it was an earthquake,” according to Anadolu.
Interior Minister Mustafa Ciftci said that emergency teams fought the blaze while searching for casualties.
“Our injured compatriots have been taken to hospitals and their health is being closely monitored,” he posted on social media.

The governor’s office said that the blast happened around noon (0900 GMT) when an overhead crane toppled into a furnace during the casting of liquid steel. It said that an investigation had been launched and Justice Minister Akin Gurlek said four public prosecutors had been assigned to the case.

Aliaga has a large port and is known for shipbreaking, which critics say has caused significant environmental damage and has led to calls to remove its shipbreaking yard from the European Union’s list of ship recycling facilities.
The disaster came as world leaders and environmental activists gathered in Antalya, on Turkey’s Mediterranean coast, for talks on curbing climate change.
The HABAS plant was established in 1987 and can produce 4.5 million tons of steel annually, according to the company’s website.

title: T. Cullen Davis, a Texas oil tycoon acquitted in a 1970s murder trial, has died at 93
summary: T
story: T

DALLAS -- T. Cullen Davis, a Texas oil tycoon acquitted of murder in a shooting at his secluded Fort Worth mansion in a 1970s case featured in true-crime shows and then acquitted again in an alleged murder-for-hire plot, has died. He was 93.
Davis, who always maintained his innocence, died Friday at his home in the Fort Worth suburb of Colleyville, his son Trey Davis said Monday.

In August 1976, Davis and his second wife, Priscilla Davis, were going through a contentious divorce when a gunman dressed in black and wearing a woman's black wig fatally shot two people at the mansion: her daughter Andrea Wilborn, 12, and her live-in boyfriend, Stan Farr, 30.
Priscilla Davis and a visitor to the mansion, Gus “Bubba” Gavrel Jr., were both wounded but survived. Gavrel's date escaped unharmed.

The three survivors identified Cullen Davis as the gunman. He was tried for capital murder in the death of Wilborn. Defended by prominent Texas attorney Richard “Racehorse” Haynes, Davis' first trial ended in a mistrial because of juror misconduct and the second ended in an acquittal in 1977.
With an oil-based empire valued at $400 million, he was said to be the wealthiest man at that point to stand trial for murder.

Nine months after the verdict, Davis was arrested and charged with solicitation of capital murder. An FBI informant swore that Davis ordered him to kill 15 people, including the judge presiding over his divorce case and the three survivors of the shooting. Davis, once again defended by Haynes, was acquitted in that case as well.
The shooting at the mansion inspired multiple books and was featured in true crime television shows. A 1995 television miniseries titled “Texas Justice” starred Heather Locklear as Priscilla Davis.
By the mid-1980s, his largely oil-based empire was crumbling. He said in the mid-1990s that his company had gone bankrupt “because of the crash of the oil industry, not because of my trials.”
Priscilla Davis died of breast cancer in 2001 at the age of 59.

Trey Davis was adopted by Cullen Davis when his mother, Karen Master, became Cullen Davis' third wife. He described Cullen Davis as someone who “stood with his arms wide open, willing to lovingly accept you regardless of where you stood in life.”
He said that when he first met Cullen Davis in the mid-1970s when his mother was dating him, Cullen Davis was “a fairly caustic person," but that changed when he became a Christian.
“He became a Christian in 1981 and a lot of things changed," Trey Davis said. "He took that very seriously, his dedication to Christ. He was a man of virtue, integrity, grit and humility.”

title: Botswana says it will increase its stake in De Beers to 30% under proposed sale
summary: Botswana’s president says that his diamond-rich southern African country will double its stake in De Beers to 30% under a proposed deal by a consortium to buy Anglo American’s shares
story: Botswana’s president says that his diamond-rich southern African country will double its stake in De Beers to 30% under a proposed deal by a consortium to buy Anglo American’s shares

GABORONE, Botswana -- Botswana's president said Monday that the diamond-rich southern African country will double its stake in De Beers to 30% under a proposed deal by a consortium of investors to buy Anglo American's shares in the company.

President Duma Boko said in a speech in Parliament that the move would make Botswana the largest single shareholder in De Beers, the world's leading diamond company. Boko said Botswana endorsed the Global Diamond Consortium of investors as the proposed buyer of De Beers.

Mining giant Anglo American put its 85% stake in De Beers up for sale in 2024 as part of a broader restructuring focused on minerals expected to boom from the transition to green energy and a downturn in the diamond market. As De Beers' other shareholder, Botswana's backing of the Global Diamond Consortium is key for the deal to proceed.
The purchase by the consortium, which is led by former De Beers CEO Gareth Penny, has not been finalized.

Botswana has long had a partnership with De Beers to operate its largest diamond mines through the Debswana joint venture. Botswana is one of the biggest natural diamond producers in the world and is looking to double down on the stones after a big dip in sales caused its diamond-dependent economy to contract last year.
The global natural diamond industry is undergoing a downturn, largely due to competition from artificial lab-grown stones and a decline in luxury spending in China, according to analysts.
Boko said fellow southern African nations Namibia and Angola would also be involved in the deal for De Beers, though he gave no details.

"For the first time, the great diamond producing nations of our region will sit together at the ownership table of the company that markets their diamonds, united by a shared belief that local resources should bring local prosperity,” Boko said.

title: France blames Iran for last month's cyberattack on supermarket fridges
summary: France has blamed Iran for a cyberattack on supermarket fridges last month
story: France has blamed Iran for a cyberattack on supermarket fridges last month

PARIS -- France on Monday blamed Iran for last month's massive cyberattack on supermarket fridges, summoned the Iranian ambassador and said it would seek European sanctions against those responsible for the attack.

The Oct. 12 attack sent refrigerator temperatures soaring, affecting about 700 of the country’s 10,000 supermarkets. In a statement Monday, prosecutors in Paris said they found that Iran’s paramilitary Revolutionary Guard was behind the large-scale cyberattack.

The French Foreign Ministry condemned the attack “in the strongest possible terms,” and French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot, speaking on the sidelines of G7 talks in Paris, said the Iranian ambassador was being summoned to “strongly protest against this extremely serious act.”

“This is an attack of unprecedented scale and aggressiveness,” Barrot said. “It is the first large-scale cyberattack aimed at sabotage on French soil, and it represents a major threat to our national interests and the security of the French people. That is why it will not go unanswered.”
“We will impose sanctions at the European level against all those responsible for this attack,” he added, vowing to take “any other measures needed” to respond to it and deter future attacks.

Paris prosecutor Laure Beccuau said in a statement that a formal judicial investigation was opened Monday into suspected organized cybercrime with the aggravating circumstance of “having been committed to serve the interests of a foreign power — in this case, Iran."

France’s national cybersecurity agency, ANSSI, attributed the attack to the Shahid Kaveh group, described as a “cyber unit” affiliated with Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. The investigation targets the leader of the group as well as his two deputies and any other individuals who might be identified in connection with the case, Beccuau said.

Investigators found that the attackers had used Farsi and IP addresses linked to devices located in Iran, Beccuau said. The Paris prosecutor’s office is seeking international arrest warrants, she said.

In the early hours of Oct. 12, attackers remotely took control of refrigeration systems in hundreds of supermarkets and independent stores across France. Temperatures reached 50 degrees Celsius (122 degrees Fahrenheit) for about six hours, forcing stores to discard fresh and frozen goods. The Intermarché supermarket chain reported losses of “tens of millions of euros” in a single day.

Last week, another cyberattack in France on several blood banks tried to raise temperatures to extremely high levels but was thwarted before it could do any damage to blood products or samples. France’s national cybersecurity agency and Paris prosecutors are investigating the incident.

Also last week, supermarkets in Sweden, Belgium, Luxembourg, Ireland and Estonia were hit by problems with freezers and fridges that apparently were caused by cyberattacks, forcing some to dispose of ruined food.

The ANSSI cybersecurity agency said it was able to attribute some other cyber attacks carried out against France since 2020 to another group named Shahid Shoostari, also affiliated with Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. They include attacks targeting satirical newspaper Charlie Hebdo in 2023 and the organization of the Paris Olympic Games in 2024.

title: Heat-trapping carbon pollution drops, but scientists cite Iran war
summary: Emissions of heat-trapping carbon dioxide from the burning of fossil fuels decreased slightly this year due to the Iran war
story: Emissions of heat-trapping carbon dioxide from the burning of fossil fuels decreased slightly this year due to the Iran war

Global carbon pollution dropped this year ever so slightly, but it's more because of oil shocks reverberating from the Iran war than anything the world has done to fight climate change, scientists said in a new study.

In 2026, the world emitted 42.2 billion tons (38.2 billion metric tons) of heat-trapping carbon dioxide from the burning of fossil fuels such as coal, oil and gas. It’s a 0.4% decrease from last year, according to the scientists of the Global Carbon Project, which publishes its estimates in the journal Earth System Science Data Discussions.

“It’s downwards which sounds good, but this is largely driven by the war in Iran, what’s happened in the Strait of Hormuz,” said study co-author Glen Peters, a scientist at the CICERO Center for International Climate Research in Norway. “So in a way, a little bit of good news, but for the wrong reasons.”
The war in Iran has effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz, a vital shipping artery for petroleum products, pushing up global prices of gasoline and oil.
They found oil emissions dropped nearly 2% and natural gas fell 0.3%, while coal was up 0.6%.

The international team of more than 140 scientists use data from around the world to calculate the yearly emissions figure, with estimates for the last few months of the year, and then present them at the U.N. climate negotiations in Antalya, Turkey. Peters said they are certain that this was related to the war-triggered energy shocks because of both the timing and type of fuel emission drops.

If the overall carbon dioxide emission drop were due solely to a rise in renewables and a systemic drop in fossil fuel use, oil emissions “would slowly come up to a peak and then slowly decline afterward, whereas what we see this year is oil emissions are going up and then suddenly BANG, down 2%,” Peters said.
This is the third time global carbon pollution dropped in the 21st century. The other two times were because of the global recession in 2009 and the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020.
In those past two crises, people hoped the recovery from the shocks would emphasize clean energy, Peters said, "but at the end of the day, we seem to go back to where we were before.”
Outside experts greeted the figures with a mix of hope and skepticism that it will last.

Niklas Höhne, co-founder of Germany’s NewClimate Institute, said “permanent shifts are happening” especially with skyrocketing switches to electric cars and trucks, especially in Asia. So he thinks the global peak of carbon emissions is near or here.

But Malte Mienshausen, a climate science and policy expert at the University of Melbourne in Australia, said oil producing nations and companies not affected by the blockage of the Strait of Hormuz reaped “tremendous windfall gains,” and it boosts their efforts to look for oil outside the Middle East. That, he said, will dampen any short-term effects of reduced carbon emissions from the war.
The 42 billion tons of carbon dioxide emitted this year comes to about 1,335 tons (1,211 metric tons) of the transparent, heat-trapping gas going into the air every second.

“We shouldn’t lose sight of the bigger picture. The world is still pumping more than a thousand (metric tons) of carbon dioxide into the atmosphere every second," Mohamed Adow, director of the environmental group Power Shift Africa, said in an email.

“It’s very abstract to think about the magnitude of stuff we throw in the atmosphere every year, but it’s a ginormous number,” Peters said. “If it was black and not transparent, the sky would be dark.”

And even though the amount of heat-trapping gases from fossil fuels dropped slightly, overall global carbon dioxide emissions went up 1%. That's because of land use changes, such as deforestation and human-caused peat fires, that increased faster than fossil fuel burning decreased, the study said.

Most of the world's biggest carbon polluting nations — China, the United States, Europe, Japan — showed about a 1% drop in emissions this year, but Peters attributed it to the oil shock. India's fossil fuel pollution went up 4.4% this year, the study found.
China's emission drop raised eyebrows and hope for some experts. Experts have been waiting for China's ever-growing emissions to start dropping.

“China is giving us real reasons to be optimistic that its emissions may have peaked," Adow said. “It’s building the world’s first major electrostate, investing at extraordinary speed and scale in solar power, wind energy, electric vehicles and the infrastructure to support them. This isn’t a temporary response to an oil crisis. It’s a fundamental transformation of China’s economy that is steadily reducing its dependence on fossil fuels.”
University of Michigan environment dean Jonathan Overpeck said, “We're not phasing out fossil fuels fast enough, but some progress is better than no progress.”

title: DOJ sues Lyft alleging discrimination against riders with disabilities
summary: The federal government is accusing Lyft of discriminating against passengers with disabilities
story: The federal government is accusing Lyft of discriminating against passengers with disabilities
The Justice Department has filed a lawsuit against Lyft, accusing the company of discriminating against passengers with disabilities who seek rides on its platform.

The federal lawsuit, filed Monday, says Lyft “is aware of, but fails to prevent and remedy” several discriminatory practices against riders who need accommodations under the Americans with Disabilities Act. That includes denying rides to people who have service animals or use stowable wheelchairs and refusing to let passengers with mobility issues sit in the front seat, the suit alleges.

“Individuals with disabilities should be able to rely on rideshare services free of discrimination,” said Jesus A. Osete, acting assistant attorney general, in a statement. “We intend to uphold the ADA’s promise that people with disabilities are entitled to equal access in every part of public life, including essential transportation services.”
Lyft firmly rejected the accusations in a statement.

The lawsuit is the latest from the federal government that targets ride-hailing companies for treatment of would-be riders with disabilities. The administration filed a similar lawsuit against Uber last year, which is ongoing. Uber settled a separate suit in 2022, and Lyft settled a different one in 2020. The companies stress that their policies and in-app tools require that drivers provide ADA accommodations and remind them of the consequences of refusing to do so.

The new lawsuit against Lyft named several examples of people across the country who hailed a ride on the platform but had one — or, in some cases, several — drivers refuse to take them to their destination, including as recently as last month. Those individuals experienced delays in getting to medical appointments, cancellation fees and other issues as a result, the suit said.

Lyft policies require drivers to accommodate riders who travel with service animals or mobility devices and “drivers who violate these policies face serious consequences, including permanent deactivation,” the company said in a statement.
“We’ve cooperated with the DOJ throughout its review and remain committed to serving every rider, including riders with disabilities,” the company said.

The lawsuit was filed in U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California. The DOJ said it is seeking $53 million for individuals who have been discriminated against and have submitted complaints to Lyft or the department.

title: Upgrading power grids to accommodate renewable energy is a key issue at climate talks
summary: Outdated power grids around the world are a major hurdle in the transition from fossil fuels to renewable energy
story: Outdated power grids around the world are a major hurdle in the transition from fossil fuels to renewable energy
Outdated power grids are a major hurdle in the transition to renewable energy, since older systems often can't absorb all the electricity from new, cleaner sources.

This threatens global efforts to curb climate change by reducing fossil fuels and switching to renewable energy such as solar and wind. At U.N. climate talks kicking off this week, co-hosts Turkey and Australia want more ambitious goals to slash fossil fuels, install renewables and upgrade grids.

Grid concerns are gaining urgency this year as nations race to improve their energy security following the Iran war. The U.N. recently launched a new initiative to rally funding for grid upgrades in Africa and Southeast Asia.

“There needs to be a massive, massive, massive scaling up of investments into grids if we are going to get close to meeting our climate, energy and development goals,” Selwin Hart, special adviser to the U.N. secretary-general on climate action, said.
At the U.N. climate talks, hosted in the Turkish resort city of Antalya, organizers describe modern and reliable electric grids as “the backbone of the clean energy system.”
But billions of dollars are needed to upgrade out-of-date grids. These steep costs could hinder further renewable energy installations.
During the U.N. General Assembly in September, the global body launched a Global Grids Accelerator to speed up international funding for electricity infrastructure in Africa and Southeast Asia.
“We’re very confident that the long-term trend is an acceleration of the pace of the energy transition, but we need the infrastructure, grids and storage, to really keep pace,” Hart said.

Annual investment in electricity generation, such as building new power plants, has risen by almost 70% since 2015, reaching $1 trillion a year, according to the International Energy Agency. Yet the agency noted annual grid spending has risen at less than half that pace.

To meet electricity demand through 2030, the IEA calculates annual grid investment must increase by about 50% from today’s $400 billion per year. Any delays will substantially increase global emissions by prolonging reliance on fossil fuels, the IEA warns.

“Power grids have not been readied enough for the scaleup of renewable electricity generation,” said Jan Rosenow, a professor of energy and climate policy at Oxford University. “We have been complacent in the past and now the grid has become a real bottleneck.”
Power grids deliver electricity from power plants to homes through a network of transmission and distribution lines, substations and transformers.

Originally designed around large, centralized power plants, many of today's power grids were built like one-way roads, with producers sending electricity to consumers. These older one-directional grids are being overwhelmed by demand surges and a boom in renewables.

Grids have a maximum capacity of electricity that they can safely store, transport and distribute. If a grid is already at capacity, solar and wind farms can be instructed to limit their electricity output, a process known as curtailment.
China and India, which have installed impressive amounts of renewables, can't take full advantage of the massive buildout for this reason.

China curtailed 360 terawatt-hours — close to the equivalent of the United Kingdom's annual electricity demand — of wind and solar electricity in the first half of 2026, according to Global Energy Monitor and the Center for Research on Energy and Clean Air.

India curtailed 11 terawatt-hours of solar generation — enough electricity to power about 10 million homes — over the course of 15 months spanning 2025 and 2026 because of insufficient transmission and storage capacity, according to the energy think tank Ember.

Curtailing solar and wind generation while fossil fuels continue to supply electricity is a blow to climate efforts, especially since China and India are among the world's largest emitters, said James Abraham, with the New Delhi-based Council on Energy, Environment and Water.
To transition away from fossil fuels, he said, "you need a grid changeover. You need a grid transformation.”

Upgrading existing grids to be more flexible could increase efficiency by allowing electricity flows to adjust to supply and demand. It could help areas with excess solar and wind energy send it to places with higher electricity demand and fewer energy resources.
Newer, more flexible grids could also make it easier for utility companies to exchange electricity with households that have solar panels or battery storage.
But many countries can't afford to take these steps, or at least not quickly enough, according to Abraham, who said “the need is now. It’s a time tension rather than anything else.”

The Iran war's energy shock built up momentum for the energy transition, especially in hard-hit regions like Southeast Asia, but investment in renewables is outpacing grid development, said Gahee Han, with the Seoul-based nonprofit Solutions for Our Climate.

“Unless we upgrade our power grid in Asia, Asia will have no choice but to rely on the conventional power plants, like gas or coal,” she said. “It’s nonsense to rely on those power plants, especially considering the energy crisis.”

One of the solutions being promoted by the Association of Southeast Asian Nations is an interconnected power grid that would allow countries to trade power more easily, adding a safeguard against future shocks.
Interest in the ambitious plan, which is still in its infancy, is growing, according to Abdul Razib Dawood, executive director of the ASEAN Center for Energy.
“We have this crisis that will unify the region. You need your neighbors," he said. “This is an opportunity for us to really strengthen the cooperation.”

title: Despite hurt wrist, Antetokounmpo scores 30 and Heat outlast Jazz 115-109
summary: Giannis Antetokounmpo scored 30 points, leading the Miami Heat to a 115-109 victory over the depleted Utah Jazz
story: Giannis Antetokounmpo scored 30 points, leading the Miami Heat to a 115-109 victory over the depleted Utah Jazz
SALT LAKE CITY -- Giannis Antetokounmpo scored 30 points, Davion Mitchell added 19 points, and the Miami Heat outlasted the depleted Utah Jazz 115-109 on Tuesday night.
The Heat also got 14 from Pelle Larsson but needed late blocks from Klay Thompson and Bam Adebayo to secure their third win in their last four games.
Antetokounmpo iced his sprained right wrist in a heavy wrap when he was on the bench but it didn’t seem to bother him on the court. He shot 12 for 21 and grabbed 11 rebounds.
He now has 21,836 points and passed Gary Payton to become the 39th leading scorer in NBA history.

Despite the Jazz's ninth straight loss, Utah's two teenagers gave the Jazz hope for the future. Rookie Darryn Peterson nearly set his career high (26) for the second game in a row with 25 points and Ace Bailey scored 23.
Utah's Isaiah Collier, a notoriously poor shooter who had not made a 3-pointer this season, made four consecutive shots from behind the arc in the fourth quarter to cut Miami's lead to 101-93.

Then Svi Mykhailiuk made back-to-back baskets to cut the lead to 112-107 in the final minute but it was too late for the Jazz, who were missing four starters to injury — Lauri Markkanen (wrist), Keyonte George (ankle), Jaren Jackson Jr. (knee), and Jusuf Nurkic (foot).
Antetokounmpo's shooting sparked the Heat to a 15-2 run in the third quarter to give the Heat the cushion they needed and send them home with a 3-2 record on their five-game road trip.
Larsson hit a 3-pointer with 6:58 left in the second quarter to cap a 13-1 run and make it 49-32 for Miami.
The Jazz, who have been hurt by turnovers all season, had 18 to just eight for the Heat.
Heat: Host Cleveland on Friday night to commence a five-game homestand.
Jazz: Host Orlando on Wednesday to complete the back-to-back set.
