Nov 11, 2026, 1:32 PM ESTIf the US attacks Pickaxe Mountain, Iran will respond by targeting all US bases, Iranian official says
Nov 11, 2026, 1:23 PM ESTTrump claims the US didn’t start the Iran war
Nov 10, 2026, 12:10 PM ESTAbu Dhabi National Oil Company vessel damaged in attack, UAE says
Nov 10, 2026, 8:35 AM ESTIran war 'not necessarily popular,' Hegseth says
If the US attacks Pickaxe Mountain, Iran will respond by targeting all US bases, Iranian official says

If the U.S. attacks Pickaxe Mountain, Iran will respond by targeting all U.S. military bases, including bases in European countries, the secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, Gen. Mohsen Rezaei, warned in an interview on Lebanon’s Al Mayadeen TV, according to IRIB.
Rezaei also said that if the enemy wants to launch a new attack against Iran, based on their own calculations, the war will not last more than 4 to 5 days, according to IRIB
Trump claims the US didn’t start the Iran war

President Donald Trump said "America did not start a war with Iran," but that "Iran has been waging war on America since 1979," while speaking at Arlington National Cemetery to commemorate Veterans’ Day.
Trump also claimed the U.S. "won" the war but that he wants to make sure "total victory" is achieved, saying it was "about time somebody fought back."
"It’ll take them 25 years to rebuild back while we have destroyed, and hopefully we won't have to destroy any more of that country. Got a lot of work to do to put it back,” Trump said.

Trump again promised that the war in Iran will end "soon," though he did not provide a concrete timeline. He also highlighted the 18 U.S. servicemembers that have fallen from hostile action since the war began in February, but he made a point to argue that active fighting only took place for "a few weeks."

“We began operations against Iran seven months ago, of which only a few weeks were active, hard fighting. We lost 18 beautiful souls, but when this conflict is over, and it will be soon, the entire world will be a much safer and better place, more peaceful place,” he said.
Abu Dhabi National Oil Company vessel damaged in attack, UAE says
A vessel with Abu Dhabi National Oil Company (ADNOC) Logistics and Services was damaged in an attack Tuesday afternoon, the United Arab Emirates state-run news agency (WAM) reported.
The attack reportedly occurred in the territorial waters of the UAE and "response efforts" were ongoing, according to WAM.
Iran war 'not necessarily popular,' Hegseth says

Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth acknowledged that the ongoing war with Iran is "not necessarily popular" among American voters, when asked about the role the conflict played in the heavy Republican defeat in the midterm elections.

Vice President JD Vance last week publicly blamed the conflict for the historic Democratic Party victory in the midterm elections. Asked about Vance's remarks, Hegseth said he did not want to engage in "finger pointing."
Hegseth said the war was launched "for the right reasons, to ensure Iran never gets a nuclear weapon."
Paraphrasing Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Hegseth said of the war, "It's not necessarily popular, but it may have been necessary. And that's certainly how I feel. It was a necessary undertaking."

title: Several Democrats missed the crucial Hegseth impeachment vote. Many blamed traffic
summary: Eleven Dems missed the critical vote, squandering Hegseth's impeachment attempt.
story: Eleven Dems missed the critical vote, squandering Hegseth's impeachment attempt.

Tuesday night's House vote on a procedural motion to kill the impeachment of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth could have gone a different way had it not been for 11 Democrats missing the vote -- with several saying a traffic incident near the Capitol kept them from casting their votes.

The GOP referred Republican Rep. Thomas Massie's impeachment resolution against Hegseth to the Judiciary Committee where it will wither and die at the end of the 119th Congress on Jan. 3, with a vote of 211-204.

While seven Republicans skipped the vote, Democrats could have prevailed had they all cast a vote in the 29 minutes that the vote, scheduled for 15 minutes, was held open. Had all 11 Democrats voted with the rest of their punctual colleagues in the chamber where Republicans enjoy a two-vote majority, the motion could have been defeated 215-211 -- and therefore the impeachment resolution would have advanced.

Democratic Reps. Julia Brownley, Lou Correa, Laura Gillen, Steven Horsford, Jonathan Jackson, Nancy Pelosi, Brittany Pettersen, Melanie Stansbury, Haley Stevens, Marilyn Strickland and Frederica Wilson all failed to show up in time to cast their no votes on referring the impeachment resolution to committee. Only Correa announced his absence in advance, citing a medical procedure that him from traveling to Washington to vote on Tuesday.

"Speaker Emerita Pelosi returned to San Francisco yesterday to join and honor local veterans at Swords to Plowshares' 30th Annual Veterans Day Celebration, an important and longstanding district tradition she regularly attends and marked for the last time as a Member of Congress," Pelosi spokesman Ian Krager told ABC News. "She supports impeaching Secretary Hegseth and would have voted ‘No’ on the motion to refer."
Other Democrats largely blamed their absence on Washington traffic -- despite knowing for at least 18 hours that the House had scheduled a 5:30 p.m. vote series on Tuesday night.
ABC News has reached out to U.S. Capitol Police about a traffic incident that several Democratic lawmakers claimed held them up, but has not yet heard back.

"Like other Members of Congress, Rep. Stansbury was blocked from entering the Capitol to vote due a traffic incident and a police escort of a bus during the vote,” her office explained in a social media post. "When she reached the chamber the vote had just gaveled out. She immediately filed a report of her vote of 'NO' to the motion meant to kill the impeachment articles and refer them to the Judiciary Committee, as documented in the Congressional Record."
Congressional record additions don't impact the result or tally of the vote.
Gillen said that she was also caught in the traffic delay.

"Like Rep. Stansbury, I was stuck behind the same police escort blocking the Capitol when Republicans closed the vote," Gillen wrote in a social media post. "I would have voted no and believe strongly that Pete Hegseth should be impeached."

Jackson said in a social media post that the traffic incident "caused a delay that resulted in the vote closing before I, along with other Members, could reach the chamber," adding that he has since entered his intent to case a "no" vote into the congressional record.
Pettersen wrote in a social media post that she was "denied the ability to vote," but didn't elaborate.

"I was driving the Congresswoman and was forced to wait for a motorcade to pass by Capitol Police, causing the Congresswoman to miss the vote by 1 minute,” Andrew Noh, Strickland’s chief of staff, told ABC. "She would have voted against the motion to refer."

After closing the vote on the motion to refer, the House proceeded next to a vote. By then, six more Democrats -- Brownley, Gillen, Jackson, Pettersen, Stansbury and Strickland -- arrived in the chamber, breaking through the traffic jam.

Had they been there for the vote on the motion to refer, their additional six votes still would have still fallen short of defeating it -- putting the prospective tally at 211-210. Horsford, Stevens, and Wilson were still inexplicably missing.
Horsford later arrived in the chamber for the following vote.
Reps. Brownley, Horsford, Stevens and Wilson have not yet responded to ABC News with an explanation of their missed vote.
Wilson did not vote on Monday or Tuesday and has faced scrutiny for missing extended periods of legislative business due to health challenges. Wilson was at the Capitol for votes on Wednesday.

Outgoing Rep. Stevens, who lost her primary for U.S. Senate, has lost most of her staff and the support of many Democratic colleagues after endorsing Michigan Republican Mike Rogers for Senate over Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed. She cast two votes on Monday evening before skipping all three votes on Tuesday. Stevens also returned for votes on Wednesday.
Democrats may pursue impeachment of Hegseth again -- once they take control of the chamber in January.

title: Discharge petition on 2nd Epstein files bill secures 218 signatures
summary: A discharge petition to force a vote on the Epstein Files Transparency Act II has amassed 218 signatures, teeing up additional floor action on the prospective bill.
story: The bill would allow the U.S. AG to be sued for withholding Epstein records.

A discharge petition sponsored by Kentucky Republican Rep. Thomas Massie to force a vote on the Epstein Files Transparency Act II amassed 218 signatures Wednesday, teeing up additional floor action on the prospective legislation, which would empower state attorneys general, victims and members of Congress to sue the U.S. attorney general for unlawfully withholding or redacting investigative records related to Jeffrey Epstein.
All 214 Democrats and four lame-duck Republicans signed the petition, including Massie and Reps. Nancy Mace, Ralph Norman and Brian Fitzpatrick.

Discharge petitions, once rare, have succeeded eight times so far in the 119th Congress. The legislative tool is used to allow lawmakers to bypass the majority's leadership and force legislation to the floor for consideration.

In November 2025, Congress overwhelmingly passed a bill ordering the release of the Justice Department's files on Epstein, the late sex offender, which President Trump ultimately signed into law. That House vote was forced by a Rep. Massie discharge petition, which secured the necessary 218 signatures at the time.

Once a discharge petition secures 218 signatures, the motion is placed on the calendar for at least seven legislative days, after which one of the signers would need to offer a motion on the discharge petition.
If that happens, the House speaker would then have two legislative days to act on the motion. If the motion passes, the House would then move to consider the legislation.
Any floor action on the proposed Epstein II bill would come after Thanksgiving recess -- potentially as early as Dec. 2 or 3.

title: Biden says he wouldn't have run for a second term in 2024 if he knew he had cancer
summary: Joe Biden says he didn't know he had cancer while he was president and wouldn't have sought a second term if he'd already been diagnosed
story: Joe Biden says he didn't know he had cancer while he was president and wouldn't have sought a second term if he'd already been diagnosed
ATLANTA (AP) — Joe Biden says he did not know he had cancer while he was president and would not have sought a second term if he already had been diagnosed.
The former Democratic president's comments came in an interview with People magazine before the release of his White House memoir on Tuesday.

“If I had known that I was feeling lousy because I had cancer,” said Biden, who turns 84 on Nov. 20, “I would’ve not gone forward” with a 2024 reelection bid that ended after a disastrous debate performance against Republican Donald Trump.
Biden was diagnosed with metastatic prostate cancer months after leaving office in 2025.
“I don’t think an 80-year-old man with cancer should be running” for president, Biden said in the interview.

Still, he argued that the June 2024 debate, less than five months before Election Day, was not a seismic event even if it accelerated Democrats' concerns about his age — he was 81 at the time — and his ability to defeat Trump.

“First of all, I thought there’d be another debate, which there wasn’t,” Biden said. “But notwithstanding the fact that there wasn’t another debate, it didn’t disturb me because it wasn’t consequential.”
Within weeks, Biden announced he was ending his campaign and endorsing his vice president, Kamala Harris, who secured the nomination and lost to Trump in the general election.
Biden insisted he was able to perform his duties while he was in office. He said age itself was not disqualifying and meant he had experience and deep personal relationships with world leaders.
“I believe that on an objective basis, I was the best-equipped person to do the job,” he said.
His son Hunter told the BBC in August that the cancer had spread and was causing his father pain. "It’s very painful and it’s very debilitating in many respects,” he said.

Since Joe Biden left office, his son has become a higher profile public presence, sparring with Republicans on social media, posting lengthy thoughts on the nation's direction and launching his own cryptocurrency.

Joe Biden defended his son's public persona and his decision to pardon Hunter Biden after the younger Biden's 2024 conviction on federal felony gun charges and his guilty plea to federal tax charges. Hunter Biden also had faced years of scrutiny and withering Republican attacks over his international business dealings.
Hunter Biden has said the pardon damaged his father's legacy, but the former president said Trump's penchant for vengeance made it necessary.

“He goes after people without any basis, whether they’re viewed as an enemy. I knew what he would do,” Joe Biden said. “If I hadn’t pardoned — not just some of my family members, anyone who’s dealt with me — he would go back and try to do harm to them.”
Biden called his son “one of the brightest men I know,” adding, “I’m really proud of him.”

title: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent moved to a military base: Sources
summary: Bessent is the latest administration official to move to a military base.
story: Bessent is the latest administration official to move to a military base.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent was quietly moved to a military base in Washington in the last few weeks because of Iranian threats, according to multiple sources familiar with the situation.
The severity and scope of the Iranian threats to Bessent are not immediately clear, and the Trump administration has not detailed the nature of the threats.
Bessent was reportedly living in Washington's Georgetown neighborhood until the move.
Other Cabinet officials including Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth and Secretary of State Marco Rubio are currently living on military bases while in Washington.

Bessent becomes the latest in a growing number of senior administration officials who have moved to military bases for their safety. Multiple senior administration officials were moved to protected housing or military bases last year, including White House chief of staff Stephen Miller.

A Treasury Department spokesperson told ABC News that the "Secretary will not be deterred by the Iranian regime’s threats and remains committed to executing Operation Economic Outcast and maintaining the blockade, which together are collapsing Iran’s economy."
Bessent has led an economic pressure campaign against Iran -- including sanctions that he said in September are meant to "economically asphyxiate this regime."

A source familiar with the matter said a media report about the location of Bessent's home increased security concerns. That media report was published in January 2025, and actions were only taken recently to move Bessent.
The Secret Service, which protects Bessent, did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The New York Times first reported Bessent's relocation.

title: House Republicans elect Jim Jordan as minority leader for the next Congress
summary: House Republicans on Tuesday elected Jim Jordan as minority leader for the next Congress, beating Majority Leader Steve Scalise, according to multiple sources.
story: Sen. John Thune will remain the party's leader in the Senate after Tuesday vote.
House Republicans on Tuesday elected Jim Jordan as minority leader for the next Congress, beating House Majority Leader Steve Scalise, according to multiple sources.
Jordan got 106 votes to Scalise's 73 votes, the sources said.
As of Tuesday, House Democrats hold a 254-166 margin over Republicans going into the 120th Congress with 15 races still undecided.

In the Senate, Sen. John Thune of South Dakota will remain as the party's leader despite some in his conference delaying the vote while they discussed the results of the midterm elections and the party's path forward.
After the vote, Jordan said Republicans will "fight for American families" in the 120th Congress.
"When Democrats offer more government, we'll offer more freedom, and we will bring that fight in committee, on the floor, and on the stump every single day," he said.

Jordan has led Republicans at the Oversight and Judiciary committees, where his hardline approach and reputation as an ardent defender of President Donald Trump have made him a popular cable TV news guest.
First elected in 2007, Jordan is a two-time NCAA champion wrestler.

Scalise, first elected in 2008, was critically injured during a shooting at practice for the congressional baseball game in 2017. He's served at the Republican leadership table for more than a decade -- including as the GOP's No. 2 leader since 2023. Scalise is also in remission from multiple myeloma, a blood cancer, which he was treated for in late 2023, taking a six-week absence to undergo chemotherapy.

Rep. Tom Emmer of Minnesota, the current majority whip, was elected to serve as GOP minority whip, beating a challenge from Texas Rep. August Pfluger. And Rep. Lisa McClain of Michigan was elected to serve as GOP conference chair -- the No. 3 position among House Republicans in the minority -- according to multiple sources. She beat challenges from Rep. Erin Houchin of Indiana and Rep. Greg Steube of Florida.
Emmer said Republicans will "regain the trust and confidence of the American people" to build back a majority in 2028.
"To our colleagues on the left, enjoy this honeymoon phase because come January 3rd, 2027, you will regret ever putting your name on a ballot," he said.
Jordan and Scalise, along with Emmer, ran for speaker in 2023 when then-Speaker Kevin McCarthy was ousted after a revolt from a small group of far-right Republicans.
Speaker Mike Johnson was elected after a chaotic battle that shut the conference down for three weeks.

Johnson announced last week that he wouldn't stand for election as minority leader, giving the GOP conference an opportunity to pick up the pieces of their shattered majority after the midterm elections by choosing fresh leadership or run it back with Johnson's top two deputies, Scalise and Emmer.

Meanwhile, Senate Republicans on Tuesday afternoon approved Thune by acclimation to remain the conference's leader in the minority after "family" discussions about the best path forward for the party.

Senate Republicans gathered Tuesday morning for what was scheduled to be their leadership elections, but rather than holding votes, they instead engaged in what was described as a "frank" discussion about how Republicans ought to respond in the wake of last week's bruising midterm elections that left Republicans down at least seven Senate seats with two races yet to be decided.

Though some Republicans said they were unsure whether they wanted to stick with Senate Majority Leader John Thune of South Dakota as their leader following voter backlash in the midterms, no one else emerged as a potential challenger.

In addition to Thune, the caucus re-elected the rest of its previous leadership: Sen. John Barrasso will remain as Senate GOP whip and Sen. Tom Cotton of Arkansas will remain Republican Conference chair.
Sen. Bernie Moreno, who was unopposed, was elected chairman of the National Republican Senatorial Committee, the Republican conference's campaign operation, replacing South Carolina Sen. Tim Scott.
Moments after being re-elected, Thune told reporters that Republicans intend to carry the lessons they learned from the punishing election cycle into the next Congress.

"Obviously, the election result was not what we had hoped for, but I think it's important that we take the lessons from that and internalize the message the American people were sending to us and focus on the things that really matter to them. And we intend to do that," he said.

In a letter sent Monday obtained by ABC News, dozens of Republican National Committee members called for Republicans to delay leadership elections in both the House and the Senate for 30 days to give the party time to evaluate its losses and how leadership candidates plan to move the party forward.

"There is no way to sugarcoat what happened on Election Day. From coast to coast, and in some of the reddest parts of the country, Republicans were humiliated. These devastating losses are historic, and they threaten to undo all the work of the last 10 years," the letter addressed to Congressional Republicans reads.

"Members deserve to understand what went wrong and hear how those seeking leadership intend to address those failures before casting their votes. That assessment should inform the choice of leadership. Holding elections first gets that backward."

title: House tables Hegseth impeachment, effectively killing it in current Congress
summary: Hegseth framed the effort as being directed at U.S. service members.
story: Hegseth framed the effort as being directed at U.S. service members.

The House of Representatives voted Tuesday to refer GOP Rep. Thomas Massie's resolution to impeach Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth to the House Judiciary Committee by a 211-204 vote, effectively killing the measure for the remainder of the Republican-controlled 119th Congress.
Massie was the only Republican to vote against tabling the measure, along with all House Democrats.
In a news conference earlier Tuesday, Hegseth dismissed the impeachment effort as "political spectacle," framing Massie's resolution as an indictment against the troops.

The vote came after calls to impeach Hegseth grew as several Republicans attributed the GOP's sweeping midterm losses to the Iran war. Massie, who lost his primary earlier this year to a challenger backed by President Donald Trump, introduced the articles of impeachment against Hegseth on the House floor Monday afternoon.

During his news conference, Hegseth said, "What one disgruntled and defeated congressman is attempting is not oversight, and it's not accountability. It's a political spectacle, a personal manifesto driven by ego and resentment."

Trump congratulated Hegseth in a post on his social media platform, saying Democrats "FAILED" to impeach Hegseth, though the effort was led by a Republican and the vote was a procedural one to refer the measure to the House Judiciary Committee, not on impeachment itself.

"The Democrats' attempt to impeach Secretary of War Pete Hegseth has miserably FAILED! Every single Republican, except Thomas Massie, a major LOSER, voted in favor of Pete," he wrote. "Again, Victories in Venezuela and Iran, the Best Recruitment Numbers in the History of the Military (Long waiting lists to get in!), and Spirit like rarely seen before, led to the EXONERATION of a Great American Patriot. The Democrats continue to weaponize and abuse the United States of America. They must be stopped!
Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell declared "TOTAL VICTORY" in a post on X with an image of Hegseth with a clenched fist.

"The referral of these baseless impeachment articles to the House Judiciary Committee marks total victory for Secretary Hegseth, the Department of War, and the American warfighter," Parnell wrote. "From the beginning, this effort has been a political exercise devoid of merit, evidence, or seriousness. It collapses under the weight of Secretary Hegseth's record of restoring the warrior ethos, delivering results, and putting the mission first."

A defiant Hegseth said in his news conference that each of the military engagements mentioned as part of the impeachment effort -- including strikes on alleged drug-smuggling boats in the Caribbean Sea and the war with Iran -- were lawful actions directed by Trump. None of the operations were approved by Congress, which Massie pointed to in his articles of impeachment.
Hegseth framed the eight articles of impeachment as being directed at U.S. military service members.

Critiques of military operations have long been divorced from the valor and sacrifice of U.S. troops, going back to after the end of Vietnam War, including Hegseth's own longstanding critiques of the chaotic withdraw from Afghanistan under President Joe Biden.
Hegseth pointed out that no Defense secretary has ever been impeached "for carrying out lawful military operations, and in our case, successful ones at that."

Hegseth said that Massie wanted to undo his work over "policy disagreements," saying none of the articles -- which range from skirting congressional approval to wage war against Iran to the unprecedented boat strikes in the Caribbean and East Pacific seas -- bring up high crimes, misdemeanors or treason.
Johnson voiced opposition to Massie's impeachment articles and said he believed Republicans would "defeat" the impeachment effort.
"We'll dispense with the impeachment gambit," Johnson said Tuesday afternoon.

After the articles of impeachment were introduced on Monday, Trump said during a press briefing that Hegseth has "won the war in Iran." Hegseth similarly declared victory during an April press conference.

"He certainly, I think, he's won the war in Iran, but he's certainly winning the war," Trump said of Hegseth. "Iran would love to make a deal. And they've been obliterated, their navy and their air force."
Hegseth on Tuesday sought to align his potential impeachment to Trump's, effectively framing it as a sequel.
"You see, we've seen this show before," Hegseth said, later adding, "both times they failed" in impeaching Trump.
"Both times he came back stronger, and the American people sent him back to the White House," he added. "Now they're trying a third time. This time against a member of his Cabinet."
Trump in a post on his social media site said that Hegseth gets an "A plus, plus, plus for his defense against" Massie.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who spoke in Paris shortly after Hegseth's Pentagon briefing, offered his own defense of Hegseth. He was asked about Hegseth's Department of Defense carrying out orders to take military action against Iran and against the Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen, along with the strikes on alleged drug boats and the U.S. capture of Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro.

"Not only did Pete execute on a direct order from the commander-in-chief, who in our constitution is empowered and trusted with the job of keeping Americans safe, but they did it quite effectively in all those fronts," Rubio said.

title: California's Prop 40 'billionaires' tax' measure is rejected, AP projects
summary: The tax was introduced in response to steep cuts to California's healthcare funding that resulted from the passage of President Donald Trump's "Big Beautiful Bill."
story: The main group opposing the tax raised $333.1 million ahead of the midterms.
Voters rejected California's so-called "billionaires' tax" ballot initiative, according to a projection from The Associated Press on Monday.
This means that the state will not levy a 5% tax on the wealth of California taxpayers and trusts with assets valued over $1 billion. This measure is known as Proposition 40.

The tax was introduced in response to steep cuts to California's healthcare funding that resulted from the passage of President Donald Trump's "Big Beautiful Bill." Yes on 40, the main group backing the measure, had said the tax would generate around $100 billion over five years. The measure would have affected roughly 200 of California's billionaires.
Building a Better California, the main group opposing the tax, raised $333.1 million since the beginning of the year. Most of that money came from billionaires.

Sergey Brin, co-founder of Google, is the organization's top donor. He gave $102 million to Building a Better California. Because of Brin, "co-founder" is the occupation that gave the most to the group overall, a total of $105.3 million. Donors who listed their occupation as "Investor/Philanthropist" gave the group $47.7 million. CEOs gave $46.6 million. People who listed their occupation as "chairman" contributed $43 million.

Naturally, many of the major donors reported being based in California. $43.9 million came from donors in San Rafael, California, a city in the San Francisco Bay Area. $40.2 million came from West Hollywood. $34.7 million came from Redwood City, another Bay Area city, and $28.4 million came from San Francisco itself.
The largest share of contributions, however, came from Sergey Brin, in Reno, Nevada.

Gov. Gavin Newsom became its most prominent opponent, arguing that the tax could be dodged by billionaires who could leave the state for another. As ABC News has reported, Newsom has shared a counterproposal: a national billionaire tax focused on loans taken against assets.
Sen. Bernie Sanders and Rep. Ro Khanna were huge proponents of the measure, arguing that it could set the stage and be an example for a national wealth tax.
Khanna told ABC News in early October that he and Newsom are "polar opposites" on the issue. Both have openly discussed that they are weighing a presidential bid in 2028.

"He [Newsom] doesn't want to offend some of the billionaires who he wants to finance his campaigns, and that's the question: Are we going to be a party for the working class? Are we going to be beholden to our donors?" Khanna said.
Tech investors pushed back hard on the measure. Vinod Khosla warned that the state's top wealth creators would leave, and Mark Cuban told Khanna he doesn't understand business.

title: Planned deportation flight to Iran is aborted for 2nd time, group says
summary: A deportation flight carrying Iranians was abruptly turned around shortly after takeoff Tuesday, according to sources, marking the second such flight to be aborted.
story: A judge recently blasted officials for trying to return Iranians during the war.
A deportation flight carrying Iranians was abruptly turned around shortly after takeoff Tuesday, according to the Iranian American Legal Defense Fund.

The deportees on Tuesday's flight were scheduled to be flown to Pakistan, which was then set to transport them to Iran, but Pakistan declined to receive them, according to two sources familiar with the situation.
It's unclear why Pakistani authorities refused to accept the plane.

The diverted flight comes after a previous attempt to deport the same group was canceled Sunday while the plane sat on the tarmac in Arizona "ready for takeoff" and the detainees were moved back to detention, an attorney for the IALDF previously told ABC News.
Both flights come after a federal judge blasted the administration for planning to send people back to Iran -- "a declared enemy" -- during the ongoing war there.

A Department of Homeland Security spokesperson said Wednesday that Tuesday's flight "contained criminal illegal aliens who have criminal histories that include arrests and convictions covering assaults, drug trafficking, child abuse, domestic battery, and illegal weapon possession."

"They all had final orders of removal," the DHS spokesperson said. "Every illegal alien has their claims heard and receives due process. If a judge finds an illegal alien has no right to be in this country, we are going to remove them. Period. As promised, the Trump Administration is employing all lawful options to carry out the largest deportation operation in history. Make no mistake, these criminals who committed heinous crimes will be deported."

According to Human Rights First, a nonprofit organization that tracks deportation flights, the small ICE Air jet carrying the Iranians departed Tuesday from Mesa, Arizona, at around 5 a.m. local time and returned within 30 minutes.

According to transcript unsealed last week of a hearing held on Oct. 15, U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes ordered the government to provide at least five days' advance notice before any individual is "placed on a transport vehicle or plane bound for removal," along with 24 hours' notice of any finalized removal plan.
There has been no public notice to the federal judge about the last two deportation attempts.

"If anything happens that violates either of those two orders, I will hold every single person associated with violating it. I will start contempt proceedings," Reyes said during the hearing last month.
Judge Reyes, in last month's hearing, slammed the government over its plans to deport the Iranians back to their home country.

"We are talking about sending individuals in our care and custody to a country that we have bombed and we may continue bombing, and is a declared enemy of this country," Reyes said. "It is like saying we have individuals in 1942 in this country that we are going to send back to Nazi Germany. That is the equivalent of what you are telling me."
Last month's hearing was part of a lawsuit brought by the IALDF alleging that the government is sharing confidential information about Iranian asylum seekers with the Iranian government.
