title: Enrolling in Medicare? Here's what to consider before Dec. 7.
summary: Medicare open enrollment, which runs from Oct.15 to Dec. 7, gives people a chance to change their health coverage. Here's what to know.
story: The Medicare open enrollment window has arrived, giving millions of seniors across the U.S. the chance to revisit their coverage choices. Even if you're happy with your plan, experts say it's still worth exploring your options.

Health plans change every year, meaning people could see updates to premium costs, prescription drug coverage and available providers in their network. New plans also come online, expanding the already broad list of coverage options.
"There's really no one who can't benefit from at least taking some time to take a look," Alex Cottrill, senior policy analyst with KFF's program on Medicare policy, told CBS News.

People enrolled in Medicare Advantage or a Part D prescription drug plan typically receive an "Annual Notice of Change" in September outlining any updates to their coverage, according to Medicare.gov, the government website for the program.

"Pay attention to those notices, and frankly, even if you don't receive an annual notice of change, you still want to review your current plan and make sure that it is the right one for you," said Jessica Rivkin, vice president of Reliance Medicare Advisors, an insurance agency that helps people enroll in Medicare Advantage plans.
Americans now have less than a month to make their Medicare choices, with open enrollment set to close Dec. 7. Here are some considerations as you navigate the process.
Choosing between Medicare and Medicare Advantage

One of the biggest decisions people face when enrolling in Medicare is whether to choose traditional Medicare or Medicare Advantage, a comprehensive plan in which private insurers are paid to manage your care.

By contrast, people who enroll in regular Medicare plans must separately select a Medicare Part D prescription drug plan and Medigap, private insurance people can layer on top of their plan to help defray out-of-pocket costs.
"You only have to pick one plan rather than having these modular options that you have in traditional Medicare," Cottrill said of Medicare Advantage.

A drawback of Medicare Advantage is its more stringent requirements. Some plans only allow you to visit in-network providers. If the plan does allow you to go out-of-network, you may face steeper cost-sharing rates, Cottrill said.

"That's a consideration for people who have either a preferred provider that they really want to stay with ...or people who have really complex health needs where they have to see maybe a lot of different specialists, or they need a very specialized type of care," he told CBS News.

For those leaning towards Medicare Advantage, Cottrill said it's worth double-checking that the providers you need are covered by the plan. People should also consider what it might mean for the Medigap coverage, he said.

If people enroll in Medicare Advantage and later switch back to traditional Medicare, they may face higher premiums due to their age or pre-existing conditions, compared to someone who enrolled in Medigap through a traditional Medicare plan from the outset, according to Cottrill.
Comparing plans

Cottrill said a good place to start is Plan Finder, a tool offered by the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) that allows people to compare Medicare Advantage plans and Part D plans and to see whether providers are in-network.
The website, however, is just a jumping-off point. People should still conduct independent research to ensure their coverage needs are met, Cottrill said.
"If something is really crucial for somebody's care, they should reach out to the plan directly, talk to their provider directly and don't just rely on the website," he told CBS News.

For general information, people can contact 1-800-Medicare, the CMS-run helpline for Medicare information, or consult their State Health Insurance Assistance Program, which provides more tailored counseling.

Seniors may also consider working with a broker who can help sort through the different options. But they should keep in mind that these people may have a financial stake in their decision, Cottrill said.
"They're often paid on commission," he said. "That's not to say that they can't be helpful, but it's worth getting a second opinion from someone who doesn't have that financial stake."
Enrollment timeline
The plan you choose during open enrollment takes effect on Jan. 1, 2027, for the full calendar year.

While the deadline to make changes is Dec. 7, some people have some extra wiggle room. Medicare Advantage enrollees can switch to another Medicare Advantage plan from Jan. 1 through March 31 during a separate enrollment period.

"You can also choose to leave your Medicare Advantage plan and return to original Medicare during that same time frame, with the option of also enrolling in a Part D plan," said Will Kinkead, associate vice president of Reliance Medicare Advisors.
Some people also qualify for special enrollment periods if they move or lose access to their current health care coverage and need to make a change.

As people research Medicare plan options, they may find they need to chase down details from their providers or consult with an expert. So it's important not to wait until the last minute to start the enrollment process, Rivkin said.

"This can be a really complicated decision for some people, so take the time to get comfortable with the questions you have, what you need in 2027, and make sure that you're getting all of your needs covered," she told CBS News.

title: Seeking relief from chronic pain
summary: With about one in four American adults living with chronic pain, Dr. Jon LaPook examines some of the current treatments, from medications and surgery, to nerve stimulation, biofeedback and self-hypnosis.
story: Veterinarian Dr. Troy Hudnall enjoyed an active practice in Missouri. But in 2022, during an intense delivery of a calf, he felt a sharp pain, and heard a strange sound: "A snap or a pop, snap's probably the best way to describe it," he said.

Herniated discs and a pinched nerve in his neck caused numbness and severe muscle loss in Hudnall's right hand: "The first thing that I really remember is, I couldn't click my mouse on my computer. I started having trouble with instruments. Anything that required much agility in the fingers was almost gone."

Hudnall had multiple surgeries to help free up the nerves, but as sensation returned, he began experiencing severe pain … pain so bad, he says, he thought about amputating his own arm. Asked to describe how it felt, Hudnall replied, "For me, it's always been electricity. If you've ever touched an electric fence on a farm, or accidentally touched both prongs while you're plugging something in, it's that, but it's repetitive, it pulses."

That chronic pain has haunted Hudnall for three years now, forcing him to stop working. He treats it with a daily handful of pills, including opioids, and has tried red light therapy, physical therapy, electrical spine stimulation, and lidocaine injections. But despite all that, he says he experiences pain every second of every day. Rating his pain level from zero to ten, Hudnall says his "best days" rank at six to eight.
About one in four American adults lives with chronic pain, defined as pain lasting more than three months. Most are still suffering a year later.
"When you have chronic pain day in, day out, you're just inundated with this signal all the time; it's crushing you completely," said pain specialist Dr. Lara Crock.
A global problem

We followed Hudnall's care at one of the nation's top pain centers, the Washington University School of Medicine Pain Center in St. Louis, where, Crock explained, patients often end up trying many different approaches. "We throw medicines at it, we try different injections, we try different procedures," she said. "But really, we don't have a full understanding of why one person with the same injury continues to hurt while the other person heals and no longer hurts."

Treating chronic pain requires understanding the different ways a body can react to a painful stimulus. For example, when a person burns their hand, an electrical signal travels up nerves in the arm to the spine, then on to brain cells that interpret that signal as pain. In most people, once the painful stimulus stops, the sensation of pain stops. But not always.

Crock said, "The tissue that was injured before may be healed, or the injury that you had is recovered, but that signal continues to go and go." Why? "We don't know!" she said. "Your arm is totally normal, every scan, everything about your arm is completely normal, but there's an area of your brain that is affecting your hand that's damaged and causes your arm to hurt all the time."

Chronic pain is a global problem. Over the last 35 years, more than 900 journals in 86 countries have published thousands of articles about chronic pain. Approaches to treatment include using devices that stimulate the vagus nerve in the neck to lower pain in patients with rheumatoid arthritis or migraine headaches. And researchers are testing new non-opioid medications that block tiny gateways in nerve cells (called sodium channels) to keep pain signals from traveling to the brain.
Biofeedback

At Washington University, researchers are trying to lower pain by "retraining" the brain. Doctors Eric Leuthardt and Simon Haroutounian have come up with a headset, wearable at home, that uses biofeedback to train patients to increase certain brain waves that ease pain. "We have conducted a pilot in a small group of about six patients with chronic pain that was non-responsive to other treatments, like surgery, medications," said Haroutounian. "And everyone improved to some extent."

The positive assets of the device, Leuthardt said, include, "It's not a drug, it's got no pathologic side effects, it's not addictive, and in many ways, [it] empowers the patient to rehabilitate their own neural circuits for improvement."
Self-hypnosis

Still in early research stages, that headset isn't ready for patients like Troy Hudnall. But since last May, Hudnall has been trying hypnosis, in sessions conducted by pain psychologist Sarah Buday. "Clinical hypnosis is not your Las Vegas stage show; I'm not trying to make anyone cluck like a chicken or be under my control," Buday said. "The way I think of it is, I'm teaching somebody the skill of self-hypnosis. We are having them go into a very deep state of relaxation, at which point, I start to make suggestions about maybe the quality of the pain or the meaning of it, their emotions."
Several weeks ago, with the help of self-hypnosis, Hudnall endured another surgery. As for his future, he says he tries to remain positive.
And Buday is positive about Hudnall's outlook as well: "I think it's good. It's already getting better. And he is somebody that has a lot of optimism and hope."

And Lara Crock says, even if – despite all you throw at it – pain is only partially relieved, "It can be the difference from being able to get up and take your kid to school or eat breakfast or dinner with your family, versus laying in bed all day. So, that can be huge."

title: Nvidia's stock dives as board weighs move to oust Jensen Huang
summary: Nvidia shares fall sharply in after-hours trading as the company's board considers whether to remove Jensen Huang as CEO.
story: Nvidia's stock price tumbled after the close of trading on Wednesday on news that the chipmaker's board of directors is preparing to oust longtime CEO Jensen Huang.

Nvidia this week launched an investigation into Huang, who admitted to having an extramarital affair. U.S. intelligence agencies have linked the CEO to a Chinese business executive, Alice Huang (no relation), who is suspected of being an asset of China's Ministry of State Security.
The Trump administration is aware of the Nvidia board's plans, sources told CBS News. The Wall Street Journal was the first to report that board members were preparing to remove Jensen Huang.

Nvidia shares fell more than 8%, to $159.51, in after-hours trading. The drop continued a steep decline in the company's market value, which has sunk more than $450 billion since Nvidia announced the probe into Jensen Huang's conduct on Nov. 8.

Jensen Huang, who co-founded Nvidia in 1993, is seen in many circles as the face of the burgeoning artificial intelligence sector, with the company's advanced chips providing the critical computing resources that power frontier AI models.
His departure would be a major blow to Nvidia, which lacks any obvious successor to fill his shoes, according to Wall Street analysts.

"The news is obviously negative, as Jensen is (arguably) the most prominent executive at the most prominent company sitting at the center of the world's most important industry — someone who foresaw the rise of AI years before ChatGPT arrived and made sure the firm he founded would be prepared to capitalize on it," Adam Crisafulli of Vital Knowledge said in a report.
Nvidia's code of conduct

Corporate governance experts said Jensen Huang's alleged relationship with Alice Huang appears to violate Nvidia's code of conduct. That policy highlights that personal relationships could create a conflict of interest for Nvidia, while Huang himself specifies in the code of conduct that the company's workers have a responsibility "to maintain high ethical standards."

Nvidia's code also instructs employees to ask themselves whether they could defend an action if it were made public on social media or known to colleagues. If not, the policy states, "do not proceed."

In a message to company employees on Sunday, Huang admitted to having an affair, and he apologized to his wife and their two children, both of whom also work at Nvidia. "There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry," he wrote.
Nvidia's 11-person board includes Jensen Huang, although the other board members are designated as independent, according to a regulatory filing.

President Trump said this week the FBI is also investigating romantic and business ties between Jensen Huang and Alice Huang, who was a senior executive at Megaspeed International. The Singapore-based company has been one of Nvidia's largest foreign customers, purchasing nearly $5 billion in AI chips and other advanced hardware.
The turmoil at Nvidia is also drawing scrutiny in Congress, with lawmakers expected to question company executives about whether its chips are being funneled to China through other countries.

Dan Ives, a tech analyst with investment adviser Yorkville Ives, said investors will now consider who might succeed Huang, what impact that could have on the company's short-term strategy and what any government investigations might reveal.

"Jensen is not replaceable by another CEO or group of interim executives, but Nvidia likely now has to move on without Jensen at the helm, which seemed like a Twilight Zone episode narrative before Sunday afternoon when the news broke," Ives said in a report.

title: Nvidia's board preparing to oust CEO Jensen Huang, sources say
summary: Nvidia's board of directors is preparing to oust CEO Jensen Huang soon, according to two sources, amid allegations Huang had an affair with a woman U.S. intelligence agencies believe was a Chinese asset.
story: Nvidia's board of directors is preparing to oust CEO Jensen Huang soon, according to two sources familiar with the matter, following allegations that Huang had an extramarital affair with a woman U.S. intelligence agencies believe was a Chinese asset.
The Trump administration is aware of the matter, the sources said.
The Wall Street Journal was first to report on the board's moves.
Nvidia's share price slid more than 8% in after-hours trading Wednesday after the Journal's report, extending a multi-day sell-off for one of the world's most valuable publicly traded companies.
The company has faced days of turmoil following reports that American intelligence agencies believed Huang was the target of a Chinese spying plot.

Nvidia was co-founded by Huang in 1993, and for years it was best known for designing graphics cards widely used for gaming. The company now designs the powerful semiconductors that fuel many of the world's leading AI firms, making its technology highly sensitive and subject to export controls limiting sales to China.

The New York Times reported last week on allegations that Huang had a close relationship with Alice Huang, who previously led a Singapore-based firm called Megaspeed International that bought billions of dollars worth of Nvidia chips and hardware. U.S. intelligence agencies have believed for months that Alice Huang — who is not related to Jensen Huang — was recruited by China's Ministry of State Security, the newspaper reported.
In a message to Nvidia employees over the weekend, Jensen Huang wrote that he was "unfaithful to my wife" and apologized for hurting her and their children. He did not name the woman involved.

Nvidia's board said Sunday it had launched an independent investigation into allegations that the CEO "has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort." The board said it had no reason to believe the company's secrets or national security were compromised. Nvidia spokesperson John Rizzo said, "We trust that if we were the target of a genuine threat, the U.S. government would have notified us."

Two law enforcement sources told CBS News the Justice Department is also investigating Megaspeed over potential violations of U.S. export restrictions on advanced AI chips. Some analysts have raised questions about whether the saga resulted in China — which is racing the U.S. for AI dominance — gaining access to Nvidia's technology through Megaspeed. The company has denied any involvement in illegal chip transfers.

China has denied all allegations, with Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesperson Guo Jiakun telling reporters on Monday that the "so-called Chinese spy narrative is entirely baseless and constitutes slander and smear."

Beyond the national security concerns, Nvidia is facing a securities lawsuit accusing the company of failing to disclose information to shareholders about Jensen Huang's relationship with the alleged spy.

Jensen Huang has a close relationship with the Trump administration. President Trump gave Nvidia permission to sell its advanced H200 computer chips to "approved customers" in China late last year, with the federal government taking a 25% cut of chip sales. The deal did not include Nvidia's more advanced Blackwell or Rubin systems.
The Nvidia CEO and other U.S. tech executives traveled to China with Mr. Trump earlier this year.

On Monday, Mr. Trump called Jensen Huang a "very high-quality person," saying during a White House briefing that "the FBI is looking into it in terms of something else, and I think that he'll be in good shape." The president said he spoke to Jensen Huang to see how he was doing, and the executive "said he had absolutely no idea that the person in question was a spy."

title: SNAP proposal would increase food insecurity, critics say
summary: Anti-hunger advocates are blasting a proposed change to SNAP rules that could cut off more than 6 million people from access to federal food aid.
story: Anti-hunger advocates are denouncing a Trump administration proposal that would tighten eligibility requirements for the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP).

The proposed rule, introduced on Tuesday by the U.S. Department of Agriculture to seek public comment, would change a policy that extends eligibility for SNAP to people who receive benefits through a social safety net program known as Temporary Assistance for Needy Families, or TANF.
If adopted, the SNAP rule would reduce public enrollment in the program by roughly 17%, the Agriculture Department projects.
White House spokeswoman Allison Schuster said the Trump administration wants to ensure that SNAP serves only "eligible Americans who need it most."

"Rather than throwing money at a broken system, the Trump Administration will continue to stop fraudsters stealing from these important programs, as well as take effective, cost-saving steps to make life more affordable for all Americans," she told CBS News in an email.
Broad push to narrow SNAP
Cutting off so many Americans from food stamps would greatly increase food insecurity at a time when many people are already struggling financially, critics said.

"Instead of listening to the public sentiment on affordability following the election, the administration is continuing its attacks on vital food assistance and the families who need help to put food on the table," Ty Jones Cox, vice president for food assistance at the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities, a nonpartisan think tank, said in a statement.

Some lawmakers also decried the proposed rule. In a statement, Rep. Angie Craig, a Democrat from Minnesota and ranking member of the House Agriculture Committee, called the proposal "heartless and cruel."

The proposal comes amid what advocates say is a broader push by the Trump administration to narrow eligibility for food stamps. The "One Big Beautiful Bill" expanded SNAP's work requirements. As of Oct. 1, states are also required to shoulder a larger share of the cost of administering SNAP, a change advocates say could lead to further benefit cuts.
According to USDA figures, more than 5 million Americans have lost access to food stamps since the "Big Beautiful Bill" was enacted in July 2025.

"Basically, what the administration is doing is continuing on this path of making sure that SNAP is dismantled," said Gina Plata-Nino, SNAP director for the Food Research and Action Center, a nonprofit advocacy group. "The states have so much on their plate that they cannot continue running the program."

Plata-Nino said the Trump administration's changes to SNAP have created additional barriers as hunger in the U.S. is becoming more pervasive. Food insecurity has surged since the pandemic, according to research from the Federal Reserve Bank of New York earlier this year.
"We do know that in terms of hunger, it is going to raise our negative health outcomes," Plata-Nino said of the proposed SNAP rule.
What would the proposed rule do?

The latest SNAP reform proposal would restrict what's known as "broad-based categorical eligibility," a policy offered by more than 40 states that allows households outside the normal SNAP eligibility income threshold to qualify for food stamps if they receive benefits through TANF.
Plata-Nino noted that the longstanding policy authorized by Congress makes SNAP more accessible and lowers costs for states administering the program.

Under the new rule, which would take effect in 2029, households above SNAP's income thresholds would not qualify for food stamps if they receive non-cash TANF benefits, such as childcare assistance or job training.
The Trump administration issued a similar proposal in 2019, but the Biden administration withdrew it two years later.
In the text of the rule, the USDA said the current SNAP eligibility standards mean that even households with $1 million in wealth but no income could technically receive food stamps.

"Broad-based categorical eligibility has bloated the welfare rolls for decades," a USDA spokesperson said in an email to CBS News. "It has allowed states to take shortcuts, error rates to balloon, and those households with income and assets far above federal limits access to a benefit meant for the neediest among us. Correcting this loophole is long overdue."
Who would it impact?
In an analysis of the rule, the USDA estimated that 6.3 million people would lose access to SNAP in 2029, the year the proposal would take effect.

The rule would also impact access to other federal assistance programs for people who qualify based on their SNAP eligibility. Nearly 1.8 million children would lose access to free school lunches, while 5,500 low-income women would lose access to supplemental food aid for women and children, according to the agency.

Plata-Nino said FRAC believes those figures could underestimate the number of people who would lose food aid under the proposed rule. "We know that the impact is going to be higher," she told CBS News.

According to the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities, the rule would cut off SNAP benefits for people with a gross household income just above 130% of the poverty line, or about $35,500 per year for a family of three.

title: Tesla extends Cybertruck production to clear backlog, Musk says
summary: Tesla CEO Elon Musk originally said Tesla would wind down production​ at its Texas factory in mid-2027.
story: Tesla is extending a deadline it set to finish Cybertruck production to give the company more time to fulfill its orders, CEO Elon Musk announced Wednesday.

In a social media post, Musk said Tesla will continue to manufacture the Cybertruck through the end of summer 2027, giving the car company a few additional months to work through its backlog. Last week, Musk originally said Tesla would wind down production by mid-2027 when he broke the Cybertruck news to customers.
Days later, he revealed Tesla would have to return some customers' deposits, noting that the Cybertruck order rate "far exceeds" the electric vehicle maker's production rate.
"We will try to make as many as possible before shutting down the line in about 8 months, but will have to return deposits for a lot of people," he said on X.
The announcement sparked backlash from some Tesla customers on social media who said they are still waiting to get their hands on the stainless-steel pickup truck.
"Like many of you, I have a 59k Cybertruck on order," one Reddit user wrote. "I've been excited for it, and I'm getting the feeling now that it may not happen."
In his X post on Wednesday, Musk said he was extending production despite it not being the best financial decision for Tesla.
"This is not the smartest move from a profit-maximizing standpoint btw, but there must be some room in this world for sentimentality or what's the point?" he wrote.

title: United bans AI agents from booking flights on behalf of travelers
summary: Using an artificial intelligence agent to make flight reservations poses security risks and could violate federal rules, according to United.
story: United Airlines said on Wednesday that it is banning artificial intelligence agents from making flight reservations on behalf of travelers, citing security risks and the possibility that such actions could violate federal rules.
Many consumers are turning to AI agents such as Meta's Muse and OpenAI's dots to complete tasks ranging from researching products and tracking down deals to making purchases.

To make an airline booking, an AI agent requires access to a customer's personal information, including credentials like payment information. United has a problem with that, saying that "sharing account credentials with personal, third-party, AI assistants can expose sensitive information, and actions taken by these tools may result in unintended purchases, account changes, or use of MileagePlus miles."

The carrier also said that using an AI agent to, for example, check in for a flight could violate federal regulations, including rules requiring travelers to verify in person that their luggage does not contain banned substances.

"As a result, United is taking steps to restrict access — directly within our digital platforms and indirectly via travel agencies and aggregators — to prohibit use by unauthorized, third-party personal AI agents or assistants," said the airline, which is updating its booking and ticketing policies to reflect the new rule.
United's new policy suggests the company wants to retain control over the customer booking process, said Henry Harteveldt, an aviation analyst at Atmosphere Research Group.

"United is saying they don't want to add yet another, and potentially even more powerful, intermediary than they already face in terms of Google search, price-comparison metasearch sites and online travel agencies," he told CBS News. "Flight searches cost airlines money, and undoubtedly United wants to avoid the expense associated with the surge of AI bot flight searches."

Other airlines are taking a different tack to the emergence of AI agents. For example, Southwest has made its flight inventory viewable to ChatGPT users, who can access the airline's website through the AI app.

United fares will continue to be bookable through flight aggregators such as Kayak, Hopper and Google Flights, Harteveldt said, adding that "consumers shouldn't find it any more difficult to find good fares on the airline."
"But by blocking the AI bots, United won't make it any easier to find its fares, either," he said.

title: Nvidia short-seller warned of Jensen Huang's ties to suspected spy
summary: A small investment firm issued a report about Nvidia in May that foreshadowed issues that have embroiled CEO Jensen Huang in scandal.
story: Recent revelations about Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's links to a suspected Chinese spy have shocked investors, with the chipmaker's valuation sinking $450 billion over two days.

But the relationship, now under investigation by Nvidia, was foreshadowed in May by a little-known Wall Street "short seller," Christian Lamarco of New York City-based Culper Research, who published a 40-page report highlighting Huang's ties to Alice Huang (no relation), a former television reporter and financial industry executive.

Short-sellers use a trading strategy that yields profits when a company's shares decline, and Culper disclosed in its report that it had bet against Nvidia's stock. Short-sellers often publish research to demonstrate why a company is overvalued, aiming to convince other investors to sell the stock, thereby driving the shares lower and boosting their profits.

Lamarco, who didn't immediately respond to requests for comment, based his report on Nvidia on interviews with employees of Chinese companies, Singaporean and Malaysian corporate filings, and social media posts that appeared to show Jensen Huang and Alice Huang socializing together at various events.

The report also outlined Culper's rationale for claiming that Nvidia's high-powered chips were being diverted to China, despite the U.S. barring the sale of such products to the People's Republic due to national security and competitive concerns.

Key to Lamarco's investigation were the actions of Megaspeed International, a Singapore-based company that has emerged as a major player in the Nvidia scandal.  Alice Huang, then a top executive at Megaspeed, is suspected by U.S. intelligence of being an asset of China's Ministry of State Security.
"Uncomfortably close"
Lamarco wrote in the report that Jensen Huang appeared to have an "uncomfortably close relationship" with Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le.

"We believe Nvidia has a significant China problem," Culper Research wrote in a May 13 social media thread. "Nvidia claims its China business went to 'zero' after April 2025 U.S. trade restrictions. We believe that in reality, over 20% of Nvidia's FY 2026 compute revenues remained driven by China via illegal GPU diversion and Southeast Asian intermediaries."

Culper also alleged that Chinese companies used Southeast Asian intermediaries to gain access to Nvidia chips. The firm said corporate filings suggest that one of those intermediaries — Megaspeed — received financing from Chinese e-commerce company Alibaba to buy the chips.
Nvidia didn't immediately respond to a request for comment.

Culper isn't the first to question whether China was using front companies to buy advanced AI chips from the U.S. In a March 23 letter to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, Sens. Elizabeth Warren and Jim Banks warned of a "large-scale diversion of advanced American AI chips to China through Southeast Asian intermediaries."

The lawmakers requested that the Commerce Department immediately suspend active export licenses for Nvidia AI chips and servers to China and to companies in Southeast Asia, including Malaysia, Thailand, Vietnam and Singapore.
Megaspeed's mega-speedy growth

Culper's report notes that Megaspeed had "relatively few assets at year-end 2023," but within a year spent $2.9 billion to purchase Nvidia-powered servers. The short-seller said it found documents that showed the Chinese tech giant Alibaba had provided billions to Megaspeed.
Megaspeed and its Malaysian affiliate, Speedmatrix, together purchased $4.8 billion of Nvidia's advanced AI equipment and processors over the last three years, according to the report.

"Megaspeed went from very little business to billions in a rapid time frame," Culper stated. "This is the exact sort of pattern that experts told us ought to raise alarm bells at Nvidia as indicative of diversion or circumvention activity."
While the firm's research didn't directly refer to a romantic relationship between Jensen Huang and Alice Huang, it included several photos and video stills showing them together at various events.

"Nvidia CEO Huang has walked alongside Megaspeed at every step, and seems to have a close relationship with Megaspeed's Alice Huang," Culper wrote in the May 13 social media thread. "They partied together in June 2024 — same month as the Apex/Alibaba pledge, then dined together in May 2025 — just after U.S. trade restrictions."

Culper, which is named after the American Revolution-era Culper Spy Ring that reported on the movement of British forces, has in recent days posted about the allegations that emerged this week about Jensen Huang's ties to Megaspeed and Alice Huang.  "We wrote about this in May," the group noted on Nov. 5.
When Culper published its report on May 13, Nvidia's stock was trading at $225.83 per share. Between that date and the close of trading on Tuesday, the shares have shed 25% of their value.
"Everyone was just mocking us, and now everyone is singing our praises," Lamarco told the New York Times in a recent interview.

title: Microsoft data center brings "a kind of boom" amid AI pushback
summary: Microsoft outlines the pledges it makes to data center communities as industry tries to sway public opinion on AI.
story: Opposition to data centers helped propel Democratic candidates who pledged to stall new construction to victory in last week's midterm elections. More than half of voters said artificial intelligence and data centers were a significant factor in their votes, according to a CBS News exit poll.
But one town says it has benefited from data centers, despite the pushback growing across the nation.
For 20 years, Microsoft has operated its Columbia Data Center in Quincy, Washington, where Mayor Paul Worley told CBS News its presence has created "a kind of boom" for the area.
Additional tax revenue from the project has funded a new high school and hospital, and helped improve other critical services, he said.
Microsoft president Brad Smith told CBS News about the pledge it makes to the communities where it builds and operates data centers.

"Basically, we will put the community first," he said. "We will not do anything that will increase the electricity rates of our neighbors. We'll ensure that we replenish more water, we put more water back into the community than we use."
He also highlighted the role data centers play in powering every action we take on our phones and other connected devices.
"Every time we tap on our phone, it's connecting through an app, it's pulling data from something like this," he said.
The industry, he said, needs to better inform opponents of data centers about the essential services the facilities enable.
"They're part of daily life, just like electricity is," Smith said.
Why Quincy?
The nearby Columbia River provides hydropower that has led seven additional companies to choose Quincy for their data centers.
It hasn't been entirely smooth. To accommodate the roughly two dozen data centers that have entered the area over the past two decades, some residents have been asked to vacate their homes.
Electricity rates per kilowatt-hour have risen by roughly 55% over the past 20 years, according to the Grant County public utility.

While that marks a steep increase, it's still lower than the average increases in national and state electricity rates over the same period. In Washington, electricity rates rose 107% over the same time period. Nationwide, they rose 66%.
Smith said he believes it is the company's "fundamental responsibility" to manage the industry's growth and the impact on residents' rising utility costs.
"You can't make the challenges go away, but you can be broad-minded, you can [be] committed, and you can take steps to manage growth well," he said.

For example, Microsoft pledges to replenish or give communities back more water than it uses. It also commits to paying for its own electricity and ensuring that its usage doesn't increase neighbors' utility rates, Smith said. He added that the facilities create local jobs, too, though many are temporary construction positions.
According to Microsoft, the company employs roughly 700 people, or almost 9% of Quincy's roughly 8,000 residents.
Questions to ask
Yale professor of environmental and energy economics Kenneth Gillingham outlined the questions communities should ask data center developers before they come to town.
They include:
What type of technology is it using for cooling?How large will it be?How is it going to generate its electricity?
What type of technology is it using for cooling?
How large will it be?
How is it going to generate its electricity?
Meanwhile, Microsoft's Smith has a clear message for Americans who say they don't want data centers in their backyards.

"Give us a chance to talk through what we want to do, and give us a chance to prove that we can do this in a way that will put the community first," he said. "We have to persuade you. But the people that you've elected, they're the ones who are gonna make a decision, not us."

title: Hoax bomb threats affect at least 20 European flights within hours
summary: At least 20 flights in Europe deal with bomb threats, adding to what one expert calls an unusual level of hoaxes in a short time period, suggesting "a very deliberate act."
story: Paris — At least 20 commercial flights in Europe had to deal with bomb threats Thursday, with at least one being diverted to a military base in France. While authorities have reported no explosives discovered on any of the jets, and they all appeared to be hoaxes, Thursday's incidents add to a fast-growing number of journeys hit by similar threats this week, which one expert said suggested a "very deliberate act."

British authorities dismissed threats to about seven flights earlier this week as hoaxes, but the number of impacted journeys soared to at least 27 on Thursday, meaning significant disruption for thousands of passengers and raising concerns about a possible coordinated effort to impact travel on the continent.
At least two more European flights, along with several Irish and British news outlets, got similar threats on Friday.

No authorities have confirmed a link between any of the threats, but Spanish Foreign Minister Jose Manuel Albares said Friday that Europe appeared to be facing "hybrid aggression and a form of psychological warfare."

David Kaminski-Morrow, Air Transport Editor with FlightGlobal, declined to speculate on who might be behind the threats to commercial flights this week, but he noted that "we currently live in a time of political aggression in regions including Europe, and it's a pretty effective tactic if someone is looking to cause disruption."

"The cluster of threats seems unusual, but it's hard to determine the extent to which they might be organized," he said, noting that "the publicity alone could spur further threats unrelated to earlier ones."

Kaminski-Morrow noted that, under an international aviation convention in place for more than 80 years, the pilot in command of a flight has the final authority over its safety, "and airlines always take threats to safety seriously. The business consequences alone of not doing so, even if the threat is proven to be a hoax, would be prohibitive – and you can imagine the cost if it turned out to be genuine."
The flights impacted on Thursday included:

A flight from Ireland to Italy that was diverted to an air base in western France Thursday because of a bomb threat, according to French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu's office. The flight landed safely and all 151 passengers and six crew members deplaned safely, while military bomb defusal teams got to work examining the plane. Flight tracking sites showed that the Aer Lingus Dublin-Rome flight turning sharply off its trajectory as it approached, and then making several loops before heading toward Evreux.A Finnair flight from Helsinki to Rome was escorted to the Italian capital by a fighter jet and was checked by bomb disposal experts, according to Italy's national news agency ANSA. Rome's Leonardo Da Vinci Airport stopped flights for 30 minutes. A second Finnair flight from Helsinki, operated by Jettime, landed as normal in Vienna, Reuters reported. A Wizz Air flight from Milan Malpensa airport to Warsaw was re-routed to Vienna after receiving a threat, also according to ANSA. A second Wizz Air flight bound for Bucharest also landed safely after being targeted, Reuters reported Romanian intelligence as saying.A flight operated by Polish Airlines LOT flying from Warsaw to Brussels landed safely in Brussels airport following security warnings. According to a statement from the airline, authorities carried out an onboard security check after it landed and "no hazardous or suspicious items were found."Three other planes, all Ryanair flights bound for Sofia, made emergency landings in Bulgaria Thursday after indications of potential danger on board, according to Bulgarian National Television (BNT). Flights from Madrid and Copenhagen landed at Vasil Levski Airport in the capital, and one from London Stansted diverted to an airport in Plovdiv. The Bulgarian transport ministry confirmed to CBS News that no explosives or suspicious items were found on any of the planes.Officials in Prague said threats were issued against four flights headed to the Czech capital Thursday. Czech police said on X that all four planes landed safely and no explosives or suspicious devices were discovered. Two of the planes were EasyJet flights, one from Newcastle, England, to Prague, and another from Glasgow, Scotland, to Prague, the airline confirmed. The other flights originated in Dublin and Athens.Italy's national news agency ANSA reported two more flights, scheduled to land Thursday at Milan's Malpensa Airport, landed safely after receiving "bomb alerts." Neither of the flights were diverted. They were Aegean Airlines flight A3552, which departed from Thessaloniki in Greece, and Ryanair flight FR8953, which arrived from Porto, Portugal. Explosives technicians were inspecting the aircraft, ANSA said.  Three flights were affected by bomb threats Thursday at Madrid's Barajas airport, the airport's management confirmed to CBS News in a statement, adding that after "relevant checks carried out by the security forces, the threats were ruled out." Iberia Airlines flights 668 from Milan and 658 from Rome were affected, and the third plane was Air Europa flight 1027, which was impacted before departing for Paris in the morning. An Air Serbia plane flying from Belgrade to Bucharest, Romania, landed safely at its destination Thursday after receiving a bomb threat, Serbia's national air carrier said in a statement shared with CBS News. Air Serbia said "following a bomb threat reported to the relevant authorities at Bucharest Airport during" the flight, the aircraft landed and security agencies found no threatening materials, "after which the aircraft was returned to regular operational service." A second Aegean flight, A3860 from Athens to Vienna, also landed safely at its intended destination Thursday after receiving a bomb threat, the airline said, adding that no threats were found. Greek Deputy Foreign Minister Tasos Chatzivasileiou said in a Facebook post he was on the flight. "Upon landing here, we were informed of a possible bomb on the plane that carried us. The inspection by the Austrian authorities showed that there was nothing," he wrote. "All is well, everyone is safe."

A flight from Ireland to Italy that was diverted to an air base in western France Thursday because of a bomb threat, according to French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu's office. The flight landed safely and all 151 passengers and six crew members deplaned safely, while military bomb defusal teams got to work examining the plane. Flight tracking sites showed that the Aer Lingus Dublin-Rome flight turning sharply off its trajectory as it approached, and then making several loops before heading toward Evreux.

A Finnair flight from Helsinki to Rome was escorted to the Italian capital by a fighter jet and was checked by bomb disposal experts, according to Italy's national news agency ANSA. Rome's Leonardo Da Vinci Airport stopped flights for 30 minutes. A second Finnair flight from Helsinki, operated by Jettime, landed as normal in Vienna, Reuters reported.

A Wizz Air flight from Milan Malpensa airport to Warsaw was re-routed to Vienna after receiving a threat, also according to ANSA. A second Wizz Air flight bound for Bucharest also landed safely after being targeted, Reuters reported Romanian intelligence as saying.

A flight operated by Polish Airlines LOT flying from Warsaw to Brussels landed safely in Brussels airport following security warnings. According to a statement from the airline, authorities carried out an onboard security check after it landed and "no hazardous or suspicious items were found."

Three other planes, all Ryanair flights bound for Sofia, made emergency landings in Bulgaria Thursday after indications of potential danger on board, according to Bulgarian National Television (BNT). Flights from Madrid and Copenhagen landed at Vasil Levski Airport in the capital, and one from London Stansted diverted to an airport in Plovdiv. The Bulgarian transport ministry confirmed to CBS News that no explosives or suspicious items were found on any of the planes.

Officials in Prague said threats were issued against four flights headed to the Czech capital Thursday. Czech police said on X that all four planes landed safely and no explosives or suspicious devices were discovered. Two of the planes were EasyJet flights, one from Newcastle, England, to Prague, and another from Glasgow, Scotland, to Prague, the airline confirmed. The other flights originated in Dublin and Athens.

Italy's national news agency ANSA reported two more flights, scheduled to land Thursday at Milan's Malpensa Airport, landed safely after receiving "bomb alerts." Neither of the flights were diverted. They were Aegean Airlines flight A3552, which departed from Thessaloniki in Greece, and Ryanair flight FR8953, which arrived from Porto, Portugal. Explosives technicians were inspecting the aircraft, ANSA said.

Three flights were affected by bomb threats Thursday at Madrid's Barajas airport, the airport's management confirmed to CBS News in a statement, adding that after "relevant checks carried out by the security forces, the threats were ruled out." Iberia Airlines flights 668 from Milan and 658 from Rome were affected, and the third plane was Air Europa flight 1027, which was impacted before departing for Paris in the morning.

An Air Serbia plane flying from Belgrade to Bucharest, Romania, landed safely at its destination Thursday after receiving a bomb threat, Serbia's national air carrier said in a statement shared with CBS News. Air Serbia said "following a bomb threat reported to the relevant authorities at Bucharest Airport during" the flight, the aircraft landed and security agencies found no threatening materials, "after which the aircraft was returned to regular operational service."

A second Aegean flight, A3860 from Athens to Vienna, also landed safely at its intended destination Thursday after receiving a bomb threat, the airline said, adding that no threats were found. Greek Deputy Foreign Minister Tasos Chatzivasileiou said in a Facebook post he was on the flight. "Upon landing here, we were informed of a possible bomb on the plane that carried us. The inspection by the Austrian authorities showed that there was nothing," he wrote. "All is well, everyone is safe."

The threats to commercial airliners Thursday came after at least seven other flights across Europe received bomb threats this week that prompted aircraft searches, diversions and in at least one other case an escort by an Italian fighter jet.
Some of the threats have been sent to airlines by email, but the nature of all of the messages has not been confirmed.
Hoaxes, but on an unusual scale

The British government described the incidents in a statement on Tuesday as hoaxes and stressed that the U.K. had "one of the most robust aviation security systems in the world, with well-tested processes for dealing with any potential threats, as well as malicious hoax threats, like those we've seen today," according to CBS News' partner network BBC.
Air transport security expert Paul Mason told BBC that threats to passenger planes "don't happen that frequently," making this week's spate of incidents "unusual."

"It sounds like they've been made in a credible manner across a broad range of airlines," Mason told the BBC's Radio 5 Live show. "That would suggest to me that it's been a very deliberate act by a typical actor rather than a load of coincidental, malicious calls."
"There are a lot of processes" that airline crew members and ground staff go through "to validate the credibility of the threat," he said.

While no individual or group has claimed responsibility for any of this week's threats, and no government or security official has pointed the finger at any, the incidents come amid rising concern in Europe about state actors, chiefly Russia and Iran, orchestrating low-level sabotage operations to undermine security on the continent.
The growing "hybrid warfare" battlefield

In October, the head of Britain's domestic spy agency MI5, Sir Ken McCallum, said security threats facing the U.K. and Europe were evolving, with malicious actors attacking not only things owned and controlled by the government, but also "aiming at people, businesses, communities."
"Russia remains aggressor number one," McCallum said.

"The Russian military and intelligence services are once again escalating their attempts at hybrid warfare," McCallum warned, adding that Moscow was "being careful to stay below the NATO Article 5 threshold" with its actions, which would trigger the alliance's collective defense principle.
"It'd be foolish for them to cross" that line, he said, and so far Russia was sticking to "tactics that stop short — though sometimes not much short — of conventional conflict."

Poland launched a large-scale security operation this week along its border with the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad as the Polish prime minister said suspicious activity was seen on the Russian side, and that the fast security response may have prevented a "serious provocation."

The flight threats also come amid a wave of cyberattacks targeting European grocery store chains' refrigerators and freezers, and even French blood banks. The hacks have forced thousands of pounds of food to be discarded in several countries, but French authorities said security systems prevented the loss of any blood stored in cooling units.
France later accused a cyber unit of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps of being behind the hacks on commercial refrigeration units across the country.
Experts told CBS News earlier this year that Russia and Iran were stepping up efforts to recruit sometimes-unwitting criminals to carry out sabotage attacks, often for small payouts.
MI5 boss McCallum, in his remarks last month, said Iran in particular was "using criminal proxies to try to intimidate oppositionists, Iranian media organizations, and Israeli sites" across Europe.

McCallum noted in particular "a wave of arson and sabotage incidents targeting Jewish communities in the U.K. and other European nations," but said Iran was also targeting "harder targets, like military sites."

Many of these attacks were claimed by a group calling itself Harakat Ashab al-Yamin al-Islamiya (HAYI), or the Islamic Movement of the Companions of the Right, which U.K. authorities have sanctioned and said is tied directly to the elite Quds Force of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, which Britain considers a terrorist organization.

A CBS News investigation in March found the group appeared to have links to Iran, and a member said it would "keep threatening U.S. and Israeli interests worldwide until we've avenged every child in Gaza, Iran, Lebanon, and the resistance nations … We urge people to stay away from Zionist and American interests and individuals to keep themselves safe."

Barry Andrews, an Irish Member of the European Parliament, referred to the diverted Aer Lingus flight to Rome on Thursday in a social media post, saying: "This after several hybrid threats and attacks across Europe, and ahead of the major European summit in #Dublin next week. Does anyone still deny Ireland faces serious security threats?"

title: Company under scrutiny for ties to Nvidia and China
summary: The unusual global footprint of Megaspeed, a major buyer of Nvidia's powerful AI computer chips, is fueling questions about whether it's a front for the Chinese government.
story: The unusual global footprint of Megaspeed International, the Singapore-based company at the center of the Nvidia Chinese spy scandal, is fueling questions about whether it's a front for the Chinese government.

One of Megaspeed's leaders is Alice Huang, the woman with whom Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was having an affair, and who is suspected by U.S. intelligence of being an asset of China's Ministry of State Security. In the past three years, Megaspeed, formerly a gaming company, has been one of Nvidia's biggest foreign customers, purchasing nearly $5 billion in AI chips and advanced hardware, The New York Times first reported.

And yet Megaspeed's corporate headquarters sat practically empty, according to The Straits Times, an English-language newspaper in Singapore. Questions have also been raised about its outposts in Australia and Malaysia.

Published reports in recent days revealed that the company listed a newspaper vendor as the director of its Australian subsidiary, and one of its Malaysia offices consisted of a dilapidated storefront outside Kuala Lumpur. Yet another Malaysia office was tucked into a shopping mall.

Megaspeed began as an offshoot of a China-based gaming firm and grew into a juggernaut by gaining access to restricted Nvidia AI computer chips. U.S. investigators say that Alice Huang used her contacts in the industry and a series of shell companies to gain access to 240,000 chips banned for export into China. Now it is being probed in both the U.S. and Singapore for allegedly smuggling those chips into China.
President Trump said this week the FBI is also investigating romantic and business ties between Nvidia's chief executive Jensen Huang and Alice Huang (who are not related).

Earlier this week, Jensen Huang, who is married, apologized for the affair in a statement to Nvidia's employees. The company launched an independent investigation of the matter, and an Nvidia shareholder filed a class action lawsuit Tuesday alleging that Huang concealed a relationship with Alice Huang and misled shareholders about national security concerns raised by the relationship.
Nvidia's board said it had no reason to believe that the company's secrets or national security were compromised.
"The Board prioritizes U.S. national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of NVIDIA and its shareholders," its statement said.

China expert Jacqueline Deal said that Nvidia's advanced AI chips could have ended up with the Chinese military. Deal, who is an adviser to State Armor, a nonprofit that studies global security threats, told CBS News, "If allegations are true, who will be fired? Nvidia has a compliance team that may have failed utterly."

She also questioned the effectiveness of the U.S. Commerce Department, which has jurisdiction over export controls that may have been bypassed, potentially giving the Chinese military access to the world's most advanced chips.
Here's what we now know about Megaspeed:

It is a major Nvidia customer. Megaspeed and its Malaysian affiliate, Speedmatrix, purchased $4.8 billion of Nvidia's advanced artificial intelligence equipment and processors over the last three years.
In 2025, Megaspeed International faced an investigation by Singapore police for alleged breaches of local laws, but no details have emerged about the probe, according to The Straits Times.
The company grew rapidly.

"Megaspeed International is a premier business partner of NVIDIA, strategically positioned in the Asia Pacific region," according to its LinkedIn profile, which claims it has between 201 and 500 employees. Three years ago it listed between two and 10 employees, according to the South China Morning Post.

Megaspeed International did not reply to a request for comment. It posted an "official statement" on its website addressing what it called "misleading information" and "incorrect insinuations" accusing it of involvement in illegal chip transfers.

"We want to be absolutely clear over the past six months our company has undergone multiple on-site inspections and reviews by key institutions, including the Bureau of Industry and Security of the US Commerce Department, the Ministry of Investment, Trade and Industry of Malaysia and NVIDIA," said the message, which also appeared on the company's LinkedIn page.
"These thorough investigations have confirmed that there has been no evidence of any violations concerning the illicit transfer of chips or any illegal activities," the company said.

Megaspeed was originally incorporated in 2015 under the name 7Road International, a subsidiary of a Chinese developer of popular video games and mobile apps based in Shenzhen, China, according to corporate filings.
Huang Le Limited, a shell company in the British Virgin Islands, acquired 7Road International in March 2023. Huang Le is the Chinese name of Alice Huang.
That same month, 7Road International was renamed Megaspeed International, and Huang became its managing director. The company also launched a subsidiary called Speedmatrix.

By the end of October 2023, Huang and another Megaspeed director, Cang Yang, resigned from the company after it was bought up by a firm called Swiftdata, whose director is based in China, documents show.

But there's some indication Huang may still be affiliated with the company. Culper Research, an activist short-selling firm, published a 40-page report on Nvidia in May that cited Megaspeed employees who said Huang was still running the company.

The report also raised some concern about Jensen Huang's relationship with Megaspeed and Alice Huang, stating, "Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has not only vouched for Megaspeed, but seems to have quite literally walked alongside Megaspeed at every step, while maintaining an uncomfortably close relationship with Megaspeed's Alice Huang, a Chinese national."
Megaspeed lists its headquarters office address on the seventh floor of the Ocean Financial Centre in Singapore, a glass office tower in Singapore's central business district.

When the Straits Times and The New York Times visited the Singapore offices around the same time late last year, they found little or no staff working. The Straits Times said the door was locked, and the Times found just two people in its office on a workday.

Megaspeed has an Australian subsidiary on the 10th floor of a commercial and retail tower in the heart of Sydney's central business district. Forty other businesses are on the same floor, and space in the building can be rented for as little as $17 per day, Australia's ABC News reported. Corporate filings name Shanghai-born Kai Kang, a 29-year-old newspaper vendor, as the director, according to Australian news reports. But Kang's newsstand is in Northern Victoria, over 400 miles from Sydney. Kang's father told Australia's ABC News this week that he had never heard of Megaspeed.

title: Enrolling in Medicare? Here's what to consider before Dec. 7.
summary: Medicare open enrollment, which runs from Oct.15 to Dec. 7, gives people a chance to change their health coverage. Here's what to know.
story: The Medicare open enrollment window has arrived, giving millions of seniors across the U.S. the chance to revisit their coverage choices. Even if you're happy with your plan, experts say it's still worth exploring your options.

Health plans change every year, meaning people could see updates to premium costs, prescription drug coverage and available providers in their network. New plans also come online, expanding the already broad list of coverage options.
"There's really no one who can't benefit from at least taking some time to take a look," Alex Cottrill, senior policy analyst with KFF's program on Medicare policy, told CBS News.

People enrolled in Medicare Advantage or a Part D prescription drug plan typically receive an "Annual Notice of Change" in September outlining any updates to their coverage, according to Medicare.gov, the government website for the program.

"Pay attention to those notices, and frankly, even if you don't receive an annual notice of change, you still want to review your current plan and make sure that it is the right one for you," said Jessica Rivkin, vice president of Reliance Medicare Advisors, an insurance agency that helps people enroll in Medicare Advantage plans.
Americans now have less than a month to make their Medicare choices, with open enrollment set to close Dec. 7. Here are some considerations as you navigate the process.
Choosing between Medicare and Medicare Advantage

One of the biggest decisions people face when enrolling in Medicare is whether to choose traditional Medicare or Medicare Advantage, a comprehensive plan in which private insurers are paid to manage your care.

By contrast, people who enroll in regular Medicare plans must separately select a Medicare Part D prescription drug plan and Medigap, private insurance people can layer on top of their plan to help defray out-of-pocket costs.
"You only have to pick one plan rather than having these modular options that you have in traditional Medicare," Cottrill said of Medicare Advantage.

A drawback of Medicare Advantage is its more stringent requirements. Some plans only allow you to visit in-network providers. If the plan does allow you to go out-of-network, you may face steeper cost-sharing rates, Cottrill said.

"That's a consideration for people who have either a preferred provider that they really want to stay with ...or people who have really complex health needs where they have to see maybe a lot of different specialists, or they need a very specialized type of care," he told CBS News.

For those leaning towards Medicare Advantage, Cottrill said it's worth double-checking that the providers you need are covered by the plan. People should also consider what it might mean for the Medigap coverage, he said.

If people enroll in Medicare Advantage and later switch back to traditional Medicare, they may face higher premiums due to their age or pre-existing conditions, compared to someone who enrolled in Medigap through a traditional Medicare plan from the outset, according to Cottrill.
Comparing plans

Cottrill said a good place to start is Plan Finder, a tool offered by the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) that allows people to compare Medicare Advantage plans and Part D plans and to see whether providers are in-network.
The website, however, is just a jumping-off point. People should still conduct independent research to ensure their coverage needs are met, Cottrill said.
"If something is really crucial for somebody's care, they should reach out to the plan directly, talk to their provider directly and don't just rely on the website," he told CBS News.

For general information, people can contact 1-800-Medicare, the CMS-run helpline for Medicare information, or consult their State Health Insurance Assistance Program, which provides more tailored counseling.

Seniors may also consider working with a broker who can help sort through the different options. But they should keep in mind that these people may have a financial stake in their decision, Cottrill said.
"They're often paid on commission," he said. "That's not to say that they can't be helpful, but it's worth getting a second opinion from someone who doesn't have that financial stake."
Enrollment timeline
The plan you choose during open enrollment takes effect on Jan. 1, 2027, for the full calendar year.

While the deadline to make changes is Dec. 7, some people have some extra wiggle room. Medicare Advantage enrollees can switch to another Medicare Advantage plan from Jan. 1 through March 31 during a separate enrollment period.

"You can also choose to leave your Medicare Advantage plan and return to original Medicare during that same time frame, with the option of also enrolling in a Part D plan," said Will Kinkead, associate vice president of Reliance Medicare Advisors.
Some people also qualify for special enrollment periods if they move or lose access to their current health care coverage and need to make a change.

As people research Medicare plan options, they may find they need to chase down details from their providers or consult with an expert. So it's important not to wait until the last minute to start the enrollment process, Rivkin said.

"This can be a really complicated decision for some people, so take the time to get comfortable with the questions you have, what you need in 2027, and make sure that you're getting all of your needs covered," she told CBS News.

title: Hotter-than-expected inflation raises chances of Fed rate hike
summary: Inflation rose at a monthly pace of 0.4%, hotter than economists had forecast and raising expectations that the Federal Reserve will increase interest rates in December.
story: Consumer prices rose more than economists expected in October on a monthly basis, offering little relief to Americans grappling with high living costs.
The Consumer Price Index, which tracks changes in prices over time, rose at a monthly pace of 0.4%, the Labor Department reported on Tuesday.
The Labor Department did not report a year-over-year inflation rate for October 2026 because the 2025 government shutdown left it without October 2025 consumer price data for comparison.
By the numbers
October's monthly inflation increase cooled from September, when headline inflation rose 0.6% on a monthly basis.
However, the figure was hotter than expected, with economists polled by FactSet predicting October prices would rise 0.3% month-over-month.
The October inflation data is one of the first snapshots of the economy following the midterm elections, which underscored Americans' frustration with high prices.

"Today's CPI report suggests underlying inflation remains more persistent than the Fed would like," Andrew Davis, head of investment strategy at Bryn Mawr Trust, said in an email. "While headline inflation moderated from September, core prices rose 0.3% for the third consecutive month, indicating that underlying price pressures have yet to meaningfully ease."

While inflation in recent months has largely been driven by higher energy prices, October's data shows that costs for other types of goods and products are also rising. Shelter costs, which rose 0.3% in October, accounted for more than 30% of the monthly all-items increase, the Labor Department said.
Food prices also accelerated, rising at a monthly pace of 0.5% last month after remaining flat in September, the data shows.
Energy prices
Energy costs, which have surged due to the Iran war, contributed less to the monthly rise in inflation than in past reports. Energy prices rose 0.7% in October, compared to 5.2% in September.
Gas prices have been falling for weeks as stations switch to cheaper winter blend and people pull back from summer travel.
Global oil costs, the main factor in setting prices at the pump, have also dipped amid hopes that the midterm elections could open the door to a deal between the U.S. and Iran to end the war.
On Tuesday, the national average prices for gasoline sank below $4 a gallon for the first time in nearly four months, according to AAA.
Core inflation, which excludes volatile energy and food prices, rose 0.3% in October, in line with September but slightly above economists' forecasts.

Josh Hirt, senior U.S. economist for Vanguard, said in an email that elevated energy prices have led to a "longer-lasting shock pass-through" to core inflation, prompting the investment company to raise its year-end 2026 core inflation forecast to 3.2%.
What this means for interest rates
Wall Street analysts predicted that firmer inflation last month will spur the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates when it meets in December.

"This is the last look at CPI inflation the Fed will get before its December meeting, and it most likely seals the deal on a rate hike to close the year," James McCann, senior economist for investment strategy at Edward Jones, said in an email. The bigger question, he added, is whether the central bank will raise its benchmark rate by a quarter or half of a percentage point.
After the latest inflation data, CME Group's FedWatch tool showed an 85% chance the Fed would raise rates by 0.25 percentage points in December and a 15% chance of a 0.50 percentage-point hike.
The central bank stayed on the sidelines at its October meeting, although two Federal Open Market Committee members voted in favor of a rate hike.

During a conference in London on Tuesday, Christopher Waller, a member of the Fed's Board of Governors, said policymakers should consider a 0.50 percentage-point increase when the central bank meets on Dec. 8-9.
"Hiking only 25 basis points would put our credibility at risk, a risk I am not eager to take," he said.

title: What stores are open and closed for Veterans Day 2026?
summary: See which businesses are operating and the deals they are offering veterans and active military members for their service.
story: Veterans Day, observed annually on November 11, honors Americans who have served in the U.S. military. Formerly known as "Armistice Day," the holiday was celebrated nationally for the first time in 1919 at the direction of former U.S. President Woodrow Wilson. Congress officially recognized it as a federal holiday in 1926.

This year, Veterans Day falls on a Wednesday. Read on to see which businesses are operating and some of the deals they are offering veterans and active military members to thank them for their service.
What stores are open on Veterans Day?
Most major grocery chains are open, including Aldi, Food Lion, Publix, Stop & Shop, Trader Joe's, Wegmans and Whole Foods.
Walgreens confirmed that it will welcome customers on Wednesday. CVS locations will be open, although some stores and pharmacies may have reduced hours, a spokesperson said.
Other retailers are also generally open on Veterans Day, although it's a good idea to check your local retailer's hours ahead of time.
Is Costco open?
The big-box store will be open for Veterans Day, according to its holiday schedule.
Is Target open?
Target stores will be open on Wednesday during regular business hours, a company spokesperson confirmed.
Is Walmart open?
Walmart stores will operate during their regular hours on Veterans Day, according to a company spokesperson.
Are banks open or closed today?
Major banks such as Bank of America, Chase and TD Bank are closed on Wednesday, as Veterans Day is a federal holiday observed by the Federal Reserve.
Americans can still visit ATMs and check online account activity. However, the holiday may affect the time it takes to process certain transactions, Bank of America says on its website.
Is the post office open or closed on Veterans Day?
All post office locations will be closed, and mail will not be delivered on Wednesday due to the federal holiday. Mailing and retail services will resume on Thursday, Nov. 12, according to the USPS.
Is the stock market open?

The U.S. stock market will be open, with Veterans Day not among the holidays observed by the New York Stock Exchange and Nasdaq. The next time markets will be closed is on Thanksgiving, which falls on Thursday, Nov. 26.
Veterans Day deals at retailers, grocery stores and restaurants
Here are a few discounts and freebies retailers are offering on Tuesday to veterans and active service members. Be prepared to show your military identification.

title: Nvidia's trillion-dollar bind: Can it afford to lose Jensen Huang?
summary: Other CEOs have been ousted over undisclosed relationships, but Nvidia's inquiry shines a spotlight on how closely the chipmaker's fortunes are tied to its co-founder.
story: Nvidia's board of directors faces a trillion-dollar dilemma: Can the chipmaker afford to part with its storied co-founder and CEO, now embroiled in multiple investigations into his affair with an alleged Chinese spy?

In recent years, several high-profile CEOs have been ousted after their relationships with employees and customers came under scrutiny, including former McDonald's CEO Steve Easterbrook and Kohl's CEO Ashley Buchanan. But none is so closely identified with their companies as Huang. Over more than three decades, he has led Nvidia as it grew into one of the world's most valuable companies, with many investors viewing him as equally critical to the company's success as Elon Musk is to SpaceX or Steve Jobs was to Apple.

Huang is facing serious challenges, including an independent inquiry by Nvidia's board into the affair, a shareholder lawsuit and questions from lawmakers. Heightening the stakes are allegations that Huang had a close relationship with a former female executive at an Nvidia customer who is also suspected of working with China's intelligence agency.
$450 billion drop
Nvidia shareholders have been spooked by the disclosure, with the company's shares shedding 10% of their value — or about $450 billion — in the last two trading days alone.
"It exposes how dependent the company is on this one person," Shiva Rajgopal, a Columbia Business School professor who studies corporate governance, told CBS News.
He added, "This is like asking if something happens to Elon Musk, what happens to Tesla and SpaceX's valuations? If something happens to Jensen Huang, what happens to Nvidia's valuation?"

Yorkville Ives tech analyst Dan Ives estimated in a research note that Nvidia could lose as much as 30% of its valuation if Huang is removed from his role, while noting that for now most investors expect the executive to retain his post at the company.

"At the end of the day, there is only one Jensen, and Nvidia will dramatically change as a company if he is no longer CEO, with a major negative ripple impact across the tech industry and AI Revolution," Ives said.
"Do not proceed"

Corporate governance experts said Huang's alleged relationship with Alice Huang — a Chinese executive linked to the Singapore-based data center company Megaspeed, which buys AI chips from Nvidia — appears to violate Nvidia's code of conduct. That policy highlights that personal relationships could create a conflict of interest for Nvidia, while Huang himself specifies in the code of conduct that the company's workers have a responsibility "to maintain high ethical standards."

Nvidia's code also instructs employees to ask themselves whether they could defend an action if it were made public on social media or known to colleagues. If not, the policy states, "do not proceed."

Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment about whether Huang had violated any company rules. In a message to company employees on Sunday, Huang admitted, "I was unfaithful to my wife," and he apologized for hurting her and their two children, both of whom also work at Nvidia. "There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry," he wrote.

But Huang's conduct "is definitely a violation," said Jay Aldebert, chief growth officer at International Services, a consulting firm that advises small and midsize businesses on issues including governance. "How he handled it based on their code of conduct is where you're going to see continued issues."
Still, while Huang may have violated company rules, he may be given more leeway than other employees due to his importance to Nvidia, governance experts said.

"This is an outlier — I don't remember a case like this," Columbia's Rajgopal said. "This company is so important to the U.S. in terms of AI, especially with China and other powers. So even if there is a violation of the code of conduct, if I were the chair of the board, I would not dismiss him."

Nvidia's 11-person board includes Huang, although the other board members are considered independent, according to a company regulatory filing. They include California Institute of Technology professor John Dabiri and former Taco Bell International president Melissa Lora. All board members except Dabiri have experience in corporate governance, the filing states.
Nvidia board members should demonstrate their independence by hiring a law firm to help with the investigation, and immediately develop a succession plan for Huang, Rajgopal said.
A common issue for Nvidia and other big tech companies led by their founders is that they are often run "like a family affair," he added.
"These are effectively run like family private companies, but they are mega-cap public companies where most of the capital comes from the public," Rajgopal said. "There is a duty above and beyond."
Succession planning

Huang has said he has more than 60 direct reports in a corporate structure that keeps him at the center of decision-making at Nvidia. As various investigations ramp up, the succession plan to replace him remains unclear, heightening pressure on the board, experts said.

"The Nvidia board is between a rock and a hard spot. They have almost no good options — Jensen is Nvidia," said David Yoffie, a professor at Harvard Business School. "And if he has done something wrong and he needs to be removed, and they have no successors, that's a terrible outcome."

If Huang resigns or is removed by the board, speculation on possible replacements has turned to figures including Nvidia co-founder Chris Malachowsky, who is a senior technology executive at the company, and Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress.
Nvidia employs more than 40,000 people worldwide, and there are "lots of other great leaders" within the company, said Bob O'Donnell, president, founder and chief analyst at TECHnalysis Research.

"I think it's important that the company starts to let some of these other folks come out as spokespeople so people feel trust, they feel good about Nvidia and their future, even without Jensen," O'Donnell said, although he said he does not think Huang will leave his post.
