title: The U.S. officials who have been targeted or threatened by Iran
summary: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent is the latest U.S. official to be threatened or targeted by Iran, but he is far from the first.
story: Washington — Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent is the latest U.S. official to be threatened or targeted by Iran, but he is far from the first.
The Iranian regime has been implicated in various plots to target top U.S. officials since 2020, when President Trump ordered the killing of Iranian general Qassem Soleimani.

Threats against Americans have ramped up since the start of the ongoing war with Iran. Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton warned in October that Iran has "substantially increased efforts to target U.S. personnel" abroad, with plots to kill Americans reaching "advanced stages" in the Middle East and other countries.
Bessent relocated from his home in the Washington, D.C., area to a military base following a series of Iranian threats against his life, CBS News confirmed Wednesday.
The threats against other officials have been detailed in court records and news reports. Here are other U.S. officials Iran has targeted or threatened in recent years:
President Trump

The U.S. charged Pakistani national Asif Merchant with plotting a murder-for-hire scheme targeting U.S. officials in documents unsealed in August 2024. Court documents didn't name his targets, but multiple sources familiar with the investigation told CBS News that President Trump was one of them. Merchant was convicted of terrorism and murder for hire in March of this year.

The Justice Department said Merchant was a trained operative of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, and that he admitted the IRGC sent him to the U.S. to arrange for political assassinations and to steal documents. Prosecutors said law enforcement thwarted his efforts and he was arrested.
At the time, then-Attorney General Pam Bondi said Merchant "landed on American soil hoping to kill President Trump — instead, he was met with the might of American law enforcement."

The Justice Department separately charged Farhad Shakeri, an alleged IRGC asset living in Tehran, in November 2024. Prosecutors said Shakeri told FBI agents that an IRGC official had directed him the month before to come up with a plan to kill Mr. Trump. If he couldn't do it in time, the official said, the IRGC would wait until after the election, believing Mr. Trump would lose and be easier to target. Shakeri told investigators he didn't intend to propose a plan within the IRGC's timeframe. He remains at large and is believed to be in Iran.

Mr. Trump also secretly switched planes before returning from a summit in Turkey over the summer, a move that came after intelligence warnings about an Iranian plot to target Air Force One with a surface-to-air missile. Mr. Trump later told reporters, "I have a lot of threats."
Former President Joe Biden
Merchant testified that his IRGC handler told him to "maybe have somebody murdered."
"He did not tell me exactly who it is, but he told me — he named three people: Donald Trump, Joe Biden and Nikki Haley," Merchant testified in court.

The Biden administration lifted some sanctions on Iranian officials as it tried to renegotiate and revive the defunct Obama-era Iran nuclear deal. But Biden imposed sanctions on Iran when those negotiations failed.
Nikki Haley, former U.S. ambassador to the U.N.
Nikki Haley, the U.S. ambassador to the United Nations during Mr. Trump's first term in office, has long been critical of Iran.
In an appearance on the "Build or Break" podcast this week, Haley talked about Merchant and the IRGC plot.

"The IRGC, the Iranian regime, paid a Pakistani businessman money to do it," Haley said. "And that's the reason why I'm so adamant about Iran is, they are targeting Americans on American soil. They have tried to get Trump multiple times. We should not be giving them even a breath when they're doing things like that. But that's because I speak out against the regime. We have to be truth tellers."
John Bolton, Trump's former national security adviser

John Bolton, Mr. Trump's national security adviser during his first term, has also received threats from the Iranian government. Bolton has long been a hard-liner on Iran, and urged Mr. Trump to increase pressure on Iran during the president's first term.

In 2022, Shahram Poursafi, a member of the IRGC, was charged with plotting Bolton's murder, the Justice Department announced at the time. The Justice Department said the plot was "likely in retaliation" for Soleimani's death.
But Poursafi was never caught. He remains wanted by the FBI. The bureau added him to its list of Most Wanted Terrorists just this week.
Mike Pompeo, former secretary of state
Mike Pompeo was Mr. Trump's secretary of state when Soleimani was killed, and led the Trump administration's so-called "maximum pressure" campaign against Iran.
Pompeo said Soleimani was "actively plotting" to take actions "that would have put dozens, if not hundreds, of American lives at risk" when the U.S. killed him.
Sources told CBS News in 2022 that Pompeo was another target of the IRGC plot against Bolton.
Brian Hook, former U.S. special representative for Iran
As the U.S. special representative for Iran, Brian Hook also led the "maximum pressure" campaign against Iran, drawing Iran's ire.

In 2022, CBS News reviewed State Department threat assessments sent to Congress citing a "serious and credible threat" to the lives of both Pompeo and Hook. The State Department was paying millions of dollars a month to protect Pompeo and Hook with 24-hour security amid threats from Iran, according to a report obtained by CBS News at the time.
The Trump administration revoked the security detail for both Hook and Pompeo in Mr. Trump's first week back in office in January 2025.
Mark Esper, former defense secretary
Mark Esper, Mr. Trump's defense secretary from 2019 to 2020, told CBS News in 2022 the government provided him "protection 24/7" when he left the federal government because of threats from Iran.
Robert O'Brien, Trump's former national security adviser

Robert O'Brien was Mr. Trump's fourth and final national security adviser during Mr. Trump's first term in office. "60 Minutes" reported that O'Brien received taxpayer-funded security protection due to potential threats from Iran, long after he left his government position.

title: Petition for new Epstein files bill gets enough support for vote
summary: GOP Rep. Thomas Massie launched a discharge petition over the summer to circumvent leadership and force a vote on the Epstein Files Transparency Act II.
story: Washington — Republican Rep. Thomas Massie has secured enough support to force a vote on legislation that would compel the release of the remaining Justice Department files related to Jeffrey Epstein.
Massie launched a discharge petition over the summer to circumvent leadership and force a vote on the bill, known as the Epstein Files Transparency Act II.

In order to bring the legislation to the floor, the discharge petition needs 218 signatures. It hit that threshold Wednesday. Four Republicans, including Massie, and all Democrats have added their names. The other Republicans who signed on are Reps. Brian Fitzgerald of Pennsylvania, Nancy Mace and Ralph Norman, both of South Carolina.

The underlying bill allows members of Congress, state attorneys general and Epstein survivors to sue the Justice Department for failing to comply with the Epstein Transparency Act, which was signed into law nearly a year ago after lawmakers pulled a similar maneuver.
Massie has accused the Justice Department of "flagrantly and consistently" ignoring the disclosure requirements of the law.

"The Department of Justice continues to unlawfully withhold over 3 million Epstein files that should be released to the public," he said in a July statement. "In addition, the DOJ is unlawfully maintaining heavy redactions on the files it is releasing."

title: Congressional Democrats target Trump's "pardon industrial complex"
summary: A new bill would bring scrutiny to pardons tied to the president's allies and donors, but legal experts say it would likely run up against the Constitution.
story: House Democrats who lead the "End Corruption Caucus" have introduced legislation seeking to rein in what has been called the "pardon economy" that has flourished during President Trump's second term, according to lawmakers and a copy of the bill.

On Wednesday, Reps. Mike Levin and Jason Crow unveiled the Abuse of the Pardon Prevention Act — a measure aimed at acts of clemency that raise possible conflicts of interest or could involve favors for the president's allies and donors.
America has "a pardon industrial complex" where "you literally, for the highest dollar amount, can go and buy a pardon," Levin said in an exclusive interview with CBS News this week.
"That is not how the Founders intended for this to work," said Levin, a California Democrat. "The pardon power is intended to be used in cases of justice and mercy."

The bill stands almost no chance of surviving Mr. Trump's veto pen, yet it offers an early look at how Democrats, fresh off sweeping midterm wins, may use their new majorities to scrutinize Mr. Trump's freewheeling use of the pardon power. A CBS News investigation found wealthy defendants have hired lobbyists and lawyers tied to Mr. Trump to press their cases with the White House. About 70% of his second-term clemency actions have bypassed the Justice Department's pardon office — 92% counting Jan. 6 defendants.

The White House has said that anyone "spending money to lobby for pardons is foolishly wasting their money" and that there is "a robust pardon review process" that includes White House counsel, the Justice Department, White House "pardon czar" Alice Johnson, and Mr. Trump "as the final decider."
"President Trump performs his constitutional duties in an ethically sound manner and to suggest so otherwise is either ill-informed or malicious," said White House Counsel Will Scharf.

The bill would direct the Justice Department's inspector general to investigate pardons that raise potential conflicts of interest. As examples, Levin pointed to Mr. Trump's pardon of Binance founder Changpeng Zhao, who pleaded guilty in 2023 to failing to maintain an effective anti-money-laundering program, and reports that Alina Habba Mildon, while a Justice Department adviser, struck a deal with the family of a Venezuelan billionaire who was pardoned weeks later. Habba Mildon has denied any role in the pardon.

The bill would also make explicit that the president and vice president can be prosecuted for trading pardons for something of value, and require pardon recipients to disclose gifts to projects tied to the president, such as his library or the White House ballroom. And it would ban self-pardons — a power Mr. Trump told "60 Minutes" this month he believes he has, though he said he doesn't expect to use it.

"No president should be able to abuse the pardon power," Crow, a Colorado Democrat, told CBS News. "We cannot accept a two-tiered system of justice that treats the wealthy and well-connected differently than working people."
Beyond the political obstacles, the bill could face legal hurdles, according to legal experts who spoke with CBS News.

Three legal experts — former Justice Department pardon attorney-adviser Samuel Morison, Josh Blackman of South Texas College of Law Houston and Brian Kalt of Michigan State University — all said key parts of the bill would likely run up against the president's constitutional pardon power.

"The constitutional remedy for the misuse of the pardon power is impeachment and removal," Morison said. "What you can't do is exactly what this bill tries to do, which is regulate the exercise of the pardon power through legislation."

Blackman said the bill's "conflict of interest" standard is so broad it could make almost any controversial pardon the subject of a criminal investigation, from Mr. Trump's actions to former President Joe Biden's pardon of his son Hunter. "I think they're trying to criminalize the political process," he said.

Kalt, who has studied the idea of presidential self-pardons, says the bill's ban on them is "purely symbolic." If the president has that power, he said, "a statute cannot take it away," and if he doesn't, "the statute changes nothing."
Levin maintained there is a path to legislate the pardon power without undermining the Constitution.

"If anything is running afoul of the Constitution, it's the way this president is misusing the pardon power," he said. "We're going to use our power of the purse to ensure the independent investigation of every department."
He said his concerns extend beyond Mr. Trump.

"I disagreed with certain pardons during the Biden years, and I disagreed with certain pardons during the Clinton years," Levin said. "Every member of Congress that actually cares about the institution, cares about checks and balances, cares about the rule of law, cares about the Constitution of the United States, will want to see reforms to the pardon power."
This story published first on CBS News at 12:36 p.m. on Nov. 11, 2026.

title: Biden targeted by protesters after event in Ireland
summary: Protesters targeted former President Joe Biden and members of his family as they exited an event in Dublin, Ireland, on Tuesday night.
story: Washington — Protesters targeted former President Joe Biden and members of his family as they exited an event in Dublin, Ireland, on Tuesday night, leading to several arrests.

Biden, former first lady Jill Biden and son Hunter Biden were at Trinity College, where Hunter Biden was being honored with a gold medal by the College Historical Society. The protests outside escalated as the Bidens were leaving, according to university spokesperson Catherine O'Mahony.

According to the University Times, the protesters chanted "shame on you" and "Genocide Joe" at the Bidens. Photos showed protesters waving a Palestinian flag. O'Mahony said the Bidens left without incident.

Irish police An Garda Síochána confirmed that three people were arrested Tuesday night in connection with the protests, and a man in his 50s has been charged. The other two men, one in his 30s and another a late teen, were released, police said.
The event coincided with publicity around Biden's new memoir, "Promise Me, America," which is set to be published next week.
On Wednesday morning, People published an on-camera interview with the former president, his first since leaving the White House.

Biden was diagnosed with Stage 4 prostate cancer shortly after leaving office, and it has spread to his bones. He told People that he would not have run for reelection had he been diagnosed while president.

"I would've not gone forward, because I don't think an 80-year-old man with cancer should be running for [president]," Biden said. "But that wasn't the case ... I believe that on an objective basis, I was the best-equipped person to do the job."
Biden writes in his book that it's a "cynical twist" that many Americans believe he hid his cancer diagnosis, when he says he was not diagnosed until May 2025.

"We let the public know when I found out, when I knew what was going on," Biden told People. "I think it's important for a national leader, as president, to let people know they go through some of the very same things that a lot of American people are going through ... I wasn't hiding it at all."

Hunter Biden told CBS News partner BBC News earlier this year that his father's cancer has "spread, metastasized into his bones and further," adding "it's very painful and it's very debilitating in many respects."

title: Did GOP efforts to redistrict the House turn into a dummymander?
summary: Republicans undertook a historic effort to redraw several states' congressional districts mid-decade in an attempt to maintain control of the House.
story: Republicans undertook a historic effort to redraw several states' congressional districts mid-decade in an attempt to maintain control of the House. That effort was rebuffed on Tuesday night as the GOP was on track to lose many of the districts it tried to gerrymander last year.

There were several reasons that states undertook what had previously been a rare practice of mid-decade redistricting. Republican efforts started when President Trump ordered Texas lawmakers to redraw their map to net up to five seats for the GOP.
But despite the all-out effort, Democrats won control of the House on Tuesday, with CBS News estimating Democrats could end up with 251 to 268 House seats.

With the House decisively swinging toward Democrats and Democrats undertaking measures in a few states to counter the GOP's efforts, Republicans are faced with the possibility of having created a so-called "dummymander," a situation in which a party tries to gerrymander, but ends up benefiting the other party.
Here's a state-by-state breakdown of how the redistricting efforts panned out:
Texas

Texas Republicans went into Election Day controlling 24 seats, while Democrats controlled 13 seats and there was one seat in a GOP-leaning district that was vacant. In redrawing the map, Republicans sought to emphasize Mr. Trump's gains in South Texas to win five more seats.
Republicans won 24 seats and Democrats won 14 seats in the midterms, making Texas a dummymander.
Ohio

A commission comprising mainly Republicans hand-picked by GOP lawmakers redrew Ohio's map to net two more seats for their party. Republicans heavily targeted longtime Democratic Rep. Marcy Kaptur's district in the northern part of the state and Rep. Greg Landsman's Cincinnati-area district.

Heading into Tuesday night, Ohio Republicans controlled 10 seats and Democrats controlled five. Eight Democrats, including Kaptur and Landsman, won Tuesday night. Republicans only won seven districts, making Ohio a dummymander.
North Carolina
Although North Carolina has a Democratic governor, Republican lawmakers have a veto-proof majority in the statehouse and pushed through a new map that attempted to oust Democratic Rep. Don Davis.

North Carolina Republicans controlled 10 House seats going into Election Day, while Democrats controlled four, including Davis' district. As of a week after the election, nine Democrats had won — including Davis — while one Republican won reelection and CBS News estimated four districts with GOP incumbents were toss-ups, making the state a dummymander.
Louisiana

Louisiana lawmakers redrew their districts after the Supreme Court ruled in June that compliance with Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act could not justify the state's use of race in redrawing its House district lines.

Louisiana went into Election Day with four House seats controlled by Republicans and two controlled by Democrats. The new map aimed to eliminate one of the majority-Black districts that currently has Democratic representatives — the 6th District.

As of Monday, Republicans had won three districts, while Democrats had won one. CBS News estimates Louisiana's 5th and 6th Districts will go to runoffs. If Democrats ultimately win either of those districts, the redistricting effort will not have netted the GOP any extra seats.
Alabama

After the same Supreme Court decision, Alabama Republicans sought to eliminate the state's two majority-Black districts, both of which are represented by Democrats. Both incumbents won reelection on Tuesday, so Republicans did not net any more than the five they already controlled.
Tennessee
Tennessee lawmakers also redrew their map after that Supreme Court decision to target the lone Democratic district in Memphis.

Going into Election Day, Republicans had eight seats, and Democrats had one. As of Monday, Republicans had won eight seats, including the newly drawn 9th District that includes Memphis, and one seat is estimated as a toss-up. If Democrats win the remaining toss-up race, the state's House delegation will remain the same.
Florida
Led by Florida's Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis, GOP lawmakers redrew their map to net up to four more seats for their party.

Heading into Election Day, Republicans controlled 20 seats and Democrats controlled eight. In the midterms, both parties won the same number of seats as before, with Democrats winning in all four districts that Republicans had targeted, meaning the redistricting effort did not net the GOP any seats.
Missouri

Missouri's GOP-led legislature last year redrew its map to make one of the state's two Democratic-held districts more friendly to Republicans. But the map's legality was challenged, and a state court ruled the map could not be used unless it was approved by voters. The Supreme Court three times blocked Missouri from using the new map, leaving the 2022 congressional districts in place for Tuesday's election.
Heading into Election Day, Republicans controlled six districts while Democrats held two. Democrats flipped another district, giving them three seats to the Republicans' five.
Indiana

Mr. Trump had also pushed lawmakers in Indiana to pass a map that would edge out the state's two Democratic lawmakers and make it a 9-0 Republican delegation. Despite pressure from Mr. Trump, the GOP-led state Senate rejected the new map.
Using the same boundaries as the last two cycles, Democrats held on to their two seats and flipped a third, making the state's representation 6-3.
South Carolina

South Carolina Republicans also sought to redraw their map after the Supreme Court decision in an effort to edge out powerful Democratic Rep. Jim Clyburn and make the state's representation 7-0 for Republicans. But the measure failed in the state Senate, and Clyburn won reelection on Tuesday. Democrats have picked up one other seat, and another race is considered a toss-up.
California

In response to Texas' redistricting efforts, California's Democratic Gov. Gavin Newsom put forth a ballot measure to redraw the map to gain five seats for Democrats, which was decisively approved by voters.

Heading into Election Day, Democrats held 43 districts and Republicans held nine. A week after the election, Democrats won in 46 districts, while CBS News estimates another two are likely Democratic. Republicans have won three districts, and one is a toss-up.
Since Democrats picked up seats in California, it is a successful gerrymander for Democrats.
Utah

A judge in 2025 rejected Utah's congressional map that favored Republicans in all four districts, and then a district court rejected the redistricting map selected by the GOP-controlled legislature and instead selected a map that would create a Democratic-leaning congressional district in Salt Lake City.
Under the new map, Democrat Ben McAdams won the 1st District in Salt Lake City by 47 points.
Virginia

Virginia voters decisively approved a ballot measure in April to redraw the congressional map to favor Democrats in 10 districts and Republicans in one. But the map was thrown out by the Virginia Supreme Court, putting back in place the map drawn in 2021.
Heading into Tuesday, Democrats held six seats while Republicans held five. Using the same boundaries as the past two cycles, Democrats won eight seats and Republicans won three.
Maryland

Maryland's state constitution requires that congressional districts be compact and connected, and Democratic Gov. Wes Moore and other Democratic lawmakers championed a ballot initiative to remove those restraints on redistricting.
The ballot initiative, known as Question 3, passed by 20 points on Tuesday, so Democrats are likely to redraw their map now to edge out their sole GOP representative.

title: Judge denies motion to dismiss Trump's defamation case against BBC
summary: A U.S. federal judge has denied a motion to dismiss President Trump's defamation case against the BBC, allowing the case to proceed.
story: A U.S. federal judge denied a motion on Tuesday to dismiss President Trump's defamation case against the BBC, allowing the case to proceed.

In December 2025, Mr. Trump filed a $10 billion lawsuit against the British Broadcasting Corporation, the U.K.'s public broadcaster, over a documentary that featured edited parts of the speech he delivered on Jan. 6, 2021, as his supporters massed around the U.S. Capitol in what would become an assault on the heart of the government.

In the lawsuit, filed in the Southern District of Florida, attorneys for Mr. Trump accuse the BBC of publishing a "false, defamatory, deceptive, disparaging, inflammatory and malicious depiction" of him in an episode of the network's "Panorama" program, which aired a week before the 2024 election.

The case alleges the BBC "intentionally and maliciously sought to fully mislead its viewers" by "splicing together" two clips of the same speech Mr. Trump gave to supporters before the riots began. The president's legal team claims the two clips were 55 minutes apart and the edit omitted "his statement calling for peace."
On Tuesday, Judge Jeffrey Kuntz denied the BBC's motion to dismiss the defamation case, effectively allowing it to proceed.
"Whether President Trump can prove these claims and establish he sustained damages at summary judgment or trial is left for another day," Kuntz wrote in his decision.
Mr. Trump hailed the decision as "A Huge Victory against Fake News BBC, a terrible abuser of the truth," in a post on his Truth Social platform.
A spokesperson for the BBC, quoted by the network's news division, said: "We are surprised by this decision but respect the Court's authority and note the case will now proceed to the next stage."
"We remain confident in our position and will continue to respond through the proper legal process," the spokesperson added.

On Oct. 22, a federal judge in Miami said Mr. Trump must sit for a deposition with BBC lawyers by Dec. 11, warning that if he did not, he could face penalties, including possible dismissal of the lawsuit, unless the period for the president and the network to collect information in the case is extended.

Mr. Trump had been due to sit for a deposition in October, but his lawyers told the BBC in late September that he would no longer be available to answer questions, "due to other matters of national importance."
The president has said he will be available for the deposition in the second or third week of January, according to the BBC.
In November 2025, the BBC issued an apology to the president over the editing of his speech as featured in the documentary.

"BBC Chair Samir Shah has separately sent a personal letter to the White House making clear to President Trump that he and the Corporation are sorry for the edit of the President's speech on 6 January 2021, which featured in the programme," the BBC Press Office said in its statement at the time.
"While the BBC sincerely regrets the manner in which the video clip was edited, we strongly disagree there is a basis for a defamation claim," the press office added.

title: Trump's judicial confirmations to face resistance in Dem-controlled Senate
summary: A Democratic-controlled Senate is unlikely to help President Trump and Republicans continue their push to remake the federal judiciary in the next two years.
story: Washington — After seeing success in reshaping the federal judiciary in his first term and the initial two years of his second administration, President Trump and Republicans' campaign to shift the courts to the right could be coming to an end with Democrats poised to take control of the Senate next year.

During his first term in office, Mr. Trump successfully put more than 230 judges on the federal bench, including three justices on the Supreme Court, remaking the judicial branch for decades. So far during his second term, the Senate has confirmed 57 of the president's judicial picks. In total, Trump nominees make up about one-third of active federal judges.

But Democrats are now poised to control at least 54 Senate seats, and as many as 56 depending on the outcome of races in Mississippi and Alaska, making it unlikely that Mr. Trump will fill many more vacancies on the U.S. district and appeals courts.

"No one, or nearly no one, is going to get confirmed, so what he does in terms of nominating people, we'll see," Ed Whelan, a distinguished senior fellow at the Ethics and Public Policy Center and former law clerk to the late Justice Antonin Scalia, told CBS News.

There are currently 28 vacancies on the federal courts and another 15 seats that will open up in the coming weeks and months. So far, the president has formally sent to the Senate 16 nominees for those existing and future vacancies, though it's possible he submits more names for consideration before the current Congress finishes its work. Mr. Trump announced on Truth Social earlier Tuesday three more nominees to district courts in Texas and South Carolina.

The GOP-led Senate Judiciary Committee is moving quickly to advance those picks before control of the upper chamber changes hands. It voted to advance four of the president's district court candidates and held confirmation hearings for four other judicial nominees Tuesday.

The panel is expected to hold more confirmation hearings next week, a break from committee practice of holding those proceedings every other week, according to a source familiar with the panel's workings.

Republicans are violating "numerous longstanding standards in a desperate attempt to confirm more than 30 qualified loyalists to lifetime appointments before Democrats take the majority," Sen. Dick Durbin, the top Democrat on the Judiciary Committee, said Tuesday.

Durbin raised concerns about two of Mr. Trump's latest picks to serve as federal judges in Texas: James Sullivan, who lost his bid for reelection to the Texas Supreme Court last week, and T. Elliot Gaiser, the head of the Justice Department's Office of Legal Counsel whose only tie to Texas is a one-year clerkship for a judge on the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 5th Circuit.

The Judiciary panel received information from Sullivan after he lost his campaign for Texas Supreme Court justice last week and from Gaiser on Nov. 8, before the president announced his intent to nominate each man, according to the source. Both are slated to appear before senators for confirmation hearings next week.

"There are many things we still can do, and I hope we'll use them. And one of them is not to expedite nominees who have not been carefully vetted," Durbin said. "I hope we don't accept that as a standard in this committee."

But Sen. Chuck Grassley, an Iowa Republican who chairs the Judiciary Committee, pushed back on Durbin's claim that he is departing from its typical practices. He argued that there are no committee rules about how quickly it can move to hold confirmation hearings or when those proceedings are held, and said chairs have discretion to set the panel's schedule.
"Historically, this committee has shortened timelines when circumstances warrant it," he said.
In anticipation of Democratic control of the upper chamber, Republicans are expected to make judicial nominees a focus of the lame-duck period.
"The priority is going to be getting the judges across the finish line," Senate Majority Leader John Thune told reporters Monday.
But seats on the federal bench that remain open come the end of the current Congress are likely to remain unfilled for at least the next two years.

"For the past two years, we've seen Trump seeking to stack our courts — district courts, circuit courts — with loyalists to him and not to the Constitution, and I think he's going to try to continue to do that," Rachel Rossi, president of the Alliance for Justice, a progressive judicial advocacy group, said. "In this moment, when Trump has clearly created this litmus test that there must be loyalty to him and not the Constitution, it's hard to see how Democrats can support nominees going forward."

It is not unprecedented in the Senate for the party in control to stymie the nominations of a president in the opposing party. During the final two years of former President Barack Obama's administration, when Republicans held the Senate majority, just 20 of his nominees to the district and appeals courts were confirmed. Obama's final judicial confirmation came six months before the end of his second term. Among the candidates that did not get a vote from the GOP-led Senate was Merrick Garland, who was nominated to replace Scalia on the Supreme Court following his death in February 2016.

"What we've seen is the federal courts being stacked with extremists and loyalists, and now Democrats have the power to stop the reshaping of our courts in a very dangerous direction," Rossi said. "I think there's increasing visibility on what judges mean and what these lifetime seats mean, and the hope is that Democrats use their power and stand against any further reshaping of our judiciary."

Of the 43 current and future vacancies, Mr. Trump has not yet announced candidates for more than half of those seats. Many of those are in states that will be represented by either two Democratic senators or one Republican and one Democratic senator next year.
Democrats could work with the White House to find consensus on candidates to serve on the district courts in their states, but it's unclear whether there is an appetite from either side to do so.

"Republicans on the Senate Judiciary Committee and the Trump administration have gutted the committee's oversight and confirmation authority," Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse, a Rhode Island Democrat who is expected to lead the panel next year, said in a statement. "There needs to be accountability for years of Republican bad behavior, and a hard reset on the nominations process next Congress."

Democrats' rout of Republicans in last week's midterm elections also makes it unlikely a Supreme Court justice appointed by a GOP president steps down in the final two years of Mr. Trump's term, given that a successor would likely not clear the Senate.

The president made a significant impact on the nation's highest court, appointing three of the nine justices. Among those was Justice Amy Coney Barrett, who filled Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg's seat following her death in September 2020, during Mr. Trump's first term.

Justices Clarence Thomas, 78, and Samuel Alito, 76, are the two oldest members of the high court, but Alito told The Wall Street Journal in August, "I'm here for another term." Alito also told CBS News chief legal correspondent Jan Crawford last month that while he considered retirement earlier this year, he feels he can still make a contribution to the Supreme Court.

With neither justice expected to step down during the lame-duck session, it could be several years before there is both a GOP president and Senate in place to confirm their potential successors on the Supreme Court, raising concerns among conservatives that a Democratic president and Senate could fill the seats of the influential conservative justices.
"Trump has managed to put in jeopardy his biggest achievement," Whelan said.

title: Kennedy family members join lawsuit to block Trump's arch
summary: Several members of the Kennedy family have joined the legal battle to prevent President Trump from building a large triumphal arch near Arlington National Cemetery.
story: Several members of the Kennedy family have joined the legal battle to prevent President Trump from building a large triumphal arch near Arlington National Cemetery.

In court filings Tuesday, nine members of the famous family — including several children and grandchildren of Attorney General Robert F. Kennedy and Sen. Ted Kennedy — argued the 250-foot-tall arch would block the sightlines of the Kennedy family's gravesites and the "Eternal Flame" commemorating President John F. Kennedy. The three brothers — Robert F. Kennedy, Ted Kennedy and John F. Kennedy — are buried at Arlington.
The family members wrote that the project will "permanently cast a shadow over the graves of servicemen and women who made the ultimate sacrifice for this country, including the Kennedy Gravesites."

The family members are seeking to intervene as plaintiffs in a lawsuit opposing the arch from the city of Washington, D.C., and the Commonwealth of Virginia. Several Vietnam War veterans are also suing the Trump administration over the arch.

"Americans from every corner of the country visit Arlington to honor those who served and sacrificed for our nation," Rory Kennedy and Maxwell Kennedy said in a statement on the lawsuit. "A towering arch casting shadows across the graves of our father, mother, and uncles, as well as the graves of so many who have served our country, would also cast a shadow over our democratic principles, undermining the safeguards established by our elected representatives to protect this hallowed ground for generations to come."
The Justice Department had no comment on the filing when reached by CBS News.

The proposed arch — slated for a traffic circle across the Potomac River from the Lincoln Memorial in D.C. — is part of a slew of construction projects in and around the nation's capital that Mr. Trump has personally pushed for. His administration says the arch would commemorate 250 years of American independence. It sought to break ground as early as this month.

But the project has drawn stiff pushback from local officials, congressional Democrats and some veterans and others with an interest in Arlington National Cemetery. Opponents argue the Trump administration did not follow the proper legal processes to build the arch, and warn it would block the sightlines between the cemetery and the Lincoln Memorial.

The National Capital Planning Commission, which is stacked with Trump allies, voted to approve plans for the arch last week. But U.S. District Judge Tanya Chutkan quickly blocked the government from starting any "construction-related activity" for 14 days, finding the plan is likely illegal. The plaintiffs have asked the court for a longer-term injunction.
The government has argued the proposed arch does not violate the law, and says the plaintiffs don't have standing to sue over the project.

White House spokesman Davis Ingle said in a statement last week: "We are confident we will be fully vindicated as this litigation proceeds and look forward to seeing the completion of this magnificent Arch — a tribute to 250 years of American greatness."

It isn't the first time that members of the Kennedy family have criticized Mr. Trump's architectural overhaul of the D.C. area. Several family members have also spoken out against Mr. Trump's attempts to add his name to the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts, including the niece and grandnephew of the center's namesake, Kerry Kennedy and Joe Kennedy III, both of whom are seeking to join the triumphal arch lawsuit as plaintiffs.

Kerry Kennedy's brother, Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., told CBS News earlier this year he was not involved in the proposed name change for the performing arts center and did not recommend against the move.
"Of course, I understand it, but I have bigger fish to fry," he said when asked about the pushback from some of his relatives.

title: Top lawyer in DOJ's Civil Division is latest in string of resignations
summary: The top lawyer in the Justice Department's Civil Division resigned on Monday, marking the latest in a wave of departures since the midterm elections.
story: The top lawyer in the Justice Department's Civil Division resigned on Monday, marking the latest in a wave of departures since Democrats won back control of both the House and Senate in the midterm elections.

Brett Shumate, the assistant attorney general of the Civil Division, tendered his resignation on Monday, leaving behind a division that has been struggling to keep pace as it defends the federal government in a flurry of lawsuits since President Trump took office.

Attorney General Todd Blanche, in a statement on X, praised Shumate for pursuing "important affirmative litigation to challenge sanctuary policies" and for "delivering key wins in lawsuits against local policies that endangered federal law enforcement."

Last week, the assistant attorneys general for the Justice Department's national security and civil rights divisions also departed, leaving those key offices without Senate-confirmed leadership as well. The U.S. Attorney in the Southern District of Florida who was overseeing the so-called "grand conspiracy" investigation into Obama and Biden-era intelligence officials also departed last week.

Blanche said Tuesday that Craig Trainor will serve as acting assistant attorney general for the Civil Rights Division. He currently serves in a Senate-confirmed leadership role at the Department of Housing and Urban Development.

T. Elliot Gaiser, the assistant attorney general for the DOJ's Office of Legal Counsel, meanwhile, is being considered by Mr. Trump to be nominated to serve as a judge for the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Texas, according to a Senate aide, who confirmed that the Justice Department had submitted his nomination paperwork. The Office of Legal Counsel offers legal advice to the executive branch, issuing opinions on thorny legal questions.

Gaiser has authored controversial legal opinions such as the classified legal justification for the U.S. military's boat strikes targeting suspected drug traffickers. He does not appear to have any direct ties to Texas, apart from a one-year clerkship in the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit.

Shumate, a former partner at the law firm Jones Day, was widely seen by attorneys in the Civil Division as a reasonable and "decent" leader at a time when chaos has descended on the Justice Department, forcing it to adopt often novel or controversial legal positions to defend the government from hundreds of lawsuits.
He also served in the Civil Division during Mr. Trump's first term in office.

Under Shumate's leadership, the department has fought to defend countless firings of career civil servants, many of whom received no explanation other than a letter citing Article II of the U.S. Constitution.

It has also defended controversial and aggressive mass deportation policies, as well as a number of controversial renovation projects that Mr. Trump has personally directed, including efforts to tear down the White House's East Wing and replace it with a ballroom, and overhauls of the Kennedy Center and the East Potomac Golf Course.

The Civil Division has also had to contend with a flood of habeas corpus petitions this year from detained immigrants, after a Justice Department-run immigration court made a sweeping determination that the government could essentially detain a large swath of immigrants indefinitely while their removal proceedings are pending.
Lawyers in the Civil Division were taken by surprise by the abrupt and unexpected nature of Shumate's resignation, which was effective immediately, sources told CBS News.
His departure comes after Stephen Miller late last week was named as White House chief of staff, replacing Susie Wiles.

One source familiar with the matter told CBS News that Miller has been critical of Shumate in the past and believes he is not aggressive enough, and this was a factor in Shumate's decision to step down.

title: Incumbent Maria Elvira Salazar wins Florida's District 27 race, CBS News projects
summary: Incumbent Rep. Maria Elvira Salazar has won the closely watched race for Florida's 27th Congressional District, CBS News projects.
story: Incumbent Republican Rep. Maria Elvira Salazar won the closely watched race for Florida's 27th Congressional District, CBS News has projected, after a machine recount was automatically triggered under Florida law.
Salazar — who has held the Miami-area seat since 2021 — claimed victory on social media after the machine recount ended, with margins about the same as before.
The new totals were announced Tuesday evening, and neither Salazar nor Democrat Eliott Rodriguez gained much ground, with a 1,086-vote margin between the two after the recount.
In her post, Salazar said the recount is over, and her victory has been reaffirmed.
"My deepest gratitude to every Republican, Democrat, and Independent who placed their trust in me. This victory sends a message beyond Miami: We prevailed because we LISTENED," she said.
By CBS News Miami's count, the recount lasted about 18 hours. The state will certify the results Nov. 17.
The legal battle surrounding the recount

Rodriguez had tried to get the Miami-Dade County Supervisor of Elections Alina Garcia removed from the canvassing board, saying she appeared to favor Salazar. However, a judge dismissed the motion and allowed the recount to proceed on Monday morning.
Garcia made a statement to CBS News Miami's partners at the Miami Herald on Election Night that the judge called "stupid," but it wasn't enough to remove an elected official from her position.
Garcia told the Herald reporter that Salazar had won the election "with or without a recount." She later clarified that it was possible Rodriguez could win, but not probable.
The judge on Monday morning said that an elected official should not be removed from her position based on the most explosive portion of an incomplete statement.
Rodriguez's attorney also pointed out that Garcia posted a photo with Elvira Salazar, but the judge said it was an older photo and was essentially irrelevant.

"It was very obvious that the judge saw the statement to the press was egregious," attorney Juan-Carlos Planas said. "In fact, the judge even called the statement stupid which I think was a big thing. Listen, we knew it was going to be a stretch and the judge stated that this was us making sure that a line was drawn. These are the people that we hold to preserve our democracy."

Salazar's attorney didn't want to speak on camera after the judge's ruling on Monday morning, but instead sent a statement to CBS News Miami saying, in part, "We stand firmly behind Alina Garcia and condemn the political attacks aimed at undermining the confidence in her office. A legally required recount is an opportunity to verify the results, not an excuse to vilify election officials because your candidate is losing."
After reading the recount results, Garcia addressed the lawsuit.

"There are no conflicts of interest," she said. "The lawsuit recently filed against me was without merit and was immediately dismissed by a federal judge. I respect the judicial process, and I will continue to perform my responsibilities in accordance with the law."
Florida's 27th Congressional District was closely watched
Florida's 27th Congressional District includes parts of the city of Miami, Coral Gables, Kendall, Key Biscayne, Pinecrest and surrounding communities.

Salazar, a former television journalist, has represented the Miami-Dade County-based district in the United States Congress for three terms. She first won the seat in 2020 after defeating Democratic U.S. Rep. Donna Shalala.

Rodriguez, a former CBS News Miami anchor, entered politics in 2026 after a nearly five-decade career in television news. He spent 25 years at CBS News Miami before leaving the station and announcing his campaign for Congress in March.
Both candidates secured their party nominations in August.
Salazar defeated attorney V. Michael Arias in the Republican primary, while Rodriguez defeated former federal prosecutor Robin Peguero for the Democratic nomination.
The district was widely seen as GOP-leaning, with Salazar winning reelection by 20 points two years ago, but Democrats had hoped to make the race competitive.

The contest drew nationwide attention in September, after Salazar taped a campaign ad warning President Trump that many of the Hispanic voters who propelled him to the White House in 2024 "feel betrayed" by immigration enforcement campaigns that have "gone too far."

title: House blocks Massie's effort to impeach Hegseth
summary: GOP Rep. Thomas Massie said Monday he would not bring up another resolution to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.
story: Washington — The House on Tuesday blocked an effort led by GOP Rep. Thomas Massie to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, largely over the war with Iran.

The House voted 211 to 204 to refer the resolution to the Judiciary Committee, effectively killing it. Massie was the lone Republican to vote with all Democrats against it. Though Republicans have been frustrated with Hegseth's handling of the war that has stretched into its ninth month, many did not think his conduct rose to the level of impeachment.

"I wasn't surprised, but I was disappointed," Massie said after the vote. "My diagnosis of Congress is these people know what to do. They just can't bring themselves to do it, even when it would benefit them politically."

Massie, a Kentucky Republican, said Monday he would not bring up another resolution to impeach Hegseth. He is retiring in early January after losing his primary earlier this year. Democrats could still force the issue, especially when they retake control of both chambers in January.
"This is not the end of it. It's just the beginning," House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, a New York Democrat, said following the vote.
Massie said Tuesday he planned to force a vote on a war powers resolution.
"We're going to see all these Republicans who said, 'Oh, we lost this election because of the war,' will they still vote for it?" Massie said.

The impeachment resolution accused Hegseth of abusing his office by launching the Iran war without congressional approval, ignoring laws designed to minimize civilian casualties, directing extrajudicial killings for the Pentagon's boat strikes in the Caribbean, directing the kidnapping of Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro and retaliating against Democratic Sen. Mark Kelly, among other allegations.
In a news conference Tuesday morning, Hegseth denounced the impeachment effort, calling it a "farce" and "political spectacle."
"None of these are high crimes or misdemeanors," Hegseth argued. "They're partisan policy disagreements from people who want to politicize our military."
President Trump mocked the impeachment effort, saying it "miserably FAILED!"
Seven Republicans and 11 Democrats missed the vote.

Only two Cabinet secretaries in U.S. history have been impeached. Secretary of War William Belknap was impeached over a corruption scandal in 1876, and Homeland Security Secretary Alejandro Mayorkas was impeached over his handling of the southern border in 2024. Belknap was acquitted by the Senate, while Mayorkas had his charges dismissed.

title: Why did Hegseth face an impeachment push? Inside the 8 articles
summary: The impeachment resolution focuses on Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth's involvement in some of the most controversial episodes of President Trump's second term.
story: Washington — Republican Rep. Thomas Massie of Kentucky led a now-blocked push to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, accusing the Pentagon chief of a broad range of high crimes and misdemeanors stemming from his conduct in office.

The charges were laid out in a 34-page impeachment resolution spanning eight articles that Massie introduced in the lower chamber on Monday. The House voted late Tuesday to refer the resolution to a committee, effectively killing it, after no Republicans joined Massie and House Democrats.

The impeachment resolution focused on Hegseth's involvement in some of the most controversial episodes of President Trump's second term: the war with Iran, boat strikes in the Caribbean, an attack on an Iranian school and the capture of then-Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro. Hegseth called the resolution "political spectacle" in a press conference Tuesday morning.
Here's a look at what the impeachment resolution says:
Article I: Starting the Iran war without authorization
The first impeachment article accuses Hegseth of following illegal orders to begin the Iran war.

"Secretary Hegseth directed and caused United States Armed Forces to be introduced into hostilities against the Islamic Republic of Iran," even though Congress had not declared war or authorized an attack, Article I says.
The resolution says Hegseth acted in violation of the War Powers Resolution of 1973, which allows the president to use force without congressional authorization in narrow circumstances.

"Secretary Hegseth nevertheless knowingly executed and implemented the order to commence such hostilities, employing the powers, personnel, weapons, and resources of the Department of Defense to initiate military action against another sovereign nation," the article says.
Article II: Ignoring Congress to continue the war
The second article accuses Hegseth of ignoring a resolution approved by both chambers of Congress that directed the administration to end the Iran war.

The House and Senate both approved a measure in June that ordered the administration to "remove United States Armed Forces from hostilities against the Islamic Republic of Iran," the mechanism for Congress to force the executive branch to end fighting under the War Powers Resolution. Massie's impeachment article notes that this was "the first successful passage of such a legislative vehicle by both chambers of Congress" in history.

"In response, and without lawful cause or excuse, Secretary Hegseth continued to direct United States Armed Forces into hostilities with the Islamic Republic of Iran on June 26, 2026, and continues to do so," the impeachment article says.
At the time, the administration argued that "hostilities" with Iran had already ended, rendering the war powers measure inapplicable.
Article III: Ignoring the War Powers Resolution's deadline
The War Powers Resolution says the executive branch must end the use of force within 60 days if Congress has not approved the operation, with another 30-day window to safely remove troops.

Mr. Trump notified Congress of the hostilities on March 2, so the 60-day window closed on May 1. In a letter that day, the administration told Congress that "hostilities" had "terminated." Hegseth told senators: "We are in a ceasefire right now, which in our understanding means the 60-day clock pauses or stops in a ceasefire."

But the impeachment resolution says Hegseth kept directing hostilities after that deadline and beyond June 1, "the date on which even the maximum possible additional 30-day withdrawal period would have expired."

The article also says Hegseth directed U.S. forces to keep fighting "in a manner calculated not to terminate the unauthorized use of such forces and bring about their prompt removal, but rather to continue prosecuting the war to pursue additional military objectives not authorized by Congress."
Article IV: Ignoring laws meant to minimize civilian casualties

The fourth article accuses Hegseth of dismantling systems and processes at the Pentagon that Congress established to minimize civilian casualties, saying that his actions led to the deadly strike on an Iranian school in the first wave of attacks against the country in February. The Tomahawk missile strike killed roughly 170 civilians, most of them children, Iranian media has reported. The U.S. has not directly accepted responsibility for the attack.

The resolution says Hegseth oversaw "the systemic deterioration and removal of Department of Defense infrastructure that Congress had mandated by law to limit collateral damage to civilians and non-military objects during military operations." The article cites Hegseth's cuts to staff dedicated to mitigating civilian casualties, his firing of the military's top lawyers and his public comments about the "stupid rules of engagement."
Hegseth's actions laid the groundwork for the strike on the school, Massie alleges.

"By directing the Department of Defense in a manner that foreseeably dismantled the safeguards necessary to distinguish civilian objects from military objectives, Secretary Hegseth thereby effected the murder of civilians," the article says.

"The strike on the elementary school was not an isolated targeting failure divorced from the conduct of the Secretary of Defense, nor can Secretary Hegseth's conduct be dismissed as a single targeting error or isolated failure in the fog of war," the resolution says.
Article V: Carrying out "extrajudicial killings" through boat strikes

The fifth article centers on the Pentagon's campaign against alleged drug-smuggling boats in the Caribbean and eastern Pacific Ocean. The resolution says the strikes have killed at least 243 people since September 2025.
Massie accuses Hegseth of using the military to target suspects of crimes.

"By subjecting persons merely suspected of criminal conduct to lethal military force without judicial process, without congressional authorization, and without establishing a lawful basis for treating such persons or vessels as military targets, Secretary Hegseth arrogated to himself and the Executive Branch the roles of judge, jury, and executioner and asserted a unilateral power to determine who may live and who may die," the article says.
The article also cites the first strike of the campaign, on Sept. 2, 2025, when the military hit the same boat a second time.

"The strike destroyed and capsized the vessel. Approximately 45 minutes later, while two survivors clung to the wreckage, a secondary strike was ordered, killing both survivors," the resolution says. "In doing so, Secretary Hegseth has endangered members of our Armed Forces in future military engagements by encouraging adversaries to subject American service members to the same treatment."
Article VI: Retaliating against Sen. Mark Kelly
The sixth article accuses Hegseth of "retaliating against a Member of Congress for constitutionally protected speech," specifically Democratic Sen. Mark Kelly of Arizona.

In November 2025, Kelly, a retired Navy captain, appeared in a video with other lawmakers to deliver a message to members of the military and intelligence community: "Our laws are clear. You can refuse illegal orders."
Hegseth issued a letter of censure and threatened to reduce Kelly's rank, which would have cut his retirement benefits. A federal judge blocked the move.

Massie's resolution says Hegseth "weaponized the Department of Defense to chill a core function of the Legislative Branch" and "place the First Amendment rights of millions of United States veterans at risk of irreparable harm."
Article VII: The capture of Venezuela's Maduro

Article VII deals with the military operation to capture Maduro and his wife in Caracas in January 2026. It calls the raid "an act of war against a sovereign country executed under the guise of narcotics law enforcement, though in actuality intended to assert U.S. control over Venezuela's oil reserves."

The resolution says the operation involved more than 200 special operations personnel and more than 150 aircraft and drones, and killed at least 83 people. It argues Hegseth acted without a declaration of war or authorization from Congress, in violation of the War Powers Resolution.
The article cites Mr. Trump's remarks after the raid that "we're going to run the country" and that U.S. oil companies would "go in… and start making money."
Hegseth "gambled the lives of Army, Navy, Air Force, and Marine Corps personnel in order to facilitate the illegal taking of national oil," the article says.
Article VIII: Strikes on Yemen
The eighth and final article focuses on more than 1,100 U.S. strikes against Houthi targets in Yemen between March and May 2025.
The article again accuses Hegseth of using military force without congressional authorization and says the strikes led to civilian casualties.
"In less than eight weeks, there were nearly as many civilian deaths in Yemen as United States military actions had caused in that country during the preceding twenty-three years," the article says.

The article cites leaked messages from Hegseth and other top officials in a group chat on Signal that The Atlantic published last year. It argues that the conversation shows the administration knew the Houthis did not pose an imminent threat that would have required an immediate U.S. response.

title: Sanders won't back Schumer as Democratic leader
summary: Sen. Bernie Sanders said Tuesday he won't support Sen. Chuck Schumer as Democratic leader in the new Congress, becoming the most prominent progressive to oppose his candidacy to date.
story: Washington — Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders said Tuesday he won't support New York Sen. Chuck Schumer as Democratic leader when the party takes control of the Senate, becoming the most prominent progressive to oppose his candidacy to date.

Sanders made the announcement at a press conference at the Capitol, saying last week's midterm elections were "about change." Democrats will control at least 54 seats when the 120th Congress convenes in January.

"It was an election across the country, in red states and blue states, where people were looking around them and saying, 'What is going on in America, when I am struggling to put food on the table, pay for healthcare, pay for housing, and I'm worried not only that my life economically is going nowhere, everything being equal, my kid in the richest country in the history of the world is going to have the lowest standard of living than I do?' And while all of this is going on, the billionaire class has never ever had it so good," Sanders said.

He added: "I personally have known Chuck Schumer for over 30 years, and I like Chuck. Nobody who works harder than Chuck Schumer. But in my view, the time is now for change, and I will not be supporting Chuck to be reelected as the Democratic leader."
Sanders, an independent who caucuses with the Democrats, called for "a vigorous debate about the direction of the Democratic Party."
"We need to have that out in the open to show the American people that a new day has come and that their votes meant a new direction in Washington," he said.

Sanders appeared alongside Michigan Democratic Sen. Elissa Slotkin, who said that "whoever wants to run this caucus should come forward with a plan on how they're going to govern differently, what they're going to do in the first 100 days to put money in people's pockets, and then in particular how they're going to communicate differently."
Slotkin said she is "not actively seeking this job" but is "seeking change."
"Whoever wants my vote is going to have to show me a concrete plan that's definitively different," Slotkin said. "I'm a no until and unless I see that from anyone."

No contender has emerged to challenge Schumer's role atop the Senate Democratic caucus, but Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland has come the closest to throwing his hat in the ring. After initially saying he would not pursue the position, Van Hollen has said this week that he's exploring a potential run.
"What I've said from the very beginning is, we shouldn't have a coronation," he said on Monday. "I'm in listening mode and haven't shut the door."
At an event on Tuesday, Van Hollen said he is "in the process right now of calling my colleagues."
"I'm actively calling my colleagues because at the end of the day, this is a vote in the Democratic caucus," he said.
Democrats are expected to hold their leadership elections in early December.

title: NASA is recruiting new astronauts. Here are the qualifications.
summary: The space agency is recruiting its next class of astronauts as the U.S. plans a new mission to the moon. Here's the kind of person NASA is looking for.
story: NASA is recruiting its next class of astronauts, inviting U.S. citizens to apply before midnight ET on Dec. 3 for the chance to "live and work" on the moon.

The space agency's application portal states there are "few vacancies" for the role, which pays $164,395 annually and requires recruits to relocate to Houston, where they'll work at the Johnson Space Center.

While the job is open to all citizens, applicants must meet certain educational criteria and possess specialized experience. In other words, not just any Tom, Dick or Harriet will qualify for the job.

The next group of astronauts is being selected as the U.S. plans to build a moon base and send crewed missions to the lunar surface. NASA's Artemis II mission recently sent a crew of four astronauts around the moon in April, setting a record for the farthest distance humans have ever traveled from our planet.

"The people we select could walk on the moon, live and work at the moon base, and help pioneer the systems and operations that will ultimately carry crews to Mars," NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said in a statement. "Those missions will demand technical excellence, sound judgment, teamwork and courage."
Here are the qualifications NASA is looking for in an astronaut.
Educational background
NASA's job application portal states that applicants must fit into one of the following four educational profiles:

A master's degree in a qualifying field of engineering, biological science, physical science, computer science or mathematics.Two academic years of qualifying doctoral coursework in one of those fields. A qualifying medical degree, such as an MD, physician assistant or nurse practitioner. Completion of a recognized test pilot school by July 2027.
A master's degree in a qualifying field of engineering, biological science, physical science, computer science or mathematics.
Two academic years of qualifying doctoral coursework in one of those fields.
A qualifying medical degree, such as an MD, physician assistant or nurse practitioner.
Completion of a recognized test pilot school by July 2027.
Specialized experience

Applicants must also select a discipline they best qualify for based on their work experience, with NASA requiring three years of professional experience after completing their degree program or pilot training.

Pilots: Must meet one of three thresholds: 750 hours as lead pilot of a high-performance jet; 1,500 hours in other fixed-wing aircraft, with 750 in command; or 1,000 hours in rotary-wing aircraft, with 300 in command. Initial flight training and drone hours are excluded.Flight test: Requires test pilot school completion or enrollment, with completion by July 2027, as well as three years of related flight test experience.Medical: At least three years of professional experience after earning a medical degree. NASA said that residencies count toward the experience.Biological and medical science: At least three years of related experience.Physical science: Three years of related work experience.Engineering: Three years of related work experience.Operations: Three years of related work experience in "high-consequence environments that require real-time decision-making and intensive teamwork, where errors carry irreversible and physical risk to personnel, missions or vehicles," NASA said.

Pilots: Must meet one of three thresholds: 750 hours as lead pilot of a high-performance jet; 1,500 hours in other fixed-wing aircraft, with 750 in command; or 1,000 hours in rotary-wing aircraft, with 300 in command. Initial flight training and drone hours are excluded.
Flight test: Requires test pilot school completion or enrollment, with completion by July 2027, as well as three years of related flight test experience.
Medical: At least three years of professional experience after earning a medical degree. NASA said that residencies count toward the experience.
Biological and medical science: At least three years of related experience.
Physical science: Three years of related work experience.
Engineering: Three years of related work experience.

Operations: Three years of related work experience in "high-consequence environments that require real-time decision-making and intensive teamwork, where errors carry irreversible and physical risk to personnel, missions or vehicles," NASA said.
Other requirements
Applicants must also pass a series of clearances, including medical and psychiatric exams; vision that can be corrected to 20/20 in each eye; and a background check and drug screening.

Aspiring astronauts must be able "to perform moderate to arduous physical activities, including heavy lifting, crouching, crawling and exposure to inclement weather" and "be willing to work in dangerous, life-threatening situations and live/work in remote, isolated, small or confined spaces for prolonged periods." Applicants also have to pass a swimming test.
On top of that, applicants must "be willing to deploy to space for 12 months or longer, accepting extreme isolation, austere living conditions and separation from loved ones."

title: Fireball traveling 47,000 mph spotted over North Carolina, Tennessee
summary: A bright fireball was spotted in skies over North Carolina and Tennessee, zooming by at 47,000 mph before disintegrating above a city near Chattanooga, NASA said.
story: A meteor lit up skies over parts of North Carolina and Tennessee on Thursday night, zooming by at 47,000 mph, according to NASA.

Eyewitnesses have shared numerous photographs on social media of the fireball, which initially sprang into view about 50 miles above the North Carolina town of Robbinsville. NASA said the meteor was also captured by its specialized imaging systems — called sky cameras — which were stationed throughout the region.

Those cameras tracked the fireball as it proceeded to travel westward into southern Tennessee, eventually dissipating once it reached a spot about 25 miles above the city of East Ridge, near Chattanooga. Just about 10 seconds passed between the meteor's first and final sighting.

NASA said it was able to analyze the meteor using the footage from sky cameras at the Tellus Science Museum in Cartersville, Georgia, and others stationed in Huntsville, Alabama, Tullahoma, Tennessee, and one more location near the Tennessee-North Carolina border. The agency determined that the object was a small piece of an asteroid, measuring two inches in diameter and weighing six ounces.

Meteors, also called "shooting stars," are the visible paths of asteroid fragments that have entered Earth's atmosphere, according to NASA. Astronomers use the term "fireball" to describe an especially bright meteor, which can be seen over a wide area because of how starkly they appear. Some fireballs are much larger than the one spotted over North Carolina and Tennessee last week, with NASA saying they can measure three feet or bigger in size.
NASA said the meteor was not part of the Taurid meteor shower, which is currently active.

title: Nvidia short-seller warned of Jensen Huang's ties to suspected spy
summary: A small investment firm issued a report about Nvidia in May that foreshadowed issues that have embroiled CEO Jensen Huang in scandal.
story: Recent revelations about Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's links to a suspected Chinese spy have shocked investors, with the chipmaker's valuation sinking $450 billion over two days.

But the relationship, now under investigation by Nvidia, was foreshadowed in May by a little-known Wall Street "short seller," Christian Lamarco of New York City-based Culper Research, who published a 40-page report highlighting Huang's ties to Alice Huang (no relation), a former television reporter and financial industry executive.

Short-sellers use a trading strategy that yields profits when a company's shares decline, and Culper disclosed in its report that it had bet against Nvidia's stock. Short-sellers often publish research to demonstrate why a company is overvalued, aiming to convince other investors to sell the stock, thereby driving the shares lower and boosting their profits.

Lamarco, who didn't immediately respond to requests for comment, based his report on Nvidia on interviews with employees of Chinese companies, Singaporean and Malaysian corporate filings, and social media posts that appeared to show Jensen Huang and Alice Huang socializing together at various events.

The report also outlined Culper's rationale for claiming that Nvidia's high-powered chips were being diverted to China, despite the U.S. barring the sale of such products to the People's Republic due to national security and competitive concerns.

Key to Lamarco's investigation were the actions of Megaspeed International, a Singapore-based company that has emerged as a major player in the Nvidia scandal.  Alice Huang, then a top executive at Megaspeed, is suspected by U.S. intelligence of being an asset of China's Ministry of State Security.
"Uncomfortably close"
Lamarco wrote in the report that Jensen Huang appeared to have an "uncomfortably close relationship" with Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le.

"We believe Nvidia has a significant China problem," Culper Research wrote in a May 13 social media thread. "Nvidia claims its China business went to 'zero' after April 2025 U.S. trade restrictions. We believe that in reality, over 20% of Nvidia's FY 2026 compute revenues remained driven by China via illegal GPU diversion and Southeast Asian intermediaries."

Culper also alleged that Chinese companies used Southeast Asian intermediaries to gain access to Nvidia chips. The firm said corporate filings suggest that one of those intermediaries — Megaspeed — received financing from Chinese e-commerce company Alibaba to buy the chips.
Nvidia didn't immediately respond to a request for comment.

Culper isn't the first to question whether China was using front companies to buy advanced AI chips from the U.S. In a March 23 letter to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, Sens. Elizabeth Warren and Jim Banks warned of a "large-scale diversion of advanced American AI chips to China through Southeast Asian intermediaries."

The lawmakers requested that the Commerce Department immediately suspend active export licenses for Nvidia AI chips and servers to China and to companies in Southeast Asia, including Malaysia, Thailand, Vietnam and Singapore.
Megaspeed's mega-speedy growth

Culper's report notes that Megaspeed had "relatively few assets at year-end 2023," but within a year spent $2.9 billion to purchase Nvidia-powered servers. The short-seller said it found documents that showed the Chinese tech giant Alibaba had provided billions to Megaspeed.
Megaspeed and its Malaysian affiliate, Speedmatrix, together purchased $4.8 billion of Nvidia's advanced AI equipment and processors over the last three years, according to the report.

"Megaspeed went from very little business to billions in a rapid time frame," Culper stated. "This is the exact sort of pattern that experts told us ought to raise alarm bells at Nvidia as indicative of diversion or circumvention activity."
While the firm's research didn't directly refer to a romantic relationship between Jensen Huang and Alice Huang, it included several photos and video stills showing them together at various events.

"Nvidia CEO Huang has walked alongside Megaspeed at every step, and seems to have a close relationship with Megaspeed's Alice Huang," Culper wrote in the May 13 social media thread. "They partied together in June 2024 — same month as the Apex/Alibaba pledge, then dined together in May 2025 — just after U.S. trade restrictions."

Culper, which is named after the American Revolution-era Culper Spy Ring that reported on the movement of British forces, has in recent days posted about the allegations that emerged this week about Jensen Huang's ties to Megaspeed and Alice Huang.  "We wrote about this in May," the group noted on Nov. 5.
When Culper published its report on May 13, Nvidia's stock was trading at $225.83 per share. Between that date and the close of trading on Tuesday, the shares have shed 25% of their value.
"Everyone was just mocking us, and now everyone is singing our praises," Lamarco told the New York Times in a recent interview.

title: Microsoft data center brings "a kind of boom" amid AI pushback
summary: Microsoft outlines the pledges it makes to data center communities as industry tries to sway public opinion on AI.
story: Opposition to data centers helped propel Democratic candidates who pledged to stall new construction to victory in last week's midterm elections. More than half of voters said artificial intelligence and data centers were a significant factor in their votes, according to a CBS News exit poll.
But one town says it has benefited from data centers, despite the pushback growing across the nation.
For 20 years, Microsoft has operated its Columbia Data Center in Quincy, Washington, where Mayor Paul Worley told CBS News its presence has created "a kind of boom" for the area.
Additional tax revenue from the project has funded a new high school and hospital, and helped improve other critical services, he said.
Microsoft president Brad Smith told CBS News about the pledge it makes to the communities where it builds and operates data centers.

"Basically, we will put the community first," he said. "We will not do anything that will increase the electricity rates of our neighbors. We'll ensure that we replenish more water, we put more water back into the community than we use."
He also highlighted the role data centers play in powering every action we take on our phones and other connected devices.
"Every time we tap on our phone, it's connecting through an app, it's pulling data from something like this," he said.
The industry, he said, needs to better inform opponents of data centers about the essential services the facilities enable.
"They're part of daily life, just like electricity is," Smith said.
Why Quincy?
The nearby Columbia River provides hydropower that has led seven additional companies to choose Quincy for their data centers.
It hasn't been entirely smooth. To accommodate the roughly two dozen data centers that have entered the area over the past two decades, some residents have been asked to vacate their homes.
Electricity rates per kilowatt-hour have risen by roughly 55% over the past 20 years, according to the Grant County public utility.

While that marks a steep increase, it's still lower than the average increases in national and state electricity rates over the same period. In Washington, electricity rates rose 107% over the same time period. Nationwide, they rose 66%.
Smith said he believes it is the company's "fundamental responsibility" to manage the industry's growth and the impact on residents' rising utility costs.
"You can't make the challenges go away, but you can be broad-minded, you can [be] committed, and you can take steps to manage growth well," he said.

For example, Microsoft pledges to replenish or give communities back more water than it uses. It also commits to paying for its own electricity and ensuring that its usage doesn't increase neighbors' utility rates, Smith said. He added that the facilities create local jobs, too, though many are temporary construction positions.
According to Microsoft, the company employs roughly 700 people, or almost 9% of Quincy's roughly 8,000 residents.
Questions to ask
Yale professor of environmental and energy economics Kenneth Gillingham outlined the questions communities should ask data center developers before they come to town.
They include:
What type of technology is it using for cooling?How large will it be?How is it going to generate its electricity?
What type of technology is it using for cooling?
How large will it be?
How is it going to generate its electricity?
Meanwhile, Microsoft's Smith has a clear message for Americans who say they don't want data centers in their backyards.

"Give us a chance to talk through what we want to do, and give us a chance to prove that we can do this in a way that will put the community first," he said. "We have to persuade you. But the people that you've elected, they're the ones who are gonna make a decision, not us."
