title: Nvidia's trillion-dollar bind: Can it afford to lose Jensen Huang?
summary: Other CEOs have been ousted over undisclosed relationships, but Nvidia's inquiry shines a spotlight on how closely the chipmaker's fortunes are tied to its co-founder.
story: Nvidia's board of directors faces a trillion-dollar dilemma: Can the chipmaker afford to part with its storied co-founder and CEO, now embroiled in multiple investigations into his affair with an alleged Chinese spy?

In recent years, several high-profile CEOs have been ousted after their relationships with employees and customers came under scrutiny, including former McDonald's CEO Steve Easterbrook and Kohl's CEO Ashley Buchanan. But none is so closely identified with their companies as Huang. Over more than three decades, he has led Nvidia as it grew into one of the world's most valuable companies, with many investors viewing him as equally critical to the company's success as Elon Musk is to SpaceX or Steve Jobs was to Apple.

Huang is facing serious challenges, including an independent inquiry by Nvidia's board into the affair, a shareholder lawsuit and questions from lawmakers. Heightening the stakes are allegations that Huang had a close relationship with a former female executive at an Nvidia customer who is also suspected of working with China's intelligence agency.
$450 billion drop
Nvidia shareholders have been spooked by the disclosure, with the company's shares shedding 10% of their value — or about $450 billion — in the last two trading days alone.
"It exposes how dependent the company is on this one person," Shiva Rajgopal, a Columbia Business School professor who studies corporate governance, told CBS News.
He added, "This is like asking if something happens to Elon Musk, what happens to Tesla and SpaceX's valuations? If something happens to Jensen Huang, what happens to Nvidia's valuation?"

Yorkville Ives tech analyst Dan Ives estimated in a research note that Nvidia could lose as much as 30% of its valuation if Huang is removed from his role, while noting that for now most investors expect the executive to retain his post at the company.

"At the end of the day, there is only one Jensen, and Nvidia will dramatically change as a company if he is no longer CEO, with a major negative ripple impact across the tech industry and AI Revolution," Ives said.
"Do not proceed"

Corporate governance experts said Huang's alleged relationship with Alice Huang — a Chinese executive linked to the Singapore-based data center company Megaspeed, which buys AI chips from Nvidia — appears to violate Nvidia's code of conduct. That policy highlights that personal relationships could create a conflict of interest for Nvidia, while Huang himself specifies in the code of conduct that the company's workers have a responsibility "to maintain high ethical standards."

Nvidia's code also instructs employees to ask themselves whether they could defend an action if it were made public on social media or known to colleagues. If not, the policy states, "do not proceed."

Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment about whether Huang had violated any company rules. In a message to company employees on Sunday, Huang admitted, "I was unfaithful to my wife," and he apologized for hurting her and their two children, both of whom also work at Nvidia. "There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry," he wrote.

But Huang's conduct "is definitely a violation," said Jay Aldebert, chief growth officer at International Services, a consulting firm that advises small and midsize businesses on issues including governance. "How he handled it based on their code of conduct is where you're going to see continued issues."
Still, while Huang may have violated company rules, he may be given more leeway than other employees due to his importance to Nvidia, governance experts said.

"This is an outlier — I don't remember a case like this," Columbia's Rajgopal said. "This company is so important to the U.S. in terms of AI, especially with China and other powers. So even if there is a violation of the code of conduct, if I were the chair of the board, I would not dismiss him."

Nvidia's 11-person board includes Huang, although the other board members are considered independent, according to a company regulatory filing. They include California Institute of Technology professor John Dabiri and former Taco Bell International president Melissa Lora. All board members except Dabiri have experience in corporate governance, the filing states.
Nvidia board members should demonstrate their independence by hiring a law firm to help with the investigation, and immediately develop a succession plan for Huang, Rajgopal said.
A common issue for Nvidia and other big tech companies led by their founders is that they are often run "like a family affair," he added.
"These are effectively run like family private companies, but they are mega-cap public companies where most of the capital comes from the public," Rajgopal said. "There is a duty above and beyond."
Succession planning

Huang has said he has more than 60 direct reports in a corporate structure that keeps him at the center of decision-making at Nvidia. As various investigations ramp up, the succession plan to replace him remains unclear, heightening pressure on the board, experts said.

"The Nvidia board is between a rock and a hard spot. They have almost no good options — Jensen is Nvidia," said David Yoffie, a professor at Harvard Business School. "And if he has done something wrong and he needs to be removed, and they have no successors, that's a terrible outcome."

If Huang resigns or is removed by the board, speculation on possible replacements has turned to figures including Nvidia co-founder Chris Malachowsky, who is a senior technology executive at the company, and Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress.
Nvidia employs more than 40,000 people worldwide, and there are "lots of other great leaders" within the company, said Bob O'Donnell, president, founder and chief analyst at TECHnalysis Research.

"I think it's important that the company starts to let some of these other folks come out as spokespeople so people feel trust, they feel good about Nvidia and their future, even without Jensen," O'Donnell said, although he said he does not think Huang will leave his post.

title: Nvidia stock slumps amid board investigation into CEO Jensen Huang
summary: Investors are questioning whether Huang's future as Nvidia's CEO may be at risk amid allegations that he was targeted in a Chinese intelligence operation.
story: Nvidia's stock price slid on Monday amid questions about CEO Jensen Huang's future at the chipmaker, following the board of directors' investigation into allegations that China targeted him in an intelligence operation.

The investigation is raising concerns about Huang's role at the company, which he co-founded and helped build into the world's second-most valuable company, with a $4.5 trillion valuation. Nvidia is barred from selling its high-end chips, specifically designed to power artificial intelligence models, to China due to competitive concerns.
Nvidia shares sank 4.3%, or $7.97, to $178.67, shrinking the chipmaker's market valuation by about $193 billion.

The allegations center around reports that Huang had a close relationship with Alice Huang, who U.S. intelligence officials believe was a spy for China's Ministry of State Security, the country's main intelligence agency. On Sunday, Nvidia's board said it is starting an "independent investigation" into the allegations, sparking questions about the CEO's future with the company.

"This is a black eye moment for Jensen and will spark multiple congressional inquiries at a minimum and will create an overhang on the stock for a myriad of reasons," Dan Ives, a tech analyst at Yorkville Ives, said in a research note. "The key question investors will be asking is: Will Jensen remain CEO of Nvidia?"

Ives added, "There is clearly risk that Jensen could be removed as CEO depending on the board investigation, and this will add risk to the stock as he is so important to the Nvidia story and strategy globally."

In a statement to CBS News, an Nvidia spokesperson said that "Jensen is committed to continuing to lead Nvidia as CEO without interruption." The company didn't respond to a question about whether Huang had violated any of its corporate policies.

The company's board said it had no reason to believe that the company's secrets or national security were compromised. John Rizzo, a spokesperson for Nvidia, told CBS News on Sunday, "We trust that if we were the target of a genuine threat, the U.S. government would have notified us."

The Chinese government dismissed allegations that it targeted Nvidia's chief executive, who co-founded the company in 1993, as part of an espionage operation. "The so-called Chinese spy narrative is entirely baseless and constitutes slander and smear," Guo Jiakun, a spokesperson for China's Ministry of Foreign Affairs, said in a statement.
Who is Alice Huang?
Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, was a former executive at a Singapore-based data center company, Megaspeed International, whose website touts its partnership with Nvidia.
Many offices in Singapore were closed on Monday for a holiday. Megaspeed and the Singapore Ministry of Home Affairs did not immediately reply to requests for comment.
Succession challenges

Replacing Jensen Huang, 63, would prove challenging because he is viewed as integral to the company's success, tech analysts said on Monday. Huang also serves as the public face of Nvidia, appearing at industry events and media interviews in his trademark black leather jacket.
Huang is the company's fifth-largest shareholder, with about 3.4% of its shares, according to financial data provider FactSet.

"There is no known succession plan, and there is no leader in the company who would be the clear next step if he had to step down. In many ways, Jensen is Nvidia's Steve Jobs," said Daniel Newman, CEO of tech consulting firm Futurum, in an email.
He added, "That does not mean they cannot find a Tim Cook in the future, but it would be a massive changing of the guard, and the company has not been set up for that."
Another blow for the AI trade

The scandal puts more pressure on Nvidia shares, which have already been bruised by mounting investor concerns about the valuations of companies driving AI growth. Prior to Monday's early decline, Nvidia's shares had tumbled almost 20% over the last month amid a broader sell-off in AI stocks.

The board investigation into Huang could loom over Nvidia and raise the risk that U.S. regulators could impose additional restrictions on the company's chip exports, according to Adam Crisafulli, an analyst at Vital Knowledge.

"The key questions are whether he was aware of any espionage activities and whether any confidential or strategically sensitive information was compromised," said George Chen, a partner and chair of digital practice at The Asia Group, a Washington-based consultancy.

In recent years, Jensen Huang has lobbied federal authorities to loosen limits on sales of Nvidia chips to China, winning approval from President Trump to sell its H200 chips this year. Those chips are not Nvidia's most advanced models, but they are still considered important products for Nvidia.
Previously, Huang also lobbied Mr. Trump to be allowed to sell Nvidia's less-advanced H20 chips, which were designed to comply with U.S. export restrictions on China.

"The real potential fallout from the Jensen Huang scandal will be the U.S. government imposing dramatically more draconian restrictions on sales of sophisticated chips to China (the issue isn't the H200 but instead the fact that a large amount of higher-end Nvidia products are still making it into the hands of Chinese buyers)," Crisafulli said in a research note.

title: Google faces mounting backlash for controversial AI school policy
summary: Google puts schools in an "impossible position" by blocking students from using its search platform unless AI tools are also enabled, Senator said.
story: Google faces mounting public pressure to change a new policy that would limit U.S. students' access to the internet giant's widely used search platform unless schools also offer its artificial intelligence-based education tools.

In a letter to Alphabet CEO Sundar Pichai on Monday, Sen. Edward Markey demanded that Google's corporate parent reverse the policy, which blocks search for K-12 student accounts that don't also provide access to apps such as Google Classroom.

Markey, a Massachusetts Democrat, said Google shouldn't use its dominance in the education technology market to effectively force AI on students by restricting their access to critical research tools like Google Search. Roughly 150 million students and teachers use Classroom.

"At a time when schools, parents and policymakers are working hard to implement safeguards on AI chatbots for our children, Google is recklessly forcing AI on schools and treating kids like collateral damage," Markey said in the letter. "Schools deserve the right to block student access to AI chatbots without also forfeiting access to an important educational tool."

Google maintains that its policy change gives schools more control over how they allow AI into schools. An Alphabet spokesperson also told CBS News that Google's AI features are now so tightly integrated into search that it cannot offer the latter without also enabling the AI services.

"We believe schools should have control over AI in their classrooms and in providing administrators with controls to help them manage their approach," Google vice president and general manager of education Chris Phillips wrote last week in a blog post announcing the policy change.
Google did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Markey's letter.

Markey said Google's decision to block search access for students who opt out of AI "places schools in an impossible position," forcing them to choose between giving students access to a potentially dangerous technology and depriving them of "a critical educational research tool."
"Although Google has a right to create and offer new educational tools, it should not use its dominant market position to force schools to adopt them," he added.

Markey is asking Alphabet if Google will commit to allowing schools to turn off AI features and chatbots in K-12 student accounts while still allowing students to access Google Search. He also requested that Google disclose any research it has conducted on the impact of its AI tools on students' mental health.
Markey has requested that Google disclose any research or testing it has conducted on the safety of its AI functions and their impact on the mental health of K-12 students.

Google's policy has drawn fire from other critics. In a statement posted on social media, New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani accused the tech giant of "trying to use its monopoly power to force AI into our public schools."

title: Data centers are unpopular — and a key motor of economic growth
summary: The political backlash against data centers is intensifying, threatening to choke off a critical source of U.S. investment, according to economists.
story: The shifting political winds surrounding data centers could buffet the entire U.S. economy, reducing investment in artificial intelligence and slowing growth, according to Wall Street analysts.

The historic tide of money pouring into AI, from data centers and frontier models to state-of-the-art chips and networking gear, has boosted business investment and financial markets in recent years. Federal Reserve researchers recently estimated that spending on data centers, power facilities and other AI-related tech equipment accounted for roughly 20% of U.S. gross domestic product over the preceding year.

In 2026, spending by "hyperscalers" such as Alphabet, Amazon, Meta and Microsoft — the companies racing to build data centers — is set to double to around $800 billion and is expected to reach $1 trillion in 2027, according to Capital Economics. Although slowing that buildout might well serve the public interest, given the widespread opposition to data centers, crimping that flow of dollars will have knock-on economic effects.

"Our economy is leveraged on this idea that AI will make us rich," economist Allison Schrager with the Manhattan Institute, a nonpartisan think tank, told CBS News. "There are risks to making it slower — it will mean slower growth."
"Detrimental effects"

Economists and investors now expect the Democrats' sweeping midterm election wins to both slow and increase the cost of data center development across the U.S. By contrast, those victories are unlikely to completely turn off the spigot, experts said, noting that political opposition to data centers isn't uniform, ranging from support for moratoriums on construction to more moderate proposals.
As a result, investment in data centers is likely to continue in the near term, both for projects currently underway and for facilities that have received permits.

For companies investing in AI, the bigger issue will be continuing such capital expenditures at the same pace even as the productivity gains and profits AI is expected to deliver remain largely unrealized for now.

"The high-level calculations essential to justify that level of CapEx, if sustained, we are talking $2 trillion in revenue for major AI companies by the early 2030s, which seems very unlikely," Capital Economics chief North America economist Stephen Brown told CBS News. "Our view is that because of that, there is likely to be some slowdown in data center construction. We are not saying it will stop altogether, but the level of investment is likely to ease. And that would have some detrimental effects on the U.S. economy."
Impact on stocks and consumer spending
Moody's Analytics chief economist Mark Zandi thinks investors are willing to continue pouring money into AI for the next couple of years, but said the long-term prospects are less clear.

"There are a lot of questions about whether that capital will continue to be there to fill that hole and, if not, AI companies will have to raise prices to cover costs. Then you won't see the same kind of investment," he said.

In 2025, investment in AI added roughly 0.3 percentage points to real GDP growth, according to Capital Economics, which expects investment in the sector to boost growth by roughly the same amount this year.

If AI investment were to fall in 2028, "It could turn into an outright drag on GDP," Capital Economics chief economic advisor Vicky Redwood said in a research note on Friday, estimating that a 10% annual drop in AI spending from current levels would knock around 0.1% off GDP growth.

If investment in AI slows, the greatest drag on growth could come from reduced consumption, Brown of Capital Economics told CBS News. Higher-income Americans who invested in AI stocks have seen their wealth grow sharply. With the S&P 500 up almost 100% over the past three years, such investors have driven increased spending.

"A big part of the wealth effect is coming from the strong rise in equity prices, and if data center construction slows, the likely weakness we'll see in the equity market is a sign of things to come," said Brown, who estimates that this "wealth effect" is boosting economic growth this year by roughly 0.5%.

If the S&P 500 were to lose 20% of its value, that boost would turn into a 0.5% drag on GDP growth, Brown said. "That would be a 1% hit to GDP," he said. "We would be talking about a sharp slowdown in GDP growth versus a recession."

title: Nvidia's stock dives as board weighs move to oust Jensen Huang
summary: Nvidia shares fall sharply in after-hours trading as the company's board considers whether to remove Jensen Huang as CEO.
story: Nvidia's stock price tumbled after the close of trading on Wednesday on news that the chipmaker's board of directors is preparing to oust longtime CEO Jensen Huang.

Nvidia this week launched an investigation into Huang, who admitted to having an extramarital affair. U.S. intelligence agencies have linked the CEO to a Chinese business executive, Alice Huang (no relation), who is suspected of being an asset of China's Ministry of State Security.
The Trump administration is aware of the Nvidia board's plans, sources told CBS News. The Wall Street Journal was the first to report that board members were preparing to remove Jensen Huang.

Nvidia shares fell more than 8%, to $159.51, in after-hours trading. The drop continued a steep decline in the company's market value, which has sunk more than $450 billion since Nvidia announced the probe into Jensen Huang's conduct on Nov. 8.

Jensen Huang, who co-founded Nvidia in 1993, is seen in many circles as the face of the burgeoning artificial intelligence sector, with the company's advanced chips providing the critical computing resources that power frontier AI models.
His departure would be a major blow to Nvidia, which lacks any obvious successor to fill his shoes, according to Wall Street analysts.

"The news is obviously negative, as Jensen is (arguably) the most prominent executive at the most prominent company sitting at the center of the world's most important industry — someone who foresaw the rise of AI years before ChatGPT arrived and made sure the firm he founded would be prepared to capitalize on it," Adam Crisafulli of Vital Knowledge said in a report.
Nvidia's code of conduct

Corporate governance experts said Jensen Huang's alleged relationship with Alice Huang appears to violate Nvidia's code of conduct. That policy highlights that personal relationships could create a conflict of interest for Nvidia, while Huang himself specifies in the code of conduct that the company's workers have a responsibility "to maintain high ethical standards."

Nvidia's code also instructs employees to ask themselves whether they could defend an action if it were made public on social media or known to colleagues. If not, the policy states, "do not proceed."

In a message to company employees on Sunday, Huang admitted to having an affair, and he apologized to his wife and their two children, both of whom also work at Nvidia. "There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry," he wrote.
Nvidia's 11-person board includes Jensen Huang, although the other board members are designated as independent, according to a regulatory filing.

President Trump said this week the FBI is also investigating romantic and business ties between Jensen Huang and Alice Huang, who was a senior executive at Megaspeed International. The Singapore-based company has been one of Nvidia's largest foreign customers, purchasing nearly $5 billion in AI chips and other advanced hardware.
The turmoil at Nvidia is also drawing scrutiny in Congress, with lawmakers expected to question company executives about whether its chips are being funneled to China through other countries.

Dan Ives, a tech analyst with investment adviser Yorkville Ives, said investors will now consider who might succeed Huang, what impact that could have on the company's short-term strategy and what any government investigations might reveal.

"Jensen is not replaceable by another CEO or group of interim executives, but Nvidia likely now has to move on without Jensen at the helm, which seemed like a Twilight Zone episode narrative before Sunday afternoon when the news broke," Ives said in a report.

title: SS United States sinks, will become world's largest artificial reef
summary: The 1,000-foot-long SS United States was sent to the bottom of the ocean in a controlled, explosive-free sinking that is taking place about 20 nautical miles off the Gulf Coast of Florida.
story: The SS United States, the fabled ocean liner, was scuttled toward the ocean floor on Wednesday in a controlled, explosive-free sinking that took place about 20 nautical miles off the Gulf Coast of Florida between the Destin-Fort Walton Beach region and Pensacola.
The 1,000-foot-long SS United States was sent to the bottom of the ocean in an hourslong sinking operation that began Wednesday afternoon and concluded later in the evening.

The ship will become the world's largest artificial reef, only adding to its long list of maritime achievements. The Destin-Fort Walton Beach metropolitan area says it already has about 580 artificial reefs off its coastline, the most for any region in the country.
The SS United States first set sail in 1952, at the time setting a transatlantic speed record for an ocean liner that still stands today.
It carried thousands of voyagers over its two decades of military service, including presidents, royalty, celebrities and even legendary CBS News broadcaster Walter Cronkite.
Its design was so revolutionary that even the Pentagon kept it a secret.

But by 1969, the SS United States was retired from service, and it wound up in Philadelphia in 1996. It remained docked there for decades, until Okaloosa County in Florida purchased the ship from the SS United States Conservancy for about $1 million in 2024 with the goal of deploying it as an artificial reef designed to provide a habitat for the Gulf's marine ecosystem.

Prior to sinking it, the county sent the ship to Mobile, Alabama, for a one-year preparation process that involved removing all environmentally unsafe materials, including non-metal items, wiring and fuel, the county said.
Holes were also strategically cut throughout the ship to ensure it remains upright when submerged.
The preparations were conducted in coordination with the Environmental Protection Agency and the Florida Department of Environmental Protection.

The approximately $13 million project to make the ship an artificial reef was funded by county tourist tax revenue. Okaloosa County hopes that the ship will serve as a jolt to the economy of the Florida Panhandle, providing a year-round destination for divers.
"I think it's going to be like Disney World," Jocelyn Collins, general manager for Emerald Coast Scuba, told CBS News. "You know, we're going to line people up and take pictures underwater."

title: Democrat Scott Colom wins Mississippi Senate race in upset
summary: Democrat Scott Colom defeated GOP Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith in the Mississippi Senate race, delivering Democrats an eighth flipped Senate seat after the dramatic race had been up in the air for days.
story: Washington — Democrat Scott Colom defeated GOP Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith in the Mississippi Senate race, CBS News projects, delivering Democrats an eighth flipped Senate seat after the dramatic race had been up in the air for days.

Colom, 43, is a district attorney and seventh-generation Mississippian. He campaigned on cost-of-living and healthcare issues, while pledging to deliver for the Magnolia State where he argued Hyde-Smith hasn't. And he saw support from top surrogates like former President Bill Clinton and former Vice President Kamala Harris, who joined Colom on the campaign trail in the weeks leading up to Election Day.
He will be the state's first Black senator since Reconstruction.
Colom thanked his supporters — and pointed to his campaign's long odds — during a victory speech late Wednesday at Tougaloo College in Jackson, Mississippi.

"Throughout this campaign, there were many times where I had to have faith. There were times that I couldn't get donors to answer the phone. They did not believe a moment like this was possible, but I kept the faith," he said. "I did my first town hall in Jackson, Mississippi. ... Less than 10 people showed up, but I kept the faith."
Hyde-Smith, 67, has been in the Senate since 2018, and was the first woman elected to represent Mississippi in Congress.

"While this is not the outcome we worked for or hoped for, I respect the decision of Mississippi voters," Hyde-Smith said in a video message Wednesday night. "I want to congratulate Scott Colom and wish him well as he takes on the tremendous responsibility of representing our great state."

The race became surprisingly competitive in deep-red Mississippi, heating up in the final weeks of the campaign. National Democrats announced last month that they were investing in ad spending in the race for the first time, and the Cook Political Report changed its rating from solidly Republican to leaning Republican, as the headwinds that faced Republicans across the map — an unpopular war in Iran and persistent affordability issues — even made their way to reliably red states.
The race appeared extremely close the day after the election, when at one point just a few dozen votes separated the candidates. But Colom's lead strengthened in the days that followed.

Heading into Election Day, the race appeared to be a steep uphill climb for Democrats. President Trump won the state by 20 points in 2024, and the state hasn't elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1982. But the contest's competitiveness in the final stages of the campaign was illustrative of the broader political environment, which put seats on the map that Democrats wouldn't have dreamed of flipping at the beginning of the cycle.

"I want to make one thing clear: An election may come to an end, but our commitment to Mississippi never will," Hyde-Smith said added in her video. "I have always believed the public service is about something much bigger than any one person or any one election. It is about the people we serve, the values we hold dear and the future we leave for our children and grandchildren. And while my time in the United States Senate may be coming to an end, my love for Mississippi and determination to stand up for what is right never will. I will always be proud to call Mississippi home."

With the projected victory, Democrats add yet another seat to their majority, marking their eighth flip after the party won seats in North Carolina, South Carolina, Texas, Ohio, Iowa, Kansas and Maine.
In January, Democrats will control at least 55 Senate seats to Republicans' 44, with Alaska's Senate race still a toss-up.

title: Bessent relocates from home to military base after Iran threats
summary: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has relocated from his home in the Washington, D.C., area to a U.S. military base.
story: Washington — Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has relocated from his home in the Washington, D.C., area to a military base following a series of Iranian threats against his life.

"The secretary will not be deterred by the Iranian regime's threats and remains committed to executing Operation Economic Outcast and maintaining the blockade, which together are collapsing Iran's economy," a Treasury Department spokesperson said.

The decision comes as Bessent has led a U.S. push to cripple Iran's economy, vowing an "economic onslaught" against Tehran through a web of sanctions. The New York Times first reported Bessent's relocation.
A source familiar with the situation pointed to a Wall Street Journal story as the impetus for the move.

"After The Wall Street Journal published an article featuring an online photo that allowed the location of the secretary's Georgetown home to be geo-located, security concerns began to increase which have now forced the secretary to relocate to a military base for his safety," the person told CBS News.
CBS News has also reached out to the White House for comment.
Last month, U.S. national intelligence chief Jay Clayton warned that Iran has "substantially increased" its efforts to target Americans in the Middle East and beyond.

Clayton's warning, contained in an unclassified memo that was sent to Secretary of State Marco Rubio and obtained by CBS News, came as the State Department adjusted staffing at diplomatic posts across the Middle East.

title: First snow of the season is coming to Northeast
summary: Parts of the Northeast could see their first snowfall of the season later this week, as a cold snap spreads over the eastern half of the U.S.
story: The first snowfall of the season is expected in parts of the Northeast later this week, although there is uncertainty over how much snow will fall and which parts of the region will be hit hardest.
Temperatures are also forecast to drop well below average for this time of year in that region and other parts of the eastern U.S., impacting a large swath of the country.
Cold snap to spread over eastern U.S. this week

A large dip in the jet stream will cause cold air to spread across the eastern half of the U.S. starting Wednesday through the end of the week, reaching from the Canadian border to the Gulf Coast. Temperatures are expected to drop between 20 and 25 degrees below average for this time of year.

Overnight feels-like temperatures are forecast to be near or below freezing in major cities, including Chicago and Atlanta. Daytime highs will only reach the mid-30s and 40s from Thursday through the upcoming weekend.
Snowfall potential
A separate storm system developing over the Midwest on Wednesday will strengthen and head to the Northeast before the end of the week, potentially helping usher in the first snowfall of the season.

Some of the moisture associated with the storm will fall as cold rain, which is expected in cities like Boston, New York, Philadelphia, Pittsburgh and Washington, D.C., even though the I-95 corridor will likely see warmer temperatures this weekend.
But places at higher elevations and those in the interior Northeast, like upstate New York, New Hampshire and Vermont, could see their first snowfall.

The storm is expected to move away from land once it reaches the Mid-Atlantic region. A second, smaller storm could potentially form off of that system and impact coastal areas from the Mid-Atlantic up to New England. The path of the second, smaller storm will determine how much snow or rain may fall in those areas, and exactly which locations could be affected.

title: The biggest races Democrats won in the midterms
summary: Democrats won pivotal races in Texas, South Carolina, Georgia, Mississippi, Michigan and elsewhere. Here are the biggest victories of the 2026 midterms.
story: Washington — Voters across the country delivered a stinging rebuke to Republicans in Congress and President Trump's agenda in the 2026 midterm elections, with Democrats capturing House and Senate seats that had seemed out of reach just a few months ago.

CBS News projects Democrats will take control of both chambers when the new Congress convenes in January, with wide margins in each. Democrats are projected to control at least 55 Senate seats, with only Alaska still unresolved. In the House, CBS News estimates the party could control between 254 and 267 when all the votes are counted.
Out of 11 Senate races that CBS News considered battlegrounds, Democrats were projected to win 10. The 11th race, in Alaska, is still rated a toss-up, with a lengthy ballot-counting process expected.
The victories weren't just limited to House and Senate races, either. Democrats captured the governor's mansion in Texas, a feat they haven't accomplished since 1990.
Here are the major races that propelled Democrats to victory, according to CBS News' projections:
Texas Senate: James Talarico
In the most expensive Senate race in Texas history, and one of the closest-watched matchups of the election cycle, Talarico defeated Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton.
Talarico, 37, is a former teacher and Presbyterian seminarian who was elected to serve in the Texas House of Representatives in 2018.

Talarico's campaign focused on corruption and lowering costs. He told "CBS Mornings" on Wednesday that his victory sent a message to Elon Musk, who spent heavily in the race, that "Texas is not for sale."
"The power in this state, in this country, belongs to the people and we've got to make sure it stays that way," he said.
Paxton was backed by Mr. Trump, who endorsed the Republican attorney general over Sen. John Cornyn in the GOP Senate primary earlier this year.

Paxton went on to defeat Cornyn in the primary runoff in May, setting the race against Talarico. Paxton had weathered numerous controversies and was impeached by the state House in 2023 on allegations of bribery, obstruction of justice and abuse of trust. He was acquitted by the state Senate.
Texas governor: Gina Hinojosa

Hinojosa, a state lawmaker, bested Republican incumbent Gov. Greg Abbott, making her the first Democrat to win the governor's mansion in more than 30 years. Hinojosa will be the third woman to lead the state.

Abbott had been in office for more than a decade and was seeking a fourth term as governor, and the race against Hinojosa narrowed in the months leading up to the election. Hinojosa focused her campaign on affordability and public education. The fight over data centers also emerged as a major issue in the governor's race.
South Carolina Senate: Annie Andrews
Andrews, a pediatrician, defeated Republican Sen. Darline Graham, the sister of the late Sen. Lindsey Graham. Andrews, 45, made healthcare access and affordability the focuses of her campaign.

Graham was appointed to finish out the remainder of her late brother's Senate term following his unexpected death in July. President Trump swiftly threw his support behind Graham and campaigned for her in South Carolina in the lead-up to the midterms.
It has been nearly 30 years since a Democrat won the Senate in South Carolina, a state Mr. Trump won by 18 points in 2024.
Kansas Senate: Adam Hamilton

Hamilton, a fifth-generation Kansan, is the leader of the largest United Methodist church in the country and is a well-known author and speaker. The 62-year-old defeated Roger Marshall, a Republican, who was seeking his second term in the Senate.
Kansas hasn't elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1932. Mr. Trump won the state by more than 16 points in the last presidential election.

In the closing weeks of the Senate campaign, Marshall, an obstetrician-gynecologist, came under scrutiny after the New York Times reported that he had filed lawsuits against hundreds of his patients over outstanding medical bills, and 81 were arrested.
Georgia governor: Keisha Lance Bottoms

In Georgia, Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms will make history as the nation's first Black woman governor. The former Atlanta mayor and senior adviser in the Biden administration defeated Republican Rick Jackson and Libertarian Chase Oliver, CBS News projects.
With 99% of the vote counted, Bottoms had 54.3% of the vote, compared to 45.7% for Jackson.
Bottoms told "CBS Mornings" on Wednesday that she was surprised that the race was called as early as it was on election night.

"I thought that it was going to be a very long night. I knew that we had done the work, but Georgia has always, for the past few years, been a purple state, so I thought it would be much closer," she said.
Michigan Senate: Abdul El-Sayed
Michigan was viewed as Republicans' best chance to flip a Senate seat, but El-Sayed's victory over GOP opponent Mike Rogers keeps it in Democrats' hands.

The Senate race emerged as one of the most contentious of the midterm election cycle. Top Republicans, led by Mr. Trump, repeatedly leveled anti-Muslim attacks against El-Sayed, calling him a "jihadist" and claiming that he is a member of the Muslim Brotherhood.
El-Sayed told Fox News in an interview last month that he has "never been a member of the Muslim Brotherhood."
El-Sayed also came under scrutiny for his opposition to U.S. support for Israel and views on Israel raising questions as to whether he could win support from Jewish and Black voters.

There was a late twist in the Senate race in Michigan when Democratic Rep. Haley Stevens, who sought the Democratic Senate nomination, endorsed Rogers and appeared alongside him at a Detroit church Sunday.
Maine Senate: Troy Jackson
Jackson was facing off against GOP Sen. Susan Collins, the only Republican running for reelection in a state won by former Vice President Kamala Harris in the 2024 presidential race.

Collins was first elected to represent Maine in the Senate in 1996 and had touted her ability to bring home benefits for the state as part of her pitch to voters. While she had survived difficult campaigns in the past, Collins was not able to fend off the challenge from Jackson.

Jackson is a fifth-generation logger who jumped into the Senate race late after Graham Platner, who initially won the Democratic Senate nomination, withdrew from the race after allegations of sexual misconduct. The former president of the Maine Senate unsuccessfully sought the Democratic nomination for governor earlier this year.
Mississippi Senate: Scott Colom

Democrat Scott Colom pulled off a stunning upset against GOP Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith in the Mississippi Senate race — a narrow victory which was projected by CBS News on Nov. 11, more than a week after Election Day.

Colom, 43, a district attorney and seventh-generation Mississippian, will be the state's first Black U.S. senator since Reconstruction. He campaigned on cost of living and healthcare issues, pledging to deliver for the state where he argued Hyde-Smith hasn't.

In 2023, then-President Joe Biden nominated Colom for a federal judgeship, but Hyde-Smith declined to back his nomination, so the Senate Judiciary Committee did not move forward with confirmation. About two and a half years later, Colom launched his campaign for Senate.
President Trump won Mississippi by 20 points in 2024, and the state hasn't elected a Democrat to the Senate in more than 40 years.
Dozens of House seats across the country
Democrats are on track to flip dozens of House seats.
In Iowa, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin, Democrats had a sweep of the most competitive seats.

Democrats defeated GOP incumbent Reps. Mariannette Miller-Meeks of Iowa, Zach Nunn of Iowa, Brian Fitzpatrick of Pennsylvania, Ryan Mackenzie of Pennsylvania, Rob Bresnahan Jr. of Pennsylvania, Scott Perry of Pennsylvania, Brian Steil of Wisconsin and Derrick Van Orden of Wisconsin. They also flipped an open Iowa seat that is currently held by the GOP.

Redistricting helped Democrats win California's 1st District and Utah's 1st District. Redistricting was expected to hamper Democrats' chances in Texas' 15th District and 23rd District, but Democrats pulled off upsets.

In Ohio, embattled GOP Reps. Max Miller and Mike Carey both lost reelection, as did Tom Kean in New Jersey, Ann Wagner in Missouri, Gabe Evans in Colorado, Victoria Spartz in Indiana and Jen Kiggans in Virginia.
Democrats also flipped open seats in Kentucky's 6th District, Nebraska's 2nd District and North Carolina's 11th District.

title: Mississippi Senate race leans Democratic as Colom's lead grows
summary: The Senate race in deep-red Mississippi remains unresolved, as Democrat Scott Colom has mounted a surprisingly competitive challenge to incumbent Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith.
story: Update: Democrat Scott Colom is projected to win, flipping the longtime Republican seat. Read the latest here. Our earlier coverage is below.
Washington — The Senate midterm race in deep-red Mississippi leans toward Democrat Scott Colom, who has mounted a surprisingly competitive challenge against incumbent GOP Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith.

As of Wednesday afternoon, Colom was leading Hyde-Smith by about 4,600 votes, with 99% of the vote in, according to CBS News projections. At one point on the morning after the election, a mere few dozen votes separated the candidates, a stunningly close result in the Magnolia State.

The state's top election official, Secretary of State Michael Watson, said in a post on X Monday that seven more counties of the state's 82 counties still needed to upload their unofficial results, with certified results due from all the counties by Friday. He also said 2,732 absentee mail ballots were still out, and the deadline for election officials to receive them would be Tuesday, Nov. 10. All counties must certify their results by Friday, Nov. 13.

Hyde-Smith, asked by CBS News' Caitlin Huey-Burns what she could have done differently during the campaign to make it less competitive, responded, "I think we worked very hard and had a very good campaign."

Hyde-Smith, 67, has been in the Senate since 2018 and is seeking reelection. But Colom, a district attorney, launched a formidable challenge in a state President Trump won by 20 points in 2024. Mississippi hasn't elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1982.

Democrats saw a slew of wins in Senate races in the midterms, including in states that President Trump won by double digits in the 2024 elections. Democrats have secured enough seats to take control of the chamber in the new year. If Colom manages to pull off a victory, he would add to their majority.

Colom, 43, is a seventh-generation Mississippian who campaigned on cost-of-living and healthcare issues. Democrats began investing in the race in recent weeks, seeing an opportunity for a pickup. But the possible outcome still appeared exceedingly unlikely heading into Election Day.
Speaking to supporters in the wee hours after election night, Colom said, "The results are all trending in our direction."
"We are trending in counties that people thought we had no chance to compete in," Colom said. "And we're winning them."
Mississippi does not allow recounts, so a winner will be decided based on a plurality of votes.
Both parties are keeping a close eye on the process. CBS News has confirmed the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee has deployed lawyers and resources to the state to monitor the count.
"I'm confident that ultimately Mississippi has decided to go in a new direction," Colom told reporters after greeting campaign volunteers Thursday morning in Jackson.

The National Republican Senatorial Committee and Hyde-Smith campaign filed a request for all counties to separate and preserve all affidavit ballots. The Colom campaign called the move a "desperate stunt." His counsel also sent a new letter to Mississippi's 82 counties asking them to respect election procedures.

Hyde-Smith predicted that she will win reelection, posting on X: "We believe thousands of votes remain to be counted from dozens of Republican counties, and we are confident those votes will reinforce her path to victory."

At a news conference Thursday, Mississippi Republican Party Chair Mike Hurst insisted the election "is far from being over" and noted the state party has attorneys and observers throughout the state to ensure all legally cast ballots are counted.
Colom and Hyde-Smith have faced off before.

Then-President Joe Biden nominated Colom for a federal judgeship in the Northern District of Mississippi, but Hyde-Smith declined to back his nomination in April 2023, citing questions about Colom's stance on transgender issues and other concerns. Colom won the support of Mississippi's other Republican senator, Roger Wicker.

Under the Senate's "blue slip" tradition, the Senate Judiciary Committee generally does not move forward with federal district court nominees unless the senators who represent the judicial district sign off — preventing Colom from being confirmed to a lifetime judicial appointment. About two and a half years later, Colom launched his campaign for Senate.
Colom told CNN that "not having a federal judgeship is not a motivating factor for me at all" in his Senate campaign, saying he forgives Hyde-Smith.

The Mississippi contest is one of two still-unresolved Senate races. Alaska's Senate race between GOP Sen. Dan Sullivan and Democrat Mary Peltola is also outstanding, leaving the size of Democrats' majority up in the air.

title: White House warns of "blatant criminality" in Democratic probes
summary: White House counsel Will Scharf warned that congressional subpoenas could lead to investigations from the executive branch.
story: Washington — The top lawyer in the White House warned the leading Democrat on the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee that investigations into the Trump administration that lawmakers plan to pursue in the next Congress "may cross the line into blatant criminality" and said congressional subpoenas could prompt probes from the executive branch.

The message from White House counsel Will Scharf to Rep. Robert Garcia, a California Democrat who is set to chair the Oversight Committee as of January, foreshadows a brewing fight between the Trump administration and congressional Democrats, who are poised to launch investigations in a slew of issues arising over the first two years of Mr. Trump's second term.
Scharf sent a letter to Garcia, dated Monday, reminding him that investigative acts by Congress must be backed by a "legitimate legislative purpose."

"Beyond being inconsistent with the clear, well-recognized constitutional limitations on your investigative functions, threats to executive branch officials designed to deter them from public service, or process designed merely to abuse or instill fear in the recipient may cross the line into blatant criminality," Scharf wrote. "And issuing unlawful subpoenas with the intention of depriving citizens of their constitutional rights and privileges may warrant further investigation."

Scharf cited recent statements from Democratic members of Congress who previewed investigations into the Trump administration they plan to pursue once they take control of the House and Senate. He claimed that Democrats are intent on crossing the Constitution's limits on congressional investigations and subpoenas.

"Abusive threats and public statements about the indiscriminate issuance of subpoenas, along with threats directed at prospective targets within the Administration make it abundantly clear that any forthcoming investigative processes will be deployed to harass and aggrandize rather than to advance any legitimate end," he wrote.
Scharf accused Democrats of making "abusive and capricious threats" and said they are seeking to "abuse the legislative process to intimidate and to interfere with lawful functioning of government."
Garcia said in response to Scharf that the White House is threatening to infringe on his committee's right to conduct oversight.

"It appears Donald Trump has something to hide," the California Democrat said in a statement. "Let's be clear: Congress' authority comes from Article I of the Constitution, not from the permission of the White House. Congress has wide latitude to conduct investigations and oversight, an authority inherent in the power to legislate."
Garcia accused the Trump administration of weaponizing the executive branch against Congress.
"We are a co-equal branch of government and will not be deterred by baseless threats from a weaponized DOJ or from the President's lawyers," he said.

House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries, who is poised to become speaker in January, told reporters that in the first two years of Mr. Trump's second term, the White House has been used to a GOP-led Congress that he said has been a "reckless rubber stamp" for the president's agenda.

"A Democratic Congress is going to be a check and balance on an out-of-control executive branch in the face of unprecedented corruption that they've unleashed on the American people, and if they don't like it, consult the Constitution," he said.
Molly Nixon, a senior fellow in executive power at the Cato Institute, said Scharf's warnings may be more political than legal in nature.

"This letter, I think, is sort of an opening salvo in what will ultimately be a political debate or a public argument about whether Congress is using its power legitimately, and I don't think that's likely to wind up in court, especially on a criminal charge, but is something Americans will be able to judge with their own eyes," she told CBS News.

While the executive branch could attempt to bring a criminal indictment, any prosecution would run into roadblocks because of the Constitution's Speech or Debate Clause, which immunizes lawmakers from criminal or civil actions stemming from legislative duties.
"I think it's incredibly unlikely that any court would find merit in any criminal charge against a member of Congress for their vote on issuing a subpoena," Nixon said.

Mr. Trump's first administration turned to the courts to fight congressional subpoenas after Democrats took control of the House in 2019, and the president could do so again to fight Democrats' demands in the final two years of his second term. In those earlier legal battles, the Justice Department argued Democrats' subpoenas for documents lacked a legitimate legislative purpose, an argument government lawyers could reprise.
While a court may agree that a subpoena does not serve a valid legislative purpose, that doesn't mean it's criminal, Nixon said.
"That might just mean the subpoena doesn't get enforced or that it's quashed," she said. "The criminality question is not coterminous with the legislative purpose question."
Following last week's midterm elections, Democrats are poised to hold at least 254 seats in the House and 54 seats in the Senate, giving them control of congressional committees and subpoena power.
Garcia had a brief message to the Trump administration on the heels of Democrats' rout of Republicans in the fight for control of Congress: "Lawyer up."

Once he takes the gavel of the Oversight Committee, the panel is expected to look into the Trump family's business dealings, corporate corruption, actions by federal immigration authorities and the scandal involving convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.
Garcia said his investigative agenda could also include:

Donald Trump Jr.'s wedding festivities in the Bahamas that were partially paid for by a Russian oligarch.A $2 billion investment that the private equity fund of Mr. Trump's son-in-law, Jared Kushner, received from Saudi Arabia's sovereign wealth fund.The Trump family's crypto ventures.Companies linked to the president's sons that have received Pentagon contracts.Allegations of a pay-to-play scheme and other kickbacks related to Department of Homeland Security contracts.Corporate donations to fund the new White House ballroom.
Donald Trump Jr.'s wedding festivities in the Bahamas that were partially paid for by a Russian oligarch.
A $2 billion investment that the private equity fund of Mr. Trump's son-in-law, Jared Kushner, received from Saudi Arabia's sovereign wealth fund.

Companies linked to the president's sons that have received Pentagon contracts.
Allegations of a pay-to-play scheme and other kickbacks related to Department of Homeland Security contracts.
Corporate donations to fund the new White House ballroom.

Faced with investigations once Democrats regain congressional majorities, Mr. Trump on Sunday accused Democrats of threatening senior members of his administration and claimed they were engaging in "extortion." The president said on Truth Social the Democrats "should be held accountable for this," and he directed the Justice Department to look into their oversight push.
"These SLEAZEBAGS should go to jail for what they are doing," he wrote in a second Truth Social post.

Democrats in Congress have in the past faced resistance from the White House in their efforts to investigate Mr. Trump and his administration. During the president's first term, Democratic-led House committees sought a trove of Mr. Trump's financial records from his accounting firm and two banks as part of an investigation into potential misconduct before and after he took office, whether he had undisclosed conflicts of interest and if he was complying with the Constitution.

Mr. Trump attempted to block the firms from complying with the subpoenas and took the dispute to the Supreme Court. In a 2020 decision, the high court declined to immediately give Congress access to the financial records, but reiterated that subpoenas must serve a "legitimate legislative purpose" and acknowledged that lawmakers have "significant legislative interests."

title: Baby found buried alive, father charged with attempted murder
summary: An infant was found alive after apparently being buried in a dog crate for about 24 hours, authorities in South Carolina said.
story: A baby was found alive in South Carolina after apparently being buried in a dog crate for about 24 hours, authorities said Tuesday.

Eleven-month-old Koah Sharp had been missing since Monday, when he was taken by his father, Michael Comer, according to the Lexington County Sheriff's Department. Comer traveled to multiple locations around Lexington County, the sheriff said, citing investigators. Comer was arrested Monday night and is charged with attempted murder, unlawful conduct toward a child, custodial interference and burglary, according to arrest warrants.

Sharp was later located inside the crate, which was wrapped in a towel, about 50 yards from the home of his grandfather, who is Comer's father, Sheriff Bryan Koon said at a news conference. Search parties, involving almost 100 law enforcement and public safety officers, had been scouring the area for the infant since he went missing. One group spotted what Koon described as a patch of "freshly disturbed dirt" in a wooded area, Koon said.
As officers started digging, they could hear Sharp cry, Koon said.
"So, as you imagine, the race was on. Everybody's getting down there, trying to get him out," the sheriff said.
The officers discovered Sharp "clinging to life," according to Koon, who called the infant's cries "the most joyful sound you ever heard of a crying baby."

Sharp was immediately taken to a hospital for medical treatment and was released Tuesday night, Koon said. The infant is now with family members and, according to information provided to investigators by his medical team, is expected to make a full recovery.

Koon said that Sharp had been in the care of his grandmother, Patricia Comer, on Monday. Michael Comer stayed with the baby at her house while she went out to run an errand, and, by the time a scheduled caregiver arrived shortly after, Comer was gone with his son.
The father was later found hiding in an outbuilding in Batesburg-Leesville, which resulted in the burglary charge, the sheriff's department said.
CBS affiliate WLTX reported that, when Patricia Comer learned the infant had been found, she jumped out of her car and shouted, "He's alive!"
The investigation into what happened to Sharp was still in its early stages when Koon spoke at Tuesday's conference.

Comer was sentenced to probation in October after pleading guilty to domestic violence and aggravated breach-of-peace charges related to an arrest in July, the Associated Press reported, citing Lexington County court records. Prosecutors dropped a gun charge as part of the plea deal.

title: SNAP proposal would increase food insecurity, critics say
summary: Anti-hunger advocates are blasting a proposed change to SNAP rules that could cut off more than 6 million people from access to federal food aid.
story: Anti-hunger advocates are denouncing a Trump administration proposal that would tighten eligibility requirements for the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP).

The proposed rule, introduced on Tuesday by the U.S. Department of Agriculture to seek public comment, would change a policy that extends eligibility for SNAP to people who receive benefits through a social safety net program known as Temporary Assistance for Needy Families, or TANF.
If adopted, the SNAP rule would reduce public enrollment in the program by roughly 17%, the Agriculture Department projects.
White House spokeswoman Allison Schuster said the Trump administration wants to ensure that SNAP serves only "eligible Americans who need it most."

"Rather than throwing money at a broken system, the Trump Administration will continue to stop fraudsters stealing from these important programs, as well as take effective, cost-saving steps to make life more affordable for all Americans," she told CBS News in an email.
Broad push to narrow SNAP
Cutting off so many Americans from food stamps would greatly increase food insecurity at a time when many people are already struggling financially, critics said.

"Instead of listening to the public sentiment on affordability following the election, the administration is continuing its attacks on vital food assistance and the families who need help to put food on the table," Ty Jones Cox, vice president for food assistance at the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities, a nonpartisan think tank, said in a statement.

Some lawmakers also decried the proposed rule. In a statement, Rep. Angie Craig, a Democrat from Minnesota and ranking member of the House Agriculture Committee, called the proposal "heartless and cruel."

The proposal comes amid what advocates say is a broader push by the Trump administration to narrow eligibility for food stamps. The "One Big Beautiful Bill" expanded SNAP's work requirements. As of Oct. 1, states are also required to shoulder a larger share of the cost of administering SNAP, a change advocates say could lead to further benefit cuts.
According to USDA figures, more than 5 million Americans have lost access to food stamps since the "Big Beautiful Bill" was enacted in July 2025.

"Basically, what the administration is doing is continuing on this path of making sure that SNAP is dismantled," said Gina Plata-Nino, SNAP director for the Food Research and Action Center, a nonprofit advocacy group. "The states have so much on their plate that they cannot continue running the program."

Plata-Nino said the Trump administration's changes to SNAP have created additional barriers as hunger in the U.S. is becoming more pervasive. Food insecurity has surged since the pandemic, according to research from the Federal Reserve Bank of New York earlier this year.
"We do know that in terms of hunger, it is going to raise our negative health outcomes," Plata-Nino said of the proposed SNAP rule.
What would the proposed rule do?

The latest SNAP reform proposal would restrict what's known as "broad-based categorical eligibility," a policy offered by more than 40 states that allows households outside the normal SNAP eligibility income threshold to qualify for food stamps if they receive benefits through TANF.
Plata-Nino noted that the longstanding policy authorized by Congress makes SNAP more accessible and lowers costs for states administering the program.

Under the new rule, which would take effect in 2029, households above SNAP's income thresholds would not qualify for food stamps if they receive non-cash TANF benefits, such as childcare assistance or job training.
The Trump administration issued a similar proposal in 2019, but the Biden administration withdrew it two years later.
In the text of the rule, the USDA said the current SNAP eligibility standards mean that even households with $1 million in wealth but no income could technically receive food stamps.

"Broad-based categorical eligibility has bloated the welfare rolls for decades," a USDA spokesperson said in an email to CBS News. "It has allowed states to take shortcuts, error rates to balloon, and those households with income and assets far above federal limits access to a benefit meant for the neediest among us. Correcting this loophole is long overdue."
Who would it impact?
In an analysis of the rule, the USDA estimated that 6.3 million people would lose access to SNAP in 2029, the year the proposal would take effect.

The rule would also impact access to other federal assistance programs for people who qualify based on their SNAP eligibility. Nearly 1.8 million children would lose access to free school lunches, while 5,500 low-income women would lose access to supplemental food aid for women and children, according to the agency.

Plata-Nino said FRAC believes those figures could underestimate the number of people who would lose food aid under the proposed rule. "We know that the impact is going to be higher," she told CBS News.

According to the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities, the rule would cut off SNAP benefits for people with a gross household income just above 130% of the poverty line, or about $35,500 per year for a family of three.

title: United bans AI agents from booking flights on behalf of travelers
summary: Using an artificial intelligence agent to make flight reservations poses security risks and could violate federal rules, according to United.
story: United Airlines said on Wednesday that it is banning artificial intelligence agents from making flight reservations on behalf of travelers, citing security risks and the possibility that such actions could violate federal rules.
Many consumers are turning to AI agents such as Meta's Muse and OpenAI's dots to complete tasks ranging from researching products and tracking down deals to making purchases.

To make an airline booking, an AI agent requires access to a customer's personal information, including credentials like payment information. United has a problem with that, saying that "sharing account credentials with personal, third-party, AI assistants can expose sensitive information, and actions taken by these tools may result in unintended purchases, account changes, or use of MileagePlus miles."

The carrier also said that using an AI agent to, for example, check in for a flight could violate federal regulations, including rules requiring travelers to verify in person that their luggage does not contain banned substances.

"As a result, United is taking steps to restrict access — directly within our digital platforms and indirectly via travel agencies and aggregators — to prohibit use by unauthorized, third-party personal AI agents or assistants," said the airline, which is updating its booking and ticketing policies to reflect the new rule.
United's new policy suggests the company wants to retain control over the customer booking process, said Henry Harteveldt, an aviation analyst at Atmosphere Research Group.

"United is saying they don't want to add yet another, and potentially even more powerful, intermediary than they already face in terms of Google search, price-comparison metasearch sites and online travel agencies," he told CBS News. "Flight searches cost airlines money, and undoubtedly United wants to avoid the expense associated with the surge of AI bot flight searches."

Other airlines are taking a different tack to the emergence of AI agents. For example, Southwest has made its flight inventory viewable to ChatGPT users, who can access the airline's website through the AI app.

United fares will continue to be bookable through flight aggregators such as Kayak, Hopper and Google Flights, Harteveldt said, adding that "consumers shouldn't find it any more difficult to find good fares on the airline."
"But by blocking the AI bots, United won't make it any easier to find its fares, either," he said.

title: Nvidia short-seller warned of Jensen Huang's ties to suspected spy
summary: A small investment firm issued a report about Nvidia in May that foreshadowed issues that have embroiled CEO Jensen Huang in scandal.
story: Recent revelations about Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's links to a suspected Chinese spy have shocked investors, with the chipmaker's valuation sinking $450 billion over two days.

But the relationship, now under investigation by Nvidia, was foreshadowed in May by a little-known Wall Street "short seller," Christian Lamarco of New York City-based Culper Research, who published a 40-page report highlighting Huang's ties to Alice Huang (no relation), a former television reporter and financial industry executive.

Short-sellers use a trading strategy that yields profits when a company's shares decline, and Culper disclosed in its report that it had bet against Nvidia's stock. Short-sellers often publish research to demonstrate why a company is overvalued, aiming to convince other investors to sell the stock, thereby driving the shares lower and boosting their profits.

Lamarco, who didn't immediately respond to requests for comment, based his report on Nvidia on interviews with employees of Chinese companies, Singaporean and Malaysian corporate filings, and social media posts that appeared to show Jensen Huang and Alice Huang socializing together at various events.

The report also outlined Culper's rationale for claiming that Nvidia's high-powered chips were being diverted to China, despite the U.S. barring the sale of such products to the People's Republic due to national security and competitive concerns.

Key to Lamarco's investigation were the actions of Megaspeed International, a Singapore-based company that has emerged as a major player in the Nvidia scandal.  Alice Huang, then a top executive at Megaspeed, is suspected by U.S. intelligence of being an asset of China's Ministry of State Security.
"Uncomfortably close"
Lamarco wrote in the report that Jensen Huang appeared to have an "uncomfortably close relationship" with Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le.

"We believe Nvidia has a significant China problem," Culper Research wrote in a May 13 social media thread. "Nvidia claims its China business went to 'zero' after April 2025 U.S. trade restrictions. We believe that in reality, over 20% of Nvidia's FY 2026 compute revenues remained driven by China via illegal GPU diversion and Southeast Asian intermediaries."

Culper also alleged that Chinese companies used Southeast Asian intermediaries to gain access to Nvidia chips. The firm said corporate filings suggest that one of those intermediaries — Megaspeed — received financing from Chinese e-commerce company Alibaba to buy the chips.
Nvidia didn't immediately respond to a request for comment.

Culper isn't the first to question whether China was using front companies to buy advanced AI chips from the U.S. In a March 23 letter to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, Sens. Elizabeth Warren and Jim Banks warned of a "large-scale diversion of advanced American AI chips to China through Southeast Asian intermediaries."

The lawmakers requested that the Commerce Department immediately suspend active export licenses for Nvidia AI chips and servers to China and to companies in Southeast Asia, including Malaysia, Thailand, Vietnam and Singapore.
Megaspeed's mega-speedy growth

Culper's report notes that Megaspeed had "relatively few assets at year-end 2023," but within a year spent $2.9 billion to purchase Nvidia-powered servers. The short-seller said it found documents that showed the Chinese tech giant Alibaba had provided billions to Megaspeed.
Megaspeed and its Malaysian affiliate, Speedmatrix, together purchased $4.8 billion of Nvidia's advanced AI equipment and processors over the last three years, according to the report.

"Megaspeed went from very little business to billions in a rapid time frame," Culper stated. "This is the exact sort of pattern that experts told us ought to raise alarm bells at Nvidia as indicative of diversion or circumvention activity."
While the firm's research didn't directly refer to a romantic relationship between Jensen Huang and Alice Huang, it included several photos and video stills showing them together at various events.

"Nvidia CEO Huang has walked alongside Megaspeed at every step, and seems to have a close relationship with Megaspeed's Alice Huang," Culper wrote in the May 13 social media thread. "They partied together in June 2024 — same month as the Apex/Alibaba pledge, then dined together in May 2025 — just after U.S. trade restrictions."

Culper, which is named after the American Revolution-era Culper Spy Ring that reported on the movement of British forces, has in recent days posted about the allegations that emerged this week about Jensen Huang's ties to Megaspeed and Alice Huang.  "We wrote about this in May," the group noted on Nov. 5.
When Culper published its report on May 13, Nvidia's stock was trading at $225.83 per share. Between that date and the close of trading on Tuesday, the shares have shed 25% of their value.
"Everyone was just mocking us, and now everyone is singing our praises," Lamarco told the New York Times in a recent interview.

title: Petition for new Epstein files bill gets enough support for vote
summary: GOP Rep. Thomas Massie launched a discharge petition over the summer to circumvent leadership and force a vote on the Epstein Files Transparency Act II.
story: Washington — Republican Rep. Thomas Massie has secured enough support to force a vote on legislation that would compel the release of the remaining Justice Department files related to Jeffrey Epstein.
Massie launched a discharge petition over the summer to circumvent leadership and force a vote on the bill, known as the Epstein Files Transparency Act II.

In order to bring the legislation to the floor, the discharge petition needs 218 signatures. It hit that threshold Wednesday. Four Republicans, including Massie, and all Democrats have added their names. The other Republicans who signed on are Reps. Brian Fitzgerald of Pennsylvania, Nancy Mace and Ralph Norman, both of South Carolina.

The underlying bill allows members of Congress, state attorneys general and Epstein survivors to sue the Justice Department for failing to comply with the Epstein Transparency Act, which was signed into law nearly a year ago after lawmakers pulled a similar maneuver.
Massie has accused the Justice Department of "flagrantly and consistently" ignoring the disclosure requirements of the law.

"The Department of Justice continues to unlawfully withhold over 3 million Epstein files that should be released to the public," he said in a July statement. "In addition, the DOJ is unlawfully maintaining heavy redactions on the files it is releasing."

title: Veterans groups keep focus on traumatic brain injuries
summary: Dozens of service members have suffered TBIs during the current conflict with Iran, and hundreds of thousands of veterans have been diagnosed in the quarter-century of the U.S.'s global war on terrorism.
story: This Veterans Day, advocates are raising awareness about traumatic brain injury and the impact of these types of wounds on the post-9/11 military generation.

Dozens of service members have suffered TBIs during the current conflict with Iran, and hundreds of thousands of veterans have been diagnosed with it over the quarter-century of the U.S.'s global war on terrorism. The recovery can be lifelong.
"The only thing I sort of remember is kind of a mayday call," Army veteran Jon Kohl told CBS News, recalling his 2013 helicopter crash in Afghanistan.
The crash happened just one month shy of Kohl's 25th birthday, leaving him gravely wounded with a spinal cord injury, broken bones and a severe TBI.
"The first moment I saw him, I said it was a miracle he was alive," said his mother, Micha Kohl.
His parents rushed to the military hospital in Landstuhl, Germany, to be by their son's side.
"They had to remove about a quarter to a third of his skull to relieve the pressure," said Paul Kohl.

It would be a year before Jon Kohl could swallow, and he spent about three years under round-the-clock care. Doctors said there was a good chance he wouldn't be able to walk or talk ever again. However, he proved them wrong.
Thirteen years later, regular art and music therapy are aiding his recovery at home as he strives to become more independent.
"One of the oddities of his brain injury is that, while he doesn't remember people talking or things he's reading, he remembers all the music he knew beforehand," his father said.

The special therapeutic services are provided through the Wounded Warrior Project's Independence Program, which aids veterans with moderate to severe brain injuries, spinal cord injuries or neurological conditions. The Wounded Warrior Project says the special therapies they offer come at no cost to the veterans who are eligible for their program.
"Since 9/11, over 530,000 service members and veterans have been diagnosed with some type of traumatic brain injury," said program director Kelly Parker.
Parker describes traumatic brain injuries as an invisible wound, with symptoms that can initially be hard to recognize.
"Some common symptoms you see is persistent headaches, challenges with memory, challenges with concentration, anxiety, depression, sleep disturbances, changes in mood and behavior," Parker said.
Experts say early intervention in treating a traumatic brain injury is critical, but also say symptoms can sometimes start weeks, months or even years after the initial injury.
The Kohl family urges other families to be proactive in getting treatment right away.
"There might be an injury that you can't see, and they still need the help and support you would have given an amputee," said Paul Kohl.
Help, hard work and perseverance have put Jon Kohl on a path to healing and inspiring others.
"Just straight up don't give up; it's all possible," he said.
