title: Trump's judicial confirmations to face resistance in Dem-controlled Senate
summary: A Democratic-controlled Senate is unlikely to help President Trump and Republicans continue their push to remake the federal judiciary in the next two years.
story: Washington — After seeing success in reshaping the federal judiciary in his first term and the initial two years of his second administration, President Trump and Republicans' campaign to shift the courts to the right could be coming to an end with Democrats poised to take control of the Senate next year.

During his first term in office, Mr. Trump successfully put more than 230 judges on the federal bench, including three justices on the Supreme Court, remaking the judicial branch for decades. So far during his second term, the Senate has confirmed 57 of the president's judicial picks. In total, Trump nominees make up about one-third of active federal judges.

But Democrats are now poised to control at least 54 Senate seats, and as many as 56 depending on the outcome of races in Mississippi and Alaska, making it unlikely that Mr. Trump will fill many more vacancies on the U.S. district and appeals courts.

"No one, or nearly no one, is going to get confirmed, so what he does in terms of nominating people, we'll see," Ed Whelan, a distinguished senior fellow at the Ethics and Public Policy Center and former law clerk to the late Justice Antonin Scalia, told CBS News.

There are currently 28 vacancies on the federal courts and another 15 seats that will open up in the coming weeks and months. So far, the president has formally sent to the Senate 16 nominees for those existing and future vacancies, though it's possible he submits more names for consideration before the current Congress finishes its work. Mr. Trump announced on Truth Social earlier Tuesday three more nominees to district courts in Texas and South Carolina.

The GOP-led Senate Judiciary Committee is moving quickly to advance those picks before control of the upper chamber changes hands. It voted to advance four of the president's district court candidates and held confirmation hearings for four other judicial nominees Tuesday.

The panel is expected to hold more confirmation hearings next week, a break from committee practice of holding those proceedings every other week, according to a source familiar with the panel's workings.

Republicans are violating "numerous longstanding standards in a desperate attempt to confirm more than 30 qualified loyalists to lifetime appointments before Democrats take the majority," Sen. Dick Durbin, the top Democrat on the Judiciary Committee, said Tuesday.

Durbin raised concerns about two of Mr. Trump's latest picks to serve as federal judges in Texas: James Sullivan, who lost his bid for reelection to the Texas Supreme Court last week, and T. Elliot Gaiser, the head of the Justice Department's Office of Legal Counsel whose only tie to Texas is a one-year clerkship for a judge on the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 5th Circuit.

The Judiciary panel received information from Sullivan after he lost his campaign for Texas Supreme Court justice last week and from Gaiser on Nov. 8, before the president announced his intent to nominate each man, according to the source. Both are slated to appear before senators for confirmation hearings next week.

"There are many things we still can do, and I hope we'll use them. And one of them is not to expedite nominees who have not been carefully vetted," Durbin said. "I hope we don't accept that as a standard in this committee."

But Sen. Chuck Grassley, an Iowa Republican who chairs the Judiciary Committee, pushed back on Durbin's claim that he is departing from its typical practices. He argued that there are no committee rules about how quickly it can move to hold confirmation hearings or when those proceedings are held, and said chairs have discretion to set the panel's schedule.
"Historically, this committee has shortened timelines when circumstances warrant it," he said.
In anticipation of Democratic control of the upper chamber, Republicans are expected to make judicial nominees a focus of the lame-duck period.
"The priority is going to be getting the judges across the finish line," Senate Majority Leader John Thune told reporters Monday.
But seats on the federal bench that remain open come the end of the current Congress are likely to remain unfilled for at least the next two years.

"For the past two years, we've seen Trump seeking to stack our courts — district courts, circuit courts — with loyalists to him and not to the Constitution, and I think he's going to try to continue to do that," Rachel Rossi, president of the Alliance for Justice, a progressive judicial advocacy group, said. "In this moment, when Trump has clearly created this litmus test that there must be loyalty to him and not the Constitution, it's hard to see how Democrats can support nominees going forward."

It is not unprecedented in the Senate for the party in control to stymie the nominations of a president in the opposing party. During the final two years of former President Barack Obama's administration, when Republicans held the Senate majority, just 20 of his nominees to the district and appeals courts were confirmed. Obama's final judicial confirmation came six months before the end of his second term. Among the candidates that did not get a vote from the GOP-led Senate was Merrick Garland, who was nominated to replace Scalia on the Supreme Court following his death in February 2016.

"What we've seen is the federal courts being stacked with extremists and loyalists, and now Democrats have the power to stop the reshaping of our courts in a very dangerous direction," Rossi said. "I think there's increasing visibility on what judges mean and what these lifetime seats mean, and the hope is that Democrats use their power and stand against any further reshaping of our judiciary."

Of the 43 current and future vacancies, Mr. Trump has not yet announced candidates for more than half of those seats. Many of those are in states that will be represented by either two Democratic senators or one Republican and one Democratic senator next year.
Democrats could work with the White House to find consensus on candidates to serve on the district courts in their states, but it's unclear whether there is an appetite from either side to do so.

"Republicans on the Senate Judiciary Committee and the Trump administration have gutted the committee's oversight and confirmation authority," Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse, a Rhode Island Democrat who is expected to lead the panel next year, said in a statement. "There needs to be accountability for years of Republican bad behavior, and a hard reset on the nominations process next Congress."

Democrats' rout of Republicans in last week's midterm elections also makes it unlikely a Supreme Court justice appointed by a GOP president steps down in the final two years of Mr. Trump's term, given that a successor would likely not clear the Senate.

The president made a significant impact on the nation's highest court, appointing three of the nine justices. Among those was Justice Amy Coney Barrett, who filled Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg's seat following her death in September 2020, during Mr. Trump's first term.

Justices Clarence Thomas, 78, and Samuel Alito, 76, are the two oldest members of the high court, but Alito told The Wall Street Journal in August, "I'm here for another term." Alito also told CBS News chief legal correspondent Jan Crawford last month that while he considered retirement earlier this year, he feels he can still make a contribution to the Supreme Court.

With neither justice expected to step down during the lame-duck session, it could be several years before there is both a GOP president and Senate in place to confirm their potential successors on the Supreme Court, raising concerns among conservatives that a Democratic president and Senate could fill the seats of the influential conservative justices.
"Trump has managed to put in jeopardy his biggest achievement," Whelan said.

title: Pope declares Peru his "homeland" in final leg of South America trip
summary: Pope Leo declared Peru his "homeland" as he arrived in Lima at the start of his historic visit​, returning to the place that taught him how to be a pastor.
story: Pope Leo XIV declared Peru his "homeland" on Wednesday as he arrived in Lima at the start of his historic visit, returning to the place that taught him how to be a pastor and where a nationwide party erupted to welcome the beloved "Padre Robert" home.

Leo seemed genuinely moved as he emerged from his charter plane, smiling broadly at nearly every turn of his first moments on Peruvian soil. The Vatican estimated that some 3 million people lined Leo's miles-long motorcade route into town, waving Peruvian and Holy See flags.

Some in the roaring crowds broke through the tight security to chase behind the car that transported him to the presidential palace, where Leo met privately with Peruvian President Keiko Fujimori. During the formal welcome ceremony in the palace courtyard, he sang the Peruvian national anthem alongside Fujimori and a children's choir.

In his first remarks to Fujimori and government officials, the Chicago-born Leo said the Peruvian citizenship he acquired in 2015 cemented a bond that began long before, crediting Peruvians with having formed him as a pastor by sharing their lives, joys and struggles with him.
"Today I understand how much of this land remains with me and how much of my own story also belongs to you," he said.
"That is why I can tell you, with deep gratitude, that I am also returning to my homeland," he said to applause.
Popemania descends on Peru, where Leo lived and served for decades

The visit to Peru marked the final leg of Leo's three-nation South America tour and its emotional highlight, given the more than two decades that Leo, formerly Cardinal Robert Prevost, spent in Peru as a missionary priest and later bishop. He has said it was here that he learned "what it means to be a shepherd." As a dual citizen of the U.S. and Peru, he's the first pope from each country.
"We love him so much because he's worked here, he knows our sufferings, he knows it all," said 85-year-old Evelina Cruz, who held a pope plush doll made by her niece as she waited for Leo to arrive.

In preparation for the pope's visit, a huge 46-foot statue of the pontiff was unveiled in the port of El Callao. Baristas in Lima, the capital, were offering cappuccinos decorated with the image of the pope.
"My heart is so excited that it makes me want to cry with joy," said Zuly Castillo, who served as Leo's
secretary when he was bishop of the northern city of Chiclayo near the Pacific Coast.
Gustavo Morello, an associate professor of sociology at Boston College and the author of "Lived Religion in Latin America," said the trip was a "return to his origins, without any doubt."
"Peru is the crown of the trip, the homecoming of the first Peruvian pope, no matter where he was born," he said.

With hands raised and voices lifted in song, hundreds awaited the pope's arrival in Lima in front of the presidential palace. "Long live Christ!" the crowd sang, following a Catholic choir on the stage.
Popemania also hit Chiclayo, where Leo arrives on Friday. Leo is painted in colorful murals, emblazoned on T-shirts, baseball hats and even bobblehead dolls.

Over the coming days, Leo will celebrate Mass in all his old stomping grounds including at the nearby sanctuary of St. Turibius of Mogrovejo in Zaña, a city that is a hub of Afro-Peruvian culture, and where the pope often visited to pray to the saint of his devotion.

Since Leo knows his adopted country so well, his speeches will be closely watched, especially one he'll deliver from the square in front of Lima's cathedral Thursday "on the challenges and hopes for the future of the Peruvian people."
Pope to honor Peru's Indigenous peoples in the Amazon

The pope will honor Peru's Indigenous peoples by traveling to Pucallpa, in Peru's Amazon, to celebrate Mass. Illegal gold mining and the cultivation of coca leaves, the raw material used to produce cocaine, are affecting Peru's Indigenous peoples.

"The Amazon is a place where critical issues affecting development — such as the environmental crisis, the exclusion of Indigenous peoples, various forms of violence, and extreme poverty — all intersect," said Pérez.

Leo will also meet with popular groups of faithful and representatives of local traditions in Cusco — the capital of the Inca Empire, an important city of Spanish colonial rule and an important cultural
destination, including the nearby ruins at Machu Picchu.
The pope will celebrate Mass in Cusco's main square, where in 1781 the Indigenous hero Túpac Amaru II was killed following the most significant rebellion against the Spanish during the colonial era.
Pope arrives in Peru about one month after undergoing lung cancer surgery

The pope's arrival in Peru comes about one month after he underwent surgery in Italy to remove a nodular lesion from his right lung, during which surgeons confirmed he had lung cancer. The Vatican announced at the time that the 71-year-old had been diagnosed with adenocarcinoma, and that the surgery had been successful.
Just two weeks after he underwent the surgery, doctors cleared him to make the South American trip, which started in Uruguay and took him to Argentina.
During an address in Uruguay last weekend, the pope used his own experience with cancer to push for access to universal healthcare.

"Recently I experienced firsthand the limitations imposed by illness, and I received care for which I am grateful," the pope said. " … Ensuring that healthcare is accessible to everyone, regardless of their resources, is a duty that confronts every society."
At the start of his trip, the pope also confirmed that he voted by mail in the U.S. midterm elections in Chicago, the first sitting pontiff to vote in a U.S. election.

title: Bessent relocates from home to military base after Iran threats
summary: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has relocated from his home in the Washington, D.C., area to a U.S. military base.
story: Washington — Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has relocated from his home in the Washington, D.C., area to a military base following a series of Iranian threats against his life.

"The secretary will not be deterred by the Iranian regime's threats and remains committed to executing Operation Economic Outcast and maintaining the blockade, which together are collapsing Iran's economy," a Treasury Department spokesperson said.

The decision comes as Bessent has led a U.S. push to cripple Iran's economy, vowing an "economic onslaught" against Tehran through a web of sanctions. The New York Times first reported Bessent's relocation.
A source familiar with the situation pointed to a Wall Street Journal story as the impetus for the move.

"After The Wall Street Journal published an article featuring an online photo that allowed the location of the secretary's Georgetown home to be geo-located, security concerns began to increase which have now forced the secretary to relocate to a military base for his safety," the person told CBS News.
CBS News has also reached out to the White House for comment.
Last month, U.S. national intelligence chief Jay Clayton warned that Iran has "substantially increased" its efforts to target Americans in the Middle East and beyond.

Clayton's warning, contained in an unclassified memo that was sent to Secretary of State Marco Rubio and obtained by CBS News, came as the State Department adjusted staffing at diplomatic posts across the Middle East.

title: Hoax bomb threats affect at least 20 European flights within hours
summary: At least 20 flights in Europe deal with bomb threats, adding to what one expert calls an unusual level of hoaxes in a short time period, suggesting "a very deliberate act."
story: Paris — At least 20 commercial flights in Europe had to deal with bomb threats Thursday, with at least one being diverted to a military base in France. While authorities have reported no explosives discovered on any of the jets, and they all appeared to be hoaxes, Thursday's incidents add to a fast-growing number of journeys hit by similar threats this week, which one expert said suggested a "very deliberate act."

British authorities dismissed threats to about seven flights earlier this week as hoaxes, but the number of impacted journeys soared to at least 27 on Thursday, meaning significant disruption for thousands of passengers and raising concerns about a possible coordinated effort to impact travel on the continent.
At least two more European flights, along with several Irish and British news outlets, got similar threats on Friday.

No authorities have confirmed a link between any of the threats, but Spanish Foreign Minister Jose Manuel Albares said Friday that Europe appeared to be facing "hybrid aggression and a form of psychological warfare."

David Kaminski-Morrow, Air Transport Editor with FlightGlobal, declined to speculate on who might be behind the threats to commercial flights this week, but he noted that "we currently live in a time of political aggression in regions including Europe, and it's a pretty effective tactic if someone is looking to cause disruption."

"The cluster of threats seems unusual, but it's hard to determine the extent to which they might be organized," he said, noting that "the publicity alone could spur further threats unrelated to earlier ones."

Kaminski-Morrow noted that, under an international aviation convention in place for more than 80 years, the pilot in command of a flight has the final authority over its safety, "and airlines always take threats to safety seriously. The business consequences alone of not doing so, even if the threat is proven to be a hoax, would be prohibitive – and you can imagine the cost if it turned out to be genuine."
The flights impacted on Thursday included:

A flight from Ireland to Italy that was diverted to an air base in western France Thursday because of a bomb threat, according to French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu's office. The flight landed safely and all 151 passengers and six crew members deplaned safely, while military bomb defusal teams got to work examining the plane. Flight tracking sites showed that the Aer Lingus Dublin-Rome flight turning sharply off its trajectory as it approached, and then making several loops before heading toward Evreux.A Finnair flight from Helsinki to Rome was escorted to the Italian capital by a fighter jet and was checked by bomb disposal experts, according to Italy's national news agency ANSA. Rome's Leonardo Da Vinci Airport stopped flights for 30 minutes. A second Finnair flight from Helsinki, operated by Jettime, landed as normal in Vienna, Reuters reported. A Wizz Air flight from Milan Malpensa airport to Warsaw was re-routed to Vienna after receiving a threat, also according to ANSA. A second Wizz Air flight bound for Bucharest also landed safely after being targeted, Reuters reported Romanian intelligence as saying.A flight operated by Polish Airlines LOT flying from Warsaw to Brussels landed safely in Brussels airport following security warnings. According to a statement from the airline, authorities carried out an onboard security check after it landed and "no hazardous or suspicious items were found."Three other planes, all Ryanair flights bound for Sofia, made emergency landings in Bulgaria Thursday after indications of potential danger on board, according to Bulgarian National Television (BNT). Flights from Madrid and Copenhagen landed at Vasil Levski Airport in the capital, and one from London Stansted diverted to an airport in Plovdiv. The Bulgarian transport ministry confirmed to CBS News that no explosives or suspicious items were found on any of the planes.Officials in Prague said threats were issued against four flights headed to the Czech capital Thursday. Czech police said on X that all four planes landed safely and no explosives or suspicious devices were discovered. Two of the planes were EasyJet flights, one from Newcastle, England, to Prague, and another from Glasgow, Scotland, to Prague, the airline confirmed. The other flights originated in Dublin and Athens.Italy's national news agency ANSA reported two more flights, scheduled to land Thursday at Milan's Malpensa Airport, landed safely after receiving "bomb alerts." Neither of the flights were diverted. They were Aegean Airlines flight A3552, which departed from Thessaloniki in Greece, and Ryanair flight FR8953, which arrived from Porto, Portugal. Explosives technicians were inspecting the aircraft, ANSA said.  Three flights were affected by bomb threats Thursday at Madrid's Barajas airport, the airport's management confirmed to CBS News in a statement, adding that after "relevant checks carried out by the security forces, the threats were ruled out." Iberia Airlines flights 668 from Milan and 658 from Rome were affected, and the third plane was Air Europa flight 1027, which was impacted before departing for Paris in the morning. An Air Serbia plane flying from Belgrade to Bucharest, Romania, landed safely at its destination Thursday after receiving a bomb threat, Serbia's national air carrier said in a statement shared with CBS News. Air Serbia said "following a bomb threat reported to the relevant authorities at Bucharest Airport during" the flight, the aircraft landed and security agencies found no threatening materials, "after which the aircraft was returned to regular operational service." A second Aegean flight, A3860 from Athens to Vienna, also landed safely at its intended destination Thursday after receiving a bomb threat, the airline said, adding that no threats were found. Greek Deputy Foreign Minister Tasos Chatzivasileiou said in a Facebook post he was on the flight. "Upon landing here, we were informed of a possible bomb on the plane that carried us. The inspection by the Austrian authorities showed that there was nothing," he wrote. "All is well, everyone is safe."

A flight from Ireland to Italy that was diverted to an air base in western France Thursday because of a bomb threat, according to French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu's office. The flight landed safely and all 151 passengers and six crew members deplaned safely, while military bomb defusal teams got to work examining the plane. Flight tracking sites showed that the Aer Lingus Dublin-Rome flight turning sharply off its trajectory as it approached, and then making several loops before heading toward Evreux.

A Finnair flight from Helsinki to Rome was escorted to the Italian capital by a fighter jet and was checked by bomb disposal experts, according to Italy's national news agency ANSA. Rome's Leonardo Da Vinci Airport stopped flights for 30 minutes. A second Finnair flight from Helsinki, operated by Jettime, landed as normal in Vienna, Reuters reported.

A Wizz Air flight from Milan Malpensa airport to Warsaw was re-routed to Vienna after receiving a threat, also according to ANSA. A second Wizz Air flight bound for Bucharest also landed safely after being targeted, Reuters reported Romanian intelligence as saying.

A flight operated by Polish Airlines LOT flying from Warsaw to Brussels landed safely in Brussels airport following security warnings. According to a statement from the airline, authorities carried out an onboard security check after it landed and "no hazardous or suspicious items were found."

Three other planes, all Ryanair flights bound for Sofia, made emergency landings in Bulgaria Thursday after indications of potential danger on board, according to Bulgarian National Television (BNT). Flights from Madrid and Copenhagen landed at Vasil Levski Airport in the capital, and one from London Stansted diverted to an airport in Plovdiv. The Bulgarian transport ministry confirmed to CBS News that no explosives or suspicious items were found on any of the planes.

Officials in Prague said threats were issued against four flights headed to the Czech capital Thursday. Czech police said on X that all four planes landed safely and no explosives or suspicious devices were discovered. Two of the planes were EasyJet flights, one from Newcastle, England, to Prague, and another from Glasgow, Scotland, to Prague, the airline confirmed. The other flights originated in Dublin and Athens.

Italy's national news agency ANSA reported two more flights, scheduled to land Thursday at Milan's Malpensa Airport, landed safely after receiving "bomb alerts." Neither of the flights were diverted. They were Aegean Airlines flight A3552, which departed from Thessaloniki in Greece, and Ryanair flight FR8953, which arrived from Porto, Portugal. Explosives technicians were inspecting the aircraft, ANSA said.

Three flights were affected by bomb threats Thursday at Madrid's Barajas airport, the airport's management confirmed to CBS News in a statement, adding that after "relevant checks carried out by the security forces, the threats were ruled out." Iberia Airlines flights 668 from Milan and 658 from Rome were affected, and the third plane was Air Europa flight 1027, which was impacted before departing for Paris in the morning.

An Air Serbia plane flying from Belgrade to Bucharest, Romania, landed safely at its destination Thursday after receiving a bomb threat, Serbia's national air carrier said in a statement shared with CBS News. Air Serbia said "following a bomb threat reported to the relevant authorities at Bucharest Airport during" the flight, the aircraft landed and security agencies found no threatening materials, "after which the aircraft was returned to regular operational service."

A second Aegean flight, A3860 from Athens to Vienna, also landed safely at its intended destination Thursday after receiving a bomb threat, the airline said, adding that no threats were found. Greek Deputy Foreign Minister Tasos Chatzivasileiou said in a Facebook post he was on the flight. "Upon landing here, we were informed of a possible bomb on the plane that carried us. The inspection by the Austrian authorities showed that there was nothing," he wrote. "All is well, everyone is safe."

The threats to commercial airliners Thursday came after at least seven other flights across Europe received bomb threats this week that prompted aircraft searches, diversions and in at least one other case an escort by an Italian fighter jet.
Some of the threats have been sent to airlines by email, but the nature of all of the messages has not been confirmed.
Hoaxes, but on an unusual scale

The British government described the incidents in a statement on Tuesday as hoaxes and stressed that the U.K. had "one of the most robust aviation security systems in the world, with well-tested processes for dealing with any potential threats, as well as malicious hoax threats, like those we've seen today," according to CBS News' partner network BBC.
Air transport security expert Paul Mason told BBC that threats to passenger planes "don't happen that frequently," making this week's spate of incidents "unusual."

"It sounds like they've been made in a credible manner across a broad range of airlines," Mason told the BBC's Radio 5 Live show. "That would suggest to me that it's been a very deliberate act by a typical actor rather than a load of coincidental, malicious calls."
"There are a lot of processes" that airline crew members and ground staff go through "to validate the credibility of the threat," he said.

While no individual or group has claimed responsibility for any of this week's threats, and no government or security official has pointed the finger at any, the incidents come amid rising concern in Europe about state actors, chiefly Russia and Iran, orchestrating low-level sabotage operations to undermine security on the continent.
The growing "hybrid warfare" battlefield

In October, the head of Britain's domestic spy agency MI5, Sir Ken McCallum, said security threats facing the U.K. and Europe were evolving, with malicious actors attacking not only things owned and controlled by the government, but also "aiming at people, businesses, communities."
"Russia remains aggressor number one," McCallum said.

"The Russian military and intelligence services are once again escalating their attempts at hybrid warfare," McCallum warned, adding that Moscow was "being careful to stay below the NATO Article 5 threshold" with its actions, which would trigger the alliance's collective defense principle.
"It'd be foolish for them to cross" that line, he said, and so far Russia was sticking to "tactics that stop short — though sometimes not much short — of conventional conflict."

Poland launched a large-scale security operation this week along its border with the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad as the Polish prime minister said suspicious activity was seen on the Russian side, and that the fast security response may have prevented a "serious provocation."

The flight threats also come amid a wave of cyberattacks targeting European grocery store chains' refrigerators and freezers, and even French blood banks. The hacks have forced thousands of pounds of food to be discarded in several countries, but French authorities said security systems prevented the loss of any blood stored in cooling units.
France later accused a cyber unit of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps of being behind the hacks on commercial refrigeration units across the country.
Experts told CBS News earlier this year that Russia and Iran were stepping up efforts to recruit sometimes-unwitting criminals to carry out sabotage attacks, often for small payouts.
MI5 boss McCallum, in his remarks last month, said Iran in particular was "using criminal proxies to try to intimidate oppositionists, Iranian media organizations, and Israeli sites" across Europe.

McCallum noted in particular "a wave of arson and sabotage incidents targeting Jewish communities in the U.K. and other European nations," but said Iran was also targeting "harder targets, like military sites."

Many of these attacks were claimed by a group calling itself Harakat Ashab al-Yamin al-Islamiya (HAYI), or the Islamic Movement of the Companions of the Right, which U.K. authorities have sanctioned and said is tied directly to the elite Quds Force of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, which Britain considers a terrorist organization.

A CBS News investigation in March found the group appeared to have links to Iran, and a member said it would "keep threatening U.S. and Israeli interests worldwide until we've avenged every child in Gaza, Iran, Lebanon, and the resistance nations … We urge people to stay away from Zionist and American interests and individuals to keep themselves safe."

Barry Andrews, an Irish Member of the European Parliament, referred to the diverted Aer Lingus flight to Rome on Thursday in a social media post, saying: "This after several hybrid threats and attacks across Europe, and ahead of the major European summit in #Dublin next week. Does anyone still deny Ireland faces serious security threats?"

title: U.S. brokers Ukraine-Russia prisoner swap, but peace not in sight
summary: The U.S. has helped broker a new Ukraine-Russia prisoner exchange and diplomacy will continue, but there's no sign of a breakthrough on a wider peace deal.
story: Officials at U.S.-mediated talks between Russia and Ukraine said Wednesday the two sides had agreed to a large exchange of prisoners of war. Russia's demand to have its seizure of a huge swath of eastern Ukraine recognized as legitimate appeared to remain a key hurdle on the path to any breakthrough on a wider peace deal, however.

"One of the positives is we agreed that we're going to have the biggest humanitarian release of prisoners, which we're going to finalize the numbers tomorrow," Jared Kushner, President Trump's son-in-law and one of the two senior U.S. negotiators at the meetings, said after the two days of talks in Abu Dhabi ended.
Vladimir Medinsky, the head of the Russian delegation, and Rustem Umerov, who led Kyiv's delegation in Abu Dhabi, confirmed the planned exchange.

Hopes had been low for any major breakthroughs in the first meeting in nine months between the delegations. Russia and Ukraine have from time to time swapped prisoners during their nearly five-year war.

U.S. officials have said they are determined to revive Washington's peace efforts, which so far have failed to deliver significant results. Kushner said he and U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff would travel to Moscow Thursday to meet with President Vladimir Putin, then fly to Dublin to meet with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
Putin's senior aide Yuri Ushakov told reporters the U.S. envoys would arrive in Moscow Thursday morning and meet with Putin in the first half of the day.

Asked if there were plans to discuss any major new proposals, including on the dispute over Russia's claim to Ukrainian territory, or security guarantees for both countries, Ushakov said the results of the negotiations in Abu Dhabi were yet to be fully understood in Moscow, but he added that Russia believed Kushner and Witkoff were "bringing something with them."

Medinsky, speaking later to Russia's Vesti program, said Russia and Ukraine had moved closer to peace following the talks, but that much would still depend on the positions of Ukraine and the U.S., as well as "on whether Europe will come to its senses."

Russia has, throughout the war, tried to drive a wedge between the U.S. and its longtime NATO allies in Europe. European nations, along with Zelenskyy, have warned for years — long before Putin ordered the ongoing full-scale invasion — that capitulating to Russia would encourage the autocratic leader in the Kremlin to seek more territorial advances. President Trump, however, has pushed Kyiv to accept a deal that Zelenskyy and the Europeans believe would strongly favor Russia.

The context of the negotiations has changed since the last meeting in February in Geneva. The Trump administration has to reckon with Democrats, who could demand more support for Ukraine, taking over the U.S. Congress in January following the U.S. midterm elections.
Also, Russia's wartime economy is under heavy strain, and Ukraine is reeling from devastating aerial attacks on its power grid.

Umerov said Kyiv's delegation was expected to meet Wednesday with European officials, and Zelenskyy, on a visit to Denmark, acknowledged the prisoner exchange agreement and said after the delegations in Abu Dhabi "discussed their views on guaranteeing security," that it was "necessary that the first step be ending this war and providing security guarantees for Ukraine."

Zelenskyy said that after Kushner and Witkoff's visit to Moscow on Thursday, "we will coordinate our positions once again and determine what next steps are possible," confirming that the American envoys would head from Moscow to Dublin to meet again with Ukrainian officials.

"Ukraine's priority is to end the war as soon as possible with a dignified peace. We believe that Europe must be represented at every stage of real diplomacy," he said. "It is essential that the United States have a strong position and exert influence on the source of this war — that is Russia — so that Russia ends the war of its own making."

Moscow has said it doesn't want European countries, which are concerned about Russia's conduct and broader intentions on the continent, involved in the direct negotiations. However, representatives of European governments, the European Union and NATO were in Abu Dhabi and consulted with the Ukrainian delegation, officials said.

Zelenskyy said Tuesday's session was "constructive and quite substantive," but he balked at what he said had been a U.S. request for Ukraine to accept territorial concessions in exchange for security guarantees that fall short of his long-stated goal of Ukrainian NATO membership.

"No one believes that Putin will stop if we give up the Donbas," Zelenskyy said Tuesday, referring to eastern regions that have been largely, but not entirely occupied by Russia. "He might pause — but then he will return in a year, two years or five years. And who will be to blame then?"

"We discussed in detail the substance of security guarantees for Ukraine and the foundations for their long-term effectiveness," he said Tuesday, stressing that Ukraine needed "practical mechanisms to prevent any recurrence of the war."

This week's talks have largely focused on humanitarian issues, including the prisoner exchange and the potential return of Ukrainian civilians in captivity, as well as children taken from the country, Zelenskyy said.
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio called the Tuesday meeting "very productive," while cautioning that a breakthrough on stopping the war would take time.
Fighting on the front line in eastern Ukraine continues unabated, meanwhile. Little territory has changed hands this year, as both countries batter each other with long-range missiles and drones.

Overnight, Russia struck the southern Zaporizhzhia region and the eastern city of Kharkiv, wounding seven civilians and damaging property. Another strike hit a busy market in the southern region of Odesa, killing three people and injuring 11 others, according to regional governor Oleh Kiper.
Russia's Defense Ministry said air defenses downed 627 Ukrainian drones overnight, 150 of them over the region around St. Petersburg, according to the regional Gov. Alexander Drozdenko.
He said the drones started a fire at the port of Ust-Luga, one of the main facilities for Russian oil exports, injuring three workers.

title: Company under scrutiny for ties to Nvidia and China
summary: The unusual global footprint of Megaspeed, a major buyer of Nvidia's powerful AI computer chips, is fueling questions about whether it's a front for the Chinese government.
story: The unusual global footprint of Megaspeed International, the Singapore-based company at the center of the Nvidia Chinese spy scandal, is fueling questions about whether it's a front for the Chinese government.

One of Megaspeed's leaders is Alice Huang, the woman with whom Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was having an affair, and who is suspected by U.S. intelligence of being an asset of China's Ministry of State Security. In the past three years, Megaspeed, formerly a gaming company, has been one of Nvidia's biggest foreign customers, purchasing nearly $5 billion in AI chips and advanced hardware, The New York Times first reported.

And yet Megaspeed's corporate headquarters sat practically empty, according to The Straits Times, an English-language newspaper in Singapore. Questions have also been raised about its outposts in Australia and Malaysia.

Published reports in recent days revealed that the company listed a newspaper vendor as the director of its Australian subsidiary, and one of its Malaysia offices consisted of a dilapidated storefront outside Kuala Lumpur. Yet another Malaysia office was tucked into a shopping mall.

Megaspeed began as an offshoot of a China-based gaming firm and grew into a juggernaut by gaining access to restricted Nvidia AI computer chips. U.S. investigators say that Alice Huang used her contacts in the industry and a series of shell companies to gain access to 240,000 chips banned for export into China. Now it is being probed in both the U.S. and Singapore for allegedly smuggling those chips into China.
President Trump said this week the FBI is also investigating romantic and business ties between Nvidia's chief executive Jensen Huang and Alice Huang (who are not related).

Earlier this week, Jensen Huang, who is married, apologized for the affair in a statement to Nvidia's employees. The company launched an independent investigation of the matter, and an Nvidia shareholder filed a class action lawsuit Tuesday alleging that Huang concealed a relationship with Alice Huang and misled shareholders about national security concerns raised by the relationship.
Nvidia's board said it had no reason to believe that the company's secrets or national security were compromised.
"The Board prioritizes U.S. national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of NVIDIA and its shareholders," its statement said.

China expert Jacqueline Deal said that Nvidia's advanced AI chips could have ended up with the Chinese military. Deal, who is an adviser to State Armor, a nonprofit that studies global security threats, told CBS News, "If allegations are true, who will be fired? Nvidia has a compliance team that may have failed utterly."

She also questioned the effectiveness of the U.S. Commerce Department, which has jurisdiction over export controls that may have been bypassed, potentially giving the Chinese military access to the world's most advanced chips.
Here's what we now know about Megaspeed:

It is a major Nvidia customer. Megaspeed and its Malaysian affiliate, Speedmatrix, purchased $4.8 billion of Nvidia's advanced artificial intelligence equipment and processors over the last three years.
In 2025, Megaspeed International faced an investigation by Singapore police for alleged breaches of local laws, but no details have emerged about the probe, according to The Straits Times.
The company grew rapidly.

"Megaspeed International is a premier business partner of NVIDIA, strategically positioned in the Asia Pacific region," according to its LinkedIn profile, which claims it has between 201 and 500 employees. Three years ago it listed between two and 10 employees, according to the South China Morning Post.

Megaspeed International did not reply to a request for comment. It posted an "official statement" on its website addressing what it called "misleading information" and "incorrect insinuations" accusing it of involvement in illegal chip transfers.

"We want to be absolutely clear over the past six months our company has undergone multiple on-site inspections and reviews by key institutions, including the Bureau of Industry and Security of the US Commerce Department, the Ministry of Investment, Trade and Industry of Malaysia and NVIDIA," said the message, which also appeared on the company's LinkedIn page.
"These thorough investigations have confirmed that there has been no evidence of any violations concerning the illicit transfer of chips or any illegal activities," the company said.

Megaspeed was originally incorporated in 2015 under the name 7Road International, a subsidiary of a Chinese developer of popular video games and mobile apps based in Shenzhen, China, according to corporate filings.
Huang Le Limited, a shell company in the British Virgin Islands, acquired 7Road International in March 2023. Huang Le is the Chinese name of Alice Huang.
That same month, 7Road International was renamed Megaspeed International, and Huang became its managing director. The company also launched a subsidiary called Speedmatrix.

By the end of October 2023, Huang and another Megaspeed director, Cang Yang, resigned from the company after it was bought up by a firm called Swiftdata, whose director is based in China, documents show.

But there's some indication Huang may still be affiliated with the company. Culper Research, an activist short-selling firm, published a 40-page report on Nvidia in May that cited Megaspeed employees who said Huang was still running the company.

The report also raised some concern about Jensen Huang's relationship with Megaspeed and Alice Huang, stating, "Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has not only vouched for Megaspeed, but seems to have quite literally walked alongside Megaspeed at every step, while maintaining an uncomfortably close relationship with Megaspeed's Alice Huang, a Chinese national."
Megaspeed lists its headquarters office address on the seventh floor of the Ocean Financial Centre in Singapore, a glass office tower in Singapore's central business district.

When the Straits Times and The New York Times visited the Singapore offices around the same time late last year, they found little or no staff working. The Straits Times said the door was locked, and the Times found just two people in its office on a workday.

Megaspeed has an Australian subsidiary on the 10th floor of a commercial and retail tower in the heart of Sydney's central business district. Forty other businesses are on the same floor, and space in the building can be rented for as little as $17 per day, Australia's ABC News reported. Corporate filings name Shanghai-born Kai Kang, a 29-year-old newspaper vendor, as the director, according to Australian news reports. But Kang's newsstand is in Northern Victoria, over 400 miles from Sydney. Kang's father told Australia's ABC News this week that he had never heard of Megaspeed.

title: Thousands of schools in Europe get hoax bomb threats
summary: Less than a week after more than 20 European flights got fake bomb threats, hundreds of schools in Italy, the U.K. and Ireland were hit by similar hoaxes.
story: Rome and London — Thousands of schools across Europe received apparently hoax bomb threats Wednesday, prompting mass evacuations in Italy. The threatening messages were sent to at least 6,300 schools in Italy alone, as well as hundreds in Ireland and across the U.K.

There have been no reports so far of explosives or suspicious devices found at any of the schools, but investigations were continuing. The threats came less than a week after more than 20 European commercial flights got fake bomb threats, forcing many to divert.

While authorities have not assigned any blame yet for the bomb hoaxes, they are fueling growing concern about the impact of wider hybrid warfare tactics that officials and security experts say Iran and Russia are using to target Europe amid the ongoing wars in the Middle East and Ukraine.

Schools in Rome, Milan, Naples, Palermo, Bologna and several other cities were affected, with lessons suspended and precautionary evacuations ordered. Police, bomb disposal specialists and the Postal Police conducted inspections and were investigating the origin of the messages.

Italian news outlets published an email they said was received by the schools across the country on Wednesday claiming to be from "Mikhail Andropov, leader of the Vilayat of Misoginistan," a Russian misogynistic extremist group that was banned by authorities in Moscow several years ago.
CBS News confirmed last week that a message attributed to the same name and same group was sent to airport authorities in Rome, threatening two of the flights affected by the mass hoaxes on Nov. 5.
"We have come to annihilate you," read the email published by Italian media on Wednesday. "I have just left a powerful explosive device with a remote detonator inside a plastic bag in your building."
The email also contained threats to Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni.
Meloni said there was no "concrete danger" behind the threats, and called it part of "a strategy aimed at causing alarm and concern."

She called a meeting for later Wednesday with Italian intelligence officials and cybersecurity experts, to discuss the potential connection with recent threats against airlines, and the identification of those responsible.

This is the third wave of bomb threats against Italian schools in a month, following messages received on Oct. 19 and then Nov. 2, when approximately 280 schools got threatening messages, according to Italian media.
Hundreds of schools in Ireland and across the United Kingdom also received threatening emails Wednesday.

Ireland's national police, the Garda, said in a statement that it was "aware of a generic communication that has been sent to a number of educational establishments" but it added that the threat had been deemed "not credible" and that the force was "not advising any educational establishment to evacuate."
Police in Northern Ireland said emails threatening schools there appeared to have originated outside the United Kingdom.

In addition to the threats to airliners last week, the school threats also come amid international investigations into cyberattacks targeting grocery store refrigeration units in both Europe and the U.S., blood banks in France, and wider "hybrid warfare" sabotage and disruption efforts attributed by Western authorities largely to Russia and Iran.

The New York Times and Reuters reported, meanwhile, that U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent had relocated from his home in Washington, D.C. to a military base following an Iranian threat to his life.
Hybrid warfare targeting "people, businesses, communities"

In October, the head of Britain's domestic spy agency MI5, Sir Ken McCallum, said security threats facing the U.K. and Europe were evolving, with malicious actors attacking not only things owned and controlled by governments, but also "aiming at people, businesses, communities."

"Russia remains aggressor number one," McCallum said, accusing its military and intelligence services of "once again escalating their attempts at hybrid warfare," and adding that Moscow was "being careful to stay below the NATO Article 5 threshold" with its actions, which would trigger the alliance's collective defense principle.

Iran, he said, had made a "major shift" in its efforts to attack the U.K., including going after harder targets such as military bases and "using criminal proxies to try to intimidate oppositionists, Iranian media organizations, and Israeli sites" across Europe.
Experts told CBS News earlier this year that Russia and Iran were stepping up efforts to recruit sometimes-unwitting criminals to carry out sabotage attacks, often for small payouts.
McCallum noted "a wave of arson and sabotage incidents targeting Jewish communities in the U.K. and other European nations," but said Iran was also targeting "harder targets, like military sites."

Many of the attacks on soft targets have been claimed by a group called Harakat Ashab al-Yamin al-Islamiya (HAYI), or the Islamic Movement of the Companions of the Right, which U.K. authorities have sanctioned and said is tied directly to the elite Quds Force of Iran's Revolutionary Guards, which Britain considers a terrorist organization.

A CBS News investigation in March found the group appeared to have links to Iran, and a member said it would "keep threatening U.S. and Israeli interests worldwide until we've avenged every child in Gaza, Iran, Lebanon, and the resistance nations … We urge people to stay away from Zionist and American interests and individuals to keep themselves safe."

title: Cartel boss helped Olympian traffic drugs, evade capture, U.S. says
summary: A cartel boss bribed Mexican public officials to help Olympian Ryan Wedding avoid capture while running a multinational drug trafficking organization, the Department of Justice said.
story: A cartel boss shot to death by police in Mexico last week helped Olympian Ryan Wedding traffic drugs and avoid the authorities before his arrest in January 2026, the U.S. Department of Justice said on Tuesday.

In an indictment unsealed Tuesday, federal prosecutors alleged that Edgar Aaron Vazquez Alvarado, or "El General," trafficked cocaine for Wedding's criminal enterprise and provided the organization with "near-daily, rotating code words" that were used for safe passage through law enforcement checkpoints. Vasquez, 42, also allegedly paid Mexican public officials to slow down criminal investigations, tamper with evidence and dismiss criminal charges.
Vasquez also helped Wedding personally avoid U.S. law enforcement for two years, the Justice Department said.

The founder of Mexico City's El Cártel Nuevo Imperio, Vasquez was shot and killed by Mexican security forces attempting to serve an arrest warrant in Naucalpan, Mexico, according to Mexico's Security Minister Omar García Harfuch. Harfuch said Vasquez fired on security forces and was responsible for the 2024 death of Milton Morales, a Mexico City police chief.

The U.S. Justice Department also announced a six-count federal indictment against Roberto Gomez, a U.S. citizen and gang member living in Mexico. Federal prosecutors allege that Gomez has spent the past decade as a drug supplier to international criminal organizations, including Wedding's.

Gomez primarily transported cocaine, methamphetamine and fentanyl from Central America to Mexico with planes and maritime vessels, then used land-based methods to bring those substances into the U.S. and Canada, prosecutors say. His efforts allegedly included attempting to broker the sale of 1,000 pounds of methamphetamine between a supplier and Wedding. The sale would have been worth about $550,000, the Justice Department said.

From 2024 to 2026, Gomez, 51, also allegedly helped Wedding avoid apprehension by U.S. authorities. The department said that Gomez's connections with cartels, including the powerful Sinaloa Cartel, and relationships with "individuals who had access to law-enforcement sensitive information from Mexican and U.S. agencies" allowed him to obtain information about law enforcement operations.
If convicted on all charges, Gomez would face a mandatory minimum sentence of 10 years in federal prison and a maximum sentence of life in prison.

The United States has made dozens of arrests while investigating Wedding's international drug trafficking network. Wedding allegedly ran the network as part of the Sinaloa Cartel and orchestrated several killings.
A Mexican judge was arrested last week and charged with taking bribes to free an accused drug trafficker linked to Wedding.
FBI Director Kash Patel has referred to the former Olympian as "a modern-day 'El Chapo." Wedding was placed on the FBI's Top Ten Most Wanted List before his arrest.

Wedding faces 17 felony charges, including those related to drug trafficking and murder, across two indictments. He has pleaded not guilty. The Justice Department said that he will remain in U.S. custody without bond.

title: U.S. soldier accused of spying linked to Russia arrested in the U.K.
summary: A U.S. official told CBS News the suspect is a senior officer based at Imjin Barracks, home to the headquarters for NATO's Allied Rapid Reaction Corps.
story: A U.S. Army soldier has been arrested in the U.K. on suspicion that he engaged in espionage linked to Russia, British and U.S. authorities announced Tuesday.

The 41-year-old suspect was not identified, but a U.S. official told CBS News he is a senior officer based at Imjin Barracks, home to the headquarters of NATO's Allied Rapid Reaction Corps. He was arrested Tuesday near Gloucester, about 100 miles west of London.

The soldier is suspected of violations under Section 1 and Section 3 of the U.K.'s National Security Act of 2023 — obtaining or disclosing protected information and assisting a foreign intelligence service, respectively. The London Metropolitan Police said the suspected activity relates to Russia and that the force was carrying out searches at two locations in Gloucestershire — the county where the base is located — related to the investigation.
The suspect was in custody in a London police station as of Tuesday, according to Brig. Gen. Sean Stinchon, commanding general of U.S. Army Counterintelligence Command.

"The allegations are serious and our investigation is very much ongoing," Deputy Assistant Commissioner Vicki Evans, senior national coordinator for the U.K.'s Counter Terrorism Policing force, said in a statement. "This activity demonstrates the strength of our UK and US law enforcement and national security partnerships, and I commend the work of all the teams involved. We will work together to take robust action against those we suspect of any criminal activity that could undermine our national security."

FBI Director Kash Patel said in a statement that "this FBI has no tolerance for anyone who breaks their oath to the United States and whose actions endanger our national security and that of our partners."
Speaking to reporters Wednesday in Moscow, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Russia had "nothing to do with" the detention of the U.S. soldier.

In an annual threat update last month, Sir Ken McCallum, the head of Britain's MI5 spy agency, accused Russia of "escalating their attempts at hybrid warfare," calling them "aggressor number one" when it comes to threats against the United Kingdom.

The arrest came as the U.S., Russia and Ukraine began a new round of trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi, the first such talks aimed at ending the war between Russia and Ukraine in about nine months. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called the discussions "constructive and quite substantive," although it seems none of the participants expect any immediate breakthroughs, with Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov rejecting European demands for an immediate ceasefire.

U.K. police said the arrest was not related to "any other ongoing Counter Terrorism Policing investigations," meaning it appears to be unrelated to the recent suspected plot at RAF Fairford, which officials have said is linked to Iran. The U.S. military last month removed its bombers from that base after a security incident that led to the arrests of five British men and one U.K.-Iranian national in late September. There are U.S. troops stationed at RAF Fairford, a British Royal Air Force base.

On Tuesday, the U.S. Justice Department announced that three people it accuses of being Iran-backed operatives were charged with plotting a terrorist attack at RAF Fairford. One of the suspects is in custody in New York. However, the other two are not in custody at this time, two sources familiar with the matter told CBS News.

title: 4 grizzly bears killed mom and daughter in Canada, DNA confirms
summary: DNA tests linked four bears to the deaths of Jenny Balcarras and her daughter, Selah Reed, officials said. All four bears were killed to protect the public.
story: Four grizzly bears captured in western Canada were responsible for killing a mother and her adult daughter this month in what investigators believe was a rare predatory attack, wildlife officials said Tuesday.

DNA tests conclusively linked a female grizzly and her three yearling cubs to the deaths of Jenny Balcarras, 48, and her 20-year-old daughter, Selah Reed, the British Columbia Conservation Officer Service said. All four bears were killed to protect the public.
"Our investigation also found that this attack likely involved predatory behavior, which I can tell you is very rare," Inspector Jeff Tyre told an online briefing.
"That is to say, we don't know how it started, but we know how it ended."
The women's remains were found about 150 meters (490 feet) apart near a trail outside Bella Coola, a remote community about 1,000 kilometers (620 miles) north of Vancouver.

Family members raised the alarm after Reed missed a routine Saturday night call with her sister. Searchers found her mother's remains first, then discovered Reed's remains in a bear cache, where bears store food.

Tyre said the bears were not involved in a separate grizzly attack last November on a group of about 20 elementary school students and teachers in the same area. Eleven people were injured, including two critically.
The latest killings have shaken the Nuxalk Nation community, which is still recovering from last year's attack. Local authorities imposed a voluntary curfew, and police escorted children to school.
"This attack has been deeply re-triggering for our community members as we continue to recover from last year's attack," said Tlhmtimut Samuel Schooner, the Nuxalk Nation's elected chief councilor.
He said community support services would remain available as long as needed.
Tyre said bears involved in fatal attacks cannot be rehabilitated or relocated because they pose an extreme risk to public safety.

"This was a heartbreaking event for the families, the Nuxalk Nation and the Bella Coola community. We hope the efforts of everyone who responded, along with these findings, bring some measure of closure," Tyre said.
Other bear attacks in British Columbia

There are between 10,000 and 13,000 grizzly bears estimated to live in British Columbia, according to the province's Ministry of Environment, Lands and Parks. The species is classified as vulnerable. Conflicts between grizzly bears and humans are considered "relatively rare," the ministry said, unless the animals are startled or protecting their cubs or food. Still, there have been a number of grizzly bear attacks in the province in recent years.

In October 2025, a grizzly bear injured two hikers in British Columbia's McGregor Mountain area, northeast of Prince George. One of the hikers was transported to the hospital in critical condition and died a few weeks later due to complications from the injuries. The grizzly bear was later found dead, according to the B.C. Conservation Officer Service.

A man suffered "significant injuries," including broken bones and lacerations, after being attacked by a grizzly bear while hunting in British Columbia's Elkford region in May 2024. He was able to shoot the bear to defend himself. The animal was later found dead. The man was flown to an area hospital for treatment.

A 21-year-old woman was seriously injured by a grizzly bear near Tumbler Ridge in British Columbia in July 2023. Authorities described the incident as a "defensive attack." The victim was transported via helicopter to an area hospital.

title: Judge denies motion to dismiss Trump's defamation case against BBC
summary: A U.S. federal judge has denied a motion to dismiss President Trump's defamation case against the BBC, allowing the case to proceed.
story: A U.S. federal judge denied a motion on Tuesday to dismiss President Trump's defamation case against the BBC, allowing the case to proceed.

In December 2025, Mr. Trump filed a $10 billion lawsuit against the British Broadcasting Corporation, the U.K.'s public broadcaster, over a documentary that featured edited parts of the speech he delivered on Jan. 6, 2021, as his supporters massed around the U.S. Capitol in what would become an assault on the heart of the government.

In the lawsuit, filed in the Southern District of Florida, attorneys for Mr. Trump accuse the BBC of publishing a "false, defamatory, deceptive, disparaging, inflammatory and malicious depiction" of him in an episode of the network's "Panorama" program, which aired a week before the 2024 election.

The case alleges the BBC "intentionally and maliciously sought to fully mislead its viewers" by "splicing together" two clips of the same speech Mr. Trump gave to supporters before the riots began. The president's legal team claims the two clips were 55 minutes apart and the edit omitted "his statement calling for peace."
On Tuesday, Judge Jeffrey Kuntz denied the BBC's motion to dismiss the defamation case, effectively allowing it to proceed.
"Whether President Trump can prove these claims and establish he sustained damages at summary judgment or trial is left for another day," Kuntz wrote in his decision.
Mr. Trump hailed the decision as "A Huge Victory against Fake News BBC, a terrible abuser of the truth," in a post on his Truth Social platform.
A spokesperson for the BBC, quoted by the network's news division, said: "We are surprised by this decision but respect the Court's authority and note the case will now proceed to the next stage."
"We remain confident in our position and will continue to respond through the proper legal process," the spokesperson added.

On Oct. 22, a federal judge in Miami said Mr. Trump must sit for a deposition with BBC lawyers by Dec. 11, warning that if he did not, he could face penalties, including possible dismissal of the lawsuit, unless the period for the president and the network to collect information in the case is extended.

Mr. Trump had been due to sit for a deposition in October, but his lawyers told the BBC in late September that he would no longer be available to answer questions, "due to other matters of national importance."
The president has said he will be available for the deposition in the second or third week of January, according to the BBC.
In November 2025, the BBC issued an apology to the president over the editing of his speech as featured in the documentary.

"BBC Chair Samir Shah has separately sent a personal letter to the White House making clear to President Trump that he and the Corporation are sorry for the edit of the President's speech on 6 January 2021, which featured in the programme," the BBC Press Office said in its statement at the time.
"While the BBC sincerely regrets the manner in which the video clip was edited, we strongly disagree there is a basis for a defamation claim," the press office added.

title: Grim details emerge after bears kill woman and daughter
summary: The delay in finding the remains of the two women was complicated by difficult terrain and the grizzly bears' behavior.
story: Selah Reed's family first knew something was wrong when the 20-year-old missed a routine Saturday night call with her sister.

When no one had heard from Reed or her mother, Jenny Balcarras, by the next morning, they asked the Royal Canadian Mounted Police to check on their home in Bella Coola on British Columbia's central coast. Balcarras' car was gone and the doors were locked. They found the car at a trailhead up the road, but Balcarras and Reed were nowhere to be found.

Family members across Canada and the U.S. started mobilizing. Jenny Balcarras' brother, Matt, headed north from Vancouver Island, and his brother left from Calgary. They met and drove through the night but got a call late Monday that their sister had been killed, likely by a grizzly.
When they arrived at the trailhead Tuesday morning, ready to join the search for Reed, her remains had also been found. The search was now a tragic recovery effort.

The killings of Jennifer Balcarras, 48, and her daughter happened only 1.8 to 2.4 miles from where a grizzly attacked a group of schoolchildren and teachers last year as they walked on a trail. Eleven were injured, two of them critically, in the Nov. 20, 2025, attack.

Jeff Tyre, an inspector with the Conservation Officer Service, said that aggressive bear was never captured, but officials were able to collect its DNA. Officials set new traps in the hopes of catching the bear involved in last weekend's attack and to learn whether it was the same bear from a year ago. On Nov. 11, the conservation service said forensic testing had confirmed that four bears — an adult female and her three offspring — captured in the traps were involved in the attack that killed Balcarras and her daughter.

"After considering the evidence and in accordance with provincial human-wildlife conflict response guidelines, conservation officers dispatched all four bears to protect public safety," the agency said, adding that the investigation "found that the encounter likely involved predatory behavior."

"This was a heartbreaking event for the families, the Nuxalk Nation and the Bella Coola community. We hope the efforts of everyone who responded, along with these findings, bring some measure of closure," Tyre said in the new statement.
The forensic testing also confirmed that the bears involved in the recent attack were not the same animals behind the attack on the school children last year.
Terry Webber, chief administrative officer for the Nuxalk Nation, said previously that the killings were triggering for the families traumatized by that attack.

"Our community is still healing," he said, adding that they've imposed a curfew and are providing mental health services for the community. "Our priority is to ensure they're safe and ensure our community is supported."
Bear attack complicated the search
The delay in finding the remains of the two women was complicated by difficult terrain, even though it was close to the trailhead, and the grizzly bear's behavior.
Searchers found Jenny Balcarras first, then her daughter. The search was helped by more resources and a cadaver dog, Matt Balcarras said.

Searchers found his niece's remains in a bear cache — a place where bears stash food, sometimes by digging a small hole and covering it with branches and vegetation to keep other animals and birds away.
"Even though it was within 100 or so meters (330 feet), locating remains in a cache is difficult," he said.

By the time officials located his niece, she could only be identified by her clothing, he said. His sister was in a similar condition, but they knew who she was thanks to several tiny tattoos, he said.
"There's no obvious body to identify," he said. "The coroner's investigation will include DNA and dental work. But there is no doubt that the remains that were found are theirs."
Balcarras was comfortable in challenging environments

Grizzly bears are common in the area surrounding the Bella Coola community, officials said. Conservation officials maintain a hotline where people can report problem bears, but no calls had been received recently, Tyre said during a media briefing.

Balcarras, an art therapist, had moved to Bella Coola during the summer. She had previously lived in Alaska, where her children were born, and was "the central organizing person in our family," Matt Balcarras said.

"In classic, strong single-mother style, she scraped together a career and a life for herself and her kids," Balcarras said. She was small in stature but strong in character and physical abilities, he said.
She was comfortable living among the wildlife, he said.

"She lived in the Bush when her kids were babies," he said. "She and my niece were not naive or foolish or uninformed. They've lived in these areas and have been around animals of countless types for years and years and decades."
Other bear attacks in British Columbia

There are between 10,000 and 13,000 grizzly bears estimated to live in British Columbia, according to the province's Ministry of Environment, Lands and Parks. The species is classified as vulnerable. Conflicts between grizzly bears and humans are considered "relatively rare," the ministry said, unless the animals are startled or protecting their cubs or food. Still, there have been a number of grizzly bear attacks in the province in recent years.

In October 2025, a grizzly bear injured two hikers in British Columbia's McGregor Mountain area, northeast of Prince George. One of the hikers was transported to the hospital in critical condition and died a few weeks later due to complications from the injuries. The grizzly bear was later found dead, according to the B.C. Conservation Officer Service.

A man suffered "significant injuries," including broken bones and lacerations, after being attacked by a grizzly bear while hunting in British Columbia's Elkford region in May 2024. He was able to shoot the bear to defend himself. The animal was later found dead. The man was flown to an area hospital for treatment.

A 21-year-old woman was seriously injured by a grizzly bear near Tumbler Ridge in British Columbia in July 2023. Authorities described the incident as a "defensive attack." The victim was transported via helicopter to an area hospital.

title: 3 Iran-backed operatives indicted for alleged role in terror plots
summary: Three Iran-linked operatives are accused of plotting a terrorist attack at an air base in the U.K. and attempting over a dozen attacks in the U.S. and Europe.
story: Three Iran-backed operatives have been charged with plotting a terrorist attack at a British Royal Air Force base in the United Kingdom where U.S. troops are stationed, the Justice Department announced on Tuesday.

Mohammad Baqer Saad Dawood Al-Saadi was indicted in May on federal charges of conspiracy to provide material support to Iran-backed terrorist organizations, including Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps and Kata'ib Hizballah. He is accused in an eight-count superseding indictment made public Tuesday of attempting to coordinate with two other operatives to attack the British Royal Air Force base in the U.K. in September.

Al-Saadi is currently in federal custody in New York. In Tuesday's filing, the Justice Department alleged that he had plotted the air base attack with Mohsen Mohajeri, an Iranian national, and Mohammad Ali al-Hassani, an Iraqi national, by "passing them coded messages through third parties."
Mohajeri and al-Hassani are not in custody, two sources familiar with the matter told CBS News.

Federal prosecutors allege that beginning in August, Al-Saadi "directed and paid" associates in the United Kingdom to prepare for and arrange an attack at RAF Fairford, including directing an unnamed individual to conduct surveillance at the air base. Al-Saadi then allegedly later paid multiple unnamed people to organize vans and barrels of fuel, and to research chemical accelerants and buy metal to be used as shrapnel for a potential attack.
The indictment alleges that three individuals would then drive the vans, filled with fuel, to RAF Fairford, where they would explode.

Prosecutors say Al-Saadi told the individuals to mark the vans with custom decals to disguise themselves as a fuel delivery or pool supply business and directed his family members to pass messages to his co-conspirators.

In one phone call with his sister from July, Al-Saadi asked his sister to pass on messages to Mohajeri about "work," referring to terrorist activity, and asked if some of their work was canceled or paused.
Al-Saadi's sister replied that the work "isn't cancelled."
On Sept. 24, Al-Saadi allegedly asked how al-Hassani was, and instructed his family to "give him money so we can do it," referring to the RAF Fairford attack.

The indictment then alleges that al-Hassani directed three individuals to drive the vans on Sept. 26 to RAF Fairford. Two of the vans encountered security checkpoints and were not able to proceed on their intended route to the base, the indictment alleges.
Federal prosecutors said that law enforcement authorities in the United Kingdom recovered three vans with fuel delivery business decals on them and arrested the drivers.

Prosecutors previously alleged that Al-Saadi had plotted to carry out terror attacks in the U.S., including at a prominent Jewish institution in New York. They also accused him of being "involved in the planning, execution and promotion" of approximately 18 reported terror attacks in Europe and two in Canada against U.S. and Israeli interests since March, in retaliation against the U.S. and Israel's military actions in Iran.
In a statement, Attorney General Todd Blanche said "anyone who plans a terrorist plot on a military base housing American servicemembers will be prosecuted by the United States government."

She was unconscious when airlifted to a hospital, and Racing NSW released a statement Tuesday from her family that she had died.

Rider Diego Montes de Oca was also dislodged from his horse during the race, Racing NSW said in a statement, adding that he suffered a foot injury but was later discharged from the hospital.
Neale had 699 career starts in her career, local media reported.

Her brother Tommy Neale wrote on Facebook that he couldn't "believe what's happened," adding: "You'll always be my lil baby sister, you were my best friend an we always was so close so I dunno how I'm gonna deal with this."
