title: France says Iran behind costly grocery store refrigeration hacks
summary: The Paris prosecutor's office says investigators have determined that a cyberattack on grocery store chains was "carried out to serve a foreign power — in this case, Iran."
story: French officials believe Iran was behind nationwide cyberattacks on commercial refrigeration units at hundreds of grocery stores in October, the Paris prosecutor's office said Monday, accusing a cyber unit of Iran's powerful Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps of carrying out the costly hacks. On Tuesday, France's foreign minister said the country "rules nothing out" in its response to what he called "a terrorist organization that has committed an attack of unprecedented scale and aggression against our country."

The Oct. 11 hacking attack struck major supermarket chains, hitting "700 retail locations across France," according to the prosecutor's office, which said the attack caused "significant food spoilage and triggered roughly twenty fires" as the temperatures in refrigeration units shot up.

The attacks on the French grocery store chains were followed weeks later by similar hacks affecting refrigerators and freezers at supermarkets in Belgium, Luxembourg and Sweden. A separate cyberattack targeted several blood banks in France, but the products and samples were not damaged.

In August, refrigeration outages at six U.S. military bases sparked an ongoing investigation by the Department of the Army Criminal Investigation Division, Thomas Hamilton, a public affairs officer for the department, told CBS News. Hamilton told CBS News this week that the division's Cyber Field Office was working with French law enforcement to understand the refrigeration outages in Europe.
There has been no assertion yet by officials in France, the U.S. or the other European nations hit by the hacks that all of the incidents were connected.

In its statement Monday, the Paris public prosecutor's office said its cybercrime division had opened a judicial investigation on charges including "fraudulent interference with an automated data-processing system and causing damage by means dangerous to persons — both committed as part of an organized group."

It said the alleged offenses were "further aggravated by the fact that they were carried out to serve a foreign power — in this case, Iran — in addition to participation in a criminal conspiracy to prepare for the commission of a serious crime (felony)."

According to the allegations, the investigation is targeting the leader of an Iranian group known as "Shahid Kaveh," which the prosecutor's office described as "a cyber-offensive unit affiliated with the Electronic and Cyber Center of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC-ECC) — as well as his two deputies and any other individuals who may be identified."

"The attackers gained remote control of the equipment via web interfaces, initiating indefinite, abnormal defrost cycles while simultaneously disabling safety alerts — alerts designed to trigger when temperatures exceeded specific thresholds," the prosecutor's office said, adding that the probe had "uncovered an attack methodology characteristic of this [Iranian] unit, including the use of the Persian (Farsi) language and IP addresses that trace back to devices located in Iran."
French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot said Tuesday that the country "rules nothing out" in terms of its response to the cyberattack.
"This is a terrorist organization that has committed an attack of unprecedented scale and aggression against our country," Barrot told French broadcaster Franceinfo.
"We are going to summon the [Iranian] ambassador and will call for European sanctions," he said, adding that "we will not stop at merely" those measures in response.
Barrot called the cyberattack "a major threat to the security of the French people" and said the government was "taking every measure to deter any further attacks."

Later Tuesday, the foreign ministry reitterated most of Barrot's remarks, and said in a statement that the hack was "unprecedented in its scale and level of aggressiveness and has been the first offensive cyber campaign carried out purely for the purposes of sabotage on French soil."

In a statement shared on social media last week, the FBI's cybercrime branch said that, along with its partners, it was "seeing malicious cyber activity targeting industrial refrigeration and cold-chain monitoring systems around the world," noting that "security weaknesses in unpatched or internet-accessible controllers can allow attackers to change system settings, potentially causing inventory loss and equipment damage."

The FBI urged all organizations that rely on such systems to take their controllers "off the public internet" and to keep access to the systems behind a firewall, in addition to other security measures.

There was no immediate response from Iranian authorities to the allegations by the French prosecutor on Monday, but the regime has threatened for months to expand its retaliation for the war launched by the U.S., and the ongoing U.S. naval blockade of its ports, using unspecified, asymmetrical means.
CBS News' Karine Barzegar contributed to this report.

title: Reported Iran threat sees U.S. move planes from second U.K. base
summary: The reported movement comes just over a month after a security incident at a separate air base hosting U.S. aircraft used in the war with Iran.
story: The U.S. military moved nine Stratotanker refueling planes from a base in England to facilities in Germany and Spain on Monday, and The Wall Street Journal quoted sources as saying they had been repositioned due to a threat from Iran.
It is unclear whether the threat was imminent or general, the sources told the newspaper.
A U.S. official told CBS News later Tuesday that there were credible threats against bases in the U.K., without specifying who was behind the threats.

CBS News Confirmed found public aircraft tracking data showing 10 KC-135 Stratotankers were moved from Royal Air Force Base Mildenhall, in southeast England to other locations. One landed at Glasgow Prestwick Airport in Scotland, while four went to Spangdahlem Air Base in Germany and one landed at Ramstein Air Base, the headquarters of the U.S. Forces Europe, also in Germany.
Four more Stratotankers left Mildenhall and arrived Monday at Morón Air Base in southern Spain.

"We take proactive measures to ensure our aircraft, our people, and our installations remain safe and secure," a U.S. official told CBS News on Tuesday, without commenting on specific aircraft movements.

Three U.S. Osprey tiltrotor transport planes also departed RAF Mildenhall and arrived Tuesday at RAF Lakenheath, another base used by the U.S. in England. It is unclear whether all of the movements were linked to the reported threat from Iran.

A spokesperson for the U.S. military's European Command said they could not comment on "specific force protection measures," adding that, "in close partnership with our host nation allies, both RAF Mildenhall and RAF Lakenheath remain vigilant" and that along with U.K. authorities, "we are taking coordinated and appropriate actions to ensure the safety and security of our U.S. service members, U.S. and host nation civilians, contractors, and all of our families."

A U.S. Air Force spokesperson told CBS News earlier Tuesday that aircraft routinely "rotate between installations and operating locations for a variety of reasons including training and real world requirements."

The spokesman added that "U.S. military aircraft are hosted in accordance with access, basing, and overflight agreements with our Allies and partners. Due to operations security, we will not provide further information on movement of assets."

The U.S. Air Force 100th Air Refueling Wing, which has been based at RAF Mildenhall for years, did not immediately respond to CBS News' request for comment on the aircraft movements. The 100th air wing is the only permanent U.S. refueling wing in Europe.

The relocation of the aircraft comes just over a month after the U.S. Air Force decided to remove all of its long-range bombers from RAF Fairford, another air base in England that had been used to launch strikes on Iran, following a security incident there.

On Sept. 27, five British men were arrested on suspicion of explosives and terrorism offenses close to the Fairford base. The suspects were later released on bail. A month later, two men were charged with security-related offenses in connection with the incident.

Mohmed Abdulkarim, 24, was charged with "assisting a foreign intelligence service" and "engaging in conduct that was likely to materially assist a foreign intelligence service in carrying out U.K.-related activities."

Nouman Essghir, also 24, was charged with a national security offense after he "approached or was in the vicinity of a prohibited place and his conduct was for a purpose that he knew, or having regards to other matters known to him ought reasonably to have known, was prejudicial to the safety or interests of the United Kingdom."
U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said at the time that Iran was believed to have "played a part" in the September incident, though he did not provide any details.

"There are strong indications that Iran played a part in what happened over the weekend at RAF Fairford, but of course it remains an ongoing, complex and serious police investigation, and of course we are working closely with our colleagues in the United States of America," Burnham told the BBC in October.

U.K. counterterrorism police said no explosives were found in extensive searches of the three vehicles operated by the men arrested near RAF Fairford, only some fuel and a number of large, mostly empty plastic drums.

title: U.S. becoming first nation to refuse U.N. Human Rights Council review
summary: "This irredeemable body makes a mockery of human rights through consistent failures to uphold its own 'values' as it pushes anti-American rhetoric," a State Department spokesperson said.
story: Geneva — The United States is set on Tuesday to become the first country to fully shun a regular review of its human rights record at the U.N.'s top rights body since it was created two decades ago.
The Trump administration last year pulled the U.S. out of the Human Rights Council, accusing it of an anti-U.S. and anti-Israel bias, and alleging that it didn't uphold the very values it promotes.

Supporters back the council's mandate to keep tabs on human rights in all U.N. member states including the U.S., which has drawn criticism for its policies including strong-arm deportations and targeted killings of alleged drug-runners in the Caribbean and Pacific — which the administration has said are designed to protect U.S. workers and help keep the country safe.
The Geneva-based council regularly examines the rights records of all 193 U.N. member states — generally about every four to five years — as part of a process known as the universal periodic review.

The United States, under President Trump, already skipped its appointment for its review a year ago. The scheduled November 2025 review was pushed back until Tuesday in hopes that the U.S. government might change its mind.
It did not.
"(W)e give no credibility to the agency," a State Department spokesperson said in an email to The Associated Press.

"This irredeemable body makes a mockery of human rights through consistent failures to uphold its own 'values' as it pushes anti-American rhetoric," the spokesperson said, alleging the council has a "persistent failure to condemn the most egregious human rights violators."
The council says the process requires participation of the country in question, and in the case of an absence of any national representatives, the review cannot go forward.

As part of such reviews, national delegations - which at times can include a dozen officials or more - make a presentation, face questions and hear recommendations from other national envoys. It's supposed to be a sweeping and constructive process, akin to holding up a mirror to governments to improve their human rights policies.
Critics of the U.S. move warn that the walkout could encourage other countries - many of which bristle about intense scrutiny from human rights monitors - to follow suit.

Jamil Dakwar, director of the American Civil Liberties Union's human rights program, said: "The administration is saying to the world, 'we don't care about whether you would review us or not, we're going to continue to violate human rights unabashed.'

"And we are saying: 'No, enough is enough. This council should hold the United States accountable,'" he told reporters Monday in Geneva, as part of a push by some groups to raise awareness about the U.S. rights record.
He said the ACLU and its allies have called on the U.N. human rights chief to respond by presenting an update on rights in the United States early next year.
Eric Tistounet, a visiting professor at the Geneva Graduate Institute, who was the council's first secretary, said the U.S. walkout could affect the credibility of the council's review system.
"If the predominant global power — which has always claimed to adhere to the human rights norms — doesn't show up and doesn't even justify why, then you are in big trouble," he said.

title: Thomas Markle Sr., Meghan's father, arrested in Florida
summary: It was reported in October that Meghan's estranged father, Thomas Markle, was under investigation by authorities in the Philippines for alleged possession of child sexual abuse materials.
story: Thomas Markle Sr., the estranged father of Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, was arrested Friday in Florida in connection with allegations he possessed child sex abuse material in storage units in California, the Justice Department announced.
The announcement came after three sources familiar with the matter confirmed the arrest to CBS News.

The Justice Department said Markle was arrested for allegedly keeping child sexual abuse material, including sexually explicit photographs of himself with prepubescent girls, in two Los Angeles-area storage units he rented for nearly two decades.

"These allegations are extremely serious, and we will prosecute Mr. Markle to the fullest extent of federal law," Bill Essayli, first assistant U.S. attorney for the Central District of California, said in a statement.

Markle, who made his first court appearance in federal court in Tampa on Friday, entered the courtroom in a wheelchair, wearing black pants and a black T-shirt with an illustration of a cat drinking a tropical drink.

Markle was advised that this hearing was related to the items found in two storage units in California. Prosecutors said they have not made a determination on whether he stays in Florida or is transferred to California, where the charges originated.

U.S. Magistrate Judge Thomas Wilson ordered Markle released on personal recognizance and ordered him to submit to home detention and electronic monitoring. Markle is also not permitted to travel outside the Middle District of Florida and the Central District of California.
No plea was taken. Markle's arraignment date in the Central District of California is not yet scheduled, but likely won't happen for at least several weeks.
The Daily Mail, a British tabloid newspaper, first reported Markle's arrest.
Allegations in Philippines lead to U.S. and Mexican investigations

Last month, it was reported that Markle was under investigation by authorities in the Philippines for alleged possession of child sexual abuse material. Markle has denied the claims against him, calling them "sick lies."
"I have never downloaded anything like that in my life," he was quoted as telling the Daily Mail.

A spokesperson for the Philippine National Police told CBS News in a statement that they launched an investigation after Markle's personal items were turned over to law enforcement by his son, Thomas Markle Jr.
Markle Jr. told the Sun tabloid last month that he reported the images to police in the Philippines and contacted the FBI.
"I have supported, cared for him and helped him for years — but that stops now," Markle Jr. told The Sun. "I won't speak to my father ever again unless I'm called to give evidence against him."
The Daily Mail reported last week that it alerted the FBI of a cache of child porn found inside a storage unit Markle Sr. had rented near his former home in Rosarito, Mexico.
In a statement on Friday, the Baja California State Attorney General's Office in Mexico confirmed to CBS News that a search was conducted on Oct. 29 after a report via the 911 emergency line.

"During the operation, three old magazines and VHS tapes containing child pornography were discovered," the office said in its statement. "The evidence and the associated case files were referred to the Attorney General's Office (FGR), which will handle the follow-up to the case."
DOJ's claims against Markle Sr.

According to an affidavit in the complaint filed in federal court, the investigation in the Philippines led law enforcement to investigate two storage units registered to Markle Sr. in the Los Angeles area that he had rented since 2008, with the most recent payments on both made last month by auto-pay.

Inside the units, agents with the FBI seized 78 items, including slides, film negatives and books that contained suspected child sexual abuse materials. In one of the units, agents found at least 18 images that appear to constitute child pornography.
Two of the images found allegedly show an adult man — whom a witness identified as Markle Sr. — with a nude prepubescent girl, the affidavit said.

A third image allegedly shows a nude prepubescent girl in a room that appears to be part of a motel chain in the Philippines. Other photos allegedly show Markle Sr. with children in various stages of undress, the affidavit said.

"Mr. Markle allegedly targeted innocent children and sought to steal their innocence through his criminal actions," FBI Director Kash Patel said in a statement, adding: "This FBI will use every single resource at our disposal to protect innocent kids – any predator who targets children will have zero safe haven in this country or anywhere they try to hide."
If convicted, Markle Sr. would face a statutory maximum sentence of 20 years in federal prison.
Meghan distanced herself because of allegations years ago

After the reports of the investigation were made public, Meghan, who recently moved back to Britain with her husband Prince Harry and their children, said in a statement sent to CBS News that she had been aware of the allegations against him since 2018 and that the allegations were shared with U.K. authorities at the time.
She said it was based on that information that she and Harry decided to cut her father off from contact with their children.

"I hope it can now be understood that, despite certain media publications' distortion over the years, any distance from my father and my choice to not allow him to have contact with our children, was for one reason: to protect them," she said.

Meghan also confronted her father last year about the child sexual abuse allegations leveled against him, according to CBS News partner BBC News. Video that the British tabloid the Daily Mail says it obtained exclusively shows Markle accepting a letter sent by his daughter in his hospital room in the U.S. in December 2025.
According to the BBC, in that letter, Meghan wrote that she and authorities "knew he had abused young girls," adding that he would never meet her and Harry's children Archie and Lilibet.
Meghan will not be commenting on the arrest at this time, sources say.

title: Kelsey Grammer still feels 'sense of smallness' for not serving in military: 'I do my best to make up for it'
summary: Kelsey Grammer's giant screen film, "America the Beautiful," celebrates national parks and military sacrifice ahead of its Veterans Day premiere.
story: The actor admitted to feeling ‘an annoying sense of smallness’ for having never served in the military but says he does what he can to 'make up for it.'
Kelsey Grammer feels he missed an opportunity to give back to his country by not serving in the military when he was younger.

During a recent interview with Fox News Digital, the 71-year-old actor discussed his latest project, "America the Beautiful," a 40-minute giant screen documentary, and why he always does his best to "show up for the military" when he is able to.
"I will always have an annoying sort of sense of smallness that I didn't serve, but I do my best to make up for it," he said.
He explained that, despite feeling that way, he is unsure if he would have made a different decision if given the opportunity to do his life over again, noting, "It was a really interesting time."

"So, I was thankful for not having to go, make that decision, but I would've gone. If my number had been up, I woulda gone. But I was, I was thankful not to," he said.

"I used to work in San Diego. It was one of my first jobs at the Shakespeare Festival there, and I would go over to the Point Loma Military Graveyard and have a lunch sometimes. I mean, with this particular thing, the 11 hour, the 11 day, 11th month, Armistice Day originally, now Veterans Day at the end of the first World War. Remarkable. The number of people who died in that war," he said.
"So, certainly the hope was that it would never happen again and, sure enough, a generation later, we were fighting World War II. Amazing. And we go on. We continue. Hopefully it'll end one day."

Grammer feels a strong connection to Veterans Day since his grandfather served as a colonel in the Army Corps of Engineers during World War II. When speaking about his grandfather, the "Frasier" star said he "was always an inspiration to me."
Grammer said his grandfather inspired him when he was younger. (Samuel Corum/Getty Images)

"I looked up to him like a kid would," he said. "I mean, he raised me, but his bravery and his courage and his commitment to the country, these were active, living, breathing things that he was … he embodied that. And, so, it's always been my hope to kind of pass that along a little bit. At least a remembrance of him, respect for what he was able to do in the face of extraordinary hardship."
CARRIE UNDERWOOD, GARY SINISE LEAD STARS WHO'VE SHARED WHY THEY'RE PROUD TO BE AMERICANS
One way in which Grammer is honoring his grandfather — and all the other men and women who have served the country — is through his new film, "America the Beautiful," which hits screens Nov. 11.
Grammer is honoring veterans with his new film, "America the Beautiful." (Michael Buckner/Variety via Getty Images)
GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE
The film was created in honor of America's 250th birthday and celebrates the beauty of the country and the love of the land Americans share for it.
WATCH: Kelsey Grammer’s new documentary, ‘America the Beautiful,’ showcases the beauty of the country

"That was the original idea of the movie, why they made it, and they invited me to join in. I think it's absolutely apropos. I mean, without the sacrifices that have been made by our military men and women, then we might not actually have this treasure of national beauty that we do have," he said.

"The Americans that have gotten to know our national forests and our national parks. They are inspired by them every day and blessed by the fact that they're still here. And I think that speaks in large part of the sacrifices that people make abroad and at home to secure our future and to defend our country."
Through making the film, he was able to understand President Theodore Roosevelt's philosophy that "we have to preserve our physical life as well as our creative and our ideological life."

He learned how Roosevelt was allotted "time to seek solace in nature" and gather inspiration and comfort from it, leading him to create the national park system, believing "everybody should be able to have" the same "personal relationship with the wilderness" as he found.
Grammer's hope for the film is that audiences are able to understand the "overwhelming beauty we have been given" in this country, calling it "powerful" and saying "it defines us."
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS
Grammer hopes audiences are overwhelmed with the beauty of America after watching his new film. (Roy Rochlin/Getty Images for Paramount+)
Of all the places he visited, he called the Badlands his favorite, saying, "I felt like I was in a holy place" while he was there, saying it felt like being "in God's land."

"It was just an amazing day we spent there and, of course, then we went and saw Mount Rushmore. We also saw on the way there … a mountain called a Crazy Horse, which is like four times bigger than Mount Rushmore," he said.

"It's an amazing thing that a private family's been working on it for 60 years, maybe longer, where it's just Crazy Horse seated on his steed, and he says, with his finger pointing outwards, sort of like this, he says, ‘My lands are where my dead lie buried.’
WATCH: Kelsey Grammer hopes viewers see ‘the overwhelming beauty we have been given’ in new documentary

"And that's powerful stuff, but I think that is an American saying. That is an American occurrence. It's these two cultures clashed, and then he became a new culture together, but it's all based on that land, this extraordinary land that we have.

"And, yeah, it's a rainbow. It's a cornucopia of life and teaming, teaming life, renewal, power, all these things that actually really are America. They live here, and I'm proud to have done the movie."

title: Antonio Sabato Jr and Virginia Madsen's son arrested in fatal hit-and-run
summary: Jack Sabato, son of Antonio Sabato Jr. and Virginia Madsen, faces felony charges after a fatal hit-and-run in Anchorage, Alaska, police say.
story: Jack Sabato allegedly struck 42-year-old Carl Simmonds while delivering for DoorDash and fled without stopping.
Antonio Sabato Jr. and Virginia Madsen’s son, Jack Sabato, has been arrested in connection with a fatal hit-and-run in Anchorage, Alaska, Fox News Digital has confirmed.

According to the Anchorage Police Department, Sabato, 32, was arrested Nov. 9 on charges of leaving the scene of an accident without assisting the injured and leaving the scene of an accident resulting in injury or death.

Police identified the victim as Carl Simmonds, 42, who was pronounced dead after officers and medics responded to reports of an unresponsive man near Airport Heights Drive and Debarr Road around 5:48 a.m. A preliminary investigation indicated a vehicle struck Simmonds and fled the scene, police said.
VIRGINIA MADSEN SAYS VETERANS AREN'T TRAINED TO COME HOME AFTER NEPHEW'S SUICIDE
Virginia Madsen and Antonio Sabato Jr.'s son, Jack, was been arrested in a fatal hit-and-run. (Getty Images)

According to court records obtained by Fox News Digital, Jack has been hit with a felony charge of leaving the scene of an accident without helping the victim, as well as a misdemeanor charge of leaving the scene of an accident involving injury or death.
Charging documents reviewed by Alaska Public Media reported that responding officers found Simmonds' body on the sidewalk off Airport Heights Drive and several car parts scattered around.

While reviewing security footage from a nearby bank, officers saw a white Chevy Tahoe striking Simmonds and not braking before or after the crash, according to the outlet.

After running the vehicle’s description into the Alaska Public Safety Information Network, law enforcement found the matching vehicle — which is registered to Jack — parked at the Anchorage Amazon warehouse. The vehicle was then seized.

According to the charging documents, Jack told police he struck "something" while driving home after delivering for DoorDash, damaging his headlights. He said he believed he hit an animal and didn’t stop because he was driving without insurance. He also said he ran a red light because he felt unsafe driving without headlights.
He said he planned to report the crash after work but contacted police after his girlfriend told him his SUV had been seized, saying he "knew the worst," according to the documents.
On Wednesday, Sabato — who's best known for his role as Jagger Cates in "General Hospital" — took to Instagram to share his thoughts.

title: Country star Craig Morgan says he's 'willing to die' for America after returning to military service
summary: Craig Morgan says he's willing to die for America's freedoms as the U.S. Army reserve officer releases his patriotic new album "My Country."
story: The country singer re-signed up for the military three years ago told Fox News Digital that every other service member feels the same way.
Country singer Craig Morgan, a U.S. Army Reserve warrant officer, says he is willing to die for his country to preserve America's freedoms.

"I am willing to go wherever they send me and do whatever it takes to ensure that we maintain the freedoms," Morgan, who reenlisted in the Army in 2023 after previously serving for nearly two decades, told Fox News Digital. "And not for me, but for my family, for my friends, for my friend's kids, and for the kids that I don't even know."
He said he thinks every American service member feels the same way he does.
AARON TIPPIN SAYS PATRIOTISM IS 'VERY STRONG IN AMERICA' AHEAD OF FORT CAMPBELL 4TH OF JULY SHOW
Craig Morgan said he's willing to die for America's freedoms. (Getty Images)
"Listen, like the [Toby Keith] song ‘American Soldier’ says, ‘I don't want to die, but if dying is asked of me, I will.’ And I believe that more people, even those that don't serve, feel that way."
The "Redneck Yacht Club" singer, who lives in Tennessee, said, "That's what we celebrate."
LEE GREENWOOD SAYS HE'S 'VERY PROUD' TO STAND NEXT TO TRUMP DURING AMERICA'S 250TH CELEBRATION

"But absolutely, I am willing to die for my country and to die for the freedoms that I get to celebrate. I want my grandchildren and their children and their grandchildren to celebrate those same freedoms."
Morgan released a new 11-song album, "My Country," on Nov. 6, which features a cover of "American Soldier."
Craig Morgan's new album was released on Nov. 6.  (Courtesy Craig Morgan)
CARRIE UNDERWOOD, GARY SINISE LEAD STARS WHO'VE SHARED WHY THEY'RE PROUD TO BE AMERICANS
"We're celebrating our 250th," he said. "I just felt like it was most appropriate as we celebrate that as a nation that I'm able to do it in my genre, in my format, in my occupation."
WATCH: CRAIG MORGAN SAYS HE IS WILLING TO DIE FOR HIS COUNTRY

He said he feels like he’s always celebrating America, "but we took it, I feel like we took it a step further with this actual project, a physical project, celebrating our nation, hence the name ‘My Country,’ but for me, it had a dual implication."
Craig Morgan served in the Army for nearly two decades before taking a break for his country music career.  (Courtesy Craig Morgan)
COUNTRY STAR CHRIS JANSON SAYS RESPECTING THE FLAG IS THE NUMBER ONE LESSON HE WANTS HIS KIDS TO LEARN
At the risk of sounding biased, Morgan said he thinks country music "celebrates the love and passion for our freedom and for our nation much more than the other genres."
KID ROCK TAPS EMINEM FOR CHRISTIAN ALBUM, PLANS BEER-AND-FAITH ARENA REVIVALS
Craig Morgan stands with an Air Force service member at the ACM Presents: An All-Star Salute To The Troops at the MGM Grand Garden Arena in Las Vegas in 2014. (Getty Images for ACM)

"We don't shy away or steer away from our belief in God, family, and country," he added, "and this project really kind of hits at both of those, both of my worlds, my military world and my music world."
The 62-year-old is especially proud of the original track "Long May You Wave," which he called "extremely personal" and emotional.
Craig Morgan at his swearing in ceremony at the Grand Ole Opry when he reenlisted in 2023.  (Courtesy Craig Morgan)
BLACK RIFLE COFFEE CO-FOUNDER RELEASES NEW MUSIC VIDEO HONORING FALLEN SOLDIERS AHEAD OF MEMORIAL DAY

"Having served in the military for over 20 years now, that flag represents something that I think — there was a time in our nation that it had been taken for granted. I do believe that we're back in a place where we respect that flag, we respect what it stands for. And I'm not saying that we didn't, but I think generally we lost sight of what it is that flag represented and the many, many men and women who have sacrificed in order to ensure that that representation is not tarnished."
Craig Morgan originally joined the Army in 1985.  (Courtesy Craig Morgan)
The song is about middle-class America — "the people that really built this country and the people whose backs we stand on," he said.
DOLLY PARTON'S ‘ALL-AMERICAN HEART’: HOW COUNTRY ICON FORGED SPECIAL BOND WITH US MILITARY
The cover of "American Soldier" is in honor of Keith "and in honor of what he stood for," he explained.
Craig Morgan wrote a song called "Long May You Wave" for his new album. (Getty Images)
"For me, that song again is extremely personal," he said. "I am an American soldier and I love my country and I love what this song says about us."

Morgan said service members don’t "stand out there and wave our flag, so to speak, but this song is a testament to, in my opinion, the moral fiber that makes up those people who serve our nation. And I'm grateful to have the honor to be able to record that song."
WATCH: CRAIG MORGAN ON WHY HE'S RELEASING HIS PATRIOTIC ‘MY COUNTRY’ ALBUM NOW
He added that country music offers listeners a "sense of reality, a sense of truth. Also, all of this wrapped up in humility, grace, and gratitude."

"The general populace of the country music format, including the artists, come from a place of humble beginnings, come from a place of Middle America," he said. "We talk about, sing about, and represent, and live the lifestyle of the people that build America, as I alluded to earlier. And I still live that lifestyle. A lot of people don't believe it. I mean, you know, I don't always cut my own grass, but I do sometimes, but I still take off my own garbage when I'm home."
Craig Morgan said he hopes his grandchildren inherit the same level of patriotism he holds dear.  (U.S. Army photographer  Robert Hold)
Speaking about his own family, Morgan said he hopes his grandchildren "inherit the attitude towards our nation that my grandfather had and that I feel like I have."

"One thing that I see now that I did not see four years ago is a sense of pride in our nation, a sense of pride in their jobs," he said.
He said he doesn’t preach his politics, "but here's what I tell every one of them: If we are not a safe nation, all of the other stuff that you celebrate will not matter. It's that simple."
Craig Morgan attended the America Salutes You Celebrating the 250th Anniversary of the U.S. Armed Forces last November. (Getty Images for ABA)
Morgan also held a Veterans Day 5K in Nashville on Veterans Day this year to bring attention to the charities he supports and raise money for them and to celebrate veterans.

Equally important to Morgan is his faith.

He’s fine with people disagreeing with him, and he doesn’t want to convert everyone, "because that's God's job. title: Katy Perry's comment that ex 'should be in jail' resurfaces after Russell Brand's prison sentencing
summary: From Kate Moss to Katy Perry to wife Laura Gallacher Brand, Russell Brand's romantic history spans high-profile romances and a headline-making divorce.
story: A London judge sentences Russell Brand to 10.5 years in prison for sexual assault. Senior foreign affairs correspondent Greg Palkot reports on the details of the case from London.
Russell Brand's romantic past is drawing renewed attention following his prison sentencing, including ex-wife Katy Perry's description of his behavior during their marriage as "very controlling."

Years before the comedian was convicted of rape and sexual assault, Perry said Brand struggled with her role as "the boss" of her own career and shared how their whirlwind marriage ended with a text message in which he announced he wanted a divorce.

Now, her past comments are resurfacing alongside renewed interest in Brand’s relationship history, from his brief romance with Spice Girls singer Geri Halliwell to his marriage to his current wife Laura Brand, who testified in his defense.
RUSSELL BRAND SENTENCED AFTER RAPE, SEXUAL ASSAULT CONVICTIONS IN UK
Here's a look back at Brand's most notable relationships.
Kate Moss — 2006
Kate Moss and Russell Brand had a brief romance in 2006. (Getty Images)
Brand described a brief romantic encounter with Kate Moss in his memoir, "Booky Wook 2: This Time It's Personal," writing that their connection elevated his celebrity status.
"I could never have anticipated the instant elevation that this liaison would afford me, it was like being awarded a celebrity Victoria Cross," he wrote, according to the New York Post.
The comedian, who met Moss through a mutual friend, expressed his admiration for the model in the book.

"Kate Moss is the prettiest girl in all our schools," he wrote. "Behold our queen, but don’t look at her directly or all else you gaze upon till death brings down your lids will be as shadows compared to her beauty."
In the book, Brand wrote that he became smitten, but their connection faded after he publicly downplayed the encounter to journalists.
Teresa Palmer — 2008
Teresa Palmer and Russell Brand attend the O2 Silver Clef Awards at the Park Lane Hilton Hotel in London on July 4, 2008. (WireImage)

Brand and Australian actress Teresa Palmer briefly dated after meeting while filming "Bedtime Stories" in 2008. By July of that year, both were publicly discussing their relationship, with Brand suggesting he was ready to leave his womanizing reputation behind.
"I’m a changed man," he said at the time, according to Cosmopolitan. "I’ve met someone very beautiful and I’ve settled down."
Palmer expressed similar enthusiasm about their budding romance.
"We’ve only been together for a month, but it’s going brilliantly," she said, according to the outlet.
The pair attended the O2 Silver Clef Awards together in London on July 4, 2008, but their relationship was short-lived. By the fall of 2008, the couple had separated.
KATY PERRY SNUBS FAMOUS EXES BEFORE SWEET NOD TO JUSTIN TRUDEAU IN CHEEKY ONSTAGE MOMENT
Katy Perry — 2009–2012

Katy Perry and Russell Brand attend the Rolling Stone after party for the 2010 American Music Awards at Rolling Stone Restaurant & Lounge on Nov. 21, 2010, in Los Angeles, California. (Jason LaVeris/FilmMagic)

Brand and Katy Perry, who met on the set of "Get Him to the Greek" in 2009, announced their engagement in January 2010 before marrying in India on Oct. 23 of that year. Their marriage lasted approximately 14 months before Brand filed for divorce in December 2011.
Perry later discussed their relationship in a 2013 Vogue interview, describing behavior she considered "controlling."
KATY PERRY FIGHTS BACK AGAINST RUBY ROSE'S 'CATEGORICALLY FALSE' SEXUAL ASSAULT ALLEGATIONS

"He didn’t like the atmosphere of me being the boss on tour. So that was really hurtful, and it was very controlling, which was upsetting," she said. "I felt a lot of responsibility for it ending, but then I found out the real truth, which I can’t necessarily disclose because I keep it locked in my safe for a rainy day. I let go, and I was like: This isn’t because of me, this is beyond me. So I have moved on from that."

During the interview, Perry said Brand informed her of his divorce plans by text message. The moment she received the message was captured on camera and featured in the pop star's 2012 documentary "Katy Perry: Part of Me."
Following Brand's sentencing, another video showing an interaction between Brand and Perry gained traction online.
Brand and Perry finalized their divorce in 2012. (Olivier Touron/AFP via Getty Images; Dave Benett/Getty Images for Experience Abu Dhabi)
During an interview at the 2010 Vanity Fair Oscar party, Brand appeared to criticize Perry for swearing on camera and displayed a badge bearing the word "Obey."
"He didn’t like her getting more attention than him," one social media user wrote on X.
Months before his conviction, Perry made a pointed remark about an ex during a concert in July at Blenheim Palace in Oxfordshire, England.

Singer Katy Perry and actor Russell Brand attend the 3rd Annual "Change Begins Within" Benefit Celebration presented by The David Lynch Foundation at LACMA in Los Angeles on Dec. 3, 2011. (Getty Images)
While playing an interactive game that asked audience members to act out their reaction to seeing an ex, Perry said, "I hope my ex isn’t here. He should be in jail," according to The Mirror.
Perry did not specifically name Brand.
Isabella Brewster — Summer 2012
Russell Brand had a brief romance with Isabella Brewster in 2012. (Getty Images)
Brand began dating Isabella Brewster, a former talent agent, following his split from Perry. The pair reportedly met at a yoga class.
He confirmed their romance during a July 18, 2012, appearance on Howard Stern's radio show, just days after his divorce became final.
"Some things in the newspaper aren’t true … that’s true, actually," Brand said when asked about Brewster, according to E! News.

Their relationship appeared to move quickly. According to Cosmopolitan, the pair were reportedly considering renting a home together in Los Angeles.
By late August, however, the romance had ended.
"Isabella and [Russell] broke it off," a source told Us Weekly at the time. "He has been in London since the Olympics and is traveling for standup."
Geri Halliwell — August 2012
Geri Halliwell was briefly romantically linked to Brand in 2012. (Getty Images)

Following his split from Brewster, Brand was briefly linked to Spice Girls singer Geri Halliwell. The pair reportedly grew close during preparations for the 2012 London Olympics' closing ceremony, at which both performed.
They were photographed holding hands during a visit to Hampton Court Palace with Halliwell’s daughter, Bluebell, and were also reportedly spotted enjoying a picnic on Hampstead Heath.
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS
Despite the attention surrounding their budding romance, the relationship reportedly ended within weeks.
"He isn’t ready to settle down so soon after coming out of marriage," a source told The Mirror.
Jemima Goldsmith — 2013–2014
Russell Brand and Jemima Khan arrive at The Hoping Foundation's Starry Starry Night benefit evening for Palestinian refugee children at Cafe de Paris in London on June 19, 2014. (Getty Images)

Brand began dating producer and journalist Jemima Goldsmith in 2013. Their relationship lasted approximately a year, during which the comedian publicly expressed his love for her and said their connection felt different from his previous romances.

"I really love her. I’m very, very happy in a relationship that feels very different from anything I’ve experienced before," Brand reportedly said during a 2014 appearance on "The Jonathan Ross Show."
Their breakup was reported in September 2014.
GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE
In November 2026, Goldsmith spoke publicly about her relationship with Brand, offering a different account of her experience with him.

In a statement posted on X following his sentencing, she accused him of "violence, coercive control and abuse." She alleged that she had called police to have him removed from her home during a violent incident in 2014.
Goldsmith said she chose not to pursue charges or speak publicly at the time because she feared the impact of media attention on her teenage children.
"I have neither seen nor spoken to Brand since that period in 2014," she wrote.
Laura Gallacher Brand — 2006–2007; reunited in 2015, married in 2017
Russell Brand arrives at Southwark Crown Court in London on Oct. 29, 2026, ahead of his trial on rape and sexual assault charges. He has denied all charges. (Getty Images)
Brand’s relationship with his current wife, Laura Gallacher Brand, began years before his marriage to Perry.

Gallacher, an author and illustrator whose sister is British broadcaster Kirsty Gallacher, first became involved with Brand in 2006. She was 19 and he was 31. Their initial relationship ended the following year amid his reported difficulty with monogamy.

"When I met him, I was aware that he liked women, and I was aware toward the latter half of that year that he was engaging with other women," Laura told the court during Brand's trial, according to Sky News. "I was not interested in having a relationship with him if he was sleeping with other people. I was invested; we both had told each other we loved each other, but it was clear it was difficult for him to be monogamous."
A court artist sketch by Elizabeth Cook of Russell Brand listening to Judge Mr Justice Bennathan at Southwark Crown Court, in London, Thursday, Nov. 5, 2026. (Elizabeth Cook/PA via AP)
After Brand’s marriage to Perry ended, he and Laura reconnected in 2015.

The couple welcomed daughter Mabel in November 2016 before marrying on Aug. 26, 2017, in a ceremony near Henley-on-Thames, England. Their family later grew with the birth of their daughter Peggy in July 2018 and a son in 2023.
Laura publicly defended her husband during his 2026 rape and sexual assault trial.
Laura described Brand as "caring and kind, a wonderful father to our children and an amazing, attentive husband," adding that he has an "eye for detail I have never known before."

"I feel very seen by him," she said. "We have a very honest, frank and clear relationship and marriage … Our relationship has always been [about] honesty. I love him very much."

title: Stacy Keach dead at 85 as ‘Mike Hammer’ star’s wife shares emotional tribute
summary: Stacy Keach's wife reveals the lengthy heart failure battle behind the iconic "Mike Hammer" actor's final days and his extraordinary courage.
story: Hollywood mourns the loss of legendary actor Stacy Keach, best known for his iconic role as detective Mike Hammer.

Stacy Keach, the legendary actor whose unmistakable voice and powerful performances captivated generations of Americans, is being remembered by his beloved wife as a devoted husband, loving father and courageous fighter after his death at 85.
Keach, best known for portraying the hard-boiled private detective Mike Hammer and for his celebrated work on stage and screen, died Tuesday, Nov. 10, at his family home in Magdalenka, Poland.
His wife, Małgosia Tomassi Keach, shared an emotional statement announcing his passing following a lengthy battle with a serious heart condition and heart failure.
PATRICK STEWART, LEGENDARY 'STAR TREK' AND 'X-MEN' ACTOR, DIES AT 86
Stacy Keach attends the Los Angeles premiere of "Taking Care," hosted by Seth Rogen and Lauren Miller Rogen, at Harmony Gold Preview House on April 16, 2025, in Los Angeles. (Getty Images)
"It is with profound sadness and a broken heart that I announce the passing of my darling husband, Stacy Keach," she said in a statement provided to Fox News Digital.

"After a long and difficult battle with a serious heart condition and heart failure, Stacy peacefully departed this world. He fought for so long, with extraordinary courage, determination and strength."
She remembered her husband as a man whose remarkable resilience extended far beyond the characters he brought to life on-screen.
"He was a true warrior, facing his illness with the same remarkable spirit and resilience that defined his life," she continued.
'TOP GUN' STAR TOM SKERRITT DEAD AT 93
Rana Ghadban, Matt LeBlanc, Stacy Keach and Malgosia Tomassi Keach attend a Hollywood event. (Penske Media via Getty Images)
"Stacy was not only a legendary actor, admired and loved by audiences the world over, but also my beloved husband, my companion and the heart of our family."

For millions of television viewers, Keach will forever be remembered as Mickey Spillane's Mike Hammer, the tough-talking private investigator he portrayed with grit, charisma and an unmistakable screen presence.
EVA MARIE SAINT, OSCAR-WINNING ‘ON THE WATERFRONT’ AND ‘NORTH BY NORTHWEST’ STAR, DEAD AT 102
James Spader as Raymond "Red" Reddington and Stacy Keach as Robert Vesco are pictured in "The Hyena," episode 1004 of "The Blacklist." (Scott Gries/NBC via Getty Images)

But his extraordinary career stretched far beyond the detective series. A gifted Shakespearean actor, Keach tackled some of theater's most demanding roles, including Hamlet, Richard III and King Lear. He also earned a Golden Globe for his portrayal of Ernest Hemingway.
His television appearances included "Blue Bloods," "Titus" and "Prison Break," while his film credits ranged from "The Long Riders" to "Nebraska" and "The Bourne Legacy."
Keach also appeared in the biblical miniseries "Jesus of Nazareth," portraying the criminal Barabbas.
In 2017, Keach suffered a heart attack while performing in a one-man production about Ernest Hemingway at Chicago's Goodman Theatre, an ordeal that forced the cancellation of the show's run.

Throughout a career spanning more than six decades, Keach earned admiration not only for his versatility but also for the unmistakable voice and commanding presence that made him one of Hollywood's most recognizable performers.
Yet for those closest to him, his greatest legacy was the love he shared with his family.
"His passing leaves an immeasurable emptiness in our lives," his wife said. "But his extraordinary spirit, his unforgettable voice and the love he gave so generously will remain with us forever."

title: ‘Yellowstone’ star Dawn Olivieri chose Arkansas ranch life over LA to reclaim her ‘freedom’
summary: "Yellowstone" star Dawn Olivieri reveals the career dry spell that drove her to leave LA for a 160-acre Arkansas ranch and animal sanctuary.
story: Dawn Olivieri, who is starring in "Homestead: The Series," explains how giving up control of her Hollywood career led to more acting opportunities and a new life in rural Arkansas.

"Yellowstone" alum Dawn Olivieri is opening up about the turning point that drove her to leave Los Angeles behind and build the life that she actually wanted on a ranch and animal sanctuary in rural Arkansas.

During an interview with Fox News Digital, the 45-year-old actress, who is starring in the second season of Angel Studios’ post-apocalyptic drama "Homestead: The Series," shared how she became disillusioned with Hollywood during a lull in her career after years of chasing acting success.
"I realized it wasn't giving me what my dream of what it was supposed to give me," Olivieri said.
Dawn Olivieri opened up about trading Hollywood for a life on a ranch in Arkansas. (Dawn Olivieri Instagram)
'VAMPIRE DIARIES' STAR IAN SOMERHALDER SAYS LEAVING HOLLYWOOD FOR FARMING 'SHIFTED MY LIFE FOREVER'
"It wasn't cooperating," she continued. "I didn't have offers, just like falling out of my phone. I went through a dry spell, and I was like, ‘Wow, so this is an illusion.'"

"I kind of saw through the veil and once I saw through veil — I realized in that moment, I have to make some decisions about my life that makes me happy — [it] isn't always waiting by the phone, losing my power, waiting for someone to hire me," Olivieri recalled. "I'm like, ‘Oh, what am I doing?’"
'HOMESTEAD' STAR BAILEY CHASE SAYS CALIFORNIA VACCINE PLANS WERE 'FINAL STRAW' THAT DROVE FAMILY OUT OF LA

"I just jumped ahead," she explained. "I go, ‘If I did make all this money and was successful, what would I do with it?’ Well, I would move to the country and have horses and OK, well, I guess let me go do that. Let me, let me see what. And so I did that with nothing. Which wasn't the dream part, but in actuality, it was what was always meant to happen because I moved toward my own authenticity."
The "Homestead" star said she became disillusioned with chasing the Hollywood dream. (Getty Images)

In 2022, the actress left LA and bought a 160-acre property outside Mena, Arkansas. The following year, Olivieri founded the nonprofit organization Moon Mountain Sanctuary and Rescue, which rescues and rehabilitates hundreds of horses and other animals.
'LIONESS' STAR JILL WAGNER RAISES DAUGHTERS IN TENNESSEE TOWN OF 800, WHERE HORSES AND BUGGIES STILL ROAM

During an August appearance on the "Let's Talk Local" podcast, Olivieri said she is currently living in a camper on the property while she continues to build and expand her ranch and animal sanctuary.

While speaking with Fox News Digital, Olivieri reflected on the unexpected result that came from her decision to leave Hollywood and create the lifestyle she had always envisioned, explaining that giving up control of her acting career ultimately improved it.
HOLLYWOOD STAR SOUNDS ALARM OVER DISAPPEARING JOBS AS PRODUCTIONS FLEE CALIFORNIA

"I think in that moment, I became a better human being," she said. "I became a better actress for sure. I started working way more than I did when I was in LA waiting for the job, waiting for the call."
The actress said she moved to a "land of no mirrors." (Dawn Olivieri Instagram)
"And I moved to a land of no mirrors is what I called it," Olivieri continued.. "I went into a deep relationship with the core of my being versus what everything looked like, what I looked like."
"And I would recommend that move to anybody," she added.

Olivieri's "Homestead: The Series" co-star Charles Esten, who joined her for the interview, agreed that letting go of the pressure to land the next role can sometimes have the opposite effect in Hollywood.
"It’s not just Hollywood, it’s the whole world that — but especially Hollywood — can smell that desperation of, ‘I need this to get that,’" Esten said.
Dawn Olivieri opened up about trading Hollywood for a life on a ranch in Arkansas. (Dawn Olivieri Instagram)
WATCH: ‘YELLOWSTONE’ STAR DAWN OLIVIERI TRADED LA FOR ARKANSAS RANCH

"The second you sort of don’t hold so tightly and you have sort of more philosophy of abundance and let it a little looser. Or another way is just give it up," he continued. "I don’t mean give it up by quit doing it, but give up the need and the desperation on it. And then they finally go, ‘Hey, you want to come do a show?’"
"Yeah, literally, that’s what happened," Olivieri replied.

Olivieri pointed out that many other actors faced a dramatic decrease in work opportunities in recent years due to the COVID-19 pandemic and the 2023 SAG-AFTRA and the Writers Guild of America (WGA) strike.
'VERONICA MARS' STAR JASON DOHRING TRADED HOLLYWOOD FOR FARMING

"But I had a very clear decision that I was willing to give up this identity of being an actress," she said. "And maybe if I had to sell farm fresh eggs on the side of the road, I would do that just to keep my freedom."
Olivieri said her acting career actually improved after she left LA. (Dawn Olivieri Instagram)

"Homestead: The Series" follows survivors living at a fortified prepper compound in the Rocky Mountains known as The Homestead after a nuclear attack on LA plunges the country into chaos. Olivieri plays Jenna Ross, the wife of Ian Ross (Neal McDonough), the wealthy prepper who established the Homestead, while Esten portrays Cain Ross, Ian's estranged brother.

After Ian is incapacitated and later dies, Jenna is pushed into a leadership role and struggles with how to protect the community while maintaining her compassionate approach toward outsiders. Meanwhile, Cain arrives at the Homestead after Ian's injury and takes a much more hardline approach to survival and leadership.
In season two, which premiered on Nov. 3, Jenna and Cain find themselves in conflict over how the compound should be run as resources dwindle.
Olivieri plays Jenna Ross and Charles Esten portrays Ian Ross in "Homestead: The Series." (Angel Studios)

Olivieri was part of the cast in the 2024 theatrical movie "Homestead," which introduces the story. Esten joined the cast for the first season of "Homestead: The Series," which picks up where the movie left off. The show also stars Kevin Lawson Emmanuel McCord, Jesse Hutch and Betzaida Landín.

While speaking with Fox News Digital, Olivieri and Esten shared their thoughts on why more Americans are increasingly interested in homesteading, growing their own food and moving away from big cities.

"People are thinking about it because everything else is becoming toxic in all truth," Olivieri said. "Our food system has gone toxic because of profit. Our way of life in a city has become toxic because of overpopulation potentially or, again, I really think the root of it is profit and money and commerce."
"In this state of government, being open and available is just a nicer experience," she added. "It is for me anyway."
Esten drew a contrast between Olivieri's homesteading and the gritty survivalism depicted on "Homestead: The Series."
Jenna is thrust into a leadership position in the compound after the death of her husband. (Angel Studios)

"Dawn's homesteading that I've noticed is beautiful," he said. "Our version of homestead is very extraordinary necessity, fear-based. Plant these fences and Dawn's is the opposite of that. Dawn's very open and welcoming and saving animals that need it and welcoming other folks on."

After Olivieri embraced rural life and stopped waiting for Hollywood to call, the actress went on to land major roles in Taylor Sheridan's universe. Olivieri played Claire Dutton, the widowed sister of James Dutton (Tim McGraw), in 2021's "1883."

From 2022 to 2024, Olivieri portrayed Sarah Atwood, the corporate strategist brought in by Market Equities who becomes involved with Jamie Dutton (Wes Bentley), in "Yellowstone." She has a recurring role as CIA officer Amber Whalen on "Lioness" and most recently made a guest appearance in "The Madison."
Season two of "Homeland: The Series" premiered on Nov. 3. ( )
While speaking with Fox News Digital, Olivieri weighed in on what she believes sets the prolific creator apart from others in Hollywood.
"He doesn't ask for permission to do anything," she said. "He listens to his North, his guide, and he writes textured, powerful human beings, especially women, which I find is very, very rare."
GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE

"He writes them like it's coming from inside of himself," Olivieri continued. "I've talked to him about this because he will write things for a strong woman that makes you read it on the page and then look around, like, ‘Is someone watching me? How are you in my head?’"
Olivieri recalled asking Sheridan how he was able to write female characters with such insight.
Olivieri has appeared in four Taylor Sheridan-created shows. (Variety via Getty Images)

"I went to him and I said, ‘How do you know how to do that?’ And he told me point blank, he said his mom was a strong woman," she remembered. "So he had a very, very, very close example of how strong women move and what they do and how they think and the way that they talk."
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

"He writes things poetically," she continued. "He has texture. There's magic in the way that he writes and it's just undeniable. And he agrees he's tapped. He'll sit and wait for the muse and the muse will share the story with him. And that's how he writes."

"It's no different than all of the great writers in the sense that they are very clear that it's not quite them," Olivieri added. "They are a conduit for some energy that flows through them. And he has told me that that's exactly what happens for him."

title: Sarah Ferguson in touch with ex-Prince Andrew as expert warns royal downfall 'has further to go' after arrest
summary: Police Scotland confirms "active inquiries" into allegations involving former Prince Andrew and Jeffrey Epstein at the Balmoral Castle royal estate.
story: Royal broadcaster Ian Pelham Turner discusses Sarah Ferguson's denial of tell-all rumors and the potential consequences for daughters Princess Beatrice and Princess Eugenie.
Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor may have lost his royal titles, but the scandal surrounding his ties to Jeffrey Epstein continues to follow him — and his ex-wife, Sarah Ferguson.
People magazine reported that while it's unclear whether the former Duchess of York has seen her ex-husband recently, the two remain in contact.
"They have an ongoing cordial and supportive relationship as co-parents and co-grandparents," a spokesperson for Ferguson told People.
FORMER PRINCE ANDREW, SARAH FERGUSON DUBBED ROYAL FAMILY’S ‘BONNIE AND CLYDE’ AS EPSTEIN FALLOUT GROWS: AUTHOR

Sarah Ferguson and Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor attend the funeral of Katharine, Duchess of Kent, at Westminster Cathedral on Sept. 16, 2025 in London. People magazine reported that the former Duchess of York has been in touch with her ex-husband. (Mark Cuthbert/UK Press via Getty Images)
Fox News Digital reached out to Ferguson's spokesperson for comment.

"It is not surprising," royal commentator Richard Fitzwilliams told Fox News Digital. "If Andrew came to court, she might well be called as a witness. Much depends on whether the police in Britain can obtain the unredacted Epstein files. But there is no way back for Andrew. He hasn't helped the FBI. He has no support. He has no reputation to lose. It can't get much worse. His fall is unique. It has further to go."
Sarah Ferguson and former Prince Andrew, Duke of York, attend day 4 of Royal Ascot at Ascot Racecourse on June 19, 2015, in Ascot, England. (Samir Hussein / WireImage)

Andrew has been issued a witness summons in a civil fraud case, marking what is believed to be the first such summons issued to a member of the British royal family since 1870, The Associated Press reported.
WATCH: SARAH FERGUSON DENIES TELL-ALL BOOK AMID ROYAL FAMILY CONCERNS: EXPERT

The summons comes after a High Court judge in London ruled in October that Andrew could be called to testify about a payment he received in connection with the case. Andrew may apply to have the summons set aside, so there is no guarantee he will testify, the AP reported.

The lawsuit was filed by Turkish national Nebahat Evyap Isbilen, who alleges that her former advisor, Selman Turk, misappropriated tens of millions of pounds of her money. As part of the case, she says Turk misled her about a 750,000-pound (approximately $1 million) payment he arranged for her to make to Andrew in 2019. The younger brother of King Charles III repaid the money in 2021, and he is not a party to the lawsuit. Turk denies dishonesty.

From left: The former Prince Andrew, King Charles III and Prince William attend Katharine, Duchess of Kent's Requiem Mass service at Westminster Cathedral on Sept. 16, 2025, in London. Andrew was arrested on Feb. 19, 2026. Thames Valley Police confirmed to Fox News Digital he was released hours later. (Max Mumby/Indigo/Getty Images)

Police Scotland confirmed to Fox News Digital that active inquiries are underway into information concerning Andrew and Epstein at Balmoral Castle, the royal family's Scottish estate. They noted that the inquiries are at a "very early stage."
Balmoral Castle in Scotland is seen here. (Tim Graham Photo Library via Getty Images)

The confirmation follows a report by the Scottish Daily Express that police inquiries concern allegations that women were trafficked to the royal estate, where Andrew hosted Epstein and his longtime associate, Ghislaine Maxwell.

"We have received information and active enquiries are ongoing, but these are at a very early stage," a Police Scotland spokesperson told Fox News Digital. "All enquiries are evidence-led, with the needs of victim survivors at the heart of those enquiries. We would never confirm details of ongoing enquiries, and it would be inappropriate to comment further."

The former Prince Andrew, Duke of York, attends the Easter service at St. George's Chapel on April 20, 2025, in Windsor, England. He lost his princely title in October of that year. (Samir Hussein/WireImage/Getty Images)

Police declined to specify the focus of the inquiries or whether Andrew is the subject of an investigation. Fox News Digital reached out to Andrew's attorney for comment. A spokesperson for Buckingham Palace told Fox News Digital the palace does not speak on Andrew's behalf because he is no longer a working royal.

title: Bruce Springsteen fan club founders say political fights, El-Sayed endorsement led to shutdown: report
summary: Bruce Springsteen's endorsement of Michigan's senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed proved the final straw for the Spring-Nuts fan club founders as group shutters.
story: A viral concert clip shows Bruce Springsteen appearing to walk past former New Jersey Gov. Chris Christie without acknowledging him as Christie reaches out during an awkward exchange.
A Bruce Springsteen fan club couldn't escape the badlands and shuttered over political commentary.

Founded more than a decade ago, the "Spring-Nuts" Facebook group dedicated to The Boss noticed its 18,000 members were no longer focused on his music as they battled against "hateful" online discourse due to Springsteen's public stances and recent endorsement of Michigan's senator-elect, Abdul El-Sayed.

"As the world grew increasingly divisive, hostile, those tensions inevitably spilled into our little corner of the E Street world," founders Julie and Howie Chaz said in a statement posted on Sunday, Nov. 8, according to Asbury Park Press.
BRUCE SPRINGSTEEN SPARKS FAN FURY AFTER BACKING ABDUL EL-SAYED IN MICHIGAN SENATE RACE
Bruce Springsteen's support of Michigan senator-elect Abdul El Sayed sparked fan fury online. (Getty Images)
"What should have been respectful differences of opinion too often deteriorated into personal attacks, bullying, insults, and some genuinely vile and hateful rhetoric."
Springsteen embarked on the "Land of Hope and Dreams" tour earlier this year with the E Street Band and legendary guitarist Tom Morello.
The 20-date tour across North America was slated in response to President Donald Trump and the "No Kings" protests.
BRUCE SPRINGSTEEN REIGNITES TRUMP FEUD, SAYS 'CRITICAL PATRIOTISM' DEFINES A PATRIOT
"We are living through dark, disturbing and dangerous times, but do not despair – the cavalry is coming," Springsteen said while announcing the tour on social media in February.

"We will be rocking your town in celebration and in defense of America – American democracy, American freedom, our American Constitution and our sacred American dream – all of which are under attack by our wannabe king and his rogue government in Washington, D.C."
Bruce Springsteen launched the "Land of Hope and Dreams" tour earlier this year in response to Donald Trump and No Kings protests. (Kevin Mazur / Getty Images)

He added, "Everyone, regardless of where you stand or what you believe in, is welcome – so come on out and join the United Free Republic of E Street Nation for an American spring of rock 'n' rebellion! I’ll see you there!"

"Spring-Nuts" founder Howie Chaz admitted that as Springsteen became "more outspoken about his politics," the group administrators were tasked with a "difficult balancing act" of respecting "his absolute right" while maintaining an ethical online community.
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

"How could we be a Bruce Springsteen fan community trying to protect that harmony and camaraderie and ignore messages and statements coming directly from the very artist who brought us all together," Howie said.
Springsteen's November endorsement of El-Sayed as "a fighter for our American Constitution" was the final straw for admins.
Bruce Springsteen endorsed Michigan senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed in November. (Getty Images)
The Boss said Michigan senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed was a "fighter for our American Constitution." (Bruce Springsteen / Instagram)
"Mr. Sayed campaigned with Hasan Piker who openly made horrific statements that America deserved 9/11," Howie said.

"After a Michigan synagogue was attacked back in March, obviously an act of terrorism, Sayed rationalized it by saying 'Hurt people hurt people' standing right next to the antisemitic streamer Hasan Piker who made the despicable 9/11 statement."

His endorsement was "deeply disappointing to us, given our concerns as proud Jews," Julie and Howie said.

"We certainly don't believe Bruce intended for his message to make fans feel unwelcome. But very unfortunately, some of his fans appointed themselves the gatekeepers of who was and wasn't worthy of belonging in the E Street community."
The "Spring-Nuts" Facebook group will continue under a different name. (Talia Sprague/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
While the group's annual Seaside Serenade and Spring-Nuts podcasts will continue under a different name, the group will rebrand with a focus on music in general, Howie told the Asbury Park Press.

"One thing we want to make absolutely clear is that Julie and I can NEVER thank Bruce Springsteen and the E Street Band enough for the decades of music, memories, inspiration, and absolute JOY they have brought into our lives," Howie said on Facebook.

title: Chris Rock says he 'was not a great husband' to Malaak Compton-Rock, admits he watched 'a lot of porn'
summary: Chris Rock admitted to cheating and porn addiction during his nearly 20-year marriage to Malaak Compton-Rock, comparing himself to a Marvel character.
story: Comedian Chris Rock compared the institutionalization of woke culture to the Salem witch trials, sparking criticism from 'The Five' for addressing the issue several years 'late.'
Chris Rock is going into detail about the end of his marriage, admitting he wasn't the best husband and took accountability for mistakes he made in the relationship.
During a recent interview with GQ, the 61-year-old comedian shared that there were many factors that caused the divorce, noting he cheated and was addicted to pornography during his marriage.
"I was not a great husband," he admitted. "I watched a lot of porn. I don’t watch porn anymore. I haven’t watched porn in five, six years."
He also admitted to cheating on his wife, noting, "It’s not anything I’m proud of, but it’s something I had to go through."
Rock took ownership of the fact that he cheated on his wife and was addicted to pornography. (Richard Burbridge/GQ)
CHRIS ROCK SHREDS 'WOKE 1.0' ERA, COMPARES MODERN OUTRAGE TO SALEM WITCH HUNTS
The comedian compared himself to a character in a Marvel movie who "has to test his powers" and see how far they can push things before they eventually "crash down."

"Every Marvel movie, man or woman, they have to test their powers," he said. "They’re a- -holes. They get these powers and they’re a- -holes, and they’re racing trains and they’re lifting up ocean liners and they try to go to the sun, then they crash down because they realize they’re not God. And then they start helping people."
Rock compared himself to a superhero learning he had powers and pushing the limits. (Simon Ackerman/Getty Images for BFI)
He explained that he "tested my powers" during his marriage by cheating on his wife, noting he "was severely humbled" when he realized he definitely "wasn't God or anywhere near him."

Rock was married to Malaak Compton-Rock for nearly 20 years. They tied the knot in 1996, separated in 2014 and finalized their divorce in 2016. They share two children together, daughters, Lola and Zahra.

title: Russell Brand sentenced after rape, sexual assault convictions in UK
summary: Russell Brand was sentenced Monday after being found guilty of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault in the U.K.
story: A judge in the United Kingdom sentenced comedian Russell Brand to 10 and a half years in prison for raping a woman and sexually assaulting three others in separate incidents from 2004 to 2009 Monday.
Russell Brand has been sentenced to 10 years and six months in prison for rape and sexual assault.
During sentencing on Monday, Judge Mr. Justice Joel Bennathan said Brand had demonstrated a "casual and arrogant disregard" for women’s right to refuse his sexual advances.
"About 20 years ago, Russell Brand, you were becoming famous," Bennathan said. "You were clever — and in many people’s eyes, funny and charismatic. You had also become a sexual predator."

The judge described one of Brand’s sexual assaults as "outrageous and possibly laddish, but also a criminal offense," adding that Brand’s behavior reflected his belief that "fame meant you could act how you liked, when you liked, unhindered by the rules by which decent people live."
RUSSELL BRAND FOUND GUILTY OF ONE COUNT OF RAPE AND THREE COUNTS OF SEXUAL ASSAULT
Nov. 9, 2026, London, UK: Court artist drawing by Elizabeth Cook of Russell Brand in the dock at Southwark Crown Court, London.  (Elizabeth Cook/PA Wire via Zuma Press)

Bennathan also said Brand’s conduct showed a "casual arrogant disregard of anyone’s right to say no," and emphasized that women retain the right to refuse sexual contact "wherever they go, indeed whatever they drink."

The judge said the victims suffered "profound and lasting" consequences, including trauma, humiliation, addiction and difficulty trusting others. He also praised the women for their "determination and bravery" after they endured Brand's assertions that they had lied about the encounters or consented to them.

Bennathan said he considered Brand’s lack of significant prior convictions, the 17 years that had passed since the offenses and his work helping people struggling with addiction. However, he said good character and exemplary conduct should not normally be given significant weight in cases involving serious sexual offenses.
Southwark Crown Court, Nov. 9, 2026: Court artist drawing of Laura Brand waving to husband, Russell Brand, as he goes down to the cells. (Priscilla Coleman/MB Media)
According to Sky News, as Brand was taken from the dock by three guards, he turned to his wife and nodded, saying, "We'll be OK."
Laura reportedly mouthed back: "I love you, I'll be OK."
WATCH: RUSSELL BRAND SENTENCED TO MORE THAN 10 YEARS IN PRISON

Last week, Brand was found guilty of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault in the U.K. He denied the charges and was acquitted of two additional rape charges and one count of attempted indecent assault.
He was immediately taken into custody following the verdict, according to the BBC.
Brand, 51, was accused of three counts of rape, three counts of sexual assault and one count of attempted indecent assault involving six women between 1999 and 2009.
Russell Brand was found guilty of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault in the U.K. (Mike Marsland/WireImage)
One woman he was convicted of sexually assaulting gave an impact statement during Monday's proceedings, while three others submitted written statements to the prosecutor.

"For many years as his star was rising it was impossible to escape seeing him all over the media, being celebrated for his disgusting behavior against women like it was all a joke," she said. "There were many times I felt visibly sick at the sight of him parading around thinking he can get away with anything."
The woman spoke out of view of the courtroom to preserve her identity.
Prosecutor Riel Karmy-Jones read statements by the other three women. Brand was convicted of sexually assaulting the first woman at a London radio station in 2005.
"Since the sexual assault ... Russell Brand has managed to move on and even forget," she wrote. "Over the years, hearing his voice on television, on social media or seeing his image made me jump."

According to Sky News, Brand acknowledged that he had been "reckless" and used his fame to pursue sexual relationships, but insisted that the encounters were consensual. He also told the jury that consent was "fundamental, essential and necessary."
Brand has denied forcing any of the women to engage in sexual activity against their will.

Brand has previously denied all allegations. (Getty Images)

Prosecutors alleged that Brand committed the offenses against six women over a 10-year period. The women testified in court about alleged encounters at a hotel, a bar, a radio station, a workplace and Brand’s home.
According to a Metropolitan Police press release, detectives began investigating Brand after allegations were made public by U.K. media outlets Channel 4 and The Sunday Times in September 2023.

The outlets launched a joint investigation into the allegations, resulting in a lengthy article on the Times' website, as well as an episode of Channel 4's documentary series, "Dispatches," called "Russell Brand: In Plain Sight." Both contained a number of anonymous complaints, with women accusing Brand of physical and emotional abuse and bullying, as well as some instances of sexual assault.

Police video released Thursday, Nov. 5 and obtained by Fox News Digital shows Brand defending his sexual history during questioning by London's Metropolitan Police.
During a December 2023 interview, Brand sat alongside his attorney and read a lengthy prepared statement to detectives, insisting that his past sexual encounters were consensual.
"As I’ve repeatedly stated publicly … I led a very promiscuous life in the past, which I’ve spent years openly denouncing. I’ve never engaged in nonconsensual sexual activity," Brand said.
Brand also criticized a September 2023 media investigation that brought allegations against him into the public spotlight.
He described the reporting as "defamatory and fictitious," suggesting that consensual encounters had been "invented or reimagined" as sexual misconduct.

In a video posted to X last year, Brand thanked his fans for messages of support, then criticized the British government and legal system before addressing the charges directly.
Russell Brand's wife, Laura Brand, took the stand in the actor's rape and sexual assault trial. (Getty Images)

He said that he "was a fool before I lived in the light of the Lord. I was a drug addict, a sex addict and an imbecile, but what I never was was a rapist. I've never engaged in nonconsensual activity. I pray that you can see that by looking in my eyes."
