title: Certain sleep habits could offer clues to hidden type of depression, scientists say
summary: A study of over 11,000 Australian adults links specific sleep habits and circadian rhythm disruptions to a newly proposed subtype of depression.
story: Metabolic health expert Jim LaValle explains how chronic stress, inadequate sleep and everyday dietary choices can affect blood sugar regulation and contribute to insulin resistance.
A person's sleep habits may help identify a newly proposed subtype of depression linked to the body's internal clock.
In a study of 11,380 Australian adults with a history of depression, about 23% met researchers' criteria for what they called "circadian depression."

The profile included at least three of six features: being an evening person, waking up feeling very tired, sleeping longer during the worst periods of depression, experiencing seasonal changes, having a later midpoint between falling asleep and waking up, and experiencing "social jetlag," a large shift in sleep timing between workdays and days off.
The seasonal changes could involve sleep, mood, activity, appetite, weight or energy.
THE DAYTIME HABIT THAT COULD TRANSFORM YOUR SLEEP, ACCORDING TO NEW STUDY
The study, published on Oct. 20 in The British Journal of Psychiatry, could eventually help guide more personalized care for patients with depression, according to the researchers.

"Depression is not a uniform illness, and understanding the characteristics of different subtypes means we can give people earlier access to treatments that will be most effective for them," first author Emiliana Tonini, Ph.D., from the University of Sydney's Brain and Mind Centre, said in a statement.
Researchers are studying whether disrupted sleep-wake rhythms may help identify a proposed subtype of depression. (iStock)
The label, however, is not a formal diagnosis and needs independent replication and further study, the researchers noted.
Treatment questions

People in the circadian group reported an earlier onset of depression and more severe symptoms than those who did not meet the criteria. They were also more likely to report weight gain during depressive episodes.

They also reported poorer responses and more side effects with two common classes of antidepressants, selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) and serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors (SNRIs).
POPULAR SLEEP AIDS BEFORE SURGERY COULD PREVENT PAINKILLER DEPENDENCE LATER
Participants reported how well their medications worked, but the study did not explain why some were less effective and did not test treatments aimed at adjusting the body’s internal clock.
Researchers said light exposure, regular sleep schedules and melatonin-related approaches warrant further study.
The proposed circadian profile includes features such as waking very tired, oversleeping during depression and being an evening person. (iStock)

Dr. Ian Hickie, a study co-author and professor of psychiatry at the University of Sydney, said the proposed profile "cuts across existing historic subtypes" of depression, most commonly atypical and bipolar depression, because they share features such as low energy and oversleeping.
COMMON GYM SUPPLEMENT COULD HELP FIGHT DEPRESSION, NEW RESEARCH SUGGESTS

Atypical depression can also involve weight gain, while bipolar depression refers to depressive episodes in people with bipolar disorder, which also involves periods of unusually elevated or irritable mood and increased energy.
"We define circadian only by sleep-wake and circadian features," Hickie told Fox News Digital.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

For some people with this profile, Hickie said sleep-wake disruption may be more than a symptom of depression. "This type of circadian disturbance is not simply a consequence, but the underlying cause," he wrote.
The study itself, however, could not establish whether body-clock disruption caused depression or resulted from it.
Staying up late or struggling to wake up does not, by itself, mean someone has depression, the researchers noted. (iStock)
Staying up late or having trouble waking does not necessarily indicate depression. Participants had already reported depression, which in some cases was severe, recurring or long-lasting.

Participants in the circadian group also reported more manic-like experiences. John Puls, a psychotherapist and adjunct professor at Florida Atlantic University, said those symptoms could help explain their reported response to antidepressants.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"SSRIs are not meant to treat these more significant mental health symptoms that go far beyond depressive symptoms," Puls, who was not involved in the study, told Fox News Digital. "In fact, some SSRIs can actually worsen manic symptoms, which lead to poor sleep."
Study limitations
There were several limitations to the study, the researchers acknowledged.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
Participants reported their own sleep patterns and treatment experiences, and the cross-sectional analysis didn't show whether sleep disruption preceded or followed depressive symptoms.
All participants were of European ancestry, so the findings may not apply to other populations.
Researchers used six sleep-related features to identify the proposed circadian depression profile, including having social jetlag and being an evening person. (iStock)
Jillian Amodio, a Maryland-based psychotherapist and founder of Moms For Mental Health, cautioned against using the findings as "a benchmark for treating each person in the same way."
"Biological, environmental, social and psychological factors all need to be accounted for," Amodio, who was not involved in the research, told Fox News Digital.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Researchers should examine more populations, including people who work night shifts, and account for differences in time zones and seasons, according to Amodio.
The study was led by researchers at the University of Sydney and QIMR Berghofer Medical Research Institute, with co-authors from institutions in Australia, the U.K. and the U.S.
Deirdre Bardolf is a lifestyle writer with Fox News Digital.

title: Popular drinks linked to heart attacks, cardiac arrest in young adults, study finds
summary: Energy drinks with caffeine and stimulants were linked to cardiac arrest reports 11 times more often than non-stimulant products, per AHA research.
story: Colin Kane, M.D., a pediatric cardiologist and professor at UT Southwestern Medical Center, discusses new research that found a connection between energy drinks, stimulant-containing supplements and reports of serious heart problems.
Energy drinks and stimulant-containing supplements have been linked to the risk of serious heart problems, including cardiac arrest and heart attacks, particularly among young adults.
That’s according to new research released by the American Heart Association, which will be presented at the AHA Scientific Sessions in Chicago, Nov. 6-9, 2026.

A retrospective observational analysis looked at more than 28,000 reports submitted to the Food and Drug Administration of cardiovascular events, including cardiac arrest, myocardial infarction (heart attack), ventricular arrhythmias (abnormal rhythms), palpitations, tachycardia (rapid heart rate), chest pain and syncope (fainting).
EVEN OCCASIONAL MARIJUANA USE LINKED TO HIGHER STROKE RISK, STUDY FINDS
Cardiac arrest appeared in reports involving caffeine- and stimulant-containing products about 11 times as often as in reports involving products without those ingredients.
Heart attacks were reported about 4½ times as often, while ventricular arrhythmias (abnormal heart rhythms) or palpitations were reported about four times as often, according to the AHA.
Energy drinks and stimulant-containing supplements have been linked to the risk of serious heart problems, including cardiac arrest and heart attacks, particularly among young adults. (iStock)
Elevated heart rate, chest pain and fainting also increased among the group consuming those substances.
Approximately 45% of reported cardiovascular events associated with stimulant products involved adults ages 18 to 34.
"We don't know how many people consumed these drinks and didn't report symptoms or those who maybe had symptoms and didn’t report them."

The stimulants included in the study were caffeine, methylxanthines, guarana, Yerba maté, synephrine, yohimbine and other compounds. They were consumed in products such as soft drinks, meal replacement shakes, protein bars, smoothies and vitamins.
Caffeine and heart risks

Colin Kane, M.D., a pediatric cardiologist and service chief at Children's Health and professor at UT Southwestern Medical Center, said the findings build on earlier case reports about potential heart risks from high caffeine intake.

"We've known through case reports and anecdotal evidence that caffeine in high amounts can be potentially dangerous to people with underlying heart conditions and even those who have normal hearts," Kane, who was not involved in the study, told Fox News Digital.
WHY STACKING SUPPLEMENTS WITHOUT A BLOOD TEST FIRST CAN DO MORE HARM THAN GOOD

It is generally safe for adults to consume up to 400 milligrams of caffeine per day, which equates to up to five 8-ounce cups of regular black caffeinated coffee, according to a 2026 American Heart Association Scientific Statement on caffeine and cardiovascular disease.

"Some energy drinks have up to three times more caffeine per fluid ounce than brewed coffee, and some pre-workout supplements have more than 12 times as much," senior study author Dr. Pamela Benavidez, a cardiothoracic anesthesiologist at Fairfield Medical Center in Lancaster, Ohio, told Fox News Digital.
Approximately 45% of reported cardiovascular events associated with stimulant products involved adults ages 18 to 34. (iStock)
"This means one small serving can easily surpass the advised daily limit or more."
Benavidez also warned that these products often include other stimulants like synephrine, yohimbine and methylhexanamine.
"These can interact with caffeine in ways that are not fully understood, especially in young, healthy people," she said.
YOUR DAILY COFFEE HABIT MAY AFFECT YOUR BRAIN AND MOOD IN UNEXPECTED WAYS, STUDY FINDS

The researchers recommend that young people carefully monitor their consumption of caffeine and watch for heart-related symptoms, such as palpitations, chest pain or tightness, lightheadedness, fainting or a racing or irregular heartbeat during or after use of these products.

"If you notice any of these symptoms, seek medical help right away," Benavidez advised. "If you have a known heart condition, a family history of sudden cardiac events or take medications that are classified as stimulants or can affect your heart rate/rhythm, you should talk to your doctor before using these products at all."
"Some energy drinks have up to three times more caffeine per fluid ounce than brewed coffee, and some pre-workout supplements have more than 12 times as much," the lead researcher said. (iStock)

Kane identified people with underlying heart conditions, particularly those with potentially dangerous heart rhythms and older adults with coronary artery disease, as groups needing particular awareness.
"And there's a whole group of people who may have an underlying heart condition that they're not diagnosed with yet," he added.
Study limitations
The findings are preliminary and have not yet been published as a full peer-reviewed manuscript.
Because the study was observational, it could only show an association and could not prove that the products caused the cardiac events.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
"We don't know how many people consumed these drinks and didn't report symptoms or those who maybe had symptoms and didn’t report them," Kane said.
Also, because the FDA reports were voluntary, they may contain incomplete, inconsistent or selectively submitted data.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
It is possible that other factors, such as alcohol or drug use, strenuous exercise and undiagnosed heart conditions, may have contributed to the cardiovascular events.
"Anytime you're mixing stimulants and other substances or medications, it can certainly bring up a potential for harm," Kane said.
Industry response
The American Beverage Association, based in Washington, D.C., sent the statement below to Fox News Digital in response to the study:
"Energy drinks have been enjoyed by billions of people around the world for more than 30 years and are recognized as safe by government food safety agencies worldwide.

"The U.S. Food and Drug Administration, Health Canada, the European Food Safety Authority all relied on the highest quality science when they determined that a moderate daily intake of 400 milligrams of caffeine from all sources is safe for adults.
The researchers recommend that young people carefully monitor their consumption of caffeine and to watch for heart-related symptoms (iStock)
"Energy drinks have less caffeine than coffeehouse coffee, and no regulatory agency has found that their other ingredients interact harmfully with caffeine."
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
Andrea Wong, chief science officer of the Council for Responsible Nutrition in Washington, D.C., also reacted to the study’s findings.

"Because the analysis does not account for how many consumers actually used these products, whether they were overused or misused or even the amount of caffeine (or other ingredients) per serving, it cannot determine the incidence of cardiovascular events or quantify the associated risk," she told Fox News Digital.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"Importantly, the reported 11-fold difference in cardiac arrest reporting does not mean consumers are 11 times more likely to experience cardiac arrest."
Melissa Rudy is senior health editor and a member of the lifestyle team at Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to melissa.rudy@fox.com.

title: Fitness influencer's vacation getaway takes scary turn after headache leads to ICU
summary: Khiana Smith was rushed by ambulance to a Bali hospital after a severe headache and light sensitivity led to a meningitis diagnosis in the ICU.
story: Emergency physician Dr. Alfred Joshua discusses a fitness influencer's reported hospitalization overseas.
A 23-year-old fitness influencer's vacation took a frightening turn after she suddenly became seriously ill in Bali.

Australian fitness coach Khiana Smith said in a TikTok video that she was hospitalized after developing a severe headache and sensitivity to light. She later revealed in another video that she had been diagnosed with meningitis.
Smith said she knew something was wrong when she woke up with what she described as the "worst headache."
DEADLY LEGIONNAIRES' DISEASE OUTBREAK SPARKS CONCERN IN MAJOR US CITY: KNOW THE SYMPTOMS
"I couldn't even get out of bed," Smith said in the TikTok video. "It was so intense I couldn't even open my eyes properly. I was really sensitive to light. I couldn't stand up without falling over."

She initially waited to see whether she would feel better, but said she woke up the following morning feeling "10 times worse." She was eventually taken to a hospital by ambulance, where testing revealed the infection.
Australian fitness coach Khiana Smith, pictured, said in a TikTok video that she was hospitalized after being diagnosed with meningitis. (Khiana Smith/Instagram)

Dr. Alfred Joshua, a California-based board-certified emergency room physician and former chief medical officer, told Fox News Digital that Smith's reported symptoms included several warning signs that should be taken seriously.
"She started having symptoms of severe headache, having difficulty with light," Joshua said. "And then she started having difficulty walking, and then eventually slurred speech."
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER
Meningitis occurs when the protective layers surrounding the brain and spinal cord become inflamed, according to Joshua.

Symptoms can include headache, fever, stiff neck and sensitivity to light. Trouble walking or speaking, confusion and extreme tiredness are more serious signs that should prompt immediate medical attention, Joshua said.
Khiana Smith, pictured left, was vacationing in Bali, pictured right, when she became seriously ill and was later diagnosed with meningitis. (Khiana Smith/Instagram; iStock)
The seriousness of the illness can also depend on what is causing it.
Joshua said viral meningitis often resolves on its own, while bacterial meningitis can progress rapidly and requires prompt treatment with antibiotics.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE STORIES
"Certain strains over a couple of hours [can cause] the person [to] get really, really sick," he said.
Doctors initially did not know whether her meningitis was bacterial or viral, according to Smith, so she was being treated for the bacterial form as a precaution.
Viral meningitis often resolves on its own, while bacterial meningitis can progress rapidly and requires prompt antibiotic treatment. (iStock)

Smith's condition later appeared to improve enough for her to leave the ICU, but she said she had to return after continuing to experience head pain, light sensitivity and slurred speech. She also reported memory loss, and said swelling in her brain was preventing her from flying home.
When meningitis is suspected, Joshua said doctors can use blood tests, brain imaging and a lumbar puncture to determine whether the infection is bacterial, viral or caused by something else.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
Smith's experience has highlighted a concern for travelers who become seriously ill far from home.
Joshua said recommended vaccines can protect against some forms of bacterial meningitis, and advised travelers to consider insurance that includes medical evacuation coverage.
"It was so intense I couldn't even open my eyes properly."
Smith's mother also stressed the importance of travel insurance, saying her daughter's hospital expenses were covered because she had purchased a policy before leaving Australia.
Joshua said worsening symptoms, including changes in speech, walking or other brain functions, should not be ignored.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"When symptoms are progressing in a more complicated manner with neurological dysfunction, do not wait and try to see this out," he said. "Go and seek prompt emergency treatment."
Fox News Digital reached out to Smith for comment.

title: Alzheimer's warning signs could emerge years before memory loss, study finds
summary: A Science Advances study reveals how brain scan connectivity patterns predict Alzheimer's disease years before memory loss or cognitive decline.
story: Dr. Jeremy Koppel, co-director of the Litwin-Zucker Center, discusses a new blood test capable of predicting Alzheimer's risk up to 10 years in advance. The test identifies elevated levels of a tau protein biomarker, P-tau217, indicating a higher likelihood of cognitive decline. Koppel highlights its potential for early diagnosis and understanding Alzheimer's progression.

Small changes in how parts of the brain communicate with one another can help predict a person’s likelihood of developing Alzheimer’s disease years before any memory lapses appear, according to a study published in Science Advances.
Stanford Medicine researchers used brain scans and a computer model to look for early clues about why some older adults develop memory and thinking problems while others stay sharp.

Investigators examined resting brain scans from two opposing groups: patients diagnosed with Alzheimer’s disease and older individuals known as "super agers," whose memory capabilities match people decades younger.
SUBTLE CHANGE IN HOW YOU SPEAK COULD BE EARLY SIGN OF DEMENTIA RISK, NEW RESEARCH SUGGESTS
Instead of looking for physical hallmarks like amyloid plaque accumulation or brain shrinkage, the researchers studied how different parts of the brain communicate with one another.

By comparing the two groups’ brain activity patterns, the researchers calculated a measurement called the Alzheimer’s resilience-vulnerability connectome score, or ARC score, that distinguishes super agers from people with Alzheimer’s with about 85% accuracy.
Researchers developed a brain activity scoring model, the ARC score, which can predict Alzheimer’s disease risk years before noticeable memory lapses occur. (iStock)

"I'm excited we established a signature that can help us better understand the difference between people who can maintain excellent cognitive performance and people who show cognitive decline," Yu Zhang, the study's senior author and an assistant professor of psychiatry and behavioral sciences at Stanford Medicine, said in a press release.
DEMENTIA RISK MAY BE LINKED TO SEEMINGLY HARMLESS DAILY HABIT, NEW RESEARCH SUGGESTS
Next, the scientists applied the scoring model to more than 1,300 cognitively unimpaired adults aged 55 to 70.

Although all the adults scored normally on memory tests, their brain scans showed differences: Some had activity patterns similar to super agers, while others had patterns more like those seen in people with Alzheimer’s.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

Over follow-up periods of up to 12 years, with most participants tracked for five to six years, those whose brain activity more closely resembled Alzheimer’s patterns showed faster declines in memory and thinking, developed more amyloid plaques and were more likely to be diagnosed with the disease, the researchers found.
The model successfully differentiated between the two extreme cognitive groups with approximately 85% accuracy. (Saul Loeb/AFP/Getty Images)
The team found that the ARC score matched or outperformed standard risk measures, including amyloid and tau biomarkers as well as genetic testing, in spotting early decline.

"We compared the ARC score with existing biomarkers in predicting people converting to Alzheimer's disease," lead author Kanhao Zhao, a postdoctoral scholar in psychiatry at Stanford Medicine, said in the release.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
"Our model shows comparable or better prediction ability, and it can do so at an earlier time point. And if we combine our score with the existing biomarkers, the prediction performance improves."
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
Alzheimer’s disease affects millions of older adults worldwide, according to major health institutions.
A central challenge in treating the disease is that physical damage often begins decades before patients notice memory lapses, at which point treatments offer limited benefit.
Across follow-up periods spanning up to 12 years, individuals with Alzheimer’s-like brain patterns experienced faster cognitive decline and higher diagnosis rates. (iStock)

Researchers stressed that the brain scan method is not yet ready for doctors to use on its own to diagnose Alzheimer’s. More studies are needed to confirm its accuracy and compare it with other new tests.

However, understanding how brain activity differs between healthy aging and neurodegeneration could help researchers test future treatments, including techniques that stimulate the brain without surgery.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"There are two main components: One is to know which part of the brain to target. The other is how we should change it," Zhang said.
"That's why identifying the super ager brain resilience pattern is a critical component — so we know what a good pattern should be."

title: Even occasional marijuana use linked to higher stroke risk, study finds
summary: A study of nearly 450,000 adults found that both casual and heavy marijuana users faced higher odds of stroke and cardiovascular disease than non-users.
story: American Heart Association expert Robert Page warns that cannabis use may increase cardiovascular risks, even in younger adults who don't smoke tobacco. He urges patients to discuss cannabis use with their doctors.
A new study of nearly 450,000 American adults links cannabis use to an increased risk of stroke and cardiovascular disease.

The findings, scheduled for presentation at the American Heart Association’s Scientific Sessions 2026 in Chicago Nov. 6–9, show that both casual and heavy marijuana users have higher odds of heart conditions compared to non-users.
Researchers analyzed survey responses collected between 2020 and 2024 through the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention's Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System.
SHARON STONE'S TERRIFYING WEED WITHDRAWAL SPARKS WARNING ABOUT TODAY'S POTENT MARIJUANA

People who reported using cannabis between one and five days per month had 23% higher odds of reporting a history of cardiovascular disease than non-users. Those using it 16 to 30 days per month had 21% higher odds.

"This study raises important concerns about cannabis use and cardiovascular health, particularly stroke," Dr. Kristen "Nicke" Worth, an Ohio-based physician and medical adviser at NuggMD, a telehealth platform for medical marijuana evaluations, told Fox News Digital.
A study of nearly 450,000 U.S. adults found that cannabis use is linked to significantly higher odds of cardiovascular disease, especially stroke. (iStock)

"One finding I found particularly interesting was that people who used cannabis just one to five days per month had somewhat higher reported odds of a previous stroke than people who used it more frequently," added Worth, who was not involved in the study.
Low-frequency users had 40% higher odds of a reported stroke, while heavy users had 25% higher odds. The study found no statistically significant link between cannabis use and heart attacks.
MARIJUANA USERS MAY FACE HIDDEN DRIVING DANGER THAT STANDARD TESTS CAN MISS

"That isn't what we'd necessarily expect from a straightforward dose-response relationship, where greater exposure is associated with greater risk. But we shouldn't interpret this as evidence that heavier use is safer," Worth said.
The method of consumption did not change the outcome. Whether participants smoked, vaped or consumed edibles like gummies, the risk remained consistent, according to the researchers.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"We were surprised to find that the link between cannabis use and cardiovascular disease was not straightforward," said lead author Dr. Aabha Divya, an assistant professor of cardiothoracic surgery at Tulane University School of Medicine, in an AHA press release.

"We expected that the chances of heart disease would gradually rise as people used cannabis more often, but that wasn't the case. Both low-use and heavy-use groups had higher odds of developing heart disease."
While the study showed a strong correlation with strokes, researchers found no statistically significant link between cannabis frequency and heart attacks. (Getty Images)

The study comes amid growing commercial availability and use of the drug across the country. According to the research team, about one in six adults reported past-month cannabis use in 2024, up from one in 10 in 2020 — a 51% increase over four years.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

Dr. Robert L. Page II, a professor of clinical pharmacy at the University of Colorado and an American Heart Association volunteer expert who was not involved in the study, said the findings challenge common assumptions about the drug's safety.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
"In patients who use both, cannabis has always been considered an innocent bystander; however, this is not the case," Page said in a press release.
"Overall, cannabis is beginning to emerge as a major contributor to premature heart disease in young and older adults, which can lead to serious cardiovascular events."
"People should not discontinue prescribed cardiovascular medications because of this report."
Page added that doctors should question patients about marijuana use just as they do with cigarettes and alcohol.

Researchers noted several key limitations to the findings. Because the study was observational and captured data from only a single point in time, it can only show a statistical link and cannot prove that cannabis causes heart disease or strokes.
Adult cannabis use has surged nationwide, rising 51% between 2020 and 2024 to reach one in six Americans. (iStock)

The data also relied on telephone surveys, leaving room for errors in participants' memory regarding their medical diagnoses and drug use. Additionally, the researchers did not track product strength, THC potency or total amounts consumed.
The findings remain preliminary until vetted through the full, peer-reviewed publication process.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"For patients, I wouldn't recommend making abrupt treatment decisions based on one preliminary study, but I wouldn't dismiss these findings," Worth said. "People should not discontinue prescribed cardiovascular medications because of this report."

"Anyone using cannabis, medically or recreationally, should discuss their cardiovascular history, existing risk factors, medications and treatment alternatives with their healthcare professional," she added.
Khloe Quill is a lifestyle writer with Fox News Digital. She and the lifestyle team cover a range of story topics including food and drink, travel, and health.

title: Wisconsin infant dies of measles as state sees first death from disease since 1990
summary: Wisconsin's health officials announced an infant's measles-associated death, marking the state's first in 36 years, amid 431 cases in 13 counties.
story: An infant in Wisconsin died of measles, marking the state’s first death linked to the disease in 36 years, according to state health officials.
An infant in Wisconsin died of measles, marking the state’s first death linked to the disease in 36 years, the state's Department of Health Services announced on Thursday.

The Department of Health Services said the child died in southwestern Wisconsin but did not provide a more precise location. The department said it would not release any additional details to protect the privacy of the family.
The coroner listed the immediate cause of death as measles.

"It is with a heavy heart we are reporting the first death of an infant connected with a measles outbreak in Wisconsin in many years. My heart is broken for the family," state Department of Health Services Secretary Kirsten Johnson said in a statement.
CHILD'S MEASLES DEATH MARKS NEW YORK STATE'S FIRST IN MORE THAN 30 YEARS AMID OUTBREAK
An infant in Wisconsin died of measles, marking the state’s first death linked to the disease in 36 years. (REUTERS/Shannon Stapleton)

"Any death of a child is a tragedy and even more so when it is related to a vaccine-preventable disease. Measles can cause serious illness and death, and it is important for all Wisconsinites to evaluate their risk and take steps to protect themselves and their family," she continued.

Measles can cause life-threatening complications, including pneumonia and swelling of the brain. The department said that while anyone can become seriously ill, children younger than 5, pregnant people and people with weakened immune systems are at increased risk of complications.

Wisconsin has reported 431 measles cases in 13 counties so far this year, reflecting the highest number of cases seen in the state in more than 35 years. Among these cases, nine people required hospitalization for severe symptoms.

State officials urged Wisconsinites to be proactive in preventing illness to protect themselves and their communities, saying the best way to prevent measles is with the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine.
Wisconsin has reported 431 measles cases in 13 counties so far this year. (Brandon Bell/Getty Images)

The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services previously told FOX News Digital that "Secretary Kennedy and CDC Director Dr. Erica Schwartz continue to make clear that the MMR vaccine is the most effective way to prevent measles."
Earlier this week, a child in New York state's Lewis County died in the first known measles-associated death in the state in more than 30 years.
New York Gov. Kathy Hochul said she was "heartbroken" to learn of the child's death.
"As a mother and grandmother, I cannot imagine what this family is going through. My heart goes out to everyone who knew and loved this child," Hochul said in a statement.
NEW YORK DECLARES MEASLES DISASTER EMERGENCY AS CASES SURGE IN PENNSYLVANIA

State officials urged Wisconsinites to be proactive in preventing illness to protect themselves and their communities, saying the best way to prevent measles is with the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine. (Raquel Natalicchio/Houston Chronicle via Getty Images)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has reported four measles-associated deaths across the country this year, although state health departments have reported higher figures.

In Pennsylvania, state health officials have confirmed six measles-associated deaths in 2026 and are investigating another reported death that has not yet met the state's criteria to be classified as measles-associated.
The Associated Press contributed to this report.

title: Twice-deported United cockpit suspect granted asylum after transgender persecution claim: DHS
summary: DHS says a twice-deported Honduran national won asylum claiming transgender persecution before allegedly trying to storm a United Airlines cockpit.
story: Retired NYPD inspector Paul Mauro explains how a twice-deported airline bomb threat suspect was granted a special immigration status on ‘The Story.’

A twice-deported Honduran national accused of trying to storm the cockpit of a United Airlines flight after allegedly claiming to have a bomb was granted asylum after telling immigration authorities he feared being killed in his home country because he was transgender, the Department of Homeland Security DHS confirmed to Fox News.

Rony Alexander Gomez-Alberto, 34, was granted asylum by an immigration judge after his third attempted illegal entry into the United States in 2019, according to DHS, which accused him of exploiting weaknesses in the asylum system.
In an excerpt of his asylum application provided by DHS, Gomez-Alberto checked "Yes" when asked whether he feared harm or mistreatment if returned to his home country.
TRUMP PUTS ASYLUM LAWYERS ‘ON NOTICE’ WITH NEW FRONT IN WAR ON FRAUD

An excerpt from Rony Alexander Gomez-Alberto's asylum application shows him claiming he feared being killed by private citizens or police because he was transgender. (Courtesy Department of Homeland Security)
"I am also afraid that I will be killed — either by private citizens or the police — in both of these countries because I am transgender," he allegedly wrote, according to the application.

"This criminal illegal alien attempted to storm the cockpit, hijack a plane and claimed he had a bomb. Thanks to law enforcement, he is now behind bars," DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin said in a statement.
"This twice-deported criminal illegal alien was allowed into our country because of a weak asylum system that allowed him to game the system."
Gomez-Alberto was arrested after United Airlines Flight 2174 landed in New Orleans Nov. 9 after the alleged attempt at a cockpit breach.
MAN ACCUSED OF THREATENING TO HIJACK UNITED FLIGHT SAYS IT WAS A DRUNKEN JOKE

Rony Alexander Gomez-Alberto, a Honduran national DHS says was deported twice, was arrested after an alleged cockpit breach attempt aboard a United Airlines flight Nov. 9, 2026.   (Courtesy Department of Homeland Security)
He is being held without bond on charges of terrorizing, communicating false information of planned arson and being a fugitive from justice, according to Fox News Digital's earlier reporting.
Newly obtained emergency radio audio, reported by Fox News Digital, captured authorities' response.
"We have him at the back door. The back door has been breached by him," someone can be heard in the radio call saying.

DHS previously confirmed that Gomez-Alberto was apprehended by Border Patrol after illegally entering the United States near El Indio, Texas, in September 2011 and Columbus, New Mexico, in October 2014. He was deported from the United States following both encounters.
EXCLUSIVE: WOMAN ALLEGEDLY RAPED BY ILLEGAL ALIEN AFTER CLINTON-APPOINTED FEDERAL JUDGE ORDERED HIS RELEASE
United Airlines confirmed that Flight 2174 landed safely in New Orleans after a passenger disturbance Monday. (Anadolu via Getty Images)
Border Patrol arrested him again in 2019 after an attempted illegal entry near San Ysidro, California.

ICE released Gomez-Alberto from custody in January 2020 following an immigration judge's order, pending removal proceedings, DHS previously said. The agency now says an immigration judge subsequently granted him asylum.

ICE lodged a detainer with the Jefferson Parish Sheriff's Office on Nov. 10, requesting notification before his release from custody.The Department of Justice and Jefferson Parish Sheriff's Office did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's requests for comment.Fox News Digital's Kelsie Cairns contributed to this reporting.

title: Jeffries leaves door open to investigating major Trump ally as Democrats prepare to take power
summary: Hakeem Jeffries says Democrats will "follow the facts" as Jamie Raskin and Robert Garcia prepare to lead oversight of Elon Musk and DOGE.
story: House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries was not opposed to an Elon Musk probe as threats to investigate the former head of DOGE continue to loom after Democrats took back both majorities in Congress. (Credit: Nicholas Ballasy for Fox News Digital)

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries left the door open to a congressional investigation into Elon Musk as threats to probe both the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) and other Trump allies continue to heat up under a new Democratic House majority.
"We're going to follow the facts," Jeffries said about the potential investigation. "We're going to apply the law. We're gonna be guided by the Constitution."
Musk has emerged as a potential target of Democratic oversight, with some lawmakers calling for scrutiny of his time as head of the DOGE.
The calls for an investigation come as Democrats have started rallying the party to look into alleged corruption under the Trump administration after coming out victorious in midterms.
SCHUMER, JEFFRIES SIDESTEP QUESTIONS ON NUKING FILIBUSTER, LAUNCHING ELON MUSK PROBE AFTER BLUE WAVE
President Donald Trump's friendship with Elon Musk is warming up again as the president reignites praise and mentions of Musk in public. (Brandon Bell/Getty Images)
Asked whether Musk should be investigated by the new Democratic majority, Jeffries declined to commit to a probe, instead pointing to the lawmakers expected to lead the party's oversight efforts.
"Jamie Raskin and Robert Garcia are going to lead our oversight efforts," Jeffries told Fox News Digital. "And I defer to them at the moment."

Raskin, D-Md., has already signaled that DOGE could face congressional scrutiny, telling Fox News Digital last week he believes an investigation is warranted, even as he acknowledged having no specific plan.
‘LAWYER UP’: DEMS IMMEDIATELY PUT TRUMP ON NOTICE AMID REPUBLICANS' MIDTERM BLOODBATH

"I had no specific plan," Raskin told Fox News Digital about the potential investigations. "Look … DOGE was a catastrophe for America, and at least one committee, I feel pretty certain, will investigate it. It needs to investigate it."
After taking the majority, the prospects for new investigations come with Raskin and Garcia positioned to be chairs of the House Judiciary and Oversight Committees.
Raskin, Garcia, Jeffries and Assistant Democratic Leader Joe Neguse have already begun strategizing plans for the investigative agenda.

Jeffries is in the running for speaker of the House after formally announcing his bid just a day after Democrats took back the majority in the midterm elections. Democrats have not been united in their decision to back Jeffries or another candidate to represent the party as House speaker.
REPORTER’S NOTEBOOK: HOUSE LEADERSHIP UP FOR GRABS AS GOP RECKONS WITH DEVASTATING LOSSES
House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries speaks alongside Rep. Pete Aguilar and Rep. Katherine Clark during a news conference in Washington, D.C., Jan. 8, 2026. (Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images)
Leadership elections for House Democrats will be held Nov. 18 and members will vote with "secret ballots" to keep their individual nominations private.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Jeffries will need a simple majority of Democrats to be nominated, but to be formally elected as House speaker, he’ll need to get 218 floor votes.
Hannah is a Production Assistant for the Politics team at Fox News Digital.

title: Hakeem Jeffries faces progressive holdouts but no rival as House speaker race takes shape
summary: New members of Congress in "The Bloc" say they're undecided on Hakeem Jeffries for House speaker, pressing for legislative guarantees before January.
story: House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries tells Fox News he is going to speak to every member ahead of leadership elections to rally support to be selected as speaker of the House.
Familiar faces populate the 110-plus new members of Congress.
A few "freshmen" are returning to the House. Even if they’ve been gone for a while.
There’s Rep.-elect Hilda Solis, D-Calif., who last served in Congress in 2009. She departed to become President Obama’s labor secretary.
Rep.-elect Jerry Carl, R-Ala., just left Capitol Hill early last year after losing a primary to Rep. Barry Moore, R-Ala., who is now moving to the Senate.
REPORTER’S NOTEBOOK: A DEMOCRATIC MAJORITY COULD EXPOSE THE LIMITS OF THE PROGRESSIVE AGENDA
And then there’s Rep.-elect Melissa Bean, D-Ill. She first won a seat in the House in 2004 and lost in 2010. Now, Bean is back.
Her advice to the rookies?
Rep.-elect Melissa Bean returns to Congress with advice for newcomers: Hire a good scheduler and make time to eat. (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images)

"Make sure you get a really good scheduler and that they schedule eating because your staff will run you all day long," Bean said. "You're kind of like the football that they pass from one staff member to the other. The whole day goes by, and you’re starving."

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., is on track to become House speaker in January. But some progressives are holding out. Bean was a moderate when she served before. Yours truly asked about the natural unease between left-wing Democrats and centrists.
"It’s a pretty united majority," replied Bean.
"Do you think that’s overstated tension?" I followed up.
"I think it always is," Bean answered. "But that’s a media thing, right?"
So to recap for new members: Get a good scheduler? Check. Make sure you have time to eat? Check. And, blame the press.
Ha.
MEET THE FAR-LEFT INSURGENTS WAGING WAR ON THE DEMOCRATIC ESTABLISHMENT IN 2026 MIDTERMS

But, seriously, there are some progressives who aren’t willing to publicly commit to supporting Jeffries as speaker. Most of these incoming members comprise what’s now known as "The Bloc." It’s kind of like "The Squad" some years ago.
And they’re not tipping their hand about Jeffries.
They’re trying to squeeze the New York Democrat and others for legislative guarantees.
"We're not withholding votes. What we're doing is saying we're undecided. We're not going to rubber-stamp anything," said Rep.-elect Adam Hamawy, D-N.J.

"I don't think it's about the individual. It’s about the agenda and the agenda that actually reflects the priorities of the American people," said Rep.-elect Melat Kiros, D-Colo. "It's about what kind of priorities, what kind of floor votes, what kind of plan do we have to actually fight for the bold change the American people sent us here to do."
"I think we need to be talking about improving the lives of working people and helping them join unions," said Rep.-elect Claire Valdez, D-N.Y.
There’s nothing groundbreaking going on here. Progressive Democrats won. Democrats won big. The Bloc wants to flex its muscles and execute its agenda.
House Democrats prepare for a new Congress as competing factions seek a say in the party’s agenda. (Alex Wong/Getty Images)
Otherwise, those members have explaining to do with their base. Thus, it’s not that extraordinary to have a group of members not automatically supporting someone for a leadership post.
They’re playing the political game to get the best deal for the people they represent. They can’t just back Jeffries out of the gate. They must first extract a concession.
Rep. Joe Courtney, D-Conn., witnessed these machinations before when former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi, D-Calif., tried to manage dissent about her leadership after elections.

"I actually think it's a weaker version [of protest] this time," said Courtney. "I think [Jeffries] did a great job of keeping the caucus really marching in the same direction in the last two years. Which was not easy."
"There's no question that as a management matter, having a bigger majority is a lot easier than having a tiny majority. That's just basic math," said Rep. Jim Himes, D-Conn.

"As a new speaker, he's going to need to do a lot of work to make sure he is listening to everybody and managing. So, it's going to be a lot easier than if it had been a four-vote majority. But managing Democrats is always a challenge."
So, for all of the talk about "issues" progressives may have with Jeffries, they’re not offering up an alternative name for speaker. And, frankly, no one could beat Jeffries in this environment.
PROGRESSIVES FUME AT HAKEEM JEFFRIES FOR SAYING DEMOCRATS WON'T 'GET EVEN' WITH TRUMP

"You can’t beat somebody with nobody. And that’s kind of where I think this ‘race’ stands," said Courtney, putting "race" in air quotes. "The worst thing that could happen is to start this Congress off like it happened in 2023, where we went through 15 ballots (before electing a speaker)."
That’s a reference to House Republicans stymieing the election of former House Speaker Kevin McCarthy, R-Calif.
Rep. Glenn Ivey, D-Md., appeared mystified at progressive machinations over Jeffries.

"It is kind of odd. You get a coach who takes his team to the Super Bowl. They win by 30 points, and then they got folks who want to fire him the next day. It's a little hard to figure out," said Ivey.

Progressives may express concerns about Jeffries. But remember that Democrats have the majority because they flipped deeply red districts. The Democrats who will represent those districts know that voters could note if they supported Jeffries — or broke with him.
Hakeem Jeffries and Chuck Schumer face pressure from incoming progressives over the Democratic Party’s legislative priorities. (Win McNamee/Getty Images)

Rep.-elect Don Leonard, D-Ohio, appears to be one of the most outspoken incoming members. Leonard emerged from nowhere to defeat Rep. Mike Carey, R-Ohio. On Instagram, Leonard said Democratic leaders informed him in "no uncertain terms" that if he didn’t support Jeffries, the party brass would make his "life a living hell" and assure he would lose re-election.
So, there are questions from the left and questions from centrists.
Yours truly pressed Jeffries about whether the skepticism from progressives was real or just politics as they try to extract legislative promises out of him.

"I'm going to work hard to talk to every single member about what we've been able to do together over the last two years and what the opportunities are for us to do together in the next two years, to deliver upon the dramatic change that the American people so decisively voted for this past Tuesday," Jeffries replied, not directly answering.
"That sounds like you don't have it nailed down. Is that right?" I followed up.
Jeffries chuckled.
"You think I don't have the vote nailed down?" he countered.
"I'm asking you. You're the vote counter. Do you have them? Yes or no?" I queried.
"I guess we'll find out next Wednesday," Jeffries said.
I have reported on the air that it would take a lot to sidetrack a prospective Jeffries speakership.
House Democrats will likely have north of 260 seats in the new Congress.

The magic number to claim the gavel on the House floor is 218. It’s hard to see Jeffries losing 42 votes. Especially when no one is competing against him. Moreover, he only needs to marshal 131 votes in the Democratic Caucus (just better than half of 260) to become the official nominee.
But that said, there is tension in the Democratic ranks.
Some of that is natural inside such a massive coalition. It’s not construed by the press corps.
The question is how will Jeffries manage those disparate factions when he clasps the gavel as speaker Jan. 3.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
The dispute now is a symptom of what problems could lie ahead.
Chad Pergram currently serves as Chief Congressional Correspondent for FOX News Channel (FNC). He joined the network in September 2007 and is based out of Washington, D.C.

title: At least 9 new Dem members will carry Al Green's mantle and try to impeach President Trump
summary: Rep. Al Green says at least nine incoming House Democratic caucus members will join his impeachment push, citing President Trump's crypto dealings and what they described as corruption.
story: Rep. Al Green is pushing the House again to vote on impeaching President Donald Trump.

EXCLUSIVE: At least 9 incoming progressive members of the House Democratic caucus are expected to support efforts to impeach President Donald Trump, continuing a push led by outgoing Rep. Al Green, D-Texas, Fox News Digital has learned.

Green and representatives from the Removal Coalition and Courage for Democracy Project discussed the effort with Fox News Digital after a Capitol Hill news conference, months after the Texas Democrat introduced articles of impeachment against Trump in August.

Green is counting on support from Reps.-elect Melat Kiros, D-Colo.; Dan Koh, D-Mass.; Chris Rabb, D-Pa.; Angela Gonzales-Torres, D-Calif.; and several other incoming Democrats to continue his impeachment efforts after he leaves Congress.
DEMOCRAT AL GREEN TO FORCE HOUSE-WIDE VOTE ON IMPEACHING TRUMP

Rep. Al Green, D-Texas, speaks at a news conference after joining Remove the Regime protesters as they march from Union Station to the Capitol Nov. 20, 2025, in Washington, D.C. (Heather Diehl/Getty Images)

"Impeachment is the only means for our future. We cannot deal with a president who engages in corruption," Green told Fox News Digital. "The end is to have the president removed from office. I applaud the courageous members carrying these efforts into the next Congress."
Green pointed to Trump's cryptocurrency dealings as one example of what he characterized as corruption by the president.
REPORTER'S NOTEBOOK: DEMOCRATS FACE AN IMPEACHMENT TRACTOR BEAM THAT COULD DERAIL THEIR AFFORDABILITY MESSAGE
Gonzales-Torres told Fox News Digital she intends to continue Green's efforts while representing the more than 100,000 Los Angeles voters she said elected her to Congress.

The coalition acknowledged uncertainty over whether its impeachment efforts would succeed, noting that even if the House approved articles against Trump, the Senate could again decline to convict him, as it did in Trump’s two previous impeachment trials.

President Donald Trump departs after signing the GENIUS Act, a bill that regulates stablecoins, a type of cryptocurrency, in the East Room of the White House July 18, 2025, in Washington. (Alex Brandon/AP Photo)
TRUMP COULD FACE IMPEACHMENT IF DEMOCRATS SEIZE HOUSE MAJORITY, GOP LEADER WARNS
However, organizers expressed confidence that growing grassroots pressure could persuade additional Democratic lawmakers to support impeachment.

"The more we articulate this effort and talk about why it is so crucial that we get rid of Trump, the more support we will have," Keira Havens, co-founder of the Courage for Democracy Project, told Fox News Digital.

Havens acknowledged that some Democrats who oppose Trump may still reject impeachment articles because they believe the allegations lack sufficient legal grounds or that conviction would fail in the Senate.

A constitutional expert affiliated with the Courage for Democracy Project also argued that Senate impeachment procedures could provide additional avenues for removing a president, citing Rule VIII. However, the Constitution gives the House the sole power of impeachment and the Senate the sole power to try impeachments.
PROGRESSIVES FUME AT HAKEEM JEFFRIES FOR SAYING DEMOCRATS WON'T 'GET EVEN' WITH TRUMP

Jessica Denson, identified as the founder of the Removal Coalition, criticized Democratic lawmakers who have prioritized congressional hearings and potential prosecutions of Trump administration officials over impeaching the president himself.

Denson called those lawmakers "spineless," arguing that grassroots pressure could eventually push them to support the coalition's demands. The coalition told Fox News Digital that "hearings and prosecutions aren't enough," and enough public backlash will lead any remaining Democratic lawmaker to get behind impeachment efforts.
The effort comes as Democrats prepare to take control of the House in January, potentially giving impeachment supporters a greater opportunity to advance resolutions against Trump.
Under the Constitution, impeachment requires a simple majority in the House, while conviction and removal from office require a two-thirds majority of senators present.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

During and after the news conference, the coalition, consisting of the two advocacy organizations and incoming and outgoing lawmakers, told Fox News Digital it also intends to pursue impeachment proceedings against War Secretary Pete Hegseth.
Eight articles of impeachment have been brought against War Secretary Pete Hegseth. (Kevin Wolf/AP)
The coalition argued that Hegseth should face impeachment alongside Trump, claiming that any wrongdoing uncovered involving the war secretary could also implicate the president.
However, a finding of wrongdoing by Hegseth would not automatically establish legal or constitutional liability for Trump.
Trump and Hegseth did not respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.

title: Dems projected to score historic upset in deep-red Mississippi, topple Trump ally Hyde-Smith
summary: U.S. Senate Republicans suffered another stunning setback as Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith is projected to lose to Democrat Scott Colom in reliably red Mississippi, according to the AP.
story: Fox News chief political analyst Brit Hume discusses the results of the 2026 midterm elections as Mississippi turns blue on 'Special Report.'
Senate Republicans are projected to suffer yet another stunning setback, this time in reliably red Mississippi.

Incumbent Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith, R-Miss., is projected to lose her bid for a second full term in the U.S. Senate to state District Attorney Scott Colom in a race that was deadlocked until the final weeks of October, according to The Associated Press.
More than a week after Election Day, the AP called the razor-thin race in favor of Colom Wednesday, pushing the Democrats' hold on the U.S. Senate to 55 seats to the Republicans' 44 in another flip.
SOROS NETWORK TARGETS DEEP-RED MISSISSIPPI IN BID TO FLIP SENATE SEAT

Democrats could gain another pending the results in Alaska, where former Rep. Mary Peltola is in a neck-and-neck contest with Sen. Dan Sullivan, R-Alaska. A source told Fox News Digital Hyde-Smith had spoken with Colom and conceded the race.
Mississippi District Attorney Scott Colom, center, ran for Senate against Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith, R-Miss., and has backers with deep pockets in the Soros family. (Courtesy of Colom Senate campaign)
Colom's victory over Hyde-Smith marked a historic moment in the Magnolia State, which hasn't elected a Democrat to the Senate since the 1980s.
Hyde-Smith, in a video posted to X, said, "While this is not the outcome we worked for or hoped for, I respect the decision of Mississippi voters.
"I want to congratulate Scott Colom and wish him well as he takes on the tremendous responsibility of representing our great state."

His win comes after President Donald Trump rallied behind Hyde-Smith and a seven-figure, last-minute ad buy by the Senate Leadership Fund, a political action committee closely tied to Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., was not enough to stop Colom’s momentum.
CHUCK SCHUMER AFTER SWEEPING DEMOCRATIC MIDTERM VICTORIES: 'I'LL BE RE-ELECTED AS MAJORITY LEADER'
U.S. Sen. Cindy-Hyde Smith, R-Miss., had eyed a second term in the upper chamber. (Al Drago/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., and Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee Chair Kirsten Gillibrand, D-N.Y., took a victory lap before the race was officially called by The Associated Press, congratulating Colom on his historic win in a state that once seemed unattainable. "Congratulations to Senator-Elect Colom on his historic win and on becoming the first Democrat to win a Mississippi Senate seat in over four decades," the lawmakers said. "We will work hand in hand with Scott to fight for Mississippians’ health care, costs and future in the 120th Congress and look forward to welcoming him to our caucus."

Hyde-Smith's loss to Colom, who she previously blocked for a district court seat under the Biden administration years ago, comes after both parties rallied big names and resources in an effort to prevent a nightmare scenario for Republicans.But in a previous interview with Fox News Digital, Colom said that wasn't his motivating factor.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"I'll tell you, as a Christian, I forgive her for that. That's not a motivating factor for me," Colom said. "I mean, as a district attorney, I have to prosecute cases where people lost their loved ones to gun violence. So, you know, and I’ve seen them forgive that person.

"So, that's not the motivating factor," he continued. "For me, it's really the betrayal of the America First movement, right? Like she was supposed to help President Trump get lower grocery prices. Well, she betrayed us. We're not getting lower grocery prices."
Alex Miller is a writer for Fox News Digital covering the U.S. Senate.

title: Army sentinel sharply reprimands Hegseth's group at Tomb of the Unknown Soldier on Veterans Day
summary: Video captures the moment a Tomb of the Unknown Soldier sentinel called for silence and respect after laughter from Pete Hegseth's departing group.
story: A soldier guarding the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier reminded visitors to maintain silence and respect after laughter was heard during a photo session involving Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth's entourage.

An Army sentinel at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier at Arlington National Cemetery called for silence and respect Wednesday after laughter was heard from departing members of Secretary of War Pete Hegseth's entourage following a Veterans Day ceremony.
Video shows the incident unfolding shortly after President Donald Trump left the memorial following a wreath-laying ceremony.

Trump left the memorial around 12:28 p.m. Hegseth and members of his entourage, including his wife, Jennifer Hegseth, began taking photos and posing on the memorial steps around 12:29 p.m., according to the video.
TRUMP UNLOADS ON AOC, MAMDANI FOR LAUGHING DURING SACRED 9/11 CEREMONY AT GROUND ZERO

Secretary of War Pete Hegseth, second from left, and first lady Melania Trump bow their heads in prayer during a Veterans Day ceremony at Arlington National Cemetery in Virginia on Nov. 11, 2026. (Mandel Ngan / AFP via Getty Images)
Roughly a minute later, laughter could be heard in the distance as members of the group departed, prompting a soldier guarding the tomb to issue a sharp reminder to those gathered.
"All visitors will maintain an atmosphere of silence and respect at all times," the soldier said.
The instruction came around 12:30 p.m., after Trump had left the ceremony.
TRAVELERS UNITE IN POWERFUL MOMENT OF SILENCE AS FALLEN US SERVICE MEMBER RETURNS HOME

Secretary of War Pete Hegseth, joined by his wife, Jennifer Hegseth, and Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff Gen. Dan Caine, left, participates in a Veterans Day wreath-laying ceremony at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier at Arlington National Cemetery in Virginia on Nov. 11, 2026. (Mandel Ngan/ AFP via Getty Images)
Chief Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell responded to the incident in a statement to Fox News, emphasizing the department's commitment to honoring fallen service members.

"The Secretary and the entire Department have always honored—and will always honor—the sacrifices our military men and women have made to keep America safe," Parnell said. "While commemorating this solemn day, a soldier correctly and respectfully reminded everyone to maintain decorum."
The soldiers who guard the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier are known as sentinels and belong to the 3rd U.S. Infantry Regiment, also known as The Old Guard.
HEGSETH DEMANDS $350B FOR MILITARY, FIRES BACK AT DEM IMPEACHMENT PUSH

Secretary of War Pete Hegseth attends a Veterans Day wreath-laying ceremony with President Donald Trump at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier at Arlington National Cemetery in Virginia on Nov. 11, 2026. (Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images)
According to Arlington National Cemetery, sentinels stand watch at the tomb 24 hours a day, 365 days a year, regardless of weather conditions.

The highly selective assignment requires extensive training, including memorizing cemetery history, mastering ceremonial procedures and maintaining strict standards of military appearance and conduct.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

The Tomb of the Unknown Soldier honors unidentified American service members who died in military conflicts. The memorial is among the nation's most solemn military sites and serves as a focal point of Veterans Day commemorations.
Brittany Miller is a Fox News Digital breaking news writer and former Independent reporter who graduated from Syracuse University in 2023.

title: Trump's ex-lawyer Alina Habba loses massive contract days after president blasts 'outrageous' deal
summary: Donald Trump personally directed Alina Habba's firing from a $50 million Concord Partners contract linked to pardoned Venezuelan banker's family.
story: Interim U.S. Attorney for New Jersey Alina Habba discusses what the Trump administration has accomplished in 100 days on ‘The Evening Edit.’

President Donald Trump's former personal attorney, Alina Habba Mildon, has lost a four-year contract worth more than $50 million to serve as general counsel for a company founded by the daughter of a Venezuelan billionaire Trump pardoned earlier this year, according to The New York Times.

Concord Partners, a Florida-based company founded by Isabela Herrera, daughter of Venezuelan banker Julio Herrera Velutini, terminated Habba Mildon’s contract after President Donald Trump urged the Herrera family to stop paying her, The Philadelphia Inquirer reported Wednesday.
A source familiar with the matter confirmed the termination to Fox News Digital.
TRUMP SIGNS PARDONS FOR ALASKA DIESEL MECHANICS ONSTAGE DURING RALLY TOUTING MAJOR ENERGY DEALS

White House Presidential Counselor Alina Habba delivers remarks before being sworn in as the interim U.S. attorney for New Jersey in the Oval Office at the White House March 28, 2025, in Washington, D.C. Habba is a former personal attorney for President Donald Trump.   (Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)
Concord Partners cited a "failure to perform duties" in a Nov. 4 termination letter obtained by The New York Times.

Trump pardoned Venezuelan banker Julio Herrera Velutini Jan. 15, 2026, just two weeks after Habba Mildon began working for the company founded by his daughter. Herrera faced federal bribery charges tied to an alleged scheme involving Puerto Rico’s governor and struck a plea deal accepting a misdemeanor campaign finance violation in August 2025.
The firing came just days after Trump publicly blasted Habba Mildon’s $50 million arrangement as excessive and said he did not want her to receive the money.

"I thought it was terrible," Trump told reporters at Mar-a-Lago Oct. 31, Reuters reported. "I told her, and I said, 'I don't want her paid.'" He called the arrangement "totally obnoxious and outrageous" and "not acceptable."

President Donald Trump listens as White House Presidential Counselor Alina Habba delivers remarks before being sworn in as interim U.S. attorney for New Jersey in the Oval Office at the White House March 28, 2025, in Washington, D.C.   (Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)
Habba Mildon has denied playing any role in securing Herrera Velutini's pardon, pushing back against questions about whether her contract was connected to the president's decision.
DOJ OPENS INVESTIGATION INTO TRUMP ALLY COREY LEWANDOWSKI

"The Fake News still seems very confused by this so let me be even more clear: I was never paid to secure a pardon. I never met with anyone at the White House or DOJ about a pardon. I’ve never done any work in any capacity whatsoever for a pardon for anyone, period," Habba Mildon wrote on X Oct. 21.

Habba Mildon signed the agreement with Concord Partners in October 2025 while serving as acting U.S. attorney for New Jersey. She began working for the company on Jan. 1, 2026, after becoming a senior advisor to Attorney General Pam Bondi, according to the outlet.
Habba Mildon had already received about $14.5 million, including an $8 million signing bonus and $6.5 million in additional payments, according to The New York Times.
MADURO ALLY DEPORTED TO US OVER ALLEGED BILLION-DOLLAR CORRUPTION SCHEME TIED TO OIL, FOOD PROGRAM
Alina Habba speaks after being sworn in as interim U.S. attorney for New Jersey in the Oval Office of the White House in Washington March 28, 2025. (Pool File via AP)

Fox News Digital reached out to Habba Mildon and the White House for comment.
Ashley J. DiMella reports on politics for Fox News Digital.

title: Longtime GOP leader faces uncertain future after Jim Jordan wins House leadership fight
summary: Steve Scalise declined to commit to serving a full term in the 120th Congress after losing the House Republican minority leader race to Jim Jordan.
story: As Scalise leaves leadership, he declines to tell Fox News’ Chad Pergram if he intends to serve a full term in the upcoming 120th Congress.

House Majority Leader Steve Scalise, R-La., the No. 2 Republican in the House of Representatives and the most tenured figure among the chamber's party leadership, declined to say whether he would commit to serving the full term in the upcoming 120th Congress.
"There’s no decision on what’s next," Scalise said on Wednesday.

"I’ve got to get through these next few weeks, and then we have a lot of decisions to make about what's life going to look like in the minority. But I sure still have a great passion for this country."
JIM JORDAN THROWS HAT IN RING FOR HOUSE MINORITY LEADER AS GOP PICKS UP PIECES AFTER BLUE WAVE

House Majority Leader Steve Scalise, R-La., speaks alongside Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., right, and Rep. Mark Messmer, R-Ind., during a news conference in the Capitol Visitor Center on June 4, 2025. (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images)

Scalise’s answer follows a loss to Rep. Jim Jordan, R-Ohio, in a bid to become the party’s new minority leader. His defeat now forces Scalise to decide whether he intends to retire or remain on Capitol Hill as a rank-and-file member of the minority as Democrats retake control of the House in January.
For now, Scalise stressed that he remains focused on securing GOP priorities before the new year.

"There’s a lot more for us to do. We have a few weeks left in the lame duck [session] and, frankly, a few big, big issues ahead. I want to see us do as much as we possibly can while we still have this majority," Scalise said.
"I’ve got a lot more gas in the tank. Obviously, all of us know there’s some real change coming in January. We still have work to do right now."
Jordan beat out Scalise in a 106-73 vote in Tuesday’s GOP elections.
Scalise, who was elected in 2008 and first joined Republican leadership in 2014, proved a steady figure and mouthpiece for conservative principles even as the party shifted dramatically around him.
Scalise originally served as House whip alongside Speaker John Boehner, R-Ohio.
JORDAN EMERGES AS POTENTIAL NEXT GOP LEADER IF DEMS SEIZE HOUSE

Speaker John Boehner, R-Ohio, left, and House Majority Whip Steve Scalise, R-La., leave after a news conference at the U.S. Capitol on June 10, 2015, in Washington, D.C. (Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images)

Although Boehner would eventually step down after the right flank of the party accused him of failing to secure GOP priorities, Scalise remained a constant, continuing to serve as whip under his successor, Speaker Paul Ryan, R-Wis. Around the same time, Donald Trump, then just a candidate for president, began gaining momentum in the GOP primary.
As the party’s core began to gravitate toward Trump, Scalise’s time in Congress and personal well-being were challenged when he was shot at a congressional baseball practice in 2017.
Although the incident left him with health complications, the attack elevated Scalise’s national profile.
"Just left hospital. Rep. Steve Scalise, one of the truly great people, is in very tough shape — but he is a real fighter. Pray for Steve!" Trump said in a post to social media at the time.
In 2023, Scalise would climb to the No. 2 job, becoming majority leader after Republicans recaptured the House of Representatives under Speaker Kevin McCarthy, R-Calif.
And when McCarthy himself was removed from the post for failing to deliver Republican demands to cut spending, Scalise launched an unsuccessful bid for speaker.
Instead, Scalise remained majority leader as Republicans rallied around Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La.
Asked if he would have done anything differently in his most recent bid to lead the House GOP, Scalise said he had no regrets.
"Nothing that could have been done differently in the leadership race," Scalise said.
MIKE JOHNSON'S NO 2 LAUNCHES GOP TAKEOVER BID AS HOUSE FALLS TO DEMOCRATS
House Majority Leader Steve Scalise on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange before morning trading on April 15. (Adam Gray/Getty Images)

title: Stephen Miller's internal memo unleashes Trump agencies after 'absolute control' under Wiles' reign
summary: A memo under new chief of staff Stephen Miller gives Cabinet secretaries messaging control, shifting from what sources say was Susie Wiles' grip.
story: Fox News' Kayleigh McEnany reacts to President Donald Trump tapping Stephen Miller as the new White House chief of staff following the departure of Susie Wiles. McEnany discusses Hakeem Jeffries' potential to become House speaker.

EXCLUSIVE: A memo describing the new White House hierarchy under chief of staff Stephen Miller circulated within the Trump administration this week, and details how Cabinet secretaries will now have more control over their own messaging.

This is a shift from what insiders say was administration-wide communications control implemented by former chief of staff Susie Wiles during the first nearly two years of President Donald Trump's second term.
"This will streamline the Cabinet, making it a more effective instrument for the President, whereas previously it was too constrained," a source familiar with the message told Fox News Digital.
The memo was sent by Miller's office after he took over the role on Monday. It was titled as a memo on administrative matters and personnel changes, the source said.

White House chief of staff Susie Wiles sits in the Oval Office, as President Donald Trump signs an executive order, at the White House in Washington, D.C., on Dec. 18, 2025. (Evelyn Hockstein/Reuters)
THE STONING OF STEPHEN MILLER, NOW RUNNING THE TRUMP WHITE HOUSE

"The White House position of Cabinet Secretary will be changed to the role of Director of Cabinet Relations, focused on providing support and reinforcement of President Trump's tremendous Cabinet Secretaries," details the memo, which Fox News Digital viewed.

"Each cabinet leader serves as the best leader and communicator for their individual Departments, and this new position will ensure our Cabinet is resourced and bolstered by the White House to deliver swift, critical, and lasting wins for the American people," the memo continues.

Another source who is familiar with day-to-day administration operations believes the memo signals a shift in communications policy, giving different agencies the ability to control their own messaging now that Miller has become chief of staff.
Stephen Miller listens during a meeting with President Donald Trump and oil company executives in the East Room of the White House on Jan. 9, 2026. (Saul Loeb/AFP via Getty Images)
The source said that previously, they believe Wiles had a chokehold on nearly all the administration's communications, and that there were "a lot of prescriptive directives" from Wiles' camp.

"I mean, to me, it reflects well on Miller and his team and I think it's really smart to be making these moves quite clear, to be communicating clearly and effectively, you know?" the source said, speaking of the policy shake-up described in the memo.
The source added that the policy change is "unleashing the Cabinet to be the captains of their own ship."

"It's more [of] a recognition that you can't possibly effectively micromanage this wide of an organization and that sometimes it might be better to trust and invest in a support system that elevates the people who are closest to the issues," the source said.
TRUMP'S NEW PRESS SECRETARY FACES FIRST MAJOR TEST AS WHITE HOUSE BRIEFING ROOM ENTERS NEW ERA
President Donald Trump attends a Cabinet meeting at the White House in Washington on May 27, 2026. (Jacquelyn Martin/AP)
WHITE HOUSE THREATENS POLITICO WITH 'CONSEQUENCES' IF IT DOESN'T RETRACT SUSIE WILES REPORTING
A former Trump administration official had much more direct criticism of Wiles' management style.
"She wants complete authority," the source said.

"The control doesn't come from, 'hey, you have to do this.' The control comes from threat of duress. Like, 'if you don't do this, I'm going to destroy you in the media,'" they continued. "The thing is, she has been very clear. 'I can't control [Trump]. I can control everything else.'"
The source accused Wiles of approaching Cabinet secretaries and warning them that if they said anything off script in the media, that midterm GOP election losses would be blamed on them.

President Donald Trump hosts a lunch with the Kennedy Center board members alongside chief of staff Susie Wiles at the White House in Washington, D.C., on March 16, 2026. (Annabelle Gordon/AFP via Getty Images)
TRUMP CLOSING IN ON NEW PRESS SECRETARY AS ADMINISTRATION OFFICIALS PUSH FOR PICK WHO COULD BREAK THE MOLD
"It's absolute control," the source said.

The memo also highlights some hierarchical changes within the administration, saying the director of presidential scheduling and the Office of Presidential Scheduling will report directly to Chamberlain Harris, the deputy director of outer oval operations.
It also confirms previous reporting that Caleb Orr, formerly the assistant secretary of state for economic and business affairs, will become the chief of staff for policy.
President Donald Trump takes questions from reporters during a press briefing at the White House on Nov. 9, 2026. (Mandel Ngan/AFP via Getty Images)

"The White House will run a clear and regular policy process through the Deputy Chief of Staff for Policy and the National Security Advisor, with clearly defined responsibilities and assignments and no overlapping policy portfolios," the memo says.
