DHS INVESTIGATES MASSIVE DATA BREACH EXPOSING 40,000 EMPLOYEES, INCLUDING ICE AND BORDER PATROL AGENTS

A massive Homeland Security data leak exposed records involving more than 41,000 employees and contractors, including personnel connected to undercover ICE operations. (Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images)
What the Homeland Security data leak exposed

On Oct. 28, the nonprofit Distributed Denial of Secrets published a collection of DHS records under the name Icepick. The information reportedly came from a group calling itself the Department of Peace, which claims it obtained access to internal government systems. The records reportedly cover DHS and seven of its component agencies, including Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP).

The files contain employee names, agency email addresses and workplace locations. They also include phone numbers, some identified as cell phone numbers, along with supervisors and internal access-group memberships. However, it has not been established that employees' private home addresses were included. CBP accounts for more than half the records, while roughly 10,000 involve ICE. Another 6,200 are tied to U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services. The records were last updated on Aug. 19, so some assignments may have changed. That's an enormous amount of organizational information to have floating around publicly. And the deeper researchers looked, the more sensitive the findings became.
Undercover ICE operations appear in leaked records

One of the most alarming findings involves internal groups associated with undercover investigations. WIRED identified 39 Homeland Security Investigations employees connected to access groups referencing certified undercover operations. Other groups reference communications interception programs and surveillance technology. The files also reveal reporting relationships that could help someone understand how different parts of DHS work together.

That raises a difficult security concern. People conducting undercover investigations depend on keeping certain relationships and assignments confidential. Revealing those connections could create risks for ongoing operations. Still, membership in an internal access group does not automatically confirm that every person listed was working undercover. The leaked records offer clues about sensitive assignments, but they don't establish every individual's operational role. Former acting ICE director John Sandweg called the exposure a "nightmare scenario". He warned that revealing agents' identities could put people in danger and interfere with criminal investigations.
Why Palantir and Grok appear in the DHS leak

Here's another part of this story that caught my attention. The leaked records reveal internal access groups referencing technology used for investigations and government operations. Some groups mention Palantir's Falcon investigative platform, which helps investigators analyze information. Others reference surveillance-related software, including tools used to examine phone records.

Then there's artificial intelligence. WIRED found groups mentioning OpenAI's ChatGPT, Google's Gemini and Microsoft's Copilot. One group labeled "Grok.com" included eight DHS technology officials. That doesn't prove these employees actively used the services or that the technology companies experienced breaches. The group names can reflect access permissions rather than actual activity. Even so, the information offers outsiders a closer look at the technologies DHS personnel may have access to. For an agency responsible for national security, those internal details can be valuable to people looking for weaknesses.
FBI SAYS SOURCE OF ITS JOBS PORTAL BREACH STILL UNKNOWN AS HACKERS ALLEGE EMPLOYEE DATA COMPROMISED
Leaked DHS records reveal internal access groups tied to surveillance technology and AI tools, including Palantir and Grok. (iStock; Victor J. Blue/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
How did hackers get access to Homeland Security records?

The group claiming responsibility says it accessed the information through DHS's Okta sign-in system. Okta provides identity and access-management technology that organizations use to control employee logins. However, Okta says it has no evidence that its own systems or data were compromised. That leaves the actual entry point unresolved.

DHS has acknowledged a potential breach and says it is investigating. The department has not publicly confirmed how the information was obtained. It's also important to understand what has been established so far. The reporting centers on personnel information and access-group details. It has not confirmed that employee passwords, intercepted communications or investigative case files were included. Until investigators explain what happened, there's no reliable basis for blaming a specific vulnerability or software provider.

We reached out to the Department of Homeland Security and Okta for additional comment. A DHS spokesperson provided the following statement: "DHS is aware of a potential breach and is actively working to address the situation swiftly and effectively. We take all security threats against our employees and officers seriously and will work to ensure all are properly protected. We will update the public when more information is available." Okta had not responded to our request for additional comment by our deadline.
DHS tries to remove leaked employee information

As the records spread online, DHS moved to limit access. On Oct. 29, a company reportedly authorized to seek content removals on behalf of ICE contacted Icelandic hosting provider FlokiNET. The request warned that the database exposed more than 40,000 identifiable individuals to potential harassment and physical harm. However, the hosting company declined to remove the material, saying the records contained workplace contact information rather than private home contact details.

The database briefly became inaccessible before appearing again elsewhere. Then, on Oct. 30, SITE Intelligence Group had reportedly identified threatening online rhetoric following the release. Some social media users reportedly threatened immigration officers and their families. Those reports raise additional concerns about what happens after sensitive personnel information becomes searchable. Even if the original files disappear, copies may already exist elsewhere.
Why this data leak should concern people outside government

You might be wondering why a federal employee database should concern someone who works in an office, owns a small business or has nothing to do with immigration enforcement. Think about how a convincing scam works. Someone contacts you claiming to be from your company's IT department. They know your supervisor's name and your work email address. They even mention an internal system you're familiar with. Suddenly, that unexpected message sounds a lot more believable.

That's the danger when attackers combine workplace records with information they find elsewhere online. They can use those details to create personalized phishing messages or impersonate trusted colleagues. We've seen related concerns before. In our reporting on the FBI hack claim involving sensitive personnel data, we examined how employee information could expose individuals and their families to additional risks. And that's what concerns me about this latest incident. Even information that seems routine can become dangerous when someone connects it to other records.
Security experts warn that exposed employee information could fuel targeted phishing attacks, impersonation scams and threats against federal workers and their families. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
Tips to protect yourself from workplace data leaks
You may have no control over how your employer stores its records. However, there are ways to reduce the amount of personal information available about you and make targeted scams harder to pull off.

If someone contacts you claiming to be from your employer's IT department, don't assume they're legitimate because they know your name or job title. Contact your IT department using a phone number or communication channel you already trust. Avoid clicking links in unexpected password-reset emails, especially when the message creates urgency. A convincing message can still lead to a fake login page designed to steal your credentials.

Your primary email account deserves special attention because criminals may use it to reset passwords for other services. Use a strong, unique password for every important account and consider a reputable password manager to create and store them. Turn on multifactor authentication or passkeys wherever available. Also review your recovery email addresses and phone numbers to make sure nobody has changed them without your permission.

Once criminals have detailed information about you, they may send phishing messages containing malicious links or infected attachments. Strong antivirus software can provide an additional layer of protection by helping detect malicious downloads, known phishing websites and malware before they cause damage. Keep your operating system and security software updated so you receive the latest protections. Antivirus software cannot remove your information from a leaked database. However, it can help protect your devices against attacks that may follow an exposure. No security tool catches every threat, so continue checking unexpected messages carefully. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android and iOS devices at CyberGuy.com.

Here's something I strongly recommend considering. Data brokers collect personal information from public records and online sources. That information can include your home address, personal phone number and details about relatives. When someone already has your workplace information, finding additional personal details may make harassment or impersonation attempts easier. A reputable data removal service can help remove your personal information from participating data broker and people-search websites. Services such as Incogni automate removal requests and continue checking for information that reappears. You can also contact individual data brokers yourself, although that takes more time and ongoing follow-up. Keep in mind that these services cannot guarantee removal from every website or erase the original DHS leak. For more information, see our guide on how to remove your personal information from the web and keep it from coming back. Check out my top picks for data removal services and get a free scan to find out if your personal information is already out on the web by visiting CyberGuy.com.

Search your own name and see what appears. You may discover old professional profiles, forgotten social media accounts or websites showing personal contact details. Check the privacy settings on your social media accounts and limit how much information strangers can see about your family. Be especially careful about publicly revealing your home location or daily routine if you work in a sensitive position. If you discover unwanted personal information online, contact the website or platform and request removal where possible.

The reported DHS records center on workplace information. So far, there has been no confirmation that Social Security numbers or financial account details were included. Still, exposed contact information can help criminals build more convincing scams. Monitor your important accounts for unfamiliar activity and pay attention to suspicious password-reset messages. If you discover that sensitive identity information has been compromised elsewhere, consider freezing your credit with Equifax, Experian and TransUnion. Identity monitoring services may also help flag certain signs of fraud. However, they cannot prevent every type of identity theft or guarantee that your information will stay private. See my tips and best picks on Best Identity Theft Protection at CyberGuy.com.

If someone uses your workplace information to impersonate a colleague or threaten you, document what happened. Save relevant emails, screenshots and messages, then report the incident to your employer's security team. If you receive threats of violence, contact law enforcement. You can also report suspected internet crime through the FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center at ic3.gov/. If you're an employee whose information may be involved in a breach, ask your employer whether you were affected and what protective steps it recommends. Don't rely on unsolicited callers claiming they can verify your exposure.
Kurt's key takeaways

What strikes me about this Homeland Security leak is how much damage a collection of workplace records could potentially cause. We're talking about information that many organizations use every day to help employees do their jobs. Yet in the wrong hands, those same details can help identify people involved in sensitive operations or make targeted scams much more convincing. I also believe there's an important conversation to be had about government transparency. Americans have a right to question how federal agencies operate and how officers are held accountable. But I worry about the consequences when information tied to undercover personnel becomes publicly searchable, especially now that threats against employees and their families have been reported. For me, the biggest unanswered question is how DHS allowed this information to become exposed in the first place. The department needs to explain what happened and how it plans to prevent another incident. In the meantime, there's a lesson here for all of us. Pay attention to how much personal information is available about you online. You may never be able to remove everything, but reducing your exposure can make it harder for someone to target you.

Do you believe exposing the identities of federal agents is justified in the name of government transparency, even when it could put undercover operations and employees' families at risk? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.

title: Fox News AI Newsletter: Voters' unmistakable message
summary: The Fox News AI Newsletter covers the latest artificial intelligence technology advancements, including the challenges and opportunities AI presents now and for the future.
story: Steamfitter Jason Jordan, 44, arranges building materials for data center infrastructure at the Silicon Valley Mechanical workshop in Sparks, Nev., Oct. 8, 2026. (Reuters/Daniel Cole)
IN TODAY’S NEWSLETTER:
- Data centers were on the ballot, and voters sent unmistakable message
- What’s fueling Wall Street’s growing concerns about AI
- Google expands voluntary buyouts to 5 countries as AI spending fuels cost cuts

NOT IN MY BACKYARD: Voters in at least 10 states delivered a sweeping rebuke to data center expansion in Tuesday's midterm elections, backing restrictions and rejecting development proposals amid growing concerns about electricity costs, land use and the rapid buildout of artificial intelligence infrastructure.
PROFIT PRESSURE: U.S. stocks plunged Thursday as investors dumped AI stocks, but market experts say Wall Street's concerns go beyond a single bad day.

title: Your old Android phone could become a walking robot
summary: UCLA's PhoneBot turns old Android phones into the brain of a two-legged humanoid robot that walks, follows people and stands up after falling.
story: UCLA researchers developed PhoneBot, a small humanoid robot that uses an Android smartphone as its brain to walk on two legs. (Ruochen Hou et al./UCLA RoMeLa)

Got an old Android phone collecting dust in a drawer? You might want to hang on to it. Researchers at UCLA have figured out how to turn an aging smartphone into the brain of a small walking robot. It's called PhoneBot, and it can walk on two legs, follow people and even get back up after falling face down.

The most surprising part? The researchers estimate the robot's hardware costs about $400, excluding the phone. So, that forgotten smartphone could have a pretty interesting second life. Here's how the researchers pulled it off and what it would take to build one yourself.
Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways to travel smarter and save money.

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed.
Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com.
GOOGLE TURNS OLD PHONES INTO CLOUD SERVERS
How UCLA turned an old Android phone into a walking robot

PhoneBot comes from UCLA's Robotics and Mechanisms Laboratory, also known as RoMeLa. The team built a miniature humanoid robot that stands about 19 inches tall and weighs roughly four pounds, including the smartphone attached to its body.

Instead of developing an expensive custom computer, researchers used technology already inside an Android phone. The robot has 13 motorized joints, with six in each leg and another that lets its upper body rotate. That extra movement allows the smartphone's camera to turn toward someone while the robot's feet stay planted.
A box filled with electronic waste and broken devices. (Getty Images)
The researchers’ goal is to make humanoid robotics more affordable for schools and research teams that cannot spend thousands of dollars on specialized machines.
Your old Android phone becomes the robot's brain

Think about everything your smartphone already does. It can recognize objects through its camera and detect movement using built-in sensors. It also has enough processing power to run sophisticated software. PhoneBot puts those capabilities to work. An Android app uses the phone's motion sensors to help the robot maintain its balance. Meanwhile, the camera helps it recognize and track people. The phone also runs an artificial intelligence-powered walking controller that tells the robot how to move. Those instructions travel over Wi-Fi to a small computer inside the robot, which communicates with the motors. The smartphone has no physical electrical connection to the robot's hardware. That design makes it easier to swap phones without rewiring the machine. Researchers trained PhoneBot's walking system in computer simulations before testing it on the actual robot. They also developed a way to improve how evenly it uses both legs. As a result, PhoneBot can walk on flat surfaces and stand up from a face-down position. For something powered largely by an old smartphone, that's quite an accomplishment.
Even a nearly 10-year-old Android phone can work

Here's something I found especially interesting. UCLA didn't need the latest expensive smartphone to make PhoneBot work. In fact, the researchers successfully tested its core functions on four different Android devices, including an Honor 9 released back in 2017. The other models included a Samsung Galaxy A16 5G and two Motorola Moto G phones from 2024 and 2025.

Researchers purchased the three prepaid models for roughly $50 to $90 each. Those were the prices reported during testing, rather than guaranteed prices today. All four phones handled the essential functions, including movement control and camera-based recognition. However, the older Honor 9 could not run one of the robot's mapping features because the required Google services were unavailable on that device in the United States. That means you cannot assume every Android phone will work. Still, the tests suggest you may not need an expensive new phone to run a capable little robot.
A WHEELED ROBOT MAY BEAT HUMANOIDS INTO YOUR HOME
UCLA's PhoneBot demonstrates its ability to walk, track a person using its smartphone camera and stand back up after falling face down. (Ruochen Hou et al./UCLA RoMeLa)
Can PhoneBot follow you around?

Yes, at least within the limits of what UCLA has demonstrated. PhoneBot can use its smartphone camera to identify a person and adjust its movement to follow them. It can also rotate its upper body to keep someone in view. The robot supports conversational interaction, too.

However, there's an important limitation. Its current system uses a separate laptop to process speech and generate AI responses. The smartphone records your voice and plays the response through its speaker. Before you start thinking about having PhoneBot clean your house, there's something else you should know. It doesn't have arms. That means it cannot pick up your laundry or carry groceries.

Researchers also trained its walking system on flat ground, so navigating stairs and uneven surfaces remains a challenge. For now, PhoneBot is best viewed as an experimental platform. UCLA has demonstrated what it can do under research conditions, but it hasn't established that the robot can independently navigate a typical home.
Could you build a walking robot with your own Android phone?

If you're comfortable with electronics and robotics, PhoneBot could become a pretty interesting project. UCLA has developed it as an open-source research platform and published hardware designs and building resources. The official PhoneBot website at phonebot.dev/ provides information about the robot's design, components and assembly process. The published hardware materials are available for noncommercial use under a Creative Commons license.

There's an important distinction, though, between having the hardware plans and being able to build a fully working robot. The project website provides hardware designs and assembly resources but does not clearly offer a download for the complete Android app and trained walking software. Although UCLA describes PhoneBot as an open-source platform, anyone hoping to reproduce its capabilities should first confirm that the necessary software is available.

And there's another consideration: the $400 price tag. It's an approximate hardware cost, and it doesn't include the smartphone. Depending on what equipment you already have, you may also need access to a 3D printer and tools for assembly. Shipping and other expenses could push the total higher. You'll also need the technical skills to put everything together and configure the software. So, don't expect to download an app and watch your old phone suddenly sprout legs. There's real engineering involved.
Why PhoneBot could make walking robots more affordable

Humanoid robots are getting a lot of attention, but building one remains expensive. Some small research models cost several thousand dollars. More advanced systems can cost considerably more. PhoneBot takes advantage of hardware that millions of people already own. By letting a smartphone handle much of the sensing and computing, researchers can avoid buying some specialized components. That helps bring the overall cost down.

The approach could also make robotics more accessible to students. Instead of requiring a large research budget, a smaller team could experiment with a relatively inexpensive walking machine. They could test new software or explore ways to improve movement without building every electronic component from scratch.

The UCLA team already has ideas for what comes next. Researchers want to improve PhoneBot's ability to handle uneven terrain and eventually give it lightweight arms. They're also exploring ways to run more conversational AI directly on the smartphone, which could reduce the need for a separate computer. Those improvements are still future goals. Even so, PhoneBot offers a promising starting point for building more affordable humanoid robots.
PhoneBot combines a smartphone with 13 motorized joints to create a walking robot that costs approximately $400 in hardware, excluding the phone. (Ruochen Hou et al./UCLA RoMeLa)
What this means to you

You probably won't see PhoneBot on store shelves anytime soon. But this research shows how much useful technology may still be inside a smartphone you've stopped using. A phone that feels outdated for daily use could still handle surprisingly demanding tasks.

If you're interested in robotics, PhoneBot could eventually offer a more affordable way to experiment with walking machines. Meanwhile, for families with kids who love technology, an accessible version of this project could make for a fascinating hands-on learning experience.

And if you've been thinking about getting rid of your old Android phone, this research offers another reason to consider what it might still be capable of. Of course, building a robot won't be for everyone. You can also sell, donate or recycle your old phone. Before you do, check out our article on securely getting rid of your old cell phone to make sure your personal information doesn't go along with it.
Kurt's key takeaways

I love the idea that a smartphone sitting forgotten in a drawer could become the brain of a walking robot. We've gotten so used to replacing our phones every few years that we sometimes overlook how powerful these devices still are. What UCLA has done with PhoneBot makes me wonder how many other uses we're missing. Now, let's be realistic. This little guy isn't ready to take over household chores, and putting one together requires some serious know-how. But the price is what caught my attention. When researchers can build a walking robot with roughly $400 in additional hardware, it opens the door to possibilities that once seemed out of reach. I'd love to see someone turn this into an affordable kit that families could build together. That could be a great way to get kids excited about engineering.
Would you spend a few hundred dollars to turn your old Android phone into a walking robot? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.

title: Suspected DUI driver arrested on 3 murder counts after deadly North Hollywood crash, police say
summary: A suspected 61-year-old DUI driver was arrested on three murder counts after a North Hollywood crash killed three women and injured two others.
story: At least three people are dead and two others are critically injured at the hospital after being hit by a car in North Hollywood. (KTTV)

A 61-year-old man suspected of driving under the influence was arrested on three counts of murder after his minivan crashed into pedestrians and a food vendor near a North Hollywood Metro station, killing three women and critically injuring two others, Los Angeles police announced Wednesday.
The Los Angeles Police Department identified the driver as Ihor Demianenko of Valley Village, who investigators determined was under the influence after Tuesday evening's deadly crash.
He was arrested on three counts of murder, and his bail was set at $6.03 million, police said.
The crash happened around 5:55 p.m. Tuesday when Demianenko was driving a white Toyota Sienna southbound on Lankershim Boulevard, just south of Chandler Boulevard, according to an LAPD news release.
MARIJUANA USERS MAY FACE HIDDEN DRIVING DANGER THAT STANDARD TESTS CAN MISS
Police identified Ihor Demianenko, 61, as the driver of a minivan that struck pedestrians and a food vendor near the North Hollywood Metro station Tuesday.  (KTTV)
Police said the minivan veered right at an unsafe speed, struck a food vendor and pedestrians near the sidewalk and continued moving before becoming stuck inside a building.

Los Angeles Fire Department paramedics pronounced three women dead at the crash site. Police said the victims were Hispanic women between 40 and 60 years old whose identities have not been released pending notification of their families.
Two other women, both Hispanic and between 50 and 55 years old, were taken to a hospital in critical condition.
CALIFORNIA MOM HAS BOTH LEGS AMPUTATED AFTER SUSPECTED IMPAIRED DRIVER PLOWS INTO HER RESTAURANT LUNCH TABLE
Three women were killed, and two others were critically injured when a minivan struck pedestrians and a food vendor in North Hollywood on Tuesday evening.  (KTTV)
Demianenko suffered minor injuries and was taken to a hospital for treatment before his arrest, police said.
Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass expressed condolences to the victims' families following the crash.
"I'm heartbroken for the families of everyone impacted," Bass said in a statement posted on X. "We will continue to provide updates as more information becomes available."
CHARTER BUS DRIVER WHO ALLEGEDLY CAUSED CRASH KILLING 5 IN VIRGINIA CHARGED WITH INVOLUNTARY MANSLAUGHTER
A minivan crashed near the North Hollywood Metro station in Los Angeles on Tuesday, killing three women. Police arrested the driver on suspicion of DUI and three counts of murder. (KTTV)
LAPD Chief Jim McDonnell previously said investigators would conduct a thorough investigation into the circumstances surrounding the collision.
"It'll be a prolonged but a very deliberate investigation to determine what happened here," McDonnell told reporters. "Our hearts go out to the families of the victims that were struck here tonight."

title: Illegal immigrant arrested after dragging, striking ICE officer in Chicago suburb: DHS
summary: Jose Garnica-Naranjo, a Mexican citizen, allegedly dragged an ICE officer through a car window during a traffic stop in Chicago Heights, DHS said.
story: Criminal defense attorney Josh Ritter and former NYPD Lt. Darrin Porcher react to the New Jersey incident in which an illegal alien allegedly rammed an ICE agent. They emphasize the staggering 3,300% increase in vehicle attacks against law enforcement officers.

FIRST ON FOX: An illegal immigrant with a prior criminal history was arrested Wednesday after allegedly dragging a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer with his car while fleeing an arrest attempt outside Chicago, federal officials said.
Jose Garnica-Naranjo, 32, a Mexican citizen, was taken into custody a day after violently resisting a targeted immigration enforcement operation, according to the Department of Homeland Security.
"This illegal alien used his vehicle to assault one of our ICE officers, hospitalizing the officer," Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said.

"Thankfully, the officer has since been released from the hospital. This is just the latest example of the staggering rise in anti-ICE violence, with our officers facing a more than 1,600% increase in assaults against them."
Photos provided to Fox News Digital appeared to show the ICE officer's wounded leg following the incident. (DHS)
VENEZUELAN NATIONAL SHOT BY ICE OFFICER IN AUSTIN CHARGED WITH ASSAULTING FEDERAL OFFICER
ICE officers spotted Garnica-Naranjo leaving a home in Chicago Heights on Tuesday morning. Officers followed his car at a distance before attempting to initiate a traffic stop, DHS said.
When officers approached the vehicle, they instructed Garnica-Naranjo to turn off the engine, but he allegedly refused to comply.

"When officers attempted to remove him from the vehicle, Garnica accelerated and fled while an ERO Chicago officer was partially inside the vehicle through the driver-side window," DHS said in a statement.
U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents walk down a street during a multi-agency targeted enforcement operation in Chicago Jan. 26, 2025. (Christopher Dilts/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
ICE SAYS OFFICER SHOT AND KILLED ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT WHO TRIED TO RAM HIM WITH CAR IN HOUSTON
Garnica-Naranjo then drove over a raised center median planted with trees, causing the officer to be thrown from the vehicle, according to authorities.

title: 'Fake' war hero allegedly posed as wounded Purple Heart recipient while stealing $81K from veterans group
summary: Prosecutors say David Agtsteribbe forged military records to join a veterans organization, then stole more than $81,000 to cover personal expenses.
story: Suffolk County DA Raymond A. Tierney accused a Long Island man of faking military honors and stealing $81,000 from a veterans organization. (Suffolk County District Attorney Ray Tierney/Facebook)

A man's alleged deception as a decorated combat veteran came crashing down this week after officials revealed he had actually been discharged from the military for bad conduct and accused him of bilking $81,000 from a veterans group.
David Agtsteribbe, 58, of Long Island, allegedly claimed to have been awarded a Purple Heart while portraying himself as a wounded war hero.
He was arrested two days before Veterans Day, the Suffolk County District Attorney's Office announced Tuesday.

Prosecutors said Agtsteribbe was discharged as a private in 1988 after serving roughly one year in the military. He was court-martialed and pleaded guilty to stealing money from another soldier in 1987.
EX-CIA OFFICER FOUND WITH OVER $40M IN GOLD BARS PLEADS GUILTY TO $194M FRAUD
David Agtsteribbe allegedly posed as a decorated war hero and stole $81,000 from a veterans' organization, prosecutors said. (David Agtsteribbe/Facebook)

He later allegedly altered his discharge documents to portray himself with an honorable military record. The forged credentials helped him secure a position as a finance officer at a local veterans' organization, where prosecutors say he stole the group's funds to cover personal expenses.
"There is something particularly despicable about fabricating a military record and claiming honors you have never earned," District Attorney Raymond A. Tierney said.

"This defendant allegedly took that disgraceful deception even further. He is accused of falsely portraying himself as a war hero, infiltrating an organization for those who actually served this country and then betraying their trust by stealing their money. Our veterans earned their honors through sacrifice and service. This defendant allegedly exploited those sacrifices for his own selfish gain. It is a shameful abuse of trust, and one that we will prosecute."
WHY SCAMMERS TARGET VETERANS AND HOW TO FIGHT BACK

A table displays military honors prosecutors said were "fake" during a news conference announcing charges against David Agtsteribbe, who allegedly posed as a decorated combat veteran. (Suffolk County District Attorney's Office)

According to prosecutors, Agtsteribbe joined the Hampton Bays American Legion, an organization that supports military veterans and service members, in 2021 after allegedly falsifying his discharge papers to qualify for membership.

The altered military records also included an elevated retirement status, which may have helped him obtain free health care and other privileges.Starting in 2022, Agtsteribbe allegedly transferred money from the organization's accounts into his personal checking account to cover personal expenses, including Amazon purchases, bills, a private business membership program, streaming services, travel, leisure activities, clothing and accessories.
The total amount allegedly stolen was $81,798.31, prosecutors said.

Prosecutors also revealed that Agtsteribbe had allegedly been applying for and obtaining memberships in other veterans organizations dating back to 2019, including the Military Order of the Purple Heart.
In 2023 and 2024, Agtsteribbe allegedly submitted falsified discharge papers to the Town of Southampton in an attempt to avoid a $50 resident permit fee and obtain a handicap parking permit.
MAN ACCUSED OF STEALING MORE THAN $735K AS POWER OF ATTORNEY TO PURCHASE PROPERTY, ONLYFANS AND LIFE COACHING
Suffolk County DA Raymond A. Tierney declared "fake, fake, fake" while exposing a man's alleged deception as a decorated combat veteran. (Suffolk County District Attorney's Office)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
In some of the documents, he also allegedly claimed to be a retired lieutenant colonel, despite having been discharged as a private.

Agtsteribbe has been charged with grand larceny in the second degree, criminal possession of a forged instrument in the second degree, two counts of offering a false instrument for filing in the first degree and three counts of falsifying business records in the first degree.
If convicted on the top count, Agtsteribbe faces 25 years to life in prison as a persistent felony offender.

Prosecutors requested substantial bail, citing his criminal history and the current charges, including $100,000 cash, a $200,000 secured bond or a $1 million partially secured surety bond to ensure his return to court.
He is due back in court on Nov. 13, 2026.

title: At least 2 dead, 17 injured after NYC building collapse
summary: Emergency crews were on the scene after a building collapsed in Brooklyn. At least two people are dead and 17 others injured in the incident's aftermath.
story: At least two people were killed in a Brooklyn building collapse that left seven children among 19 reported patients, as rescue crews searched unstable rubble near an active construction site. (Credit: WYBW)
At least two people were killed and more than a dozen injured, including seven children, after a three-story building collapsed in New York City on Wednesday, officials said.

FDNY Commissioner Lillian Bonsignore provided updated casualty figures, reporting 19 patients, including two fatalities, four people in critical condition and 12 in stable condition. A firefighter also suffered minor injuries during the emergency response.

The collapse occurred in Brooklyn's Flatbush neighborhood, where emergency crews continued searching for anyone who may still be trapped beneath the rubble. It remains unclear how many people may still be trapped inside the building or what caused the collapse.

New York City Mayor Mamdani said the FDNY received a 911 call reporting the collapse at 1321 Flatbush Avenue at 4:01 p.m., with firefighters arriving within one minute and immediately launching search-and-rescue operations.

Firefighters search through rubble for survivors following a building collapse in Brooklyn, New York. (NNYW)
"I am heartbroken to share that at this time, at least two New Yorkers have passed away," Mamdani said during an evening news conference.
An unidentified person was killed when a building in Brooklyn's Flatbush neighborhood suddenly collapsed, the FDNY previously told Fox News Digital.
During the news conference, officials did not identify the ages of the children or establish whether either of the deceased was a minor.
Upwards of 250 fire and EMS personnel were at the scene.
First responders work the scene after a building collapsed in the Brooklyn borough of New York, Wednesday, Nov. 11, 2026. (AP Photo/Ryan Murphy)
FDNY Chief of Department John Esposito warned about the risk of another collapse, calling the scene an "extremely dangerous operation for all of our people."

Bonsignore emphasized the dangers facing first responders as they carefully searched through the unstable rubble.
"Every move is choreographed and critically important to patient outcomes and member safety," she said.
The building collapsed into an adjacent property that was an active construction site, officials said.
Department of Buildings Commissioner Ahmed Tigani said workers were conducting excavation work at the neighboring construction site when the collapse occurred.
The site had approved plans for a three-story building, while plans for a nine-story building were still awaiting approval, Tigani said.

"We’re praying for the safety of anyone who may be trapped and for the first responders working to reach them. Our thoughts are with everyone affected and their loved ones."

The City's Emergency Management office has opened a reception center for impacted residents with the Red Cross nearby.

title: MICHAEL RUIZ: JonBenét Ramsey's father challenges DA after report says family shouldn't have been cleared
summary: Boulder County DA Michael Dougherty's remarks on the JonBenét Ramsey cold case sparked a fierce response from her father over DNA evidence use.
story: John Bennett Ramsey details how new DNA technology could help solve JonBenét Ramsey's decades-long murder case, while calling on President Donald Trump to aid in the search for his daughter's killer. (Julia Bonavita/Fox News Digital)

JonBenét Ramsey's father has issued a fiery response to a report that a Colorado prosecutor now handling his daughter's cold case murder would not have ruled the family out as suspects if he'd been in charge when a predecessor did so in 2008, even as the family shared that investigators gave them an optimistic update on the case earlier this year.

"After 30 years, if they still think I am guilty, then please file charges, and we will settle this in court based on facts and evidence," John Ramsey told Fox News Digital Wednesday after Boulder County District Attorney Michael Dougherty said in a recent interview with local reporters that he "would not have" publicly ruled out the family as suspects like his predecessor, Mary Lacy, did in 2008.

"They can’t selectively apply the unknown male DNA both ways," Ramsey said. "They have cleared a number of interesting suspects based on their DNA not matching unidentified male No. 1 DNA recovered from JonBenet’s person."
JONBENET RAMSEY'S FATHER ASKS TRUMP FOR HELP IN DAUGHTER'S UNSOLVED MURDER CASE

John Ramsey speaks with Fox News Digital in Las Vegas in April 2022. He is the father of JonBenét Ramsey, the Colorado 6-year-old whose murder on Dec. 26, 1996, remains unsolved nearly 30 years later. (Michael Ruiz/Fox News Digital)

Dougherty declined a Fox News Digital interview request Wednesday, but his office said he planned to post video from his local interview online amid concerns his remarks were taken out of context under a headline reading, "Boulder County DA says Ramseys shouldn’t have been cleared in JonBenét's murder."

"I’ve never ruled out people in a case that’s unsolved," he told local reporters Tuesday, according to The Boulder Daily Camera newspaper. "Doing right by the victim demands that I remain open-minded and committed to following the evidence wherever it leads."
JONBENET RAMSEY'S FATHER UNVEILS PETITION PRESSING COLORADO GOVERNOR TO ADVANCE DAUGHTER'S MURDER CASE
JonBenét Ramsey pictured in an undated portrait. The Colorado 6-year-old was found dead in her home Dec. 26, 1996, in one of America's most high-profile unsolved cases. (Splash News)
This is a routine investigatory position, according to retired FBI agent Jason Pack, who has followed the case for decades.

"If new evidence challenges an assumption made years ago, they need to take another look," he told Fox News Digital. "That doesn’t mean accusing somebody all over again. It means being willing to let the evidence change the direction of the investigation."
JONBENET RAMSEY CASE: FATHER TO PURSUE LEGAL ACTION IF COLORADO IGNORES REQUEST FOR INDEPENDENT DNA TESTING

The 6-year-old died of strangulation and head trauma, according to the Boulder City medical examiner. Her family reported her missing only to find her dead in their basement the day after Christmas in 1996.
Since then, investigators have examined more than 20,000 tips and hundreds of pieces of evidence. They've checked previously recovered DNA against more than 750 "reference samples."
Either they believe they have the killer's DNA — or not.
As Fox News Digital has reported previously, early DNA testing results did not show matches for JonBenét's immediate family, but police continued to eye her parents as potential suspects for years.

"Either they believe they have the killer's DNA or not," the family patriarch said. "This problem of selective use of evidence to try and fit things to their opinion rather than use evidence to solve the crime has been the problem from the beginning."

The home in Boulder, Colorado, where JonBenét Ramsey was murdered in December 1996 is pictured Aug. 17, 2006. Investigators have said renewed DNA testing has raised hopes of solving the decades-old cold case. (Doug Pensinger/Getty Images)
DNA TECHNOLOGY LEADS TO ARREST IN 1988 KILLING OF ORLANDO WOMAN AFTER NEARLY FOUR DECADES

As recently as last year, police still had some untested DNA collected from the 1996 crime scene, and the elder Ramsey has called on authorities to use modern investigative genetic genealogy methods to try and gin up new leads.

title: Foreign spy ‘honeytraps’ targeting America’s tech elite spark alarm amid Nvidia CEO scandal

story: Foreign intelligence services are using corporate cover and executive networking to gain multi-year access to tech leadership, according to a former NSA analyst, Ira Winkler.

American tech executives are facing escalated and systematic campaigns by foreign intelligence services using a variety of spy tactics to get the upper hand, including "honeytraps," to infiltrate U.S. expert controls, supply chains and other intelligence, experts say.

The warning comes amid reports revealing NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang's extramarital relationship with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, whom U.S. intelligence identified as a Chinese intelligence asset operating under corporate cover.

Foreign espionage operations targeting high-profile tech figures are not isolated incidents but reflect an ongoing, long-term threat designed to exploit business environments, former National Security Agency analyst and corporate cybersecurity expert Ira Winkler told Fox News Digital.

"These types of cases have gone on over the last few decades and arguably since the days of Samson, if you want to get biblical on how long honey pots have been around."
Unlike traditional covert intelligence operations, foreign adversaries routinely target tech executives through legitimate business settings when their defenses are lowered, Winkler said.

"This is where they had long-term access and clear cooperation in many cases, to go ahead to try to avoid export restrictions, to potentially get information," Winkler said. title: Former West Point cadet sued over alleged drugging, forced abortion of ex-girlfriend: 'Horrifying'
summary: A former West Point cadet drugged his girlfriend and forced abortion pills into her mouth and vagina, according to a lawsuit filed by the victim.
story: Alliance Defending Freedom attorney Erin Hawley says the alleged assault by former West Point cadet Caleb Suh, who pleaded guilty after drugging his pregnant ex-girlfriend and administering abortion pills without her consent, was "horrifying."

A former West Point cadet who pleaded guilty to drugging his then-girlfriend and administering abortion pills without her consent, causing a miscarriage, is facing a civil lawsuit that seeks unspecified damages.

Caleb Suh pleaded guilty in June to assault resulting in substantial bodily injury to a dating partner in connection with the March 2022 incident involving the woman, who was also a cadet at the U.S. Military Academy at the time.

Suh studied at two Ivy League universities since the incident, including one where he began attending classes after his guilty plea. He graduated from Cornell University this year and was enrolled as a graduate student at Columbia University when the woman filed a lawsuit Oct. 28.

The woman wanted to have the baby, but Suh did not want her to keep the child. Suh told the judge that he used the woman's identity to set up an online pharmacy account, ordered abortion drugs through the mail, obtained Xanax from a friend to use as a sedative and tricked his girlfriend into drinking what he claimed was a prenatal protein shake. When she fell asleep, Suh inserted the abortion pills into her mouth and vagina.
PRO-LIFE LEADER SOUNDS ALARM AFTER DOCTOR GETS 6 MONTHS FOR FORCING ABORTION PILLS ON GIRLFRIEND
Caleb Suh pleaded guilty this summer to the March 2022 assault on the woman, who was also a cadet. (AP Photo/Julia Demaree Nikhinson)
Erin Hawley, a lawyer with the pro-life legal group Alliance Defending Freedom who played a key role in helping overturn Roe v. Wade, said the woman was put in an "absolutely horrific situation."

"She was expecting a child she very much wanted, was drugged and assaulted," Hawley, who is not representing the woman, told Fox News Digital. "The horrifying assault ended up causing the death of her very much wanted child — something no woman should ever have to endure. It has obviously caused a lot of harm and trauma, in addition to the loss of the baby she very much wanted."
"She was drugged and assaulted with abortion pills, even though Mr. Suh knew she very much wanted that child. I expect that he will be prosecuted to the full extent of the law," she added.
Suh is still awaiting sentencing.
Suh left the woman alone and incapacitated and ignored her attempts to reach him once she woke up and noticed that she was bleeding, according to the lawsuit. She was then hospitalized.

As the woman was receiving medical attention, Suh returned to the online pharmacy's website and posted questions about whether doctors could detect the medication he administered, according to the lawsuit.
"She’s suffered a life-changing event that she is still dealing with and will be dealing with for the rest of her life," her lawyer, Russell Kornblith, told The Associated Press last week.
"We hope that by our client coming forward with this lawsuit, it will, at least, ensure that this never happens to anyone else," Kornblith said.
INSIDE EXPLOSIVE CORNELL RAPE ALLEGATIONS: 7 MEN ACCUSED, CONFLICTING ACCOUNTS AND A POLITICAL FIRESTORM
Caleb Suh graduated from Cornell University this year and was a graduate student at Columbia University when the woman filed a lawsuit late last month. (TW Farlow/Getty Images)
Fox News Digital reached out to Suh's attorney for comment.
During a court hearing in June, Suh said that he was "deeply and immeasurably sorry for my actions and the pain that I have caused."
Suh's sentencing has been postponed until Jan. 21, 2027, at his attorney's request, allowing him to finish the semester at Columbia. Prosecutors did not oppose the delay for Suh's sentencing.
He has also been taking a three-month life skills course for people facing federal charges, his attorney said in a letter to the court.

Suh transferred to Cornell during the 2023-2024 school year. The university said in a statement last week that he answered "no" on an application when asked if he had been found responsible for a disciplinary violation at any previous institution.

The university said West Point noted that he was in good academic standing and was eligible to return. He had been involved in health and medicine at Cornell and wanted to become a physician, according to the university's website.

In September, Suh started a master's program at Columbia University's Mailman School of Public Health, his lawyer wrote to the judge in his federal case. A person familiar with the matter told The Associated Press that Mailman applicants are not asked about their criminal records but are questioned about whether they have ever been disciplined for student conduct violations or poor academic performance.
Suh’s application never made any mention of past disciplinary proceedings, the person told the outlet.

As the woman was receiving medical attention, Caleb Suh returned to the online pharmacy's website and posted questions about whether doctors could detect the medication he administered. (Soumyabrata Roy/NurPhoto via Getty Images)

"Regardless of one’s position on abortion, it is not good medicine to allow an abortion drug to be shipped across the country to a dorm room or a home without a woman ever having talked to a doctor," Hawley said.

"The defendant in this case impersonated his girlfriend, had those drugs shipped and then assaulted her with them. That would never have happened if the FDA had done its job in 2023. Hopefully, when the courts do their job and reinstate that safeguard, it won’t continue to happen," she continued, referring to Alliance Defending Freedom's lawsuit challenging the Food and Drug Administration's 2023 decision to remove the in-person dispensing requirement for mifepristone, after the agency had already stopped enforcing the requirement in 2021.

However, the assault occurred in March 2022, before the FDA's 2023 decision. The agency had already announced in April 2021 that it would temporarily stop enforcing the in-person dispensing requirement during the COVID-19 public health emergency. In December 2021, the FDA announced plans to permanently remove the requirement, a change formally implemented in January 2023.
The FDA has said its decision to remove the requirement followed a review of available evidence. Other restrictions, including prescriber certification requirements, remained in place.
Hawley added that the case at West Point would never have happened if that requirement had been in place.
"Horrific incidents like that throughout the country would never have happened if that basic safeguard had been in place," she said.

title: MICHAEL RUIZ: Lindsay Clancy judge denies double jeopardy motion and explains jury notes after deadlock
summary: Judge William Sullivan denied Lindsay Clancy's double jeopardy motion, ruling there was manifest necessity for the mistrial in her murder case.
story: Attorney Randolph Rice says prosecutors can use lessons from the first trial to refine their case. He also explains why he believes Judge William Sullivan’s order rejected Clancy’s double-jeopardy argument.

The Massachusetts judge overseeing the murder case against Lindsay Clancy has denied her motion to dismiss the case on double jeopardy claims, clearing the way for a retrial in the strangling deaths of her three young children that some experts believe could have a better chance at a guilty verdict.

"Because the Court concludes that there was a manifest necessity for a mistrial based on the jury’s deadlock, a retrial on the murder indictments does not violate Clancy’s right not to be placed in double jeopardy," Judge William Sullivan wrote in a 17-page order and memorandum made public Monday.

Clancy's 26-day trial ended with a deadlocked jury on Sept. 4, with jurors later saying publicly that 11 of them accepted her insanity defense and one wanted to find her guilty of first-degree murder for what the holdout called the "methodical" slayings of Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and Callan, 8 months.
LINDSAY CLANCY DEFENSE FILES MOTION TO DISMISS UNDER DOUBLE JEOPARDY GROUNDS, WITH FOCUS ON HOLDOUT JUROR

Judge William Sullivan indicates he was going to declare a mistrial before changing course and giving Lindsay Clancy's defense attorney one hour to appeal, as the jury in the case has indicated that they are unable to reach a verdict on Friday, Sept. 4, 2026, in Plymouth, Mass. (Greg Derr/The Patriot Ledger via AP, Pool)
Had the motion been granted, Clancy would not face a potential second trial, said Randolph Rice, a trial attorney and former prosecutor who is not connected to the case.
Now, he says, the order gives prosecutors a chance to address what went wrong with their case in the first trial.
"I think there's real possibility that DA [Tim] Cruz says, 'We're going back to trial ... and we have learned from our mistakes,'" Rice said.
Among the lessons learned, Rice said, may be that Plymouth County prosecutors did not show jurors enough empathy when presenting their case after 11 of the 12 jurors voted against them.
What a second trial may look like remains unclear as prosecutors have so far declined to publicly commit to bringing the same or different charges.

Lindsay Clancy looks at jurors as Judge Sullivan asks them to start deliberations for a sixth day during her murder trial on Thursday, Sept. 3, 2026, in Plymouth, Mass. (Pool Photo by Greg Derr/The Patriot Ledger)
Deliberations began on Aug. 27. On Sept. 1, they sent the first of several notes explaining their deadlocked situation.
"After many hours of deliberation, we are unable to come to a unanimous verdict," that first note said, according to Sullivan, who instructed them to keep trying.

They sent a similar note on Sept. 2, and Sullivan, without objection from lawyers on either side, read them what's known as a Tuey-Rodriguez charge — an instruction given to hung jurors encouraging them to reexamine their views with an open mind while reminding jurors they should not abandon honestly held beliefs to reach their verdict.
On Sept. 3, Sullivan received another note reading, "A member of the jury is unable to follow the instructions regarding reasonable doubt. How should we proceed?"
ATTORNEY FOR LONE HOLDOUT JUROR IN LINDSAY CLANCY MISTRIAL PUSHES BACK ON CLAIMS OF REFUSING THE LAW
Michael P. Desronvil, the juror whose refusal to join the other 11 led to a mistrial in the Lindsay Clancy murder trial. (Fugitive TV)

In his order, Sullivan wrote that he was skeptical of the allegation that the holdout was "genuinely" unable to follow instructions regarding reasonable doubt and decided to hold a "limited inquiry" into each juror's ability to follow the law.

Prosecutors had opposed voir dire, and the defense asked for the holdout to be replaced with an alternate. The defense then asked for the judge to ask the foreperson to expand on what she meant in her latest note, and prosecutors objected, arguing that a question like that would improperly intrude into the deliberation process. Sullivan agreed with the commonwealth and asked each juror, "Are you able to follow my instructions on the law that were given to you earlier in the trial?"
LINDSAY CLANCY HOLDOUT JUROR WON'T HAVE TO TURN OVER PHONE OR FACE INQUIRY, JUDGE SAYS
District Attorney Timothy Cruz leaves Plymouth Superior Court, Plymouth, Mass., on Thursday, September, 3, 2026. (David McGlynn for Fox News Digital)
Each juror answered "affirmatively and credibly," Sullivan wrote.
FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X

Prosecutors and the defense agreed that the court should also reinstruct the jury, as a whole, about reasonable doubt, and Sullivan did so. Afterward, however, Clancy's defense attorney, Kevin Reddington, again asked for the holdout to be replaced with an alternate, and Sullivan denied his motion.
LINDSAY CLANCY'S PUSH TO PROBE HOLDOUT JUROR HITS SNAG BEFORE PIVOTAL RETRIAL HEARING
Later on Sept. 3, the foreperson sent another note, directly accusing the holdout of ignoring reasonable doubts about the case, according to Sullivan.
LINDSAY CLANCY HOLDOUT PRAISED AS 'AMERICAN HERO' BY LAWYER WHO SAYS HE REPRESENTS HIM
Callan, left, Dawson and Cora Clancy. The three children were killed at their Duxbury, Massachusetts, home in January 2023. (Lindsay Marie Clancy/Facebook)
SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS
"[Juror Doe] has made statements acknowledging doubt but refuses to apply it to the verdict as the law states," she wrote. "This is why we cannot come to a unanimous decision."
CLICK HERE FOR MORE FROM THE FOX TRUE CRIME HUB

Jurors were sent home for the day. Before deliberations resumed on Sept. 4, Sullivan and counsel on both sides discussed the latest note. Sullivan gave jurors another instruction on reasonable doubt and following the law and told them that future notes should not identify anyone's vote based on their juror number. Two hours later, with no movement in the deliberation room, Sullivan said he planned to declare a mistrial, over Reddington's objection.
SEND US A TIP
He granted a one-hour stay as the defense appealed to the state's Supreme Judicial Court. A single justice summarily denied the defense’s emergency request, then Sullivan declared a mistrial.
LINDSAY CLANCY LAWYER SAYS HE PLANS NEW MOTION TO DISMISS AFTER JURORS SPEAK OUT ON MISTRIAL: REPORT

Clancy's defense later filed a motion to dismiss on double jeopardy grounds, arguing that there was no "manifest necessity" for the court to declare a mistrial and that as a result, a new trial would violate Clancy's Fifth Amendment rights.
LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST

"Clancy contends that there was no manifest necessity for a mistrial because the Court failed to consider the alternative of inquiring into the meaning of the foreperson's notes and questioning Juror Doe to determine whether there was good cause to discharge Juror Doe," Sullivan wrote.

That's the motion he denied Monday.

title: Cruise ship murder victim ID'd as suspect's wife; child found at scene of deadly attack
summary: Jason Leon Watford told FBI investigators he snapped during an argument before beating and choking his wife aboard the MSC Seascape cruise ship.
story: A man was taken into custody after MSC Seascape abruptly returned to Galveston less than a day into Caribbean voyage. (Credit: @villamosbiztonsag via Storyful)

A cruise ship passenger accused of killing his wife aboard the MSC Seascape told FBI investigators he "snap[ped]" during an argument before beating and choking her for up to five minutes, according to newly filed federal court documents.

A criminal complaint filed in the Southern District of Texas shows that Jason Leon Watford, 48, has been charged with murder in connection with the death of his wife, Susan Watford, aboard the cruise ship while it was sailing in international waters on Sunday.

FBI spokesperson Connor Hagan identified the woman killed aboard the ship as Watford's wife, Susan Watford, the Associated Press reported. Hagan also said a child was found unharmed when law enforcement responded.
Court records show Watford had previously pleaded guilty to assaulting Susan in 2024.
TEEN ACCUSED OF STEPSISTER’S CRUISE SHIP MURDER BUYS TIME TO CONSIDER PLEA BUT WON’T GET ‘SWEET’ DEAL: EXPERT
Jason Leon Watford was booked into the Galveston County Jail on a federal hold. (Galveston County Sheriff's Office)

Surveillance footage showed Watford entering the cabin at about 7:46 p.m., followed by the woman about 25 minutes later, investigators said. No one else was seen entering or leaving the cabin before she was discovered.
Watford told investigators the two had been arguing while eating at a restaurant aboard the ship before returning to the cabin, where the argument continued, according to the affidavit.

Investigators said Watford admitted that he "snap[ped]" and struck his wife multiple times, causing blood to come from her mouth and land on his shirt, pants and hands. His bloodstained clothing was later found on the cabin floor.
ANNA KEPNER’S STEPBROTHER CHARGED AS ADULT WITH MURDER, SEXUAL ABUSE IN FLORIDA TEEN’S CRUISE SHIP DEATH
Watford allegedly admitted to choking her with both hands before wrapping his right arm around her neck from behind as she was lying down.
He told investigators he applied pressure to her neck for about four to five minutes, releasing her only after becoming exhausted.

The MSC Seascape is seen at the Port of Galveston in Texas. The ship later left the port and resumed its planned itinerary as the FBI investigated a suspected homicide aboard the vessel. (Photo by Kirk Sides/Houston Chronicle via Getty Images)
Investigators found Susan Watford dead with multiple facial injuries, according to the criminal complaint.
Susan remained motionless on the floor for about 10 minutes, but Watford did not contact ship security or medical personnel, investigators said.
Susan Watford, 31, was identified as the woman killed aboard the MSC Seascape. Her husband, Jason Leon Watford, has been charged with murder in connection with her death. (Credit: LinkedIn)
At about 9:02 p.m., a housekeeper arrived at the cabin to deliver towels and knocked on the door.
SECRET EVIDENCE FILED IN ANNA KEPNER CARNIVAL CRUISE MURDER CASE AS FEDS PUSH TO JAIL ACCUSED STEPBROTHER

Watford answered and briefly spoke with the housekeeper, who reported seeing what she believed was blood on his hands and pants and the woman lying face down and motionless on the floor, the affidavit says.

The housekeeper then contacted other MSC employees.

He then sat on the hallway floor outside the cabin and scrolled on his smartphone, investigators said.

MSC security detained Watford as a suspect, and the cruise line contacted the FBI's Texas City Resident Agency at about 11 p.m. to report a suspected homicide aboard the ship.

Jason Leon Watford, 48, is escorted by law enforcement after the MSC Seascape returned to Galveston, Texas. Watford has been charged with murder in connection with a woman's death aboard the cruise ship. (CREDIT: @villamosbiztonsag via Storyful)
The Seascape returned to the Port of Galveston early Monday, where FBI personnel boarded the vessel and began investigating.
Watford appeared in federal court Tuesday and requested a court-appointed attorney, federal court records show. He waived a detention hearing and was ordered held pending trial.
A preliminary examination hearing is scheduled for Monday at 1 p.m. before U.S. Magistrate Judge Andrew Edison.
If convicted, Watford faces up to life in federal prison and a possible $250,000 fine, according to the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of Texas.

Watford had previously been prosecuted in Texas for assaulting a family member, Smith County court records show.
The victim in that case was his wife, Susan, according to the Associated Press.

He was arrested in September 2024 on a charge of assault causing bodily injury to a family member and was sentenced that November to 15 months of probation and 30 hours of community service.

Law enforcement officers escort Jason Leon Watford from the MSC Seascape after the cruise ship returned to Galveston, Texas. Federal prosecutors have charged Watford with murder in connection with a woman's death aboard the ship. (CREDIT: @villamosbiztonsag via Storyful)

Illinois court records show he was found guilty of attempted first-degree murder, aggravated battery with a firearm and unlawful use of a weapon following a bench trial in 1996.

Susan also had a criminal case pending in Texas in the years before her death.

She was arrested in March 2024 on charges accusing her of intentionally injuring a child, elderly or disabled person, Smith County records show. She later pleaded guilty to one felony charge and was placed on 10 years of community supervision with 600 hours of community service.

title: Tennessee warns executions could grind to a halt if Christa Pike's lawyers see a single drug label: court docs
summary: Tennessee officials warn that exposing their pentobarbital supplier could halt all future executions after Christa Pike survived two lethal doses.
story: Anesthesiologist Dr. Joel Zivot joins Bill Hemmer to discuss the legal fallout after a judge ordered Tennessee officials to preserve evidence from the botched execution of Christa Pike. Zivot, who advised Pike's attorneys, explains the complications surrounding the lethal injection drugs used in the state's attempt. Pike remains on death row following the failed execution attempt.

Tennessee officials are urging a judge to keep their lethal injection drug supplier secret, warning in court documents that executions could come to a halt if the vendor is exposed to retaliation after Christa Pike's botched execution.

Pike had been set for execution on Sept. 30 after the Supreme Court vacated a last-minute stay. She was convicted of the murder of 19-year-old classmate Colleen Slemmer in Knoxville and received a death sentence.

She stood to become the first woman put to death in Tennessee in more than two centuries, yet she survived after two administered doses of the lethal injection drug pentobarbital did not result in her death.

In a motion filed in the Davidson County Chancery Court on Friday, a Tennessee Department of Correction employee said that providers of the chemical used in the execution attempt have grown skittish. In the filing, the employee described being responsible for procuring the state's pentobarbital execution drug.
TENNESSEE DEATH ROW INMATE SURVIVES 2 LETHAL INJECTION DOSES IN FAILED EXECUTION ATTEMPT
Christa Gail Pike was scheduled to be executed on Sept. 30, 2026. (Tennessee Department of Correction via AP)

"Suppliers have stated that they are concerned about threats, harassment, and boycotts because of their lawful decision to supply state correctional departments with drugs used to carry out lawful executions," the employee wrote.

State officials filed the motion in response to an Oct. 10 order from Chancellor I'Ashea Myles requiring them to preserve all physical evidence tied to the botched execution, including needles, drug vials and any "residual pentobarbital."
911 OPERATORS QUESTIONED WHETHER CHRISTA PIKE FAILED EXECUTION CALL WAS PRANK, AUDIO REVEALS
READ THE COURT FILING HERE:

Warning that a label on one of those items could expose Tennessee's pentobarbital supplier, the unnamed state employee said the vendor has "made it clear" it will cut ties with the state if identified.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE FROM THE FOX TRUE CRIME HUB
Christa Gail Pike appears remotely from Deborah K. Johnson Rehabilitation for her hearing in Knox County Criminal Court in Knoxville, Tenn., on Aug. 11, 2026. (USA TODAY Network via Reuters Connect)
Losing that supplier could bring executions in Tennessee to a halt, the employee wrote, adding that finding a replacement would be unlikely.
SEND US A TIP

"If counsel or experts for Plaintiffs [Pike] are allowed to view the labels on any vials of pentobarbital or handle the vials, TDOC would likely lose access to pentobarbital and thus be unable to carry out executions using it," the employee said. "And in my experience, if that were to happen, it is unlikely Tennessee would be in a position to find another supplier willing to provide pentobarbital for carrying out executions."
Myles hasn't made a decision on the matter.

Convicted killer Christa Gail Pike listens to proceedings on April 2008 in Knox County Criminal Court in a bid for a new trial in the 1995 killing of fellow Job Corps student Colleen Slemmer. (USA TODAY Network via Reuters Connect)

"This pod houses inmates with significant histories of assaults and disciplinary problems," the motion states.
