title: Behind the data: How NBC News tracked the decline in childhood vaccinations
summary: How an NBC News data investigation tracked vaccination and school exemption rates across thousands of counties in the U.S.
story: Editor’s note: This 2026 NBC News data investigation is an update of The Vaccine Divide, which was originally published in September 2025. The methodology for both projects is similar. The new data was collected from June to October 2026.
For Subscribers

For “The Vaccine Divide,” NBC News gathered massive amounts of data from state governments and archives of public records. With the help of infectious disease researchers at Stanford University, NBC News filed scores of requests for documents, including materials obtained under the Freedom of Information Act, and wrestled different types of data into a standardized format to map and compare rates across thousands of counties.
Methodology

NBC News built a database of childhood vaccination and exemption information using data provided by state governments, primarily health agencies. The data combines public information available for some states and data provided directly to NBC News.
The data covers kindergartner vaccinations for each academic year.
For Subscribers
After collection, the data was collated, and exemption rates were calculated in order to be analyzed. The analysis focuses on four facets of the data:
Medical exemptions: Exemptions granted when students have medical conditions that could make vaccination harmful.
Nonmedical exemptions: Exemptions for students who opt out of required vaccinations because of personal beliefs or religious convictions.

MMR (measles-mumps-rubella) vaccinations: For states where data is subdivided by number of doses, MMR vaccination is counted by the second dose. Some states track measles, mumps and rubella immunization separately; in those states, measles was used to represent MMR rates.
Up-to-date vaccinations: Students are considered “up to date” with their vaccinations if they have received the full vaccination series required for enrollment in their schools.
With a hodgepodge of formats, jurisdictions and collection practices across states, the task required extensive work to ensure that possible inconsistencies in the data were managed.

Certain states, such as Ohio and New York, required further calculations to aggregate the state-supplied data.Other states required hand input of hundreds of rows of tabular data.All data was checked for accuracy.
Certain states, such as Ohio and New York, required further calculations to aggregate the state-supplied data.
Other states required hand input of hundreds of rows of tabular data.
All data was checked for accuracy.

This analysis of childhood MMR vaccination rates focused on states that provided MMR figures for the 2025-26 school year. Accompanying the analysis were several variant analyses, which confirmed that the results were robust. The variant analyses all yielded similar results, mostly within 1 percentage point. We also examined the scale of MMR vaccination rate decline across counties, with almost 4 in 10 counties declining by over 5 percentage points since 2019 and about 1 in 8 declining by that amount since 2024. Fewer than 2% of counties declined by 0.1 percentage points or less since 2019.

Many states collect and report their data differently. Some use health districts instead of counties. Some states provided over a decade of data; others provided only two years’ worth. Some states redacted certain data because of privacy concerns.

Not all states have recent data. Florida did not provide data on kindergarten exemptions after the 2021-22 school year. Montana stopped collecting vaccine and exemption data after 2019, first because of Covid and thereafter because of the passage of a state bill (HB 334) in 2021 that struck down the mandate for the state to collect data on immunizations.Certain states (such as Arizona and Minnesota) do not collect overall “up-to-date” figures representing the percentage of kindergartners who are compliant with all required vaccines. Others (such as Florida, New Hampshire and South Carolina) provided only “up-to-date” numbers. In other states — Mississippi, New Hampshire and South Carolina — data was provided only for years K-12, rather than specifically kindergartners. West Virginia also falls into this category for its exemption data. Some states — Illinois and New York — do not collect data at grade level, so data is for elementary schools as a whole (up to K-8 for Illinois, and New York was based on headcounts, with elementary schools defined as having less than 3% enrollment above grades K-6), rather than kindergartners specifically. Hawaii also fell into this category (up to pre-K-5), as its school-level data was more consistent than its kindergarten-specific data.Other states did not provide data on a county level. Alaska and Nebraska provided data for other jurisdictions. Delaware and Rhode Island were unable to provide data at the county level; state-level figures were used instead. Indiana was unable to provide county-level exemption data. West Virginia was unable to provide county-level immunization data, but igt was able to provide exemption data per county, starting in January 2025.Some states (such as Michigan) collect data by calendar year, rather than school year.Wyoming did not consistently report data among kindergartners, so the most consistent reported value was used, instead: one-dose MMR among 19- to 35-month-olds. Accordingly, exemptions among children younger than 5 were used to correspond with this age group.Alaska was unable to provide regional exemption data for privacy reasons because of small sample sizes.

Not all states have recent data. Florida did not provide data on kindergarten exemptions after the 2021-22 school year. Montana stopped collecting vaccine and exemption data after 2019, first because of Covid and thereafter because of the passage of a state bill (HB 334) in 2021 that struck down the mandate for the state to collect data on immunizations.

Certain states (such as Arizona and Minnesota) do not collect overall “up-to-date” figures representing the percentage of kindergartners who are compliant with all required vaccines. Others (such as Florida, New Hampshire and South Carolina) provided only “up-to-date” numbers.

In other states — Mississippi, New Hampshire and South Carolina — data was provided only for years K-12, rather than specifically kindergartners. West Virginia also falls into this category for its exemption data. Some states — Illinois and New York — do not collect data at grade level, so data is for elementary schools as a whole (up to K-8 for Illinois, and New York was based on headcounts, with elementary schools defined as having less than 3% enrollment above grades K-6), rather than kindergartners specifically. Hawaii also fell into this category (up to pre-K-5), as its school-level data was more consistent than its kindergarten-specific data.

Other states did not provide data on a county level. Alaska and Nebraska provided data for other jurisdictions. Delaware and Rhode Island were unable to provide data at the county level; state-level figures were used instead. Indiana was unable to provide county-level exemption data. West Virginia was unable to provide county-level immunization data, but igt was able to provide exemption data per county, starting in January 2025.
Some states (such as Michigan) collect data by calendar year, rather than school year.

Wyoming did not consistently report data among kindergartners, so the most consistent reported value was used, instead: one-dose MMR among 19- to 35-month-olds. Accordingly, exemptions among children younger than 5 were used to correspond with this age group.
Alaska was unable to provide regional exemption data for privacy reasons because of small sample sizes.

title: Sen. Richard Blumenthal ordered to preserve documents from inquiry into Trump ballroom
summary: The official’s letter comes on the day the White House told congressional Democrats that investigations into the administration could be a crime.
story: A Justice Department official called on Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., on Wednesday to preserve documents related to what he claims is harassment of citizens during Blumenthal’s investigation into White House ballroom donors, threatening “significant legal consequences” if he does not comply.

The U.S. attorney for the Southern District of Texas, Aaron Reitz, alleged in a letter to Blumenthal that his investigation equated to threatening “citizens for associating themselves with the President and other public officials.” The White House warned congressional Democrats on Wednesday that efforts to investigate the administration could be a crime.

In a post on X with a copy of the letter attached, Reitz equated Blumenthal’s investigation examining anonymous donors for the roughly $400 million project on White House grounds with wielding Congress as a “weapon” against Americans.
“I’m taking the first step to stop this abuse of power,” Reitz said.

Acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter, the second-highest-ranking official at the Justice Department, responded to Reitz’s post, saying, “The First Amendment expressly prohibits Congress from infringing the speech and association rights of Americans.”
“DOJ will defend against threats to those rights, period,” McCotter wrote.

Blumenthal said in a statement responding to the letter that he “will not be intimidated,” vowing to “vigorously pursue investigations into this Administration’s persistent misuse of taxpayer dollars and any corporate entity that has enabled their boundless corruption.”
For Subscribers

“The Trump Administration is so afraid of transparency and oversight that they are weaponizing the Department of Justice to baselessly target Congress in direct violation of the Constitution,” Blumenthal wrote.

Blumenthal is the top Democrat on the Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations. The subcommittee is tasked with studying the economics and efficiency of government operations.

Blumenthal sent letters last month to a list of people whom a Washington Post report identified as having donated private funds to the ballroom’s construction. A news release said he was “leading an inquiry into waste, fraud, and abuse associated with the White House ballroom and other projects throughout the nation’s capital.”
For Subscribers

President Donald Trump had vowed to release the names of the private donors, but he has made only a partial list public. A few donors have acknowledged their donations, including Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who is under investigation by the company and the FBI for an affair with an alleged Chinese spy. Trump defended Huang in remarks to reporters this week.
Reitz’s letter cited the federal conspiracy against rights statute, as well as the federal deprivation of rights under color of law statute.

Such an overt investigative measure against a sitting member of Congress would typically have undergone an extensive review process within the Justice Department’s Public Integrity Office, but that office has been shrunk and sidelined in the second Trump term.

A Justice Department spokesperson said in a statement that “the Department routinely requests that records be preserved when public officials take such extreme actions,” alleging that Blumenthal’s letters were an attempt to “suppress their First Amendment activities, including their philanthropic practices.”

Reitz, a former chief of staff to Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, headed the Justice Department’s Office of Legal Policy for a few months last year before he launched an unsuccessful campaign for Texas attorney general. He has been U.S. attorney since July.
Trump’s ballroom project has faced a series of legal hurdles, but the Supreme Court ultimately decided in August that it could go forth indefinitely.

Blumenthal on Wednesday night responded to Reitz’s letter with a record preservation request of his own, calling his efforts to investigate the ballroom donations “appropriate” and part of his “constitutional duties.”

“Since you appear to have evidence of the Trump Administration’s efforts to protect corporate donors and Administration officials from legitimate oversight, I accordingly direct you to preserve all records and correspondence, including all communications with the White House or senior officials at the Department of Justice, related to the decision to draft and post your letter,” Blumenthal wrote.

title: 2 dead, at least 17 hurt in NYC building collapse, authorities say
summary: The collapse occurred around 4 p.m. in the Flatbush neighborhood. Rescuers were trying to reach people trapped in the rubble.
story: Two people died and at least 17 others were hurt — including seven children — when a building collapsed Wednesday at the edge of a construction site in New York City, officials said, sparking a frantic search by firefighters combing through large piles of rubble.

The collapse occurred around 4 p.m. near the intersection of Bedford and Flatbush avenues in the Flatbush neighborhood of Brooklyn, the Fire Department of New York said. It was not known what caused or led up to it.

The FDNY said two people were removed from the rubble soon after the collapse. Aerial video showed dozens of firefighters scouring for others, at least two of whom were trapped in the wreckage. A senior city official later said those two were in the process of being freed just before 5 p.m.

Two people died and four of the injured were in critical condition, FDNY officials said at a news conference Wednesday night. Seven children and a firefighter were among the injured, according to the FDNY.
The fire department noted that the number of victims could increase, since it was not known how many people were in the building when it collapsed or whether everyone had been accounted for.
FDNY Commissioner Lillian Bonsignore said the number could change “by the minute” as the operation, which is expected to take days, continues.

“This is such a very fragile situation here. ... We’ll continue to look until we find everybody,” Bonsignore said, noting that victims included construction workers and those who were inside the building at the time.
The FDNY did not share the ages or identities of the two people killed, nor did it say whether any children died.
A man told NBC New York his brother, Jose Luis Caguana, was killed in the collapse.

The 26-year-old immigrant from Ecuador had been in the U.S. for about six years, his brother said, working construction to support his family. Caguana’s wife, who is pregnant and due very soon, was too distraught to speak with reporters on camera. The couple also have another young child.

“Her husband has passed away; he was the sole provider for the family. Now that he’s gone, she is going through an immense amount of pain. She is in a very bad state right now — she’s completely overwhelmed and can’t even find the words to speak,” Caguana’s brother, Carlos, said in Spanish.

Video from NBC New York’s Chopper 4 showed firefighters pulling an injured person from the rubble around 4:45 p.m. He was taken away on a stretcher. Another person was seen being taken away on a stretcher just after 6:30 p.m.

The building that collapsed appeared to have been three stories tall, with a business on the ground floor. It was next to an excavation site after a one-story building that had previously been there was fully demolished.

title: Nvidia shares drop after hours as board meets over CEO Jensen Huang’s future
summary: The New York Times reported that Huang had a relationship with an Nvidia executive following reports that he’d had a relationship with a suspected Chinese spy.
story: Shares of Nvidia dropped almost 9% in after-hours trading amid multiple reports that the company’s board would meet Wednesday night to discuss CEO Jensen Huang’s future after The New York Times reported that he had a relationship with an executive who reported to him.

Nvidia’s board was addressing Huang’s future at the company, two sources familiar with the matter told NBC News. The meeting is happening Wednesday evening, and the White House is aware, a source said.

The New York Times reported, citing five people who worked at Nvidia, that Huang had been involved in a relationship with a woman who reported to him, in addition to a woman who was suspected of being a Chinese spy.
NBC News has not confirmed the Times report. The Wall Street Journal first reported the board’s meeting, citing people familiar with the matter.

Huang wrote in a note to employees Sunday that he had been “unfaithful to his wife,” though he did not specify details. NBC News reported that U.S. intelligence agencies had determined that the first woman, Alice Huang, was a Chinese intelligence operative.
China has denied the allegations, calling them “purely unsubstantiated and directed at smearing China.”
Nvidia did not respond to multiple requests for comment Wednesday.
If Nvidia’s stock drop after hours holds through Thursday’s opening bell, it would erase more than $350 billion in value.

Jeffrey Sonnenfeld, an expert on corporate governance and executive leadership and senior associate dean for leadership studies at Yale School of Management, hailed Huang’s contributions to the industry but said the board should move to oust him.
Huang “has lost his legitimacy to lead internally in the eyes of the company, and he’s lost his external credibility in the eyes of key constituents, including customers,” he told NBC News.
Huang is among the most important people underpinning the AI boom and the trillions of dollars of investments tech giants are pouring into it around the globe.

Nvidia chips are the cornerstone of the artificial intelligence boom, powering all of the top developers, from OpenAI to Anthropic. Huang founded the company and has been its leader since 1993, taking the graphics processing chip company from nothing to a valuation of more than $4 trillion.
On Monday, longtime chip sector analyst Stacy Rasgon wrote that removing Huang from the company could pose massive problems for the trillion-dollar firm.
“NVIDIA is not an ordinary company and Jensen is not an ordinary CEO; he IS NVIDIA,” Rasgon wrote. “The primary beneficiary of Jensen’s removal as NVIDIA’s CEO would clearly be China.”

Rasgon said the revelations, first announced Sunday by Nvidia and Huang, also had wider implications. “It brings the stewardship of one of America’s most important companies, and the architect of the US AI trajectory, under debate,” he wrote in a note.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers
In overnight trading, Nvidia shares were not the only ones to sink. Shares of chipmakers Intel, Qualcomm and ARM Holdings also fell in after-hours trading as Nvidia dragged the entire sector lower.
As of 9:40 p.m. ET, Nasdaq futures were also lower, pointing to the losses the U.S. tech industry was set to face at Thursday’s opening bell.

On Wednesday night, as the Nvidia board met, Sens. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., and Chris Coons, D-Del., announced they had written to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick with a request to preserve records as the dramatic events engulfed the company.

“We write to request that the Department of Commerce, the Department of State, and the White House preserve all documents, communications, records, and other materials regarding the export of NVIDIA’s advanced AI chips to China or to entities that may divert such chips to China,” they said.
They requested that “all records and materials specifically related to this reported intelligence operation” regarding Huang and the Chinese business executive also be preserved.
In the coming months, Democrats will hold control of both the House and the Senate and, as a result, will have subpoena power.

Warren and Coons added in their letter: “This incident raises significant concerns about the federal government’s ability to effectively enforce our export controls and protect our national security.”

Lawmakers have become alarmed by the events surrounding Nvidia and Huang in recent days because Nvidia chips are effectively how the United States has, so far, led the AI revolution. Chinese President Xi Jinping recently set a deadline of 2030 for his country’s companies to catch up with or surpass the capabilities of American AI systems.

The request from the lawmakers also comes just days before President Donald Trump embarks on a visit to Asia for meetings of both the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation and the Association of Southeast Asian Nations.
During the trip, Trump is widely expected to meet with Xi for the third time this year.
At a briefing with reporters this week at the White House, Trump was asked whether Huang could accompany him on the trip, as he did earlier this year on a trip to Beijing.
“I don’t know, but I’d certainly take him,” Trump said.

title: Father charged with attempted murder after baby survives being buried in crate
summary: Koah Sharp, an 11-month-old boy, was found alive Tuesday after being buried in a wire crate, which was wrapped in a towel, for around 24 hours, police said.
story: The father of an 11-month-old boy found alive after having been buried in a dog crate has been charged with attempted murder and other counts, authorities said Wednesday.
The baby, Koah Sharp, was taken by his father, Michael Comer, 25, on Monday, and he was dug out of the ground Tuesday afternoon, the sheriff of Lexington County, South Carolina, alleged.
The baby is expected to make a full recovery. He is believed to have been buried in the wire crate, which was wrapped in a towel, for around 24 hours, Sheriff Bryan “Jay” Koon said.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers
The towel likely created an air pocket that allowed Koah to breathe, and cool weather may have also helped him survive, Koon said.

Comer, who was arrested on a burglary charge after he was found in an outbuilding Monday night, is charged with attempted murder, unlawful conduct toward a child, custodial interference and burglary, the sheriff’s office said Wednesday.
Searchers investigating a patch of disturbed earth near a home owned by Comer’s father heard the baby’s cries and quickly unearthed him, Koon said.
Koah was released from the hospital Tuesday, the sheriff’s office said, and he is with family members.

Koah was reported missing early Monday afternoon, authorities said. The report set off a search that included the FBI; firefighters; the federal Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives; and local law enforcement agencies.
Comer was in custody Wednesday, jail records showed. It was not immediately clear whether he had an attorney who could speak on his behalf.

Koah’s mother has custody of the child, Comer’s mother has said. Koah’s mother told a sheriff’s deputy that she allowed Comer to briefly have the child but expected that to last only a day or two, according to a police report.
She told the deputy that Comer had threatened her over Facebook Messenger that he would keep Koah, according to the police report.
CORRECTION (Nov. 12, 2026, 2 a.m. ET): A pervious version of this article misspelled the name of the Lexington County, South Carolina, sheriff. He is Bryan Koon, not Brayn Koon.

title: Democrat Scott Colom wins Mississippi Senate seat, breaking GOP’s grip on the state
summary: Colom pulled off an upset over Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith, becoming the first Democrat elected to the Senate in Mississippi since 1982.
story: In a major upset, Scott Colom has defeated Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith in Mississippi, NBC News projects, capping off a string of Democratic victories by flipping the reddest seat yet in this year’s midterms.

Mississippi last elected a Democrat to the Senate 44 years ago, just a few weeks before Colom was born in 1982. Colom will become Mississippi’s first Black U.S. senator since the post-Civil War Reconstruction era.

The historic win comes after days of uncertainty in the race, with Colom holding a razor-thin lead over Hyde-Smith as more votes continued to be counted. Colom, a district attorney, remained confident throughout the vote counting that he would prevail.

“For months and months, I’ve been telling everybody, everywhere I go, that we’re going to win this election. I was saying it eight and nine months ago,” Colom told a crowd of his supporters in Jackson on Wednesday night.
Colom emphasized that what he described as the “Mississippi faith tradition” guided his campaign and said, “This journey started with a prayer.”

“All I did was have the courage to imagine a night like this,” he said. “I had the courage to believe in Mississippi. I had the courage to understand that we can show the country that Mississippi matters.”
Colom said that “in Mississippi, our prayers have often changed the course of history,” noting that the first Black senator ever elected in the U.S. came from Mississippi.
He ended his remarks by promising to represent all Mississippians, including “the ones that voted for me, the ones that didn’t vote for me and the ones that didn’t vote.”
Hyde-Smith congratulated Colom in a video message Wednesday evening.

“While this is not the outcome we worked for or hoped for, I respect the decision of Mississippi voters,” she said. “I want to congratulate Scott Colom and wish him well as he takes on the tremendous responsibility of representing our great state.”
Colom’s campaign confirmed to NBC News that Hyde-Smith had called him to concede.
Colom’s victory means Democrats will hold at least 55 Senate seats next year. The only Senate race left to be called is in Alaska.

In the next Congress, no Democratic senator will represent a redder state than Colom. Donald Trump carried Mississippi by 23 percentage points in 2024. Colom’s victory also underscores the Trump administration’s broad unpopularity with voters just two years after that presidential election, even in parts of the ruby-red Deep South.

A majority of Mississippi voters said they disapproved of Trump’s overall job performance, according to NBC News exit polling. Majorities also said that his policies, including tariffs, hurt the economy and that it was wrong for the U.S. to take military action in Iran.

Colom, the eighth Democrat to flip a Republican-held Senate seat so far this year, long believed Democrats had an opportunity to win Mississippi, given its sizable Black population and plenty of white voters in rural areas who he thought could back a Democrat. He chided his party for writing off the state.

“We were never a lost cause. We were a betrayed cause,” Colom recently told NBC News. “We were betrayed by Cindy Hyde-Smith because she allowed tariffs to hurt us. She allowed people — hundreds of thousands of Mississippians — to lose healthcare. She gave away our voice in the war in Iran, which drove up costs for farmers and for truckers and for businesses.”
“But for too long we were also a betrayed cause by the national party, because they did not compete in this state,” Colom added.

In late October, the Senate Majority PAC, a top Democratic super PAC, announced an ad campaign in the state through Election Day, starting with a 30-second spot that presented Colom as a crusader who would “fight corruption in both parties.” The group ended up spending nearly $2.1 million on the airwaves, according to the ad-tracking firm AdImpact.
The GOP super PAC Senate Leadership Fund responded with a similar-sized buy, airing ads that painted Colom as “too liberal” and “too radical.”

The race also drew high-profile surrogates from both parties. Trump traveled to Mississippi eight days before the election, while Democrats such as former Vice President Kamala Harris and Sens. Cory Booker of New Jersey and Raphael Warnock of Georgia hit the campaign trail for Colom. Former President Barack Obama also appeared in an ad that the Colom campaign launched on digital platforms.

Republicans tried to leverage those surrogates against Colom, with the Senate Leadership Fund launching one ad with a narrator saying, “Colom proudly campaigns with Kamala Harris because Colom supports their radical agenda.”

But it was not enough to defeat Colom, who sharply criticized Hyde-Smith’s vote for Trump’s “big, beautiful bill,” which cut Medicaid funds. Colom also faulted Hyde-Smith’s support for the Trump administration’s tariff regime and the costly war with Iran, labeling his opponent “Cindy High Prices.”

Colom’s campaign also created a viral video highlighting Hyde-Smith’s comments that Mississippians struggling with high beef prices “have so many proteins to choose from.” The video featured clips of people saying: “Pick another protein? I’d rather pick another senator.”
NAACP President Derrick Johnson praised Colom’s victory, calling it proof that Mississippi and other states in the South were “underinvested in.”

“The Scott Colom campaign proves that it is possible to win in the South when there’s investment,” Johnson said in an interview, adding that he hopes Colom’s victory will show that a state like Mississippi is not “deep red,” but rather “an opportunity state.”

Johnson added that the Supreme Court’s April decision gutting the Voting Rights Act was “a direct attack on the rights of Black voters,” saying it was one of the many realities that urged people to turn out to vote. He also cited affordability and foreign wars as motivators.

“Folks were seeing that we were losing grip in this country, that we were losing our democracy, that our very essence as a community, our community, was under attack, and people stood up and fought back at the ballot box,” Johnson said.

Hyde-Smith, a former state agriculture commissioner who was appointed to the Senate in 2018 and won a full term in 2020, campaigned as a reliable conservative and tried to portray Colom as a “radical” progressive. She also touted her loyalty to Trump, who endorsed her more than a year before the midterms and said she was “100% MAGA.”

Hyde-Smith said that over the last week, her campaign team “worked tirelessly to ensure every legally cast vote was counted and that the people of Mississippi received a fair and transparent election.”
“I am proud of what we have accomplished together, but I want to make one thing very clear: An election may come to an end, but our commitment to Mississippi never will,” she said.

Colom and Hyde-Smith had crossed paths before this year’s midterm elections. She blocked his nomination for a federal judgeship during the Biden administration. Colom recently told NBC News that he had forgiven her.

title: Miller’s moment: From the Politics Desk
summary: In today’s edition, we explore how Stephen Miller’s appointment as White House chief of staff is already making waves across Washington.
story: Welcome to From the Politics Desk, a daily newsletter that brings you the NBC News Politics team’s latest reporting and analysis from the White House, Capitol Hill and the campaign trail.

In today’s edition, we explore how Stephen Miller’s appointment as White House chief of staff is already making waves across Washington. Plus, Andrea Mitchell digs into the alleged spy scandal that’s ensnared a top tech CEO.
— Adam Wollner
Democrats are deeply skeptical Trump wants to work with them after Stephen Miller’s elevation

After the Republican drubbing in the midterm elections, President Donald Trump said he’s open to cutting a deal with Democrats on immigration and showing he can work cooperatively with the opposition.

But what Trump actually did was far more illustrative of what’s to come, as Democrats see it. Trump ousted Susie Wiles and installed as his new White House chief of staff Stephen Miller, the face of hard-line immigration enforcement and an operative who has swung a rhetorical cleaver at the party that will soon control Congress.

Miller won’t get a honeymoon from ascendant Democratic lawmakers whose party he likened last year to a “domestic extremist organization.” He’d need to shed the persona of an uncompromising Trump loyalist, and the early signs suggest he won’t, Democratic lawmakers told NBC News.

Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., who is expected to become House speaker when the new Congress convenes in January, called Miller a “stone-cold racist” in remarks to reporters Monday. Jeffries said he has “zero interest” in working with Miller.
A reporter asked if Miller can be a viable partner to Democrats.
“No,” Jeffries said. “Stephen Miller is a stone-cold racist. His track record speaks for itself. And I’ve got zero interest in working with that kind of individual.”

To that end: The country’s top 16 Latino advocacy organizations are calling on the next Congress to subpoena Miller to answer for Trump’s mass deportation actions, Natasha Korecki reports. They’re also asking Congress to freeze any new funding for ICE until there is transparency in how money has already been spent.

Friends in high places: Meanwhile, advocates of the “Make America Healthy Again” movement are enthusiastically embracing Miller as a new champion of their agenda in the White House, Aria Bendix writes. The group, which had been vocal about its disappointment with the Trump administration before the midterms, cheered Wiles’ exit.
Read more →
The alleged spy scandal shaking Washington and Silicon Valley

It’s a Washington scandal that has the plot lines of pulp fiction: an alleged Chinese spy, exposed in a suspected romantic relationship with one of the world’s richest and most influential tech giants.
As the president of the United States expresses sympathy for his friend and business ally, rather than disappointment or condemnation, questions persist about who knew what and when.
For Subscribers

The context is potentially even more damaging. Last year, Secretary of State and national security adviser Marco Rubio wrote a classified memo warning that Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang might be compromised by his friendship with a Chinese intelligence asset, according to The New York Times, citing multiple people briefed on the matter. The Times also reported that Rubio repeated that warning in May, en route to a Beijing summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping.
For Subscribers

Nevertheless, Huang was added to the corporate delegation traveling with President Donald Trump when Air Force One stopped to refuel in Alaska. He was also literally seated at the president’s right hand when Xi visited the White House last month.

Asked Monday if he’d read Rubio’s memo when he brought Huang to Beijing, Trump said, “They could have been mentioned. Certainly, it didn’t make much of an impact on me.” Trump also said during the same exchange: “No, I didn’t hear about it then, but a lot of people have heard about it, and Jensen totally denies that he had, he — I asked him today because I did speak to him today just to see if he’s feeling all right. … I asked him that question. ‘Did you have any idea that she was a spy?’ He said, ‘I had no idea that she was a spy,’ and I really believe him.”

There have apparently been U.S. suspicions about Huang’s alleged romantic partner, Alice Huang (no relation), for a while. A former Chinese state media reporter, she purchased a subsidiary of a Chinese video gaming company that she turned into Megaspeed International, a Singapore-based technology company. The Commerce Department began investigating Megaspeed at least a year ago over alleged backdoor shipments of Nvidia’s most prized advanced chips to Beijing — chips that the U.S. bans for sale to China under export controls.

Nvidia’s most powerful chips dominate the market for data centers that are essential for artificial intelligence in the U.S. and Southeast Asia. In addition to his company being a top donor to the White House ballroom, according to documents obtained by The Washington Post, Huang has become a key adviser to Trump on major AI policy decisions. This year, Huang led a successful campaign to push back against government regulation of AI, instead arguing for the industry to adopt voluntary practices to keep new models safe.

China has denounced the espionage allegations as a smear. Jensen Huang acknowledged being “unfaithful” to his wife over the weekend, but did not mention Alice Huang. Rubio has declined to comment on the scandal, nor has the White House explained Trump’s Monday statements that he did not recall being warned. Nvidia is investigating but asserted it does not believe any corporate or U.S. secrets were compromised. The company’s stock has also taken a hit this week.

Huang has no known succession plan in place in case action is taken to remove him from his hugely profitable company, with fears this scandal could even affect the U.S. economy, which has been heavily dependent on the AI boom.

title: Record credit card balances, fewer trips to McDonald’s: More signs of strain ahead of the holidays
summary: Federal data shows savings rates have dipped below 4% of total income, well below pre-pandemic levels, revealing a fraying financial safety cushion.
story: Big credit card bills are supposed to show up after the holiday shopping season. This year, Christmas came early.
Just one week after affordability took center stage in the midterm elections, fresh data shows Americans are heading into the holiday shopping season saddled with record credit card balances.

Americans’ total credit card debt hit $1.29 trillion in the three months that ended in September — a rise of $22 billion over that period, according to the Federal Reserve Bank of New York’s latest quarterly report on household debt and credit. That’s 67% higher compared with the first quarter of 2021, when pandemic restrictions limited spending on things like travel and dining out.

“The consumer is in a fragile state,” Steve Cahillane, the CEO of Kraft Heinz, said on the company’s quarterly earnings call this month. He said the company, which makes everything from ketchup to cream cheese, plans to hold off on significant price increases “in order to meet the consumers where they are.”

Total household debt, which includes mortgages, student and auto loans, credit cards, home equity lines of credit and other borrowing, rose by $334 billion in the third quarter to $19.1 trillion. That’s $5 trillion more than at the end of 2019, just before the pandemic-driven recession.

“Last week, voters expressed their anger at the high cost of living. With prices up an average of 30% since 2019, millions of Americans have depleted their savings and taken on debt to make ends meet,” said Ted Rossman, principal consumer finance analyst at Money Management International, a nonprofit credit counseling agency.
Federal data also shows savings rates have dipped below 4% of total income, well below pre-pandemic levels, revealing a fraying financial safety cushion.

title: Frankie Muniz hospitalized after crash during practice at Daytona
summary: Muniz was taken to a medical facility for evaluation and is awake and alert, Team Reaume said on social media.
story: Actor Frankie Muniz was released from the hospital Wednesday after he was involved in a crash during practice at Daytona International Speedway in Florida.

Muniz, the 40-year-old actor-turned-race car driver, was taken to a local medical facility for evaluation and is awake and alert, Team Reaume said Wednesday afternoon on social media. Muniz became a full-time driver with Reaume Brothers Racing in the 2025 racing season.
Ford Racing said Wednesday evening that Muniz had been released from the hospital.
Muniz said in a statement he’s a “little sore” from the incident, “but my Mustang did its job in protecting me.”
Muniz was set to participate in the Ford Proud to Honor Veterans Classic at Daytona on Wednesday evening.

“I am disappointed I won’t be able to take part in Ford’s Proud to Honor event tonight,” Muniz said. “I was looking forward to honoring the service of our veterans and racing against these other amazing drivers.”
Muniz thanked Ford Racing, Daytona, hospital staff members and well-wishers for their support.
The race broadcast acknowledged Muniz’s absence.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers
“After a practice crash earlier today, Frankie Muniz will not start the race tonight,” an announcer said.
Jenson Altzman took his place and wrote on Instagram, “I’ll be sure to represent the #30 well tonight.”

Wednesday evening’s race featured six teams, each named in honor of a branch of the U.S. military, and a performance by the Zac Brown Band. Muniz was set to drive on Team Air Force with Austin Cindric, who won the race.
Muniz, an Emmy-nominated actor who rose to fame as a child star in the Fox sitcom “Malcolm in the Middle,” started racing in 2004 and focused on stock car racing in 2021.
He also competes in the NASCAR Craftsman Truck Series, as No. 33 in a Ford F-150.

title: Pete Hegseth and others reprimanded by guard at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier
summary: An Arlington National Cemetery guard told the defense secretary and his companions to maintain a respectful atmosphere during a Veterans Day visit.
story: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth was reprimanded Wednesday by an Army sentinel guarding the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier who asked him and his guests to maintain an atmosphere of “silence and respect.”

Hegseth, his wife, Jennifer, and some of his top aides were taking pictures, talking and laughing in front of the tomb, a memorial to unidentified service members killed in battle located at Arlington National Cemetery. Hegseth had been attending a Veterans Day ceremony at which President Donald Trump laid a wreath in honor of fallen service members.
The incident puts Hegseth’s name back in the headlines just one day after he narrowly dodged impeachment.
Hegseth and his wife were taking pictures alongside some of his top aides when the sentinel shouted at the group: “All visitors will maintain an atmosphere of silence and respect at all times.”
Hegseth made no acknowledgment of the reprimand, looking over his shoulder and continuing to walk up a set of stairs.
Asked for comment on the interaction, chief Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell said Hegseth and the department “have always honored” service members’ sacrifices.
“While commemorating this solemn day, a soldier correctly and respectfully reminded everyone to maintain decorum,” Parnell said in a statement.
For Subscribers
Soldiers stand watch over the tomb 24 hours a day, complete with an elaborate changing of the guard ceremony that happens at least once every hour.
For Subscribers

Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., a vocal critic of the Iran war who was unseated following a Trump-led effort, introduced articles of impeachment against Hegseth this week. The Republican-led House voted 211-204 to shelve the resolution. But Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., who is poised to become speaker of the House come January, has signaled Democrats will not dial back efforts to oust Hegseth.
Hegseth has downplayed the efforts, calling them “political spectacle.”
Trump has repeatedly expressed support for Hegseth, and he has said he would back him even if he were to be impeached.

title: In return to NFL coverage, Dianna Russini doesn’t address Mike Vrabel relationship
summary: “I have had a lot of time to think about my life and my priorities and the person I want to be,” Russini said on the debut of her new show.
story: Dianna Russini returned to covering the NFL on Wednesday with a new show but did not address the relationship with New England Patriots coach Mike Vrabel that cost her her perch as one of the league’s highest-profile reporters.

Seven months after the New York Post published photos of Russini and Vrabel together at an Arizona resort and Russini resigned from The Athletic amid the outlet’s investigation into her previous coverage, she announced a new show this week sponsored by BetUS, an online betting sportsbook.

“The Russini Report” was scheduled to air live at 12 p.m. ET Wednesday, but it did not air for at least 45 minutes before a full version of the episode was uploaded. On social media, some users said that the BetUS site would not load or that the stream had crashed. “Well... you broke it,” wrote the X account associated with Russini’s show.

In a column on the BetUS website, Russini had written that “I have a lot to say” about her seven months away from coverage of the NFL. But when her show began, before appearances by former NFL coach Bill Parcells and other guests, Russini did not address Vrabel, the nature of their relationship or her decision to resign from The Athletic, instead offering “a personal note.”

“You know, over the last few months, I have had a lot of time to think about my life and my priorities and the person I want to be moving forward and being home in New Jersey with my husband and our two little boys and being truly present. It gave me so much perspective that I didn’t even know I needed,” Russini said.

“I’ve also had a lot of long conversations with people all around football. You know, some were about the game, and others were just about life,” she said. “To the people who picked up the phone and checked in and offered both encouragement and honest advice, from the bottom of my heart, thank you. Those conversations helped me find my way back to the work I love and back to myself, right here hosting the show.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers

“So, anyone who knows me knows I have always been obsessed with the NFL. But maybe because I wasn’t around it so much the last few months, my passion for covering this league has never been stronger. I’m so grateful, so grateful for this chance to do it again.”

Russini became a national reporter while she was working at ESPN before she joined The Athletic in 2023. There, she wrote columns and hosted a podcast and was one of the company’s most visible and highest-paid writerreporters, according to The New York Times, which owns The Athletic.

Russini had not spoken publicly since she issued statements in April after the Post published photos of her and Vrabel together in Sedona. The Post published subsequent photos of the two in other locations. Vrabel missed the third day of the NFL draft in April to attend counseling with the Patriots’ support. After the photos were published, Vrabel told reporters that he’d “had some difficult conversations with people I care about — with my family, the organization, the coaches, the players.”

Less than a week after the initial Post story, Russini resigned from The Athletic, writing in a letter to the publication’s top editor, “I have covered the NFL with professionalism and dedication throughout my career, and I stand behind every story I have ever published.”

An internal investigation by The Athletic that ended in September determined that although there were no clear indications of bias showing that Russini’s coverage helped promote Vrabel, she had a “clear conflict of interest” that was not disclosed to her editors but should have been. “The appearances surrounding her relationship with Vrabel undermines our audience’s confidence in her impartiality,” the report’s author wrote.

title: Delaware residents file lawsuit seeking a second House seat for the First State
summary: They want a federal court to overturn the House’s 435-seat cap and create a second congressional district for Delaware.
story: A pair of Delaware voters sued Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick in an effort to increase Delaware’s representation in Congress.

The plaintiffs, University of Delaware professor David Redlawsk and Delaware resident Kevin Price, argue in the suit, filed Tuesday, that Delaware residents are underrepresented in the House, with only one at-large seat for roughly 991,000 people.
That’s less representation per person than in any other state, they argue, noting that Montana — with just under 1.1 million residents — has two House seats.

“The 435-seat limitation imposes a severe and avoidable disparity on Delaware’s voters,” their lawsuit says, adding that “Plaintiffs suffer a concrete and particularized injury from the dilution of their representation in the House.”

They are asking a three-judge panel of the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia ro declare the House’s 435-seat limitation under the Permanent Apportionment Act of 1929 unconstitutional — and to create one more seat for Delaware, bringing the full House to 436 representatives.

The suit names Lutnick because the Commerce Department oversees the Census Bureau, whose population count every 10 ears is used to apportion House seats. Also named are Commerce Deputy Under Secretary George Cook, who is fulfilling the duties of the director of the Census Bureau, and House Clerk Kevin McCumber.
Redlawsk and Price’s attorney Andrew Tutt argues in the lawsuit that the U.S. population grows “while the statutory apportionment mechanism carries the same total of seats forward” in the House.

Tutt said that as a result of the 2020 census, that year’s apportionment divided seats among more than 331 million people, “more than three-and-a-half times the 92 million Americans counted in the 1910 census, before the current House size was set in 1911—leaving Delaware’s 990,837 people with a single Representative.”
For Subscribers
For Subscribers
Redlawsk and Price want the court to create an additional House seat for their state in time for the 2028 presidential election.

“Delaware would have two Representatives for its 990,837 people, an average of approximately 495,419 people per Representative,” the lawsuit says. “The House would have 436 Members. The remedy would give Delaware’s voters the additional representation their population requires and leave the allocations of the other 49 States intact.”
The lawsuit asks that if Congress fails to act on the request, the court should order that the House’s composition be increased to 436 members.
The Commerce Department and the House clerk didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment.

title: White House warns congressional Democrats: Investigating us may be a crime
summary: Rep. Robert Garcia, the incoming House Oversight Committee chair, noted that the Constitution grants Congress “latitude to conduct investigations.”
story: WASHINGTON — Previewing the partisan battles to come, the White House fired a warning shot at House Democrats’ top investigator Wednesday.

The Trump administration is “monitoring” Democrats’ “abusive and capricious threats” to launch congressional probes, White House counsel Will Scharf said in a letter to Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., who is poised to become chairman of the powerful Oversight Committee starting in January.
And, Scharf warned, those threats may be criminal and warrant their own executive branch investigations. His letter was shared with NBC News by a White House official.
While threats of political reprisal for partisan investigations are commonplace, the suggestion of a congressional probe constituting criminality is not.

When President Joe Biden occupied the White House, and Republicans took control of Congress, Democrats cried foul that Trump’s allies were only interested in launching partisan probes that damaged their political enemies.

But those high-profile investigations continued unimpeded. House Oversight Chairman James Comer, R-Ky., led probes into the international business dealings of Biden’s son Hunter Biden and brother James Biden.

In the letter dated Monday, Scharf rattled off numerous examples of Democratic lawmakers making cavalier threats of issuing subpoenas. For example, Rep. Analilia Mejia, D-N.J., wrote on X, “We’re going to toss out subpoenas like Mardi Gras beads,” while Rep. Emily Randall, D-Wash., said they’ll be passed out “like candy.”

The White House pointed to Supreme Court rulings that have held that congressional investigations must be tied to a legitimate legislative purpose and must not be used to punish political opponents. But House and Senate committees under both parties have broad authority to investigate a range of matters, and they’ve rarely been stopped by the courts.

Likely House Speaker Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., called the Scharf letter “outrageous,” telling reporters on Capitol Hill on Wednesday: “It’s factually inaccurate. It’s legally inaccurate, and it’s inaccurate in terms of the Constitution.”

“A Democratic Congress is going to be a check and balance on an out-of-control executive branch in the face of unprecedented corruption that they’ve unleashed on the American people. And if they don’t like it, consult the Constitution,” Jeffries said.

Scharf in his letter accused Democrats of seeking “to abuse the legislative process to intimidate and to interfere with the lawful functioning of government,” adding that “threats to executive branch officials designed to deter them from public service, or process designed merely to abuse or instill fear in the recipient may cross the line into blatant criminality.”

Trump himself has used his office to target his political enemies. A year ago, the president accused Democrats of criminality, saying on social media that a video posted by Sen. Mark Kelly, D-Ariz., and other Democrats telling service members not to follow illegal orders amounted to “SEDITIOUS BEHAVIOR, punishable by DEATH!”

The Trump administration failed to secure an indictment against those Democrats over the video, and a judge later found that their speech was protected by the First Amendment in blocking the Pentagon’s attempt to punish Kelly.

The president has also publicly called on his Justice Department to investigate Democrats who probed his family and business dealings, including Sen. Adam Schiff, D-Calif., former FBI Director James Comey and New York Attorney General Letitia James.

Responding to Scharf’s letter, Garcia invoked the separation of powers in a statement and said newly empowered congressional Democrats will stay the course in investigating the president and his administration.

“It appears Donald Trump has something to hide. Let’s be clear: Congress’ authority comes from Article I of the Constitution, not from the permission of the White House. Congress has wide latitude to conduct investigations and oversight, an authority inherent in the power to legislate,” Garcia said in a statement.

Garcia and other Democrats who will lead congressional committees beginning in January have made no secret of their interest in investigating Trump, as well as his family, businesses and administration.

As NBC News reported this month, the White House was gearing up for a defense even before Election Day, hiring staff in the counsel’s office, while individual current and former aides have hired lawyers.

“The American people voted overwhelmingly for us to pass laws to root out corruption and abuse,” Garcia said. “The Trump Administration continues to weaponize the government with threats of unconstitutional attacks on Congress. We are a co-equal branch of government and will not be deterred by baseless threats from a weaponized DOJ or from the President’s lawyers.”

title: Brandon Sklenar Opens Up About Experiencing Body Dysmorphia Since He Was 12
summary: Actor Brandon Sklenar opens up about struggling with body dysmorphia from a young age and how the experience inspired his performance in the upcoming sports drama “Iron Jane.”
story: Actor Brandon Sklenar is opening up about struggling with body dysmorphia from a young age and how the experience inspired his performance in the upcoming sports drama “Iron Jane.”

The “1923” star, 36, explained his personal connection to his next project, which also stars Eiza González, in an interview with The Hollywood Reporter. “Iron Jane” tells the story of a woman (González) who undergoes an intense transformation to become a competitive bodybuilder following a difficult childhood. Sklenar plays the former champion who guides her.
Sklenar told the magazine he was intrigued by the film after previously working in an underground bodybuilding gym.

“I personally was drawn to it because I grew up in northern New Jersey working in an underground bodybuilding gym. When I was 15, I was cleaning the floors, and by 18, I was a trainer, training everybody and running the whole gym,” he shared. “There was an MMA gym upstairs, and I would just train MMA all day and then train other people. I started doing martial arts when I was really little, like six.”
Since he used to work and train in that world, he saw firsthand the posing, diets and steroids that are involved.

Sklenar noted, “There is an element of ‘Iron Jane’ that really goes into body image and body dysmorphia, which is something that I just really feel needs to be talked about more, especially in this age of social media and fitness influencers.”

“This is something I’ve struggled with, so we really wanted to translate that, and (director Lissette Feliciano) was really open to working with me on getting across (my character) Josh’s dysmorphia and what he goes through,” he added.
“The Housemaid” star shared more details about his past struggles, revealing that they began when he was a child.

“I was a little kid — short, chunky. I swam in a T-shirt and got made fun of. Then I had a growth spurt and became really lanky, and I got made fun of for that,” he recalled. “So I started training a lot and got obsessed with working out, like, ‘I’ll show them.’”
The desire to prove them wrong turned into “a kind of obsession,” he said.
“It becomes a very weird thing, where you see yourself completely differently than pretty much anybody else does, and usually in not a good way,” he explained.
Sklenar said he is still tackling his body image issues.

“Therapy helps for sure. If you look at me now as a 36-year-old man, you’d never guess it, but I still very much feel like that 12-year-old chunky kid — that sense of nothing is ever good enough,” he revealed. “You have to find a way to check your self-talk, because that’s really where it begins and ends — but it’s easier said than done.”
He said that working on “Iron Jane” allowed him to confront some of his insecurities. He shared details of one scene that includes a full-body shot as he poses.

“I’ve been pretty much naked in a film before, but it’s a whole different thing to literally be posing and have the camera panning up and down your body, detailing everything. When I was shooting that scene, I was so uncomfortable. Dealing with my issues, it was very challenging to work through that,” he pointed out.
But, Sklenar said he reminded himself that González had to shoot that same type of scene repeatedly throughout filming.
“Eiza trained her a** off, and she got in incredible shape for this film. I just have so much respect for her,” he praised.
“Iron Jane,” which marks Sklenar’s first producer credit under his Vista Lane Pictures banner, is expected to debut at festivals next year.

title: Frankie Muniz Hospitalized After Race Car Incident During Daytona Practice
summary: Frankie Muniz was taken to the hospital after he was involved in an incident during a practice at Daytona International Speedway.
story: Frankie Muniz, actor-turned-race-car-driver, was hospitalized on Wednesday, Nov. 11, after an “incident” while practicing at the Daytona International Speedway.
His NASCAR team, Team Reaume, shared the news on Instagram, noting that he was taken to a medical facility to receive care.

“Frankie Muniz was involved in an incident while practicing for today’s Proud to Honor event at Daytona International Speedway,” the statement reads. “He was taken to a local medical facility for further evaluation and is awake and alert.”
“We’ll share updates as they become available,” the statement continued, thanking people for their support. They also asked to respect Muniz’s privacy at this time.

Muniz, best known for his roles in “Malcolm in the Middle” and “Agent Cody Banks,” has been racing for over 20 years. Currently competing in the NASCAR Craftsman Truck Series, he was going to be participating in the Ford Proud to Honor Veterans Classic at Daytona Wednesday evening.

Muniz, 40, has been vocal about the struggles he’s faced this year. Back in July, he announced that he and wife Paige Price Muniz were divorcing after 10 years together. The two share 5-year-old son Mauz. The actor, however, removed his original post after receiving backlash from people. The announcement featured both of them dancing with the son and noted, “Who says you can’t stay best friends with your baby momma?”
His estranged wife would go on to defend him, according to People, saying sorry that he felt the need to remove the video because “people are so cruel to you.”
In September, he posted a lengthy post about experiencing a “heavy” time in his life.

“The last 6 weeks of my life have been a nightmare I’m praying to wake up from. Everything felt heavy, unclear, and like it was falling apart at the same time. I wouldn’t wish this season on anyone,” he wrote on X. “The unexpected gift in the middle of it is that I’ve had nowhere to hide. I’ve had time to sit with myself, do real self-reflection, and finally see the areas of my life that need work if I want to become a better version of me. Not the polished version I show the world...the actual one.”
He added, in part, that he was committed to “doing the work” and choosing to treat this chapter of his life as “the foundation, not the finish line.”

title: Amanda Seyfried on ‘You Can See Everything’ Scene With Billy Evans: ‘There Was No Reason for Him to Get That Aggressive’
summary: Among the most tension-filled moments of A24’s bombshell documentary “You Can See Everything,” about disgraced Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes, is the contentious dinner exchange between Amanda Seyfried and Holmes’ partner, Billy Evans.
story: Among the most tension-filled moments of A24’s bombshell documentary “You Can See Everything,” about disgraced Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes, is the contentious dinner exchange between Amanda Seyfried and Holmes’ partner, Billy Evans.
Nearly a month after the movie’s premiere, Seyfried is finally opening up about it.

The actor joined co-directors Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim for a conversation published by Rolling Stone magazine Nov. 11, in which the trio discussed her surprise appearance in the documentary.

In it, Seyfried — who had previously portrayed Holmes in Hulu series “The Dropout” and reprised the role for several scenes in the documentary — had the opportunity to chat with Evans in his home for a meal that quickly devolved into an near-explosive argument.

“There was no reason for him to get that aggressive. (Pauses.) That’s the word I’m going to use, as it’s more diplomatic,” she said in the Rolling Stone interview, her first extensive comments about the film. “If my jaw wasn’t obviously on the floor, you could tell, like, it had come unhinged.”
Evans did not immediately respond to TODAY.com’s request for comment.

The film, released Oct. 16, documents the family life of Holmes and Evans before and during the tech founder’s prison sentence. Holmes, who reported to the Bryan, Texas federal prison camp in May 2023, had been convicted of fraud. It was only after the film’s release that Seyfried’s involvement was revealed.

In the film, Seyfried is featured in several scenes, drawing on her past experiences, studying the once-promising tech leader’s mannerisms and movements to help Fielder analyze Holmes’ behavior in footage. Because Holmes is behind bars for much of the making of the film, Seyfried ends up stepping into the Theranos founder’s shoes for several reenactments.

Things hit a fever pitch when Seyfried and Fielder visit Evans’ Texas house while Holmes is in prison. It’s during this visit that he reveals he has been impersonating Holmes on her social media accounts. Seyfried, who immediately expresses her opposition to what she perceives as Evans’ controlling behavior, gets into a heated argument with him over dinner.

In their conversation in Rolling Stone, Seyfried told the filmmakers that she went into the conversation with Evans, “honestly trying to connect.” She also mentioned that she was aware his kids, whom he shares with Holmes, were in the house and that she wanted to be open-minded.

“We were all sitting there eating really good Chinese food, and, obviously, there were questions we wanted to ask. But for me, since I’m not an interviewer or an investigator, I’m not so good at asking questions and getting the timing right. And Nathan, you had a rapport with him. I was still creating this rapport.”
Seyfried told Fielder and Oppenheim that her mindset shifted, however, as the meal went on.
“I don’t want to provoke him, but at this point, it’s kind of like, the gloves are off. Because this guy has disrespected me in such a way that I was like, ‘Oh, I don’t think so, buddy,’” she said.

“I was in the frame of mind where I’m like, ‘OK, this guy is disrespectful, and I’m here in his home, I’m gonna argue this because I actually have a pretty solid stance on things. I don’t like the way he’s using this human being, his wife — the person he says he’s ‘building monuments of love’ to — as a tool. Maybe he does respect her, but he’s behaving like he does not respect her.’”
The actor added that she was attempting to be “protective” of herself while also “maintaining some kind of rapport with him, so I can stay and he doesn’t kick us out, you know?”
Seyfried revealed in the same interview that she had wanted to meet Evans after seeing the documentary footage of him and getting “such strong negative feelings from him.”
“I felt like I needed to meet this guy,” she said. “It was exciting to me, and it was scary, and it was questionable.”
The chat with Evans did little to change her opinion of him. In fact, Seyfried told the outlet, it “only got worse.”

Seyfried also spoke to the filmmakers about the unplanned call that Evans got from Holmes herself while they were at his house. It was during that call that she and Fielder had the opportunity to speak to Holmes, who was in prison. As Seyfried tells it, the moment was shocking.

“We didn’t know she was gonna call right then. And I am sitting there with her children and cuddling with her dog! While she’s in prison!” Seyfried said. “And then she calls, and … someone asked me if that was real, if that was really her on the phone. And I’m like, ‘It’s a documentary. Who else would it be?’”
The actor was mum about the entire project, even after its release. When asked about her thoughts on the Holmes-centered documentary in October, Seyfried brushed off the question.
“It’s interesting, yeah, it’s interesting,” she told the Hollywood Reporter.

title: Sheinelle Jones Has ‘Pinch-Me’ Moment With Debbie Allen Reflecting on Her Legacy, Perseverance
summary: Sheinelle Jones spoke with Debbie Allen after the two were recently honored at the 2026 Ebony Power 100 Gala.
story: Sheinelle Jones’ childhood dream came true when she was able to sit down with Debbie Allen to discuss her decades-long illustrious career and recent honor from Ebony magazine.

Both the TODAY with Jenna & Sheinelle co-host and the icon were among the inspirational figures in the Black community honored at the 2026 Ebony Power 100 Gala, which was held at the Hollywood Palladium in Los Angeles on Nov. 9.

“It was a night to celebrate excellence in all fields from media and the arts, to trailblazers in science … we’re all just trying to be the best versions of ourselves while paving the way for those coming behind us,” Sheinelle said of the event on Instagram Nov. 10.
After being recognized for their contributions to the culture, Sheinelle sat down with Allen and shared why she has been her “personal hero” for decades.

“I have to let you know how special this moment is for me. The viewers will know of the show because I’ve talked about it so many times. I used to have a cabbage patch. Her name was Lily Debbie Allen,” Sheinelle said.
“Wow, that is so loving,” Allen replied. “Thank you.”
During the Nov. 11 episode of TODAY with Jenna & Sheinelle, she reflected on the special moment of being honored alongside one of her childhood heroes.

“From the moment I arrived, I could feel the energy,” Sheinelle said. “There was so much joy, so much history and so much greatness, and I had my own pinch-me moment sitting down with fellow honoree, dancer, choreographer and just legend, Debbie Allen.”

The two chatted about the multi-hyphenate breaking down racial barriers from a young age to pursue her dream, becoming the first Black dance student at the Houston Ballet at age 14. Later, she was rejected from a university program due to her body type. But her mom, Vivian Ayers Allen, wouldn’t let her throw a “pity party” and encouraged her to keep dancing.
“What’s it like for you then in this seat now, to look back and reflect a message that you would want to give others? What would you say?” Sheinelle asked.
“I would say look in the mirror, know who’s looking back, get into that blood memory DNA, and believe in yourself,” Allen said.
“I’m one who has basically made dreams come true. I worked,” she added.

The Ebony Power 100 list features leaders, visionaries and changemakers. Sheinelle was named a “media maven” for joining TODAY with Jenna & Sheinelle in January and becoming a New York Times best-selling author with her literary debut, “Through Mom’s Eyes.”

Allen was named one of the Artists in Residence, who “through theater, dance, art, photography and literature have altered culture as we see it today,” according to the magazine. Her accolades include choreographing for Michael Jackson and Dolly Parton, directing episodes of “Scandal,” starring in “Grey’s Anatomy” and founding her nonprofit, the Debbie Allen Dance Academy.

She also produced and directed “A Different World” and was an executive producer for the 2026 Netflix reboot. A devoted fan of the show, Sheinelle revealed that several months ago, she bought a T-shirt printed with Debbie Allen’s 1992 Jet magazine cover on the front. She later gave that shirt to Maleah Joi Moon, star of Netflix’s “A Different World,” on TODAY for her birthday.
“I love this so much,” Allen said.

Speaking about the significance of making the Ebony Power 100 list, Allen pointed out the legacy of the magazine and Johnson Publishing Company, which was founded in 1942 and launched Ebony three years later.
“People around the world were reading these magazines and seeing these pictures, and wanting to channel themselves into it, wanting to share who we are, wanting to be who we are,” she said.
The 2026 Ebony Power 100 honorees also include WNBA star Flau’jae Johnson, food critic Keith Lee, filmmaker Lena Waithe, businessman Byron Allen, musician Brandy and astronaut Victor Glover.

title: Jenna Bush Hager Announces a One-Night-Only Event with ‘Theo of Golden’ Author Allen Levi in Columbus, Georgia

story: Jenna Bush Hager is headed on a literary vacation, and you’re invited!

title: See How TODAY Covered Prince Charles and Princess Diana’s Wedding in 1981
summary: TODAY covered the wedding of Prince Charles and Princess Diana in 1981. We look back on the day.
story: As TODAY marks its 75th anniversary, the TODAY Archive is revisiting legendary interviews, stories that moved us and other iconic moments from our 75 years on the air. These are the segments that shaped TODAY and created a lasting legacy. Today, we look back at the wedding of Prince Charles and Princess Diana on July 29, 1981.
The term “fairy tale wedding” looked like it came to life when Prince Charles and Lady Diana Spencer got married on July 29, 1981 at St. Paul’s Cathedral in London, England.
It was one of the most high profile weddings of the 20th century, completely capturing the public’s attention. The broadcast was watched by 750 million people in 74 countries, according to the BBC.
TODAY Had a ‘Splendid Morning’ From the UK
Tom Brokaw and Jane Pauley were on hand in the U.K. to report on the royal wedding. The two anchors sat at a desk decked out in the  Union Flag.

“Good morning everyone and welcome to the NBC News coverage  of the royal wedding,” Brokaw said at the top of the show. “By now, we should not have to tell you it is the royal wedding of his Royal Highness, the Prince of Wales, to Lady Diana Spencer, who in just a few hours will become the Princess of Wales.”
As he introduced himself and Pauley, she called it “a splendid morning.”
A View of Queen Elizabeth II, Prince Philip and Guests
Before the soon-to-be-husband and wife made their grand appearance, TODAY showed Queen Elizabeth II and husband Prince Philip with their traditional escorts, waving to people from their carriage.
Viewers then saw the bride and groom making their grand appearances in their respective carriages.
“Here comes the bride,” said Pauley.
Other noteworthy guests included Nancy Reagan and Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher.
Diana’s Grand and Elegant Entrance
Viewers got to see Diana in an ivory taffeta gown adorned with sequins and 10,000 pearls. It also had a 25-foot train that was longer than any other worn before her by a British royal bride.

“Why, she’s floating,” Pauley said as the bride emerged from her carriage to enter St. Paul’s Cathedral. “The dress does appear to float up the steps and I had underestimated the length of a 25-foot train.”
A Slight Mistake In the Ceremony
The ceremony did feature one flub, though. During the vows, Diana referred to Charles as “Philip Charles Arthur George” rather than Charles Philip Arthur George.
“Well, he does have a lot of names and she got them slightly out of sequence,” Brokaw said, reading off the correct order of the groom’s names. “Nervousness is to be expected.”
Procession Back to Buckingham Palace and Balcony Appearance
After their wedding ceremony, they rode back to Buckingham Palace together.
“The curtains are open, that’s the signal,” Pauley said as the newlyweds made their way to the balcony.

Princess Diana would go on to reflect on her wedding in the 2017 National Geographic documentary, “Diana: In Her Own Words,” which used audio from a series of interviews she gave for her biography, “Diana: Her True Story.”

“I remember being so in love with my husband that I couldn’t take my eyes off him. I just absolutely thought I was the luckiest girl in the world and you know, he was going to look after me,” she said.
However, Princess Diana would go on to call the wedding “the worst day of my life” in the documentary, also expressing doubts about the marriage after the engagement.

The two welcomed their first child, William, in 1982, followed by Harry in 1984. The couple ultimately separated in 1992 before they officially divorced in 1996. Princess Diana would die in a car accident in 1997.

title: ‘DWTS’ Grammy Night Ends In Jaw-Dropping, Shocking Elimination. See Who’s Headed to Semifinals

story: Grammy Night on “Dancing With the Stars” celebrated award-winning hits and delivered can’t-miss performances.
The Nov. 10 episode saw the remaining seven couples bring their best foot forward as they continued showcasing what they’ve learned over the last weeks.
As the show kicked off, hosts Alfonso Ribeiro and Julianne Hough announced the return of the Dance-Offs, where two couples faced off against each other in the same style at the same time.
The winners of the three Dance-Offs received bonus points that were added to the scores they received from judges Carrie Ann Ibana, Derek Hough and Bruno Tonioli.

During last week’s episode, Harry Shum Jr. and Jenna Johnson received immunity and didn’t have to partake in the Dance-Offs, which included  performances by Brandy and Monica, Maren Morris and Sheryl Crow.
Read all about what went down during the Nov. 10 episode of “DWTS,” including the dances, scores of each couple and who got eliminated.

Amber Glenn delivered a powerful paso roble that Derek called “phenomenal,” while Bruno said it was “everything a paso doble should be” and included “Pasha’s pecs.” Carrie Ann, however, did note that her foot came off the ground, which left her and Pasha Pashkov a bit stunned.

Maura Higgins, meanwhile, had to navigate a rib injury while attempting to do the Argentine tango. Despite the setback, Bruno called it sensual and elegant, while Carrie Ann called her a warrior and the performance “a work of art.” It also took Derek’s “breathe away.”

title: Brandy and Monica Bring the Nostalgia With ‘Boy Is Mine’ Performance on ‘DWTS’
summary: Brandy and Monica brought the nostalgia and glam to “Dancing With the Stars.” They also announced a Las Vegas residency.
story: Brandy and Monica brought nostalgia and glam to “Dancing With the Stars.”
The singers performed their hit song “The Boy Is Mine” during the Nov. 10 episode of the dancing competition show.

During Grammy Night, couples competing had to go up against each other during the Dance-Off portion of the episode. Brandy and Monica were on hand to sing their iconic track while Amber Glenn and partner Pasha Pashkov went up against Ezra Frech and partner Daniella Karagach.

As they wrapped up their performance and the couples closed out their routines, co-host Alfonso Ribeiro praised the singers adding, “My whole childhood, I wish I was that boy.”
He then shared an exciting announcement, noting that fans of the duo can catch the superstars at their first-ever Las Vegas residency.
Starting May 29, 2027, “The Boy Is Mine Vegas Residency” will consist of 10 performances at Resorts World Theatre at Resorts World Las Vegas. Tickets go on sale to the general public on Nov. 20.
